Jet-powered Russian drones strain Ukraine's air defences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
09:59:30 UTC
18:59:30 KST

Jet-powered Russian drones strain Ukraine's air defences
KYIV, Sept 22 - Vasyl, a portable rocket operator in one of Ukraine's many mobile air defence groups, was dismayed when he checked his screen. The Russian jet-powered Shahed drone moving towards his position was flying far too high for him to shoot it down.
"Before, Shaheds used to fly lower — one or 1.5 kilometres (above ground) and we could work on them," said Vasyl, who goes by the call sign Racoon, while on a mission to protect the capital Kyiv and the surrounding region with a shoulder-fired ground-to-air missile.
"But jet-powered drones now fly at four, five, even seven kilometres. It's not realistic for us to down them," the 26-year-old said.
Since Russia started widely using jet-powered drones this summer, hundreds have crashed into Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities in recent weeks, evading air defences. The new drones fly at high speeds and high altitudes, blurring the line between drones and cruise missiles.
The result has been disruption to businesses, government and ordinary life on a much bigger scale than in the previous four-and-a-half years of the war since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
In the first three weeks of September, Russia launched 2,100 jet-powered attack drones and 136 missiles at Ukraine, killing 288 people, including four children, according to Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi.
In August, Russia launched more than 2,800 such drones, he said. Moscow denies targeting civilians despite the growing civilian death toll and the devastation caused to cities across Ukraine.
HIGH ALTITUDES AND SECONDS TO REACT
Vasyl and his mobile drone-hunting crew of three people have only seconds to react to attacks by jet-powered drones, instead of minutes with the propeller versions of the Shahed. Russia is also now launching drones round the clock instead of largely at night.
"It's aiming to wear down our air defences," said Vasyl, adding that drones had been flying all day. "It all takes its toll, because we're out on duty and we're not really getting any sleep."
Ukraine is intercepting only about 60% of the jet-powered drones, compared to the more than 90% of earlier models that were routinely intercepted, said Yurii Ihnat, the Ukrainian air force's spokesperson.
The new drones are more expensive than propeller versions, but are still cheaper than the cruise missiles that Russia has been firing at Ukraine.
BROADER RANGE OF TARGETS
In recent months, Moscow has systematically targeted the pillars of Ukraine's economy including its Black Sea grain ports, railways and the steel and logistics sectors.
Hundreds of thousands of square meters of warehouses and commercial properties have been destroyed in Ukraine. Russia has disrupted supplies of food products, medicines, and other daily-use products for the first time since the early days of the war.
Moscow has used the new tactic as its advances on the battlefield stalled. Ukraine has also ramped up its own strikes on Russia, hitting its oil and fuel infrastructure and weapon production companies.
The shift in Russian tactics was anticipated, said Fedir Venislavskyi, a lawmaker in President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's ruling party and a member of parliament's security committee, adding that efforts were now underway to come up with effective defences.
Ukrainian officials have reported several successful combat uses of drone interceptors against jet-propelled Russian drones, but their mass production and other potential solutions would require time and money.
Money is in short supply: Zelenskiy has announced an unexpected defence funding shortfall for this year of $27 billion as the war has become more expensive. Kyiv is in talks with its partners on how to cover the gap.
"I believe that we will resolve the issue of jet-powered drones in the short term. But as with all other aspects of buying weapons, everything comes down to financial resources," Venislavskyi said. REUTERS

European experts observe blast tests on civil defence shelters in Rovaniemi
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:58:47 EEST
18:58:47 KST

European experts observe blast tests on civil defence shelters in Rovaniemi
The Ministry of the Interior and the Finnish Defence Forces organised blast tests in Lapland to assess Finnish civil defence shelters. The event was attended by experts from the international Civil Protection Shelter Coalition for Ukraine, led by Finland and Ukraine, as well as from other partner countries interested in developing shelters. An eight-member delegation from Ukrainian ministries responsible for civil defence shelters and from the State Emergency Service of Ukraine also took part. The aim of the event was to develop the Finnish system of civil defence shelters, draw on lessons learned from Ukraine and strengthen international cooperation in civil defence.
Blast tests help ensure that Finnish shelter solutions are effective against the threats posed by modern warfare. Similar tests were last carried out in 1992.
International experts observed the tests
Alongside the tests, the Ministry of the Interior organised a three-day event that brought together civil defence experts from across Europe. Participants observed the tests and discussed lessons learned from Russia’s war of aggression, the need for civil defence shelters in present-day Europe and the elements of an effective shelter system.
The event was attended by representatives of authorities responsible for civil defence shelters in countries participating in the Civil Protection Shelter Coalition for Ukraine, co-chaired by Finland and Ukraine. Representatives from other European partner countries interested in developing civil defence also took part.
Finland supports Ukraine while developing its own shelters
The event in Rovaniemi formed part of wider international cooperation in the civil defence shelter sector. Finland and Ukraine have intensified their cooperation on civil defence as part of Finland’s support for Ukraine, in line with the Government Programme. Civil defence cooperation between Finland and Ukraine strengthens Ukraine’s resilience and societal preparedness and supports the country’s reconstruction.
The Finnish Ministry of the Interior and the State Emergency Service of Ukraine are implementing a project funded by the Finnish Ministry for Foreign Affairs. Through the project, Finland is supporting Ukraine in developing its system of civil defence shelters. At the same time, Finland is learning from Ukraine’s experience of modern warfare and from the kinds of solutions needed to maintain an effective shelter system.
The project is part of the international Civil Protection Shelter Coalition for Ukraine, which supports Ukraine in expanding its network of civil defence shelters. The coalition was established in May 2025 through a joint statement by the Prime Ministers of Finland and Ukraine, and its activities began at the end of 2025. In addition, the coalition is mobilising international funding for the construction of civil defence shelters, and the first projects it funds are already under way.

West Bank's farmers fear settler attacks as olive harvest nears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
09:58:41 UTC
18:58:41 KST

Breadcrumb
As olive harvest season approaches, West Bank's Palestinian farmers fear Israeli settler attacks and restrictions
With olive harvest season approaching in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian farmers are preparing for a crop that has long been far more than an agricultural event.
For generations, families have gathered in their fields during the harvest, with men, women and children picking olives together before taking them to local presses to be turned into oil–a staple of Palestinian households and an important source of income.
This year, the season approaches under growing anxiety.
Speaking separately with The New Arab, Palestinian farmers and officials said Israeli settler attacks, Israeli military restrictions, the expansion of illegal Israeli settlement outposts and growing barriers to agricultural land since the outbreak of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023 have transformed the harvest into a season of uncertainty.
"The olive season is no longer what it used to be," Samir Jaradat, a farmer from Hebron, remarked to TNA.
Prior to Israel's genocidal war, Jaradat said, his family planned the harvest around the olives' ripeness and the availability of relatives to help. They could spend hours on their land without worrying about whether they would be allowed to enter or leave.
"Before the war, we used to await the olive season with great anticipation. We would go to our land whenever we pleased, spend hours there, tend to the trees and harvest the fruit with our families," he said.
Today, even reaching the land has become a source of concern.
"I own land in Area B, yet I cannot easily access it. The issue is no longer the quantity of olives the land will yield, but rather my ability to reach the land in the first place," Jaradat described.
The change has altered how farmers plan the harvest.
"In the past, we would schedule the harvest based on fruit ripeness and family availability. Today, our first thoughts are: Can we get there? Is the road open? Will we be able to return from the land without incident?" he said.
Threat to the harvest
The concerns come as Palestinian officials expect a stronger olive crop this year than last.
The Palestinian agriculture ministry estimates that the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip could produce around 21,000 tonnes of olives this season, a level officials say would meet local demand while leaving a surplus for storage or export.
But a larger crop does not necessarily mean farmers will be able to reach their trees.
Samer Samara, director general at the Palestinian agriculture ministry and head of the Higher Committee for the Olive Harvest Campaign, said that around 200,000 dunams of olive groves face access problems due to their proximity to settlements, bypass roads, military bases, and outposts.
Tens of thousands of additional dunams lie beyond the separation wall, which is considered illegal under international law, further complicating access, he added.
Data from the Palestinian Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission indicates that about 49,000 olive trees were targeted during the first eight months of 2026, compared with 18,964 in 2023, 10,459 in 2024 and 26,988 in 2025.
Palestinian officials have also reported in recent weeks that Israeli bulldozers uprooted hundreds of dunams planted with old olive trees in the Arraba area south of Jenin.
In some cases, farmers were reportedly left trying to collect olives from trees that had already been cut down, even though the fruit had not fully ripened.
For Jamil Abu Naim, from Al-Mughayyir village east of Ramallah, such developments have changed what was once a cherished family tradition.
"Before the war, the olive season meant family and land to us. We would go out in the morning, men, women and children together, and stay on the land all day. The work was arduous, but fear wasn't the first thing on our minds," he told TNA.
Now, fear accompanies the journey to the fields.
"When we go to the land now, we don't just think about the quantity of olives on the trees. We also think about the settlers, the possibility that they might come and attack us or block our access," Abu Naim said.
"We approach the olive season now without knowing if we'll be able to finish the harvest," he added.
For Abu Naim, the significance of the olive trees extends beyond their economic value. Many have been passed down through generations, making their loss difficult to measure simply in terms of agricultural production.
"We do not plant olive trees for just a single year. These trees are decades old; some were planted by our fathers and grandfathers. When a tree is uprooted or burned, it cannot be replaced in a single season," he said.
Farmers' concerns have also increased following Israeli reports about possible changes to procedures governing the harvest.
According to the reports, Palestinians could be barred from accessing olive trees located on land Israel classifies as "state land", while access could remain possible on land where Israeli authorities recognise private Palestinian ownership.
The reports also indicate that additional checkpoints could be established, with no coordination mechanism available in areas without recognised private ownership.
Israeli media outlets have described the proposed measures in terms of security and operational considerations, including efforts to reduce friction during the harvest.
Palestinian officials, however, say the measures would further restrict farmers' access to their land.
Much of the land affected is in Area C, which makes up about 60 percent of the West Bank and contains large areas of agricultural land and olive groves.
Farmers turn to collective harvesting
In Deir Istiya, in the Salfit governorate, concerns over access have prompted local officials to seek collective solutions.
The municipality has called a meeting with farmers from the western parts of the town, where the proximity of an outpost has complicated access, to discuss harvesting procedures and the possibility of organising collective harvesting campaigns on Fridays and Saturdays.
The Palestinian agriculture ministry is also running a campaign with local committees across governorates, towns and villages, involving local authorities, the Palestinian Red Crescent, Civil Defence, civilian and security agencies, and volunteers.
Samara said the aim is to ensure that farmers in particularly vulnerable areas do not have to enter their land alone.
In what the ministry calls "hotspots", larger groups of farmers and volunteers can harvest together, providing collective assistance and a degree of protection.
Samara said the number of such areas has increased. From around 10 hotspots per governorate in previous years, the number rose to about 20 last year, with officials expecting it to increase again this season.
"The priority is to protect the farmers and their property, and then to enable them to harvest the largest possible area of their land," Samara said.
The effort comes after a particularly poor harvest last year, when production fell to around 7,000 tonnes, according to the ministry.
The decline left some families unable to produce enough olive oil for their own household consumption, adding an economic burden to a season already marked by growing restrictions and insecurity.

Retreat; The only option facing US to exit from Iran war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
09:57:47 UTC
18:57:47 KST

The war of aggression waged by the US, after months of conflict, has yet to achieve Washington’s maximalist objectives while simultaneously driving up military and economic costs for the United States.
In this regard, Colonel Daniel Davis—a retired US Army officer and military analyst—believes that if Donald Trump wishes to emerge from a war with Iran with what could be termed a "victory," he must achieve objectives far beyond merely delivering military blows; these objectives include fundamentally altering Iran's political and military structures and eliminating the country's capacity to continue its missile and drone operations. From Davis's perspective, the fundamental problem is that the US military lacks the capacity to impose such an outcome.
This remark cannot be viewed merely as a personal stance; the issue Davis raises touches upon one of the fundamental challenges of warfare for Washington: the distinction between "military superiority" and "political victory." While the United States could leverage its air, naval, and intelligence capabilities to strike key targets in Iran and inflict significant damage on military infrastructure, turning this military superiority into a lasting shift in a nation's behavior or political structure is an entirely different matter.
The official and media reports also indicate that the war has not been without cost for the United States. According to estimates by the US Congressional Budget Office, the country's military operations had cost approximately $38 billion by August 1, a figure that rises by an average of about $3 billion per month. A report by the US Department of War Inspector General has also highlighted ammunition shortages and bottlenecks in production and replenishment capacities.
On the other hand, an assessment by the US Congressional Research Service indicates that by September 2026, the conflict has effectively reached a state of mutual attrition; this means that despite the damage it has sustained, Iran retains the capability to continue its attacks, while the United States and its partners face constraints regarding military capacity, economic costs, and political pressures. The report outlines four primary paths for Washington: maintaining the status quo, securing a ceasefire, escalating military operations, or negotiating a broader agreement.
This situation clears a significant part of Davis’s argument. If the US objective is merely to degrade a portion of Iran’s military capabilities, Washington can point to its operational achievements. However, if the goal is to completely eliminate Iran’s capacity for a military response, alter its political structure, and establish a new order, the gap between what is militarily feasible and what is politically achievable widens considerably.
A more significant issue is that the continuation of the war would not necessarily narrow this gap. While an escalation of attacks could inflict greater damage on Iran, it would simultaneously drive up costs for the United States and heighten the risk of the conflict spreading across the region. In recent weeks, Washington has remained undecided regarding the continuation or resumption of military operations. On September 17, Trump spoke of approaching a critical decision point concerning the war, stating that he was weighing various options for the future course of operations.
Amidst this situation, the discussion regarding US military capabilities has also gained greater significance. Recent reports indicate a depletion of certain ammunition stockpiles and strain on US production capacity—an issue that extends beyond a potential conflict with Iran and could impact Washington’s readiness for other contingencies, particularly those involving major powers.
From this perspective, the "withdrawal" Davis speaks of does not merely signify the physical departure of U.S. forces from the region. The core issue is devising a political exit strategy from the war—one that allows Washington to halt military operations without explicitly admitting defeat and to define the war's outcome through an agreement or new regional arrangements.
This is precisely the point where the conflict with Iran has become a strategic dilemma for the Trump administration. While prolonging the conflict might exert greater pressure on Iran, it offers no guarantee that America’s maximalist objectives will be achieved. Conversely, backing down or accepting a ceasefire could be interpreted within the US political landscape as a departure from the initially stated goals.
Consequently, Washington’s primary challenge is no longer merely whether the U.S. has the capacity to deliver further blows; the more critical question is whether those blows can yield the political outcome the U.S. desires. Daniel Davis’s position focuses precisely on this disconnect: a nation may possess air and military superiority on the battlefield yet fail to translate that advantage into its intended political result.
From this perspective, if Washington concludes that maximalist war objectives cannot be achieved through military means, a retreat might not signify an end to the pressure on Iran, but rather a shift in the tools of pressure—moving from direct warfare to negotiations, sanctions, and regional containment. Ultimately, the factor determining how the war concludes will not be merely the extent of U.S. capacity to sustain attacks, but the balance between the cost of continuing the war and the achievable political gains.

Danish consumer confidence falls as households grow more worried about personal finances

How to break the negative habit of 'toxic multitasking'?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
09:54:02 UTC
18:54:02 KST

How to break the negative habit of 'toxic multitasking'?
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
PRESS REVIEW – Tuesday, September 22: The Moscow Times talks about mobilisation rumours scaring anti-war activists in Russia. Next: The New York Times interviews South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung. Also: why is multitasking bad for the brain and the nervous system? Finally: this year's Fat Bear contest is starting in Alaska. Who's going to be the chonkiest chonk?
Independent paper The Moscow Times says there are rumours that the Kremlin could order another mobilisation to sustain its Ukraine invasion. The paper spoke to anti-war activists who say that anxiety is rising, even though helping Russians avoid the military is a routine part of their work. They remember September 2022, when 300,000 reservists were called up – Russia's first mobilisation since the Second World War. According to an independent source, more than 20,000 of the men who were mobilised then were later confirmed killed. Many activists worry that a new call-up could come faster and be even harder to avoid.
Another independent paper, Novaya Gazeta, writes about Yulia Kuznetsova's State Duma election experience. She was a candidate who abruptly went missing on the eve of Russia's three-day voting, shortly after meeting with voters. On Sunday, she said in a Telegram post that she and her husband are safe, but didn't really explain what happened. Kuznetsova's platform called for peace, the admission of all candidates and parties to the elections, media freedom and the release of political prisoners.
Next: The New York Times interviews South Korea's President Lee Jae-myung. He urges the United States to ease its sanctions on North Korea – saying that Trump should demand that Pyongyang freeze, not eliminate its nuclear weapons programme. He adds that "there is a significant value in a trade-off between sanctions" and "the world has no realistic alternative". He is making those claims as Pyongyang is increasingly showing off its nuclear missiles against the South and as both Russia and China have embraced North Korea as a strategic partner. Lee also told the NYT that Trump is the only leader "capable of drawing Mr. Kim back to the negotiating table".
Also: The Washington Post writes that "Toxic multitasking is breaking your brain" and explains how to "take control". In today's always plugged-in world, performing several tasks at the same time has become the new normal – scrolling while watching TV, reading emails while in a meeting. It can become addictive, especially when it involves screens. An expert who spoke to the paper says that it's only an "illusion of productivity" and "our brains simply aren't wired for it". It turns out that toxic multitasking can actually harm the functioning of our brain and the nervous system. This is because of the constant "context switching" that's detrimental to our brains without a break. The experts say that not all multitasking is bad, but the one we do the most – digital multitasking, or using more than one screen at a time – has an ironically negative effect on our ability to multitask when it can actually be beneficial. So how to break the toxic habit? The paper says we should try meditation, practice single-tasking or "design your environment for success" – silencing notifications, limiting your screen time, etc.
Another thing that helps? Sleep. The Times writes about some 1,000 teenagers who took part in a dream study – they were paid to sleep at least seven hours on weeknights. Not only were they well rested for school, their academic performance also increased!
Finally, Fat Bear Week is back and it has "unleashed its chonkiest contest yet", The Daily Beast reports. The annual contest determines which brown bear in Alaska's Katmai National Park has gained the most weight before the hibernation season. This year we have 16 chonky contestants and voting will begin later on Tuesday. Last year, 1.7 million people voted from across the world.

Foreign Minister Petrova: Europe needs leadership that builds trust
Tuesday 22 September 2026 11:07
Tuesday, 22 September 2026, 11:07
PHOTO MFA
Font size
Europe needs leadership that builds trust and delivers concrete results amid growing uncertainty, Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova said in New York, where she is part of the Bulgarian delegation attending the 81st session of the UN General Assembly. Speaking at the Her Power @ UNGA81 forum, organised by US international affairs magazine Foreign Policy, Petrova pointed to military conflicts and geopolitical competition as some of the challenges facing Europe.
Petrova said Bulgaria’s membership of the EU, Schengen and the eurozone marked the completion of its European integration, and that the next step was to contribute more actively to common European decisions.
Petrova also pointed to Bulgaria’s role in Europe’s security, energy and transport links.
“Security, energy and connectivity are no longer separate policies. Together, they determine Europe’s resilience, and Bulgaria has an important role in all three,” she said.
In New York, the minister also said that through its role in the EU, Bulgaria was working with other countries actively involved in efforts to achieve peace, particularly in conflicts close to the region and of direct importance to Bulgaria.

The Board of Peace — a multilateral initiative launched by US President Donald Trump in January and backed by a UN resolution to coordinate the reconstruction of Gaza and establish a security framework for the Palestinian enclave — has called for international support for its roadmap, reaffirming its objectives ahead of the UN General Assembly in New York.

It said an agreement reached with Hamas on July 30 provides a roadmap for the next stages of the ceasefire, including demilitarisation, Israeli withdrawal, Palestinian administration and reconstruction.

The board said the peace plan had paved the way for the release and return of all Israeli hostages and the Gaza Peace Summit in Sharm El-Sheikh, followed by UN Security Council Resolution 2803 and the board’s establishment.
It stressed the role of diplomacy in securing lasting peace and security in Gaza.
Since October 8, 2023, Israel has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000 others in its genocidal war on Gaza, while around 90 percent of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.

First Afghan US Congress member Aisha Wahab spotlights community
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
09:49:18 UTC
18:49:18 KST

Breadcrumb
First-ever Afghan US Congress member Aisha Wahab puts her district's community on the map
Aisha Wahab has been in Congress for less than a month, and she is widely considered a point of pride for the tight-knit Afghan community across the US.
As the first Afghan American member of Congress, Wahab has deep roots in the city of Fremont, sometimes affectionately referred to as Little Kabul, where she grew up, studied, organised for social causes, and worked her way up the ranks of local politics, starting as a city council member in nearby Hayward.
“What’s important about her work, her race and what we’re building together is that she didn’t just show up yesterday asking for our vote. She has been building and learning with us and alongside us for so long,” said Zahra Biloo, executive director of the San Francisco Bay Area chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, at a recent fundraising event for Wahab at a ballroom in Fremont.
At the same event, Nahid Aria, a member of the local Afghan Women's Book Club, who wore matching white outfits, called Wahab "a hero".
In another part of town, Wais Omar is working on remodeling his family restaurant De Afghanan, a longtime favorite restaurant of Wahab’s, where she would often order marinated kebabs. He has known her for 20 years and describes the congresswoman as humble, down-to-earth and smart.
As part of the older wave of Afghan immigrants, Omar, who arrived in 1979, says he is proud of the younger generation.
"She's shown the world that Afghan women can be anything they want to be," he told The New Arab. "Everybody is happy. We feel like we’re part of it."
Abdullah Danishmal, an Uber driver in Fremont who has never met her but voted for her, is also excited to see her in Congress.
"We're proud of her," he told TNA. "The position she’s reached is not easy."
Afghans have long been part of the US fabric, with the most significant waves arriving in the 1970s and 1980s with the Soviet invasion, the 1990s, early 2000s and most recently starting five years ago with the US withdrawal of forces and the subsequent Taliban takeover.
Wahab’s family arrived in the US as Afghan refugees in the 1980s. Shortly after her birth, her father was murdered, and her mother’s died soon afterwards, leaving her as an orphan in foster care. She was then adopted by an Afghan family in Fremont, where she grew up and established herself. She did her doctorate in social work at the University of Southern California and worked as management and consulting before entering politics. Over the years, she has spoken about her personal history as a motivation for getting into politics.
In her most recent congressional race, Wahab's campaign website highlighted her family’s history and her voting record after her opponent, Melissa Hernandez, supported with an estimated $6 million to $7 million from AIPAC, accused her of being soft on crime.
Wahab is now campaigning for a fourth time against the same candidate for California’s District 14. It is again a hard-fought race, though one where she will have the support of the Afghan community.
At the recent fundraiser in Fremont, she said that since arriving in Washington, DC all of her Uber drivers have been Afghans, and as soon as they recognise her, they extend their hospitality and tell their stories.
"They'll say we’re extremely proud. It’s an honour to hear that from our community," she said. "The reason why I say that is because our community has always had to face disaster and death and darkness. For fifty years, this community has largely seen war or been affected by war."
"And all of us have had the experience where we’ve had different generations that have come to the United States and start from scratch. And they have hope in their hearts," she added.

With Limitations apartment reveals unvarnished glimpse into life as a London designer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
09:45:55 UTC
18:45:55 KST

With Limitations apartment reveals unvarnished glimpse into life as a London designer
A lack of money, materials or equipment shaped every object in this mock apartment, which has taken over the basement of London shop Aram as part of an exhibition by guerrilla design collective Design Everything.
With Limitations, which debuted as part of the London Design Festival, takes the form of an imagined designer's apartment to offer a glimpse behind the curtain at how young creatives are managing to survive in one of the world's most expensive cities.
Every piece in the show was made by one of 102 emerging designers and reflects not just the hurdles they faced in the making process but also the weird, wonderful and ingenious ways they've found to overcome them.
"We hope this will enable you to peek behind the veneer of the design industry – the glossy photographs and Instagram reels – to see an honest portrayal of life as an emerging designer today," Design Everything wrote in the exhibition's introductory text.
In total, the exhibition features 130 objects organised into three distinct rooms – a kitchen, living room and bedroom. And although each was born from different constraints, a lack of funds seemed to be at the root of most limitations faced by young designers.
Stuck for time between her two part-time jobs, designer Symran Shah took to knitting during her commutes as a way of rapid prototyping. Once she was happy with the shape, she sand-cast one of her creations to burn away the cotton yarn and leave behind a deceptively soft-looking metal tray for the bedside table.
Faced with skyrocketing material costs, others resorted to creating new objects from off-the-shelf components, scavenged objects and offcuts.
Among them is a bow-shaped light in the kitchen, made by Design Everything co-founder Lewish Duckworth using an old tent pole and a tensioning guy rope. Nearby, another lamp was assembled from found nitrous oxide canisters by Absolute Beginners, a factory in Park Royal that teaches young people how to make everyday products.
"Funnily enough, NOS canisters came up a lot in the open call," Duckworth laughed.
South London designer Felix Fried lent out his own bed, cobbled together using offcuts from a fabrication job, for the sake of the exhibition and is currently sleeping on a mattress on the floor until the show finishes on 10 October.
Unable to access expensive industrial equipment, others turned to creating improvised production lines in their own homes and hacking their existing machinery.
The speckled backsplash in the apartment's kitchen was made by Royal College of Art student Olivia Webb using wilted flowers from local supermarkets and a DIY tile factory she set up in her flatshare.
In the absence of a welding machine, Jake Robertson instead made a floor lamp by cutting and bending an aluminium tube "like peeling a banana", and Sam Braid created his Pylon lights from craft wire and masking tape.
"It's almost like a prototype that is so beautiful in its execution, it becomes the final thing," Duckworth said.
Design Everything has made a splash at LDF in recent years by hosting guerrilla shows that offer young and emerging talent a space to exhibit their work for free.
It's a radical departure from existing participation fee models, where even dedicated emerging designer exhibitions, such as Isola, can allegedly charge around £900 per square metre.
"It's very, very inaccessible," explained Design Everything co-founder Tabatha Pearce Chedier, who is exhibiting a series of lights made from wall mouldings.
"I never thought I could show at LDF at all," she admitted.
Instead of a conventional exhibition, last year's LDF saw Design Everything show 36 chairs by emerging designers from the back of a travelling van. The year before, Duckworth turned the renovation of his friends' record shop into an opportunity to commission work from other young designers he admired.
"The whole point of that show was that you saw the work being used, which became the basis of a lot of what Design Everything is now," he remembered.
"It's about being interactive and playful, about bringing people together, making design feel accessible, and trying to build a community."
This year's show at Aram – a stalwart of the London design scene since 1964 – marks the first time that the collective has gone mainstream.
"They kind of liked our 'punk energy'," Duckworth said.
It's an energy that's very much alive in the Aram show, which doesn't charge a participation fee and encourages visitors to interact with the designs on show instead of placing them on a plinth.
At any given time during the exhibition, Design Everything members, designers and visitors could be found playing with a flat-pack cardboard chess set by Maja Rowecka, perched on sofas made from road signs and bales of cardboard boxes by Charlie Boyden and Max Hayward.
There's also a Jenga set, although this game can't be played since designer Hao Chen has reimagined it as a tiny chest of drawers for holding incense and matchsticks.
In the kitchen, heated conversations about the state of the design industry could be overheard around a dining table assembled from off-the-shelf materials by David Searcy, surrounded by a mishmash of chairs by Jamie Reed, Abby Ghent, Cam Rowley and Gloriana Valverde.
The soundtrack was provided courtesy of a stereo speaker, which designer and DJ David Chen assembled from two £15 IKEA work lamps, 3D-printed adapters and a set of Beyma tweeters.
"I think a lot of us create quite wacky objects," Duckworth said. "And I think being able to engage with them, like actually spend a day with that object, you're like: oh, I actually really like this, and I can see how it would fit within my life."
Throughout the week, the exhibition also hosted live making sessions with some of the designers.
Oliver Linnell assembled a candelabra of nuts and bolts from B&Q's pick-and-mix section, Polly Jennings showed how she slip-casts cups using DIY cardboard moulds, and Anna McAllister used a vegetable steamer and an electric hob to mould balsa wood into a minimalist wall clock, using a process she developed in her own kitchen.
In total, the exhibition features 130 objects by 102 designers, which might sound like a lot but is only a fraction of the 520 submissions that Design Everything received to its open call – more than three times as many as last year.
"I hope it's because we feel accessible that people apply with stuff that they've made and feel like there's an opportunity there instead of being intimidated and put off," Duckworth said.
The Design Everything team – Jacob Marks, Eleanor Murphy, Sammi Cherryman, Izi Thexton, Duckworth and Pearce Chedier – went through each project and developed a points system to rank them based on how well they fit the theme and what was needed for the apartment.
Duckworth also interviewed each of the 102 participants about the limitations they face and photographed their workshops, with the results collated in the final part of the exhibition.
In total, the process of organising the exhibition took around six months, during which the members also created their own contributions to the show and held down their day jobs.
"Everyone's kind of got their bread and butter," Duckworth explained. "It's a bit of a passion project for now. But we're hoping that we can get some funding soon."
The photography is by Kane Hulse.
With Limitations is on show from 11 September to 10 October 2026 as part of London Design Festival. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Man jailed for murder after denying son, 14, treatment for Covid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Man jailed for murder after denying son, 14, treatment for Covid
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A Dutch man whose 14-year-old son died after he was denied medical treatment for Covid-19 has been jailed for 23 years by a court in Belgium.
Rennlhy Manuela covered up the death of his son, Jairon, for eight weeks, refusing to let his siblings enter his bedroom and telling his mother he was out of the house when she tried to visit him.
Manuela, who belonged to a strict Pentecostal sect, refused to consult a doctor when Jairon fell ill at the end of 2021, instead relying on paracetamol, a liquid diet and prayers for his recovery.
The court of justice in Antwerp said Manuela “made his child’s life subordinate to his radical religious convictions”. He was convicted of murder by a jury and sentenced to 23 years in prison, three years more than prosecutors demanded.
The boy died in the night of January 3 and 4 after falling in the bath. When police were called to the house, they found his body underneath a blanket in an advanced state of decay, with traces of ketamine in his blood.
Manuela and his adult housemates had hoped God would answer their prayers to bring Jairon back to life.
Mother raised alarm
Jairon’s mother, Danica, raised the alarm after she contacted the boy’s school across the Dutch border in Tilburg, only to be told he had been signed out months earlier.
She had been denied access to the villa in Turnhout, where Manuela lived with his children and several other members of the religious community.
Four other adults were given sentences of between one and three years in the case. The jury said Manuela had caused “irreperable suffering” by “preventing [Jairon’s] mother and brothers saying goodbye in a humane manner”.

Barcelona FC faces backlash over Israel-linked Babylon Park deal

Breadcrumb
Barcelona FC faces backlash over 25-year deal with Israel-linked Babylon Park
Barcelona has faced criticism from supporters after approving a 25-year agreement with entertainment company Babylon Park to establish a family entertainment centre inside the Camp Nou.
Club members approved the agreement ahead of Barcelona's match against Sevilla, granting Babylon Park Spain SL a concession to develop a 900-square-metre interactive entertainment centre at the stadium.
Although the company involved in the deal is registered in Spain, corporate records cited by Spanish media link it to the wider Babylon Park group, owned by Israeli businessman Efi Malka, who lives in Tel Aviv.
The agreement was approved by 252 votes, or 57.15%, compared with 158 votes against and 31 invalid ballots, while 10 members abstained.
The deal had already faced political opposition before the vote. Jaume Asens, a Catalan member of the European Parliament from the Comuns party, wrote to Barcelona president Joan Laporta calling for the agreement to be withdrawn from the general assembly agenda.
Asens called on the club to investigate the company's ownership and investors and determine whether its parent company or other businesses within the group have activities or economic links to Israeli settlements, the occupied Palestinian territories or institutions accused of contributing to the continuation of the occupation.
He proposed that, if the deal was not withdrawn, the vote should be suspended pending an independent assessment of its potential legal, institutional, reputational and human rights implications.
The agreement has since prompted criticism from some Barcelona supporters on social media.
One fan posted on Reddit that they were "so disappointed in the club", writing that the agreement went against what Barcelona and Catalan identity represented and drawing parallels between Palestinian and Catalan struggles.
"Lliure Palestina, lliure Catalunya," the supporter wrote, meaning, "Free Palestine, free Catalonia".
Another Reddit user criticised the commercial considerations behind the agreement, writing: "Disappointing seeing this from a fan-owned club, unfortunately seems like that matters less these days than pure commercial interests pushed by the board."
Barcelona has long promoted the slogan "Més que un club", or "More than a club", reflecting its historic association with Catalan identity and its role beyond football.
The latest agreement has led some supporters to question whether the partnership is compatible with those values, while also drawing attention to the balance between the fan-owned club's identity and the commercial interests pursued by its board.
The controversy comes amid heightened scrutiny of sporting institutions and clubs over their commercial relationships with Israeli companies amid Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, expansion of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and continued occupation of southern Lebanon and southern Syria.

Russia, Ukraine trade blows ahead of Zelenskyy meeting with Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
09:42:00 UTC
18:42:00 KST

Russian missile and drone strikes across Ukraine killed at least four people overnight, officials said Tuesday, while a Ukrainian long-range strike damaged another Russian oil refinery.
The ongoing exchange of daily aerial attacks, while positions on the battlefield's front line barely change, provided a backdrop to the visit by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to the United States.
Zelenskyy was due to meet other world leaders, including U.S. President Donald Trump, at the U.N. General Assembly in New York. The Ukrainian leader is hoping to recruit their help to end Russia's more than 41/2-year-old full-scale invasion of his country.
Russian President Vladimir Putin isn't due to attend the annual event.
The war, which Western officials say has killed more than 500,000 Russian troops, has had global repercussions.
The repeated attacks on Russian refineries, following Moscow's strikes on Ukraine's power grid, have caused international shortages of diesel and price spikes, according to Trump. However, the global crunch also came after the Iran war led to curtailed oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
Zelenskyy also wants help to ensure the flow of Ukrainian grain and other farm products to world markets through the Black Sea. Russian attacks on cargo vessels have severely disrupted Kyiv's exports, hurting its economy and threatening global supplies.
French President Emmanuel Macron said Tuesday that his country would provide Ukraine with more radars to help protect its power grid.
He said on social media that he discussed with Trump the possibility of a truce between Moscow and Kyiv on strikes on energy infrastructure and a "moratorium" on Black Sea attacks.
Zelenskyy began his New York visit by meeting with U.S. senators, thanking them for what he called strong bipartisan support for Ukraine and for recently passing a tougher Russian sanctions bill that Trump has signed into law.
Peace and security will be closer once the bill is fully implemented, he said.
Zelenskyy said on social media that he briefed senators on his proposals for de-escalation measures that he intends to discuss with Trump later Tuesday.
The Ukrainian leader also plans to again press Trump to send more U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems that Kyiv desperately needs to stop Russia's ballistic missiles.
Ukraine said that it struck the Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara, southeast of Moscow, in an overnight attack.
Several drones hit their targets, sparking a large fire at the facility, according to a statement from Ukrainian special forces.
The refinery, owned by Rosneft, is a key fuel supplier for central Russia, producing gasoline, diesel, fuel oil and other petroleum products, the statement said. Ukraine said that it struck the same refinery last June.
One person was killed and four others were wounded in the Samara attack, regional Gov. Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said. He said that "the enemy targeted industrial facilities," but didn't specify which ones.
The Russian Defense Ministry Tuesday said that its forces downed 297 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions overnight, as well as the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula.
Russia's overnight attack on Ukraine included anti-ship missiles, ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and more than 200 drones, Ukraine's air force said.
The strikes killed four people in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk regional military administration.
The strikes across Ukrainian regions damaged homes, businesses and storage facilities, wounding at least five people, authorities said. Five people were wounded in the capital, Kyiv, according to officials.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Tuesday that its forces struck metallurgical and chemical industries, the fuel and energy sector, and the military-industrial complex, as well as port infrastructure facilities in four regions of Ukraine.
They included a Fire Point plant in Kyiv producing components for long-range cruise missiles and a tobacco factory in the central Poltava region used to make small arms ammunition, it said.

18:41:23 KST

Reza Valizadeh, a dual US-Iranian citizen and former journalist for RFE/RL's Radio Farda, is marking two years behind bars in Iran.
Valizadeh was sentenced to 10 years in prison on charges of "collaborating with a hostile government" in December 2024, a conviction his supporters and press-freedom groups reject. His appeal was rejected.
Valizadeh resigned from Radio Farda in November 2022 after a decade of work. He returned to Iran in early 2024 to visit his family but was arrested on September 22 of that year and kept in pretrial detention.
Since the death of Mahsa Amini in September 2022, Iranian authorities have launched a brutal, and sometimes deadly, crackdown on any dissent. Amini died while in custody of Iran's so-called morality police for an alleged violation of the country's headscarf law.
Her case sparked the Women, Life, Freedom movement that rattled the hard-line authorities.
Valizadeh also accused the Iranian authorities of inviting war in the country of some 90 million people, citing its disputed nuclear program and human rights violations.
The United States and Israel launched a bombing campaign of Iran in late February. The war has killed hundreds of Iranians, worsened the already acute economic crisis in the country, and led to a tightening of the crackdown on dissent.
Sources close to Valizadeh claim he fell into a "security trap" despite receiving unofficial assurances from Iranian security officials that he would not face legal troubles upon returning to Iran.
The US State Department has condemned Valizadeh’s detention, calling it "unjust" and inconsistent with international legal standards.
Press freedom organizations, including Reporters Without Borders and the Committee to Protect Journalists, have urged Iranian authorities to release Valizadeh immediately.
Iran is routinely accused of arresting dual nationals and foreign citizens on false charges to use them to pressure Western countries. In September 2023, Iran released five Americans jailed in Iran in a prisoner swap.
Earlier this month, 71-year-old Iranian-American citizen Kamran Hekmati was released from Tehran's notorious Evin prison, but his family said he is unable to leave the country due to a travel ban.
Iran is also among the most repressive countries in terms of freedom of the press. Reporters Without Borders ranked Iran 177th out of 180 countries in its 2026 World Press Freedom Index. Only China, North Korea, and Eritrea scored lower.
The Paris-based media watchdog said Iran is also one of the world’s biggest jailers of journalists.

Two men who registered 14 Starlink terminals for the Russian military were detained in Lviv
Kyiv • UNN
Two Lviv residents registered Starlink terminals under the names of nominees for the Russian military. All illegally connected terminals were blocked.
Two Lviv residents, aged 26 and 20, organized the illegal registration and verification of 14 Starlink terminals using the details of front persons so that the terminals could be used by representatives of the Russian Federation. This was reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General, UNN reports.
Details
According to the investigation, in May 2026, the men contacted via Telegram an individual who offered them money for cooperating with the aggressor state. Their task was to ensure the registration of Starlink satellite communication terminals in the names of front persons.
To do this, they involved 14 citizens who were unaware of their intentions. Starlink terminals were registered using their personal details, and the required verification was completed. All that was needed was to provide a photo of the device’s box showing its serial number. In this way, the actual users of the terminals remained outside the official registration procedure. Subsequently, these communication devices were used by representatives of the Russian Federation to conduct combat operations against Ukraine
At the same time, the terminals themselves were located in temporarily occupied territory, where restrictions on their use are in effect. According to the available information, the men received payment for their services after transferring the authorization data for the terminals to the handler.
Under the procedural guidance of the Lviv Regional Prosecutor’s Office, they were served notices of suspicion under Part 2 of Article 28 and Part 1 of Article 111-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
All illegally connected terminals that were identified have been blocked. The legality of the verification of more than 40 additional devices is also being checked. At the request of the prosecution, the suspects were remanded in custody without the right to bail
Recall
The Russian company "Bureau 1440," which is creating the low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation "Rassvet" as an analogue of Starlink, said it was ahead of schedule amid reports of problems with the launched spacecraft.

TJO Youth-Galilee, a delegation from the Jerusalem Orchestra East & West, is in New York this week for a series of performances, including an appearance Tuesday evening at an event marking the opening of the annual United Nations General Assembly session.

Group's UN repertoire intended to bridge cultures

Cohen described the meeting with Broza as particularly meaningful for both the young musicians and for him personally.
“During this trip to New York, the soloists of our youth orchestra had the privilege of meeting an artist they admire, and the person who helped me, as an enthusiastic child full of dreams, become the mature musician I am today,” Cohen said.
“The same generosity David showed me two decades ago, he gave with endless patience and love to our young musicians, who eagerly absorbed everything they could from this special encounter. Together, we experienced once again that when you follow the path of music — particularly the musical paths of David and of our orchestra — there is the potential for a colorful and exciting future in the meeting between East and West.”

Children under the age of 15 will soon be offered training to join the Islamic Republic’s Janfada (self-sacrifice) campaign, the campaign’s spokesperson, Sasan Zare, confirmed to the Iranian Labour News Agency last week.
Acknowledging that individuals as young as 15 have already begun training, Zare said that, due to high demand, “special training appropriate for younger ages will also be arranged.”
Zare, however, asserted that only male children would be provided with training, while women would need to enlist after reaching the age of 18.
The planned recruitment of children comes despite international humanitarian law, including the Geneva Conventions, prohibiting the recruitment of minors under the age of 15 by both state armed forces and non-state armed groups. The Islamic Republic has nevertheless admitted to recruiting children as young as 12.
In March, Rahim Nadali, the cultural and artistic deputy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)’s Mohammad Rasoulollah Corps, told Iran’s Defa Press Agency that the minimum age for joining the homeland defense fighters was set at 12. Days after Nadali’s announcement, 11-year-old Alireza Jafari was killed at a military checkpoint, according to Iranian state media. The Basij Teachers Organization confirmed that the minor was killed “on duty.”
The Jerusalem Post has contacted the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict for comment on the planned recruitment of minors for the Janfada Campaign.
Military training set to begin this week in Tehran
Military training for the campaign is set to begin in Tehran this week. Training exercises will be carried out at military centers and in “high-traffic squares,” Zare said, admitting that the major public Imam Hussein Square would be converted into a “fully equipped military training pseudo-camp.”
Those who sign up will be trained in “ensuring local security, general war preparations, observation, surveillance, and intelligence measures,” as well as “guiding micro-aircraft (drones), which are used in military operations,” and “the possibility of using shoulder-launched weapons.”
“The training platform is the Basij community, and the content is approved by the Basij organization, and the training capacity of all armed forces will be used,” he said. “There is also full preparation to ensure the security of the training sites.”
Zare further alleged that of the 31 million Iranians he said had enlisted in the campaign, 26% had signed up for military and security duties.
Zare: campaign centered on slogan: 'We have one life, and we give it for Iran'
He said the campaign was centered on the cultural slogan, “We have one life, and we give it for Iran,” which he acknowledged had drawn international criticism.
Zare also alleged that many Iranians living abroad had signed up for the campaign and would soon be included in “cultural and educational events.”

Attempts to expand the “gray zone” and armored vehicles for the autumn — the Defense Forces revealed the Russians’ tactics near Dobropillia
Kyiv • UNN
Russia is trying to expand the “gray zone” in the Dobropillia area, but the Defense Forces are holding back the attacks. Ukrainian intelligence is preventing the enemy from deploying armored vehicles.
Despite the occupiers’ attempts to expand the "gray zone" in the Dobropillia sector of the front, it would not be entirely accurate to speak of any major gains by the enemy, as the Defense Forces are stopping and neutralizing the adversary to the maximum extent. Meanwhile, against the backdrop of the beginning of the autumn campaign, increased activity by enemy armored groups is expected, but it is extremely difficult for the occupiers to transfer equipment to the Dobropillia area amid the development of Ukrainian reconnaissance capabilities. This was reported by Ihor Yaremenko, chief of staff of the artillery reconnaissance division of a separate artillery brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine, during a national telethon on September 22, UNN reports.
Details
"We clearly see and understand (...) that the enemy is, in principle, periodically expanding the ‘gray zone,’ since there really are a great many assault operations taking place. But, for their part, the Defense Forces are stopping and neutralizing the enemy to the maximum extent, and great importance is attached to infiltration groups, which are constantly being detected and neutralized. Therefore, to say that the enemy has made any major gains does not quite correspond to reality. But because there is a constant and large number of assault operations, plus we should not forget that the enemy continues to employ a scorched-earth tactic. That is, constant artillery shelling, constant raids by large numbers of UAVs, and, most importantly, strikes with guided aerial bombs, which simply destroy and wipe off the face of the earth all infrastructure in any cities and settlements that the enemy can reach," Yaremenko said.
"The Defense Forces are actively fighting not only infiltration groups, but many plans for counteroffensive actions are also being developed. We clearly see that the Defense Forces are also achieving success in this regard. Therefore, we are holding the line," the serviceman emphasized.
At the same time, he noted that "the enemy is not going to end the hostilities. It constantly changes its plans and deadlines for capturing the entire Donetsk agglomeration, but (...) I believe these plans are unattainable. The enemy is losing an enormous number of personnel."
The serviceman also noted the beginning of the autumn campaign, with the appearance of dense fogs.
"We clearly understand that we have already entered the autumn campaign, (...) and it is precisely in this weather that the enemy is trying to transfer equipment. And I think that in the near future we will see activity specifically by armored groups, which the enemy barely used during the summer campaign. But I emphasize that during the summer campaign, the Defense Forces developed their reconnaissance capabilities very actively," Yaremenko said.
"Therefore, it is extremely difficult for the enemy to transfer equipment specifically to the Dobropillia area, since with the help of such means as optical reconnaissance systems and radar systems—and we should not forget the active work of UAVs—it is extremely difficult for the enemy to move its armored vehicles undetected and transfer them to any sector or area of the front. Plus, we should not forget that the so-called Middle Strike assets are actively operating—systems that constantly destroy both the enemy’s logistics routes and the depots where the enemy concentrates and stores its equipment to the greatest extent," Yaremenko noted.
"Therefore, the enemy is making attempts, but realistically, it has almost no positive movement," the serviceman emphasized.
Additional information
In its report for September 21, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine noted that the Pokrovsk sector remains the hottest area of the front, with enemy assaults also recorded in the Dobropillia area.
On the Pokrovsk sector, Ukrainian troops repelled 33 enemy attacks over the past day, out of 248 across the front.

Focus Survey Research conducted the landline poll from July 31 to Aug. 3, collecting 1,502 valid responses from adults in 19 coastal cities and counties. Samples in Keelung, Yilan, Taitung, Pingtung, and Penghu were expanded to 100 respondents each, Greenpeace said. The results were weighted by demographic data and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.53 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — National Taiwan University Hospital said Tuesday that its new Health Building has officially opened, per CNA.
The hospital spent more than 20 years planning the building and eight years constructing it. The facility had a soft opening on July 27 before beginning full operations Tuesday.
Located next to the hospital’s pediatric facility, the building has 14 aboveground floors and four basement levels for medical care, teaching, research, and administration. It has capacity for 330 general beds and 10 intensive care beds, along with 16 operating rooms, 24 postsurgical recovery beds, 69 consultation rooms, and a 30-bed chemotherapy area.
Several departments formerly based at the west campus, including otolaryngology, dermatology, and urology, have moved into the building. Head and neck ultrasound services from the east campus have also relocated, providing patients with one-stop care.
NTUH Superintendent Yu Chong-jen (余忠仁) said more than 190 beds are currently in use, with additional beds expected to open later. He said the expansion would ease congestion and allow the hospital to admit new patients each day.
Yu said the hospital has also taken steps to alleviate emergency department congestion ahead of the fall and winter. The emergency department lobby is now free of patients awaiting beds more than 90% of the time, he said.
The relocation of several departments has freed space for a post-emergency admission ward, Yu said. He added that reducing traffic at the historic west campus would also ease pressure on its 105-year-old building.

"He later said that they had no such information and then at another point he claimed that the relatives of the deceased were against disclosing this information, while no one knows the names of the relatives either. This is a truly striking fact," Russia’s top diplomat noted.
Lavrov stressed that Moscow "had already realized that it should not depend on the UN Secretariat’s assistance."
On March 30, 2022, Russia, as a sign of goodwill amid negotiations with Ukraine in Istanbul, withdrew from the area around Kiev, including from the town of Bucha. On March 31, this was confirmed on camera by the head of the local administration. A few days later, Western television broadcast footage showing - in contrast to an earlier recording - that the bodies of people who had allegedly been murdered were lying in the streets. In Russia, a criminal case was opened over the provocation involving the spread of deliberately false information about the Russian Armed Forces.
The Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum is a global platform for discussing methods to combat disinformation and develop fact-checking technologies. The event is taking place at the Russia National Center with the participation of over 2,000 journalists, experts and businesspeople from 80 countries. It is organized by the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN), established in 2025 by the TASS news agency, the autonomous nonprofit organization "Dialogue Regions," and the New Media Workshop.
TASS is the forum’s strategic media partner.

Pepe Losada joins Iran football team coaching staff
TEHRAN - Following the departure of Andranik Teymourian and Aliasghar Ghorbanalipour from the Iran national team coaching staff, head coach Amir Ghalenoei has bolstered his backroom team with the additions of Mehrdad Khanban and Pepe Losada.
The Football Federation of Iran began negotiations with several candidates identified by Ghalenoei to complete the coaching staff, eventually confirming the appointments of Khanban and Losada as the national team prepare for the next stage of their campaign.
Khanban, 44, is a familiar figure within Iranian football and has extensive experience with the national team. He began his professional coaching career with Persepolis club and later worked under Carlos Queiroz with Iran. His first spell with the national team lasted until 2018, when he left the coaching staff ahead of the FIFA World Cup in Russia.
Following Dragan Skocic’s appointment as Iran head coach, Khanban returned to the national team setup. He subsequently spent several years at Persepolis, working alongside coaches including Gabriel Calderon, Yahya Golmohammadi and Osmar .
Khanban was part of the Persepolis staff during their title-winning campaign before moving to Tractor. Last season, he worked on the coaching staff under Dragan Skocic and Mohammad Rabiei. He also took charge of Tractor on an interim basis during their AFC Champions League Elite clash with Al-Gharafa.
Khanban will now return to the national team, although in a different capacity, joining Ghalenoei’s staff as one of his assistant coaches.
Meanwhile, Spanish fitness coach Pepe Losada has been appointed as the national team’s new conditioning coach.
The 50-year-old has extensive experience in physical preparation and has previously worked in Iranian football with Persepolis, Nassaji Mazandaran and Gol Gohar.
Losada enjoyed one of the most successful spells of his career at Persepolis. During the 2022/23 season, he was part of the squad that won the Iranian Pro League, Hazfi Cup and Iranian Super Cup. The following season, he remained with the club as Persepolis again lifted the league title and Super Cup.
According to Spanish club Balompédica Linense, Losada has more than two decades of experience in physical preparation. Earlier in his career, he also spent around 12 years working within the Cádiz setup in Spain.
With Khanban and Losada now joining Ghalenoei’s staff, Iran have reshaped their coaching team as preparations continue for the next stage of the national team’s campaign and the 2027 AFC Asian Cup.

‘Apartheid 2.0’: South Africa condemns US refugee program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22

‘Apartheid 2.0’: South Africa condemns US refugee program
South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola has denounced US President Donald Trump’s program for resettling Afrikaners, a white ethnic minority in South Africa, as refugees, describing it as “Apartheid 2.0.”
Lamola made the remarks at an African Diaspora Forum in Washington, according to footage posted on Sunday by South Africa’s Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO). The minister argued that the program gives preferential treatment to white South Africans while excluding other racial groups.
“Only white Afrikaners from South Africa are allowed to be refugees here. And all of you or any other race is not allowed. It’s a race-based policy, which we call the Apartheid 2.0,” he said.
The Democratic Alliance, the second-largest party in South Africa’s coalition government, welcomed Lamola’s condemnation and urged him to oppose race-based policies at home. It called for economic justice and opportunity “without permanently reducing citizens to arbitrary racial categories.”
Afrikaners are a predominantly white, Afrikaans-speaking ethnic group descended mainly from Dutch, German and French settlers who began arriving in southern Africa during the 17th century. Afrikaner-led governments instituted apartheid, the system of racial segregation that ended in 1994.
Trump established the resettlement initiative through an executive order signed in February 2025, alleging that Afrikaners faced state-sponsored racial discrimination, violence, and farmland confiscation under South Africa’s Expropriation Act.
There is no genocide against white people in South Africa. #UnityInDiversity#SouthAfrica@UbuntuRadioZA@GovernmentZApic.twitter.com/ROLKbFHqkD
— DIRCO South Africa (@DIRCO_ZA) September 20, 2026
Pretoria has rejected the allegations, insisting that the legislation is intended to address land inequalities inherited from apartheid and that no private property has been confiscated under it.
Trump expanded the initiative in May 2026, raising the annual US refugee admissions ceiling from 7,500 to 17,500 and reserving the additional places for Afrikaners, citing an “unforeseen emergency refugee situation.”
AfriForum, which had lobbied Washington over alleged discrimination against Afrikaners, said it “does not have information” about the claimed emergency. The group said its priority was creating conditions that would allow Afrikaners to remain in South Africa. More than 13,000 South Africans have since been resettled in the US, according to State Department figures, even as Washington sharply restricted refugee arrivals from most other countries.
Applicants must establish past persecution or a credible fear of future persecution and undergo security screening. Dozens have reportedly received rejection notices that provide no detailed explanation and cannot be appealed. Cases examined through information requests included denials linked to criminal records and public-safety concerns.

Cork wall by GenCork
Dezeen Showroom: Portuguese brand GenCork combines one of the world's most sustainable natural materials with customisable algorithmically generated design, creating an insulating wall cladding that makes a strong visual impression.
GenCork's cork wall is made using the Corkvectors algorithm, which blends organic patterns inspired by nature with geometric structure to create a dynamic 3D surface design.
The panels make use of cork, which is a highly renewable material, harvested from trees without cutting them down and so allowing forests to continually regenerate.
GenCork's owner and producer Sofalca lowers the environmental impact even further with its expanded black cork, which is made using a zero-waste process where steam from waste biomass from the cork's cleaning and milling bonds the material together with only its natural resin.
This process also gives the panels their distinctive rich colour, darker and earthier than raw cork, while CNC milling gives it its precise relief.
The computational design system allows the pattern to be customised to the dimensions of the wall or other parameters, while cork's strong thermal and acoustic insulating properties make the product as functional as it is aesthetic.
"Corkvectors [is] a bridge between nature and design, evoking the beauty of both," said GenCork.

EU split over Russian tycoon pushes entire sanctions regime to the edge
The EU is at an impasse over the proposed de-sanctioning of Russian businessman Alisher Usmanov, with Latvia flat out rejecting demands by fellow states to lift the restrictions during an ambassador meeting on Tuesday.
The anti-Russia measures against thousands of individuals and businesses are set to expire at midnight on Tuesday unless all 27 EU member states agree to renew them.
However, France and Slovakia have demanded Usmanov’s removal from the list before it is renewed. Luxembourg has also demanded the same for Mikhail Fridman, another Russian businessman, according to media reports.
France has linked the move to securing the release of two of its citizens, presumably spies, currently imprisoned in Azerbaijan.
After extended deliberations over the de-sanctioning of the businessmen, Ireland, which holds the EU’s rotating presidency, proposed a compromise. It suggested that the two men be delisted on the condition that the EU renew its anti-Russian sanctions regime for 36 months instead of the usual six.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, who has held office for just over 100 days and faces a general election next month, rejected the proposal, taking to social media overnight to insist that he would not allow “one of Putin’s oligarchs” to be de-sanctioned, insisting that the EU’s “pressure must become stronger.”
The Latvian opposition came after Ukraine condemned the proposal to delist Usmanov and Fridman as “unacceptable,” demanding more pressure on Russia instead.
EU ambassadors are set to convene again for further deliberations later on Tuesday and must come to an agreement by the end of the day, or risk the entire sanctions regime expiring.
Commenting on the delisting proposals, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov stressed that Moscow considers all Western sanctions illegal, and demanded that they be lifted from Usmanov, Fridman, as well as all other Russian businessmen and citizens.
Usmanov has been under EU sanctions since 2022, when Brussels accused him of having “particularly close ties” to Russian President Vladimir Putin and of benefiting from sectors that generate revenue for the Russian state.
The businessman has repeatedly denied the allegations. His lawyers have argued that the case against him was built on sketchy media reports, most of which have already been legally proven false. More than 3,200 articles concerning Usmanov have been corrected since 2022, while another 1,300 have been deleted entirely, his lawyers reportedly claimed in a letter to the European Council. At least 18 documents have also reportedly been removed from the EU’s own evidence file.
The businessman has also won legal cases against several major European media outlets over claims about his supposed links to the Kremlin, including Germany’s Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung and public broadcaster ARD.

====================================================================================================

A New Chatbot Wants to Unlock the Secrets in Tattered Ancient Greek Records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Academic libraries across the globe are stuffed with hundreds of thousands of Ancient Greek papyrus fragments. Though many are so damaged that their meaning is probably lost, scholars have the ability to restore the rest by methodically filling in missing words or phrases. To accelerate that laborious task, researchers have turned to artificial intelligence.
On Wednesday, the Austrian Academy of Science will release “the world’s first advanced large language model for Ancient Greek,” developed in partnership with French AI lab Mistral and technology services firm Sail Reply. The model, Apollo, is trained on roughly 600 million historical Greek words drawn from manuscripts, papyri, and inscriptions.
The model will be freely available to academics through a chatbot interface. The ambition is to help scholars to more rapidly identify papyrus fragments relevant to their specific sub-disciplines, as well as promising new avenues of research. Where documents are tattered and torn, Apollo is built to fill in the blanks with the most statistically likely words or passages, potentially revealing hidden details about historical events and practices.
Dimitris Vlitas, partner at Sail Reply, tells WIRED that unlocking knowledge in this way “was unthinkable a year ago.”
Until now, restoring a tattered piece of papyrus has required a skilled academic to first identify the word divisions—there are no gaps in Ancient Greek writing—then accurately date the document, weigh the appropriate socio-political contexts, and consult reference materials to help choose suitable words to fill in the gaps. “There are very few people in the world who are that good at Greek history,” says Stephen Colvin, a professor of classics and historical linguistics at University College London.
But all of that specialized knowledge is baked into Apollo. “When it sees Homer, it supplements Homeric Greek. When it sees an inscription in Doric dialect, it uses Doric dialect,” says Anna Dolganov, a historian and papyrologist at the Austrian Academy of Science.
Academics who find themselves bogged down in painstaking reconstruction work expect Apollo to accelerate things, allowing them to focus on the implications of historical documents, rather than figuring out what they say.
“I think it’s very exciting,” says Armand D'Angour, a professor of classical languages and literature at the University of Oxford, home to the world’s largest ancient papyrus collection. “If I had a machine telling me, ‘Here are the three possible words that could fit into that gap,’ it would speed up matters considerably.”
Apollo is unlikely to change the broad-strokes understanding of the ancient world; many papyri are yet to be restored precisely because they are mundane—personal letters, marital contracts, civil service papers. “If you were a layperson, you might think suddenly we’ll get a few new plays by Sophocles, but that’s not going to happen,” Colvin says. However, the model could help to uncover new details about life in antiquity and substantiate existing scholarly assumptions. “Every time something is produced, it adds a tiny element of knowledge about the ancient world,” D’Angour says.
If Apollo is a success, says Vlitas, the same technique could be readily applied to other ancient languages—Latin or Egyptian, say—or any other academic discipline that would benefit from the distillation and indexing of a large corpus of material. AI has had notable success in some areas; OpenAI recently said its AI models solved a 200-year-old math problem, while Google DeepMind released a vast dataset that maps how genetic mutations affect molecular biology, which it compiled using AI.
One concern might be that relying on a language model—which deals in probabilities—to fill in gaps in ancient documents risks polluting the historical record with errors. But to head off that issue, Apollo is built to propose a selection of word options for a scholar to select between. “The crucial point is that human competence needs to remain,” says Dolganov. “If we become totally reliant on AI transcriptions and interpretations of historical material, that’s when the problems start.”

Bank of Estonia issues Forest Brothers commemorative coin
