US says Australian digital care bill would 'facilitate censorship'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:47:01 UTC
17:47:01 KST

Trump administration attacks Australia's 'opt-out' algorithm law in rare intervention
In short:
In an extremely uncommon move, the US government has publicly criticised an Australian government policy proposal.
It wants US social media companies excluded from digital duty of care laws, which would give Australians the option to opt out of algorithmic feeds.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is in New York promoting Australian tech policies at the United Nations.
The Trump administration has made an extraordinary public intervention into Australia's debate about its proposed digital duty of care, warning the Albanese government that the policy would be "extraterritorial censorship of protected speech".
It called for the Australian government to exclude US social media companies from its plans to give users the option to opt into algorithmic recommendation feeds — a decision that would effectively neuter the law, removing the biggest platforms from its application.
The rare public rebuke took the form of a response to a consultation on the draft digital duty of care bill, which would force platforms to take actions to mitigate and respond to harms caused by digital platforms.
The submission, published by the US Embassy today, said Washington had "serious concerns" about how Australia would decide what counts as "foreseeable harm".
This comes with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese currently in the middle of a United States trip to promote his government's tech policy agenda at the United Nations General Assembly.
His support for international AI regulation and his government's teen social media ban have increasingly earned the ire of the Trump administration.
Washington objects to harm rules and feed mandates
In the submission, the US government said it was concerned by what it described as rigid, one-size-fits-all design requirements.
Such mandates, it argued, would push platforms to demote sensitive or controversial topics to comply, reducing the reach of independent journalists and other voices.
"The US government would likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship," the submission said.
It put a number of questions to the Australian government, including how Australia would define "harm" and "risks", how they would be adjudicated, by whom, and whether platforms or users could appeal. It also asked about the role of the eSafety Commissioner and impacts on privacy.
While it is common for governments to express their views on other countries' policies, those views are usually communicated through private channels.
It is exceedingly rare for a foreign government to make a direct, public intervention into a domestic debate like this.
The US government's hostility toward the digital duty of care was signposted earlier this month in a statement from White House spokesperson Kush Desai to the Guardian Australia.
He said President Donald Trump had warned other nations against imposing "digital services taxes, fines, and other forms of extortion on America's leading technology sector".
Warning Australia's tech policies could spread elsewhere
The submission argued forced changes to mitigate Australia-specific risks could change how users everywhere, including Americans, experienced the platforms.
If other jurisdictions adopted conflicting duty-of-care mandates, platforms could face incompatible design requirements not technically or commercially scalable in parallel, it said.
Australia's teen social media ban inspired a number of other countries to introduce, or pledge to introduce, similar restrictions.
Earlier today, it was reported by Politico Australia that the American industry body representing American tech companies had joined in a High Court challenge to Australia's teen social media ban.
The group, NetChoice, described it as "the most extensive prohibition on youth access to social media in force in any liberal democracy".
The digital duty of care draft shows how the government plans to create a legal obligation for online services, including social media, gaming and other platforms, to create a safe experience for users through its design.
The Albanese government said it would use this law, if passed, to force platforms like Facebook, Instagram and TikTok to send users a pop-up offering a choice between a personalised algorithmic feed and a feed limited to accounts they follow.
Communications Minister Anika Wells last week downplayed the White House's warning as "broad" and said she had not directly received such a warning from a US representative.
When asked about the US government's intervention, Ms Wells's office and the US Embassy both declined to comment.

But as major networks boycotted pool coverage of the President over his ban on multiple news outlets, the White House promoted a new 24/7 video feed focusing on Trump and his achievements.
It’s unclear if the YouTube-hosted stream, called “Trump TV,” is meant to potentially fill the void of television pool coverage of the President’s events. But it went live at 7 p.m. ET, according to the White House, with a rerun of Trump’s speech at Mount Rushmore on July 3.

Kaelan Dorr, a deputy assistant to the President and head of digital strategy at the White House, posted on social media about how Trump TV would show “the Administration’s greatest hits, unfiltered.” Dorr added: “The press, in some cases, reported inaccurately or not at all on the Administration’s many record breaking accomplishments on behalf of all Americans.”
CNN was supposed to shoot for the pool on Monday, with footage distributed to other networks, but it was one of the three organizations, alongside MS NOW and Politico, which were banned from the White House on Friday over their negative coverage of the President. The outlets have sued the Administration on free speech grounds, and, in seeming solidarity against the ban, ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC subsequently suspended television pool coverage of presidential events. “No Administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting,” their joint statement said.
Critics slam ‘state-run’ TV

Gavin Newsom, the Democratic Governor of California widely seen as a presidential contender for the 2028 election, described “Trump TV” as “state-run.”

This is truly autocratic behavior from a failed President.”
Democratic U.S. Senator for Arizona Mark Kelly also slammed the Trump Administration’s recent spate of actions in a social media post: “State run media, state owned enterprises, prosecuting political opponents, gifts from foreign countries, selling pardons, massive amounts of money flowing into the President’s bank account, and banners with his head plastered on government buildings. NONE OF THIS IS NORMAL.”
Stephanie Grisham, Trump’s former White House Press Secretary during his first term, suggested on social media that “Trump TV” is similar to what U.S. adversaries use. “You know who else does this? Russia, China, and Iran to name a few…”
Before the launch of Trump TV, former White House Correspondents’ Association President and CBS News senior White House correspondent Weijia Jiang already warned on Fox News Sunday about increasing attempts by the government to shape news coverage in light of the press ban.
“America cannot have state TV,” Jiang said. “That’s what makes America America … You need independent actors to be able to be the observers. And if the government is only showing you what it wants, then you have to question: What are we missing?”

Context
Under the proposal, sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman would be lifted, while sanctions against approximately 3,000 other Russia-linked individuals and organizations would be extended for three years.

Latvia blocks
Extending the sanctions for 36 months would be the right step. However, the price for this should not simply be removing both individuals from the sanctions list. Latvia cannot accept such a proposal

France took this step after coming under pressure from Azerbaijan, amid the country’s detention of at least two French citizens, three European diplomats told Reuters last week. A senior Azerbaijani diplomat denied these claims on Friday.
Both men challenged the cases against them and took legal action to try to have the sanctions lifted.
Fridman is seeking $16 billion from Luxembourg in a case that has gone to arbitration. EU diplomats said Luxembourg argues that its case for maintaining EU sanctions against Fridman could be weakened if sanctions against Usmanov are lifted.
Kulbergs said he would convene an emergency cabinet meeting on Tuesday, September 22, to discuss the issue. He said Latvia would cooperate with Brussels and Paris "to find a solution that meets Latvia’s interests."
Talks continue
EU member-state ambassadors were due to resume talks on Tuesday morning, September 22, in an attempt to resolve the issue, diplomats said.
Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty journalist Rikard Jozwiak reported on X on September 22 that EU ambassadors had met again this morning.
"Another written procedure has been launched, with a deadline of 2 p.m. It remains the case that Usmanov and Fridman will be removed from the list and that the 36-month extension will be adopted," Jozwiak indicated.

China’s Vice President Han Zheng will address the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, Beijing announced Tuesday, saying he will stress revitalizing the authority of the world body.
Han will be in New York on Sept. 24-26 to attend the general debate of the General Assembly, China’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
The General Assembly will hear the address from the Chinese representative on Saturday.
During his visit, 72-year-old Han will also attend the high-level dialogue on the 5th anniversary of the Global Development Initiative hosted by China, and meet with the UN secretary-general, the president of the 81st UN General Assembly, and leaders of relevant countries, the statement added.

“This year marks the 55th anniversary of the restoration of China's lawful seat in the UN,” he noted.
China was granted its seat in the UN on Oct. 25, 1971, when the General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758.
Guo said that during the General Debate, Han will “present China's views and positions on the current international landscape, major international and regional issues, and the work of the UN.”
Han “will outline China's concrete actions to practice true multilateralism and promote world peace and development, and call on the world to revitalize the authority and role of the UN, build greater synergy for reforming and improving global governance, and work together in the right direction of building a community with a shared future for humanity,” Guo added.

A squeeze usually destroys open interest. This one did not, which means positions are immediately being replaced. Traders are chasing the move rather than reducing risk. That is why the next 5% in either direction will be faster than expected

Peace in southern Lebanon remains ‘elusive’: UN mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:42:47 UTC
17:42:47 KST

Wassim Samih Seifeddine and Lina Altawell
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
The UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) said Tuesday that peace in southern Lebanon remains "elusive," stressing that permanently ending the conflict requires political will from the parties.
The remarks came in a statement marking the International Day of Peace, observed annually on Sept. 21, which UNIFIL commemorated Monday evening with a ceremony at its headquarters in the southern Lebanese town of Naqoura.
“Today, peace in south Lebanon remains elusive, but the hope for peace endures,” UNIFIL said, stressing that lasting peace requires “political commitments and solutions from the parties themselves.”
“Peacekeepers can help restore stability, avoid misunderstandings, and reduce the risk of escalation -- but they cannot replace the political will and decisions needed to end the conflict permanently,” it said.
"Peace is not something we address once a year; it is an enduring responsibility," UNIFIL Head of Mission and Force Commander Major General Diodato Abagnara said.
“We patrol, we keep channels of communication open with the parties to reduce the risk of misunderstanding and escalation. We work with the Lebanese Armed Forces as they assume greater responsibilities in the south,” Abagnara said.
He stressed that responsibility for reaching a political solution rests with the parties, while “UNIFIL will continue to do its part, keeping communication open, reducing the risk of escalation, and supporting diplomatic efforts.”
The full implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701 "remains the objective and the basis for lasting peace and stability in south Lebanon," Abagnara added.
“Continued cooperation between the Lebanese Armed Forces and peacekeepers remains central to maintaining stability and supporting the extension of state authority in the south,” he added.
The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 1701 in August 2006 following a 33-day war between the Israeli army and Hezbollah.
The resolution calls for a complete cessation of hostilities between Lebanon and Israel and for an area between the Blue Line and the Litani River in southern Lebanon to be free of weapons and armed personnel except those of the Lebanese army and UNIFIL.
 
Disrupted livelihoods
UNIFIL said the current conflict has forced thousands of people from their homes, with many remaining displaced.
“It has disrupted livelihoods, caused widespread damage to homes and infrastructure, and resulted in civilian deaths and injuries,” it added.
This year's International Day of Peace is the last UNIFIL will observe before its mandate expires at the end of 2026, following a UN Security Council decision in 2025 to end the mission.
The UN General Assembly established the International Day of Peace in 1981 to promote ceasefires, nonviolence, tolerance, justice and human rights.
Israeli attacks on Lebanon since March 2 have killed at least 4,386 people, injured 12,407 others and displaced more than 1 million, according to Lebanese authorities.
The attacks have continued despite the two countries signing a US-brokered framework agreement on June 26 providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of Hezbollah.
Israel occupies areas in southern Lebanon, some for decades and others since the 2023-2024 war, while Israeli forces have advanced more than 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) during the current offensive.

Historic Kawabata Bridge reopens between Taipei and New Taipei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:40:14 UTC
17:40:14 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The historic Kawabata Bridge, built in 1937 and one of the few substantially preserved large bridges from the Japanese colonial period, reopened Monday as a pedestrian and bicycle route connecting Taipei and New Taipei.
The bridge crosses the Xindian River. Following the completion of the new Zhongzheng Bridge, the old structure was restored and repurposed to connect surrounding riverside parks and provide views of the river, per a press release.
New Taipei Mayor Hou Yu-ih (侯友宜) and Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) attended the evening reopening ceremony and walked across the restored bridge.
The project included structural reinforcement, restoration of the bridge’s steel beams, and improvements to the surrounding area. The bridge retains its distinctive double-column arched piers and steel-beam structure from the Japanese colonial period. Railings modeled on its original design were also installed.
Hou said the bridge represented the longstanding connection between Taipei and New Taipei and praised cooperation between the two municipalities in preserving it. He also credited Lee Shu-chuan (李四川), who served as deputy mayor in New Taipei, Kaohsiung, and Taipei, for his role in the project, per CNA.
Chiang said the restoration demonstrated the two cities’ commitment to preserving historic structures while giving them new functions. “Today we witnessed the rebirth of the Kawabata Bridge,” Chiang said, noting that the cities had worked together to preserve the historic piers, Japanese-era steel beams, and original-style railings.
New Taipei’s Public Works Department said the restoration team discovered extensive corrosion in parts of the old bridge’s steel beams. The project therefore included reinforcement and restoration of the original paintwork while retaining the historic structural elements.
The bridge was expanded in 1962 and again in 1972 as traffic increased. After the new Zhongzheng Bridge was completed, the historic structure was retained rather than demolished.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) outlined the government’s efforts Tuesday to promote more balanced development across Taiwan as the economy is expected to grow by more than 11% this year, CTEE reported.
Hsiao said a key priority is spreading economic growth and resources more evenly across the country. Differences in development, geography, and local conditions have contributed to disparities in economic development and resource distribution among regions, according to Hanlin.
Since late last year, the government has promoted regional development while accelerating more than 140 infrastructure projects. The plans include further metropolitan development in northern Taiwan, stronger technology industries in Taoyuan, Hsinchu, and Miaoli, and greater support for precision manufacturing and smart industries in central Taiwan.
Southern Taiwan will expand its technology industries, while eastern Taiwan and the offshore islands will focus on sustainable development, low-carbon initiatives, and tourism, according to the National Development Council.
Hsiao also emphasized balanced development among businesses of different sizes. She said the government would continue supporting large companies as they expand overseas.
At the same time, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) remain a key part of Taiwan’s economy. The country had 1.715 million SMEs in 2024, accounting for 98.8% of all businesses. They employed 9.19 million people, or nearly 80% of the workforce, according to UDN Money.
President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) has proposed a NT$100 billion (US$3.15 billion) support program over eight years to help SMEs expand overseas and connect with global markets through financing, talent development, and assistance with business transformation.
Hsiao said the government’s third priority is balanced development across industries. While AI, semiconductors, and other high-tech sectors remain important, it also aims to support industries including finance, services, and tourism.

Türkiye set for rainy autumn despite above-normal temperatures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:39:58 UTC
17:39:58 KST

(AA Photo)
Türkiye is expected to experience a warmer-than-normal autumn but receive above-average rainfall across much of the country, according to a climate scientist, who said the outlook marks a departure from last year’s drier autumn.
Murat Türkeş, a member of the executive board of Boğaziçi University’s Center for Climate Change and Policy Research, said temperatures are likely to remain above seasonal averages in October, November and December, meaning Türkiye is expected to enter winter under warmer-than-normal conditions.
“Unlike last year, I expect this autumn to be rainy,” Türkeş said, forecasting above-normal precipitation across a large part of the country during the three-month period. He said rainfall in western and northwestern Türkiye is expected to remain around or below seasonal averages, while most other regions are likely to receive more precipitation than normal.
Türkeş attributed the outlook to the expected influence of frontal low-pressure systems originating from the North Atlantic and, at times, the Mediterranean over the northern Mediterranean basin, southern Europe, the Balkans and Türkiye.
However, he cautioned that higher temperatures could still intensify the effects of drought by increasing evaporation from ecosystems, soil and water resources and reducing soil moisture. Warmer conditions can also contribute to agricultural drought even when rainfall is adequate.
Türkeş noted that above-normal precipitation from last autumn through the summer had already eased hydrological and agricultural drought across much of Türkiye. Prolonged drought remains a concern in parts of the northwest, the Marmara and northern Aegean regions, as well as central parts of southeastern Türkiye.
Despite the expected rise in temperatures, he said rainfall could limit the severity of drought conditions during the coming season.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has said she will soon propose measures to cap the number of foreign students in classrooms and ban burqas and niqabs in schools.
Meloni told the youth wing of her nationalist conservative Brothers of Italy party on Sunday that the measure would also make Italian language lessons compulsory for parents of foreign students having "serious difficulties integrating into the school system."

Once approved by the government, the measure would need parliamentary approval within 60 days to pass into law.
Meloni, who has political roots in the far-right, has consistently been hawkish on migration. But she has evolved politically over her tenure as prime minister, shifting from a nationalist outlier to an establishment figure among European Union politicians.
However, she's also keen to boost her popularity before a general election next year and is introducing a string of policies that achieve that aim, including an exemption from a hated property tax on small- and medium-sized cars and scooters.
Earlier this month, Meloni’s conservative administration became Italy’s longest-serving uninterrupted government since World War II.

National statistics agency Istat said Tuesday that Italy's deficit-to-GDP ratio for 2025 was 3.1%, confirming the provisional figure it gave in April and dashing hopes the country would be able emerge from its EU excessive-deficit infringement procedure. 
    The government had been hoping the final figure would be revised down to bring it within the 3% threshold laid down in the EU budget rules.

'Swang Song': New book by Princess Diana's brother drops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:36:00 UTC
17:36:00 KST

'Swan Song': New book by Princess Diana's brother drops
September 22, 2026
Charles Spencer's book about his late sister Princess Diana's life and former marriage to Britain's now King Charles III hit bookstores on Tuesday.
The book titled "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister" is being published globally by Penguin and has been translated into 12 languages.
The memoir triggered a royal row even before it went on sale, after some of its pre-published extracts — laden with Spencer's explosive claims — received a rare reaction and rebuttal from the king.
Charles Spencer, the 9th Earl Spencer, is Diana's younger brother and has long clashed with the royal House of Windsor over how they treated the princess.
What does Charles Spencer say in his memoir of Princess Diana?
In one of the claims that made a splash ahead the new book's release, Spencer accused Charles of sounding "giddily elated" and "like a lottery winner" when he had called him after Diana's death.
Spencer also writes that he had argued against plans for Charles and Diana's sons, William and Harry, to walk in their mother's funeral procession in 1997, saying that she would not have wanted them to go through that ordeal.
Spencer claims Charles "went ballistic" during the argument , telling him: "Rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough."
William was 15-years-old at the time and Harry was 12.
The world was moved by somber visuals of the young princes walking behind Diana's coffin.
How has King Charles III reacted to Spencer's claims?
Following the release of the book's excerpts last week, Buckingham Palace published a strongly-worded statement.
"His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," it said in a statement considered rare as far as responses from the royal household go.
Princess Diana's life and death
In 1981, a 20-year-old Lady Diana Spencer married a 32-year-old Charles, who was then the Prince of Wales, in a fairytale wedding that was televised globally.
Their whirlwind romance soon hit rock bottom and culminated in a public breakdown of their marriage. Diana famously told the BBC in an interview that "there were three of us in this marriage, so it was a bit crowded" in reference to Charles' relationship with Camilla Parker Bowles.
Diana, known as the people's princess, was loved by people from all over the world. Her popularity led to her experiencing a media frenzy that lasted nearly all her adult life.
The royal couple divorced in 1996 and Diana died a year later, aged 36, in a car crash in Paris as she was being pursued by paparazzi.
Charles married Parker Bowles in 2005.
Edited by: Rana Taha

One-third of drinking water supplies contain high levels of PFAS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:35:52 UTC
17:35:52 KST

One-third of drinking water supplies contain high levels of PFAS
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Water companies have called for PFAS chemicals to be banned in pesticides after a study showed that one-third of people are exposed to high levels of the “forever chemicals” in drinking water.
An analysis by Greenpeace of every postcode in the Netherlands showed that the water in 32% of areas contains PFAS levels that are at least 1.5 times the recommended safe level.
The environmental inspection agency ILT blames the increased use of trifluoroacetic acid in pesticides by agricultural sectors such as potato farming, which has almost doubled in the last two years. The ILT says two tonnes of the chemical end up in the water supply per year.
The highest concentrations are in the provinces of Noord-Holland, Zuid-Holland and Zeeland, with towns such as Zaandam, Purmerend and IJmuiden recording 14.3 nanograms per litre.
PFAS is a collective label for thousands of highly stable chemical compounds that are used extensively in packaging, liquid chemicals and products such as waterproof clothing and non-stick cooking pans.
They are attractive to industry because they are extremely durable, but prolonged exposure increases the risk of cancer, immune system problems, low fertility and damage to unborn babies.
High blood levels
A recent study by the public health agency RIVM showed almost everyone in the Netherlands has unhealthy levels of PFAS in their blood.
Greenpeace compiled a dataset and built an online tool allowing householders to see how much PFAS is in their drinking water, with a map to show the most polluted and least polluted areas.
“We think this information should be available to everyone, so we asked a data analyst to set out clearly how much pollution is in the water per location,” campaign leader Eline Bosman told NRC.
There are strong regional variations, with the northern provinces of Drenthe, Friesland and Groningen showing almost no PFAS chemicals in drinking water.
Patricia van der Linden of Vewin, the association of Dutch drinking water suppliers, said the west of the country drew its water supply from rivers and reservoirs, which are more polluted than water sources in rural areas.
“Ground water contains less pollution than surface water,” she said. “In places where we use surface water for drinking water, we have to take more steps to purify the water.”
Immune system
Although none of the water supplies exceed the legal limit set by the European Union, they are well above the RIVM’s advisory limit of 4.4 nanograms.
The agency lowered the guideline level in 2023 in the light of new information that showed PFAS chemicals have a greater impact on the immune system than previously thought.
Germany, the Netherlands and the Scandinavian nations have been lobbying since February 2023 for a total ban on PFAS in pesticides throughout the EU.
RIVM spokesman Coen Berends told NRC: “We can see that banning individual types of PFAS makes a difference, but really the whole group should be banned.”

====================================================================================================

South African firm unveils V-Raven unmanned aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:30:15 UTC
17:30:15 KST

- Paramount unveiled V-Raven, a reusable vertical-takeoff drone, at the Africa Aerospace and Defence exhibition in South Africa on Sept. 19.
- The petrol-powered version can fly up to eight hours and 1,200 km, while a planned armed variant will carry precision-guided glide munitions.
South African defense company Paramount unveiled a new reusable drone called V-Raven at the Africa Aerospace and Defence exhibition in South Africa on Sept. 19, replacing an earlier catapult-launched design with an aircraft that takes off and lands vertically without a runway.
V-Raven grew out of Paramount’s earlier N-Raven program, a swarming drone the company first showed in 2021. That version launched from a catapult and weighed 41 kg, cruised at about 180 km/h and could fly for roughly two hours. V-Raven drops the catapult in favor of vertical takeoff and landing, which Paramount says lets forces launch and recover the aircraft from remote locations without fixed infrastructure.
“The V-Raven has been developed for the realities of the modern African battlefield,” said Sello Ntshiele of Paramount. “Vast operating areas, remote terrain, dispersed threats and the increasing use of drones mean that forces need to be able to see further and stay on station longer. V-Raven brings those capabilities together in a highly flexible, reusable unmanned system.”
The drone comes in two power configurations. The petrol-powered version can fly for up to eight hours, cover a range of up to 1,200 km and cruise at about 140 km/h, with a communications range of up to 150 km from its ground station. An electric version trades range and endurance for a smaller footprint, flying for up to two hours over a maximum range of 250 km. Both share the same airframe: a 3.6-meter wingspan, a 2.1-meter fuselage and a maximum takeoff weight of 65 kg.
Unlike a one-way loitering munition, V-Raven is built to fly a mission and land for reuse. The base ISR version carries an electro-optical sensor for day and night surveillance, with automatic target tracking and support for interchangeable electro-optical and infrared sensors. Paramount is also developing a second configuration that adds precision-guided glide munitions for strikes on selected targets; DefenceWeb reported the weapon under development is Paramount’s LongClaw glide bomb. That armed version will go through further systems integration, ground testing and flight trials before it is ready to field.
“What we are unveiling at AAD is the next stage of the V-Raven journey,” Ntshiele said. “It is a common aircraft architecture that can evolve as operational requirements develop. The immediate focus is a highly capable ISR platform, while the family architecture provides a pathway towards additional mission configurations, including light attack.”
Paramount pointed to security challenges in the Sahel and northern Mozambique as examples of the kind of terrain V-Raven is meant to cover, where forces often lack conventional airfields to operate from. AAD 2026 drew 287 companies and 33 countries to Waterkloof Air Force Base near Pretoria, South Africa’s defense minister, Angelina Motshekga, said at the show’s opening.

Hong Kong lacks a climate narrative to unify its efforts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:30:05 UTC
17:30:05 KST

Hong Kong lacks a climate narrative to unify its efforts
Hong Kong does not mention ‘climate change’ in its five-year plan, yet it already has many ingredients of climate leadership
Hong Kong deserves credit for its first five-year plan, accompanied by a detailed policy address. The plan establishes a useful framework beyond the annual policy cycle. Precisely because this is an important first effort, it is worth asking what could make the framework even stronger.
One striking omission is that the five-year plan never explicitly mentions climate change. This does not mean Hong Kong is failing to act.
Consider the binding indicators. They include the long-standing reduction in carbon emissions per unit of gross domestic product and increasing the proportion of zero-carbon energy in electricity generation. The plan also addresses cleaner power, electric vehicles, green maritime fuels, sustainable aviation fuel, energy efficiency, hydrogen, waste reduction and carbon trading.

Israeli sentenced to 55 months in prison for spying for Iran, photographing Gallant's house
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:29:49 UTC
17:29:49 KST

An Israeli citizen was convicted of contact with an Iranian foreign agent on Tuesday, with the tasks he carried out including hiding phones in Haifa and Kiryat Haim and photographing streets near the home of former defense minister Yoav Gallant.
The Haifa District Court sentenced Fares Abu al-Hija, 32, of Kaukab Abu al-Hija, to 55 months in prison after he was convicted as part of a plea agreement, which did not include an agreement regarding sentencing, for contact with a foreign agent.
According to the amended indictment, to which he confessed, Hija carried out a series of tasks for an individual identified by the Shin Bet (Israeli Security Agency) as an Iranian intelligence operative, including photographing streets near Gallant's home.
According to the indictment, between October 2025 and January 2026, Hija was in contact via Telegram with a person who called himself "Martin," and carried out a series of tasks for him in exchange for payments transferred through the Binance app.
During his interrogation, it emerged that Hija had begun to suspect that the individual was connected to Iranian intelligence. The Shin Bet identified the person he had been in contact with as an Iranian intelligence operative.
Hija hid cell phones, delivered cryptocurrency account information
As part of the assignments, Hija purchased cellphones and a charger and hid them at several locations in Haifa and Kiryat Haim. He activated the devices, installed communications applications on them, documented the locations where they had been hidden, and sent the documentation to his handler.
He was later asked to deliver an envelope containing an access code to a cryptocurrency account to a location in Zichron Yaakov, and to photograph a cafe in Tel Aviv.
In January 2026, Hija was asked to travel to the community of Amikam and photograph streets near Gallant's home. He took the photographs and sent them to his handler, after which he was arrested in an operation by the Shin Bet and the Menashe District Central Unit of the Israel Police's Coastal District.
Judge weighs Hija's confession, life circumstances over deterrence
In his sentencing decision, Judge Avi Levy noted that Hija's confession, acceptance of responsibility, expression of remorse, and the judicial time saved weighed in his favor. The court also took into account his family circumstances, including his father's serious medical condition and the impact of his arrest on his family.
At the same time, the court emphasized the severity of the offenses and the need for deterrence. The judge said the court must take into account "in light of the defendant's dangerous conduct," and added that general deterrence should be included among the considerations determining the sentencing range, given the growing prevalence of the phenomenon.
The court ultimately sentenced Abu al-Hija to 55 months in prison, with time already served in detention deducted from the sentence, as well as a 24-month suspended sentence for three years and a NIS 10,000 fine.

Canadian police have yet to formally determine the motive behind the shooting outside Congregation Beth Jacob in Belleville, Canada, which occured as worshipers gathered for Yom Kippur prayers on Sunday.
Shortly after the shooting, Israel's Ambassador to Canada Iddo Moed described the incident as a "terror attack" and called for an immediate increase in protection for the Jewish community.
Belleville Police Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks said during a briefing that the shooter was 29-year-old Sean Ward of nearby Quinte West, about 18 kilometers from Belleville. He remains hospitalized with life-threatening injuries.
Meeks identified the wounded officer as Jeff Smith, a veteran police officer who has served for 13 years. She said Smith was hospitalized in intensive care and faces a significant recovery, but that his condition had stabilized.
Kristy Denette, a spokeswoman for Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU), which is investigating the incident, said in response to a question that logic pointed toward a terrorist incident targeting the Jewish community. She stressed, however, that the SIU's investigation was focused on the actions of the police officer.
Denette said the scene was complex and that forensic investigators would need several days to complete their work there.
Belleville Mayor Neil Ellis said it was "too early to determine that this was a hate crime," but noted that the location and timing, outside a synagogue on the eve of Yom Kippur, "point in that direction."
None of synagogue's 24 worshippers injured in attack
About 24 worshipers were inside the synagogue at the time of the shooting, Meeks said. None were injured. She added that antisemitism, hatred, and violence were unacceptable in the community.
Following the incident, police increased their presence across the city, including around houses of worship.
Israel's Foreign Ministry in Jerusalem said the terror attack against Congregation Beth Jacob in Belleville on the eve of Yom Kippur marked a further escalation in Canada's antisemitism crisis.
"Our thoughts are with the police officer who acted with extraordinary courage and was wounded in the line of duty. We pray for his full and speedy recovery," the Israeli Foreign Ministry said. "Israel stands in solidarity with the Jewish community in Canada, which is confronting an increasingly threatening reality."
The ministry added that "open incitement that goes untreated in the public sphere, together with anti-Israel policies, fuels antisemitism. A change is needed."
Denette said Belleville Police were conducting a parallel investigation that included examining the suspect's motive. She declined to say whether others directed or activated the suspect, repeatedly saying the question fell outside the scope of the SIU's investigation.
On-duty police officer guarding synagogue was first target of shooting
According to Denette, the suspect arrived in his vehicle, believed to have been a pickup truck, at around 7 p.m. while armed with a shotgun. He fired first, initially targeting the on-duty police officer who was securing the synagogue.
The officer returned fire, and a second officer later arrived and also opened fire. The suspect and the first officer were both struck.
The scene extended for roughly half a block. Witness accounts and the preliminary investigation indicated that as many as 30 rounds were fired. A police cruiser, other vehicles, and nearby homes were hit.
A team of four investigators and two forensic investigators was assigned to the case. They collected evidence, reviewed security footage, police body-camera recordings, and vehicle-camera footage, and took witness statements.

E. coli contamination in Saue private wells unresolved after month-long investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:29:00 UTC
17:29:00 KST

E. coli contamination in Saue private wells unresolved after month-long investigation
E. coli contamination found in private wells in Saue, near Tallinn, in mid-August remains without an identified source after extensive investigation, the local municipality said.
On August 17, the municipal government received its first report of a possible water quality problem, in the northwestern part of town. Three more reports followed the next day, and residents were informed of contamination in private wells. A crisis committee convened on August 19, bringing in relevant authorities and taking the first water samples.
A total of 11 samples were taken — three from the public water supply, all found safe, and eight from private wells, seven of which were contaminated with E. coli. No contamination was found in the public supply.
Water and soil samples were taken, wastewater systems and pipelines inspected, and the Environmental Board, Health Board, Rescue Board, AS Tallinna Vesi and the Geological Survey of Estonia all involved in assessing the situation.
Drinking water tanks were set up in the town for local residents affected by the contamination.
Andres Marandi, a hydrogeologist at the Geological Survey of Estonia (Eesti geoloogiateenistus), said the evidence suggests several factors may have coincided: microbiological contamination may already have been present in the area's soil and shallow groundwater, while low summer water levels, the condition of private wells and excavation work on Rauna tänav may have affected water movement through the soil.
Deficiencies were found in on-site wastewater treatment systems at several properties, but in none of the cases could these be conclusively linked to the well contamination. A tip alleging a sewer pipe leak on Rauna tänav during construction was investigated by the Environmental Board; the municipality said isolated minor leaks may have occurred but were not extensive enough to cause widespread groundwater contamination. CCTV inspections by AS Tallinna Vesi found no broken pipes.
Repeat samples taken on September 2 showed coliform bacteria levels had fallen in several wells, indicating improvement, though the original source remains unknown. Soil samples from five locations also failed to identify a single source.
The municipal government said it would continue spot checks of well water in the affected area.

Will Germany have enough gas this winter?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:25:00 UTC
17:25:00 KST

Will Germany have enough gas this winter?
September 22, 2026
As of mid-September 2026, Germany had stored just about 141 terawatt-hours of gas, accounting for around 57% of the country's total storage capacity.
Last winter just under 134 terawatt-hours of gas were withdrawn from storage, according to the Federal Network Agency, the agency that monitors the country's electricity and gas networks.
At first glance, the numbers sounds reassuring, especially since last winter was quite cold and therefore required a lot of heating. But compared to previous years, natural gas storage levels are low.
On September 4, Markus Söder, the premier of Bavaria, called for intervention by the federal government.
A few days later, the opposition Green Party accused the economy minister of negligence. "The gas storage facilities are not full. We are facing a potential shortage," said Britta Hasselmann, co-leader of the Greens' parliamentary group.
Such statements have raised concerns about potential gas shortages in Germany this winter.
To assess the current situation, however, various factors such as imports and the diversification of supply sources need to be taken into account , not least since Germany is no longer as dependent on a single importer as it was on Russia until 2022.
Will Germany have enough gas?
Most experts interviewed by DW are not concerned about the winter gas supply.
Charlie Grüneberg, spokesperson for the German Gas and Hydrogen Industry association, points to the contracts that have been signed for the medium term. "Anyone who has contractually secured their gas needs for the winter with a reliable supplier will receive the agreed quantities," he said.
Sebastian Heinermann, managing director of INES, a German association for gas and hydrogen storage system operators, is more cautious.
He pointed out that it's technically possible to fill gas storage facilities in Germany to around 77%, but this would require filling at a level that "has not been observed even once in the past three weeks," Heinermann said. "If this trend continues unchanged, the fill level will reach only about 65% by November 1."
Still, the Federal Network Agency sees no cause for concern.
"The gas supply in Germany is stable," the agency's spokesperson, Nadia Affani, told DW. "Security of supply is currently guaranteed. Based on the latest information, the Federal Network Agency continues to assess the risk of a gas supply crunch as low."
Germany's Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy shared a similar assessment. The ministry "is monitoring all developments very closely to ensure security of supply. There are currently no signs of a supply shortage," said spokesperson Susanne Ungrad.
Officials downplay supply risks
She also pointed to an array of factors that determine the price of natural gas like available storage, ongoing imports via pipelines and LNG terminals, demand and the situation on the international energy markets.
"We are prepared for further developments," Ungrad stressed.
Grüneberg also takes a more holistic view.
"The key factor is whether enough gas can be procured and transported to and through Germany. Supply contracts, storage facilities, pipeline imports and LNG are all interlinked," he underscored.
"Thanks to investments in LNG terminals, new import routes and reverse-flow capabilities, the infrastructure is now significantly more robust than it was in 2022."
Gas prices rise ahead of winter
As the winter approaches and people start heating their homes more, gas prices tend to climb. This trend is already evident, said Heinermann.
"In the second quarter, the gas price across various contracts on the futures market stood at around €46 ($52) per megawatt-hour. Recently, the gas price has risen to over €80."
Olaf Geyer from the US consulting firm Arthur D. Little, who has been monitoring the German market, said there is no immediate supply problem, but: "If the winter turns out to be cold or there are disruptions on the import side, prices could rise quickly."
Grüneberg said "reliable price forecasts" are difficult to make and noted that low storage levels could cause prices to rise "if additional volumes have to be procured on the market."
However, there are no signs of a shortage on the supply side. "As things stand today, there are no indications of a physical shortage of supply by the end of winter. The futures markets are not signaling this at the moment either," said Grüneberg.
The German economy ministry points out that "the prices currently quoted for forward contracts for the winter are only slightly higher than the spot market prices for immediate transactions."
"The usual summer-winter spread, which made it economically viable to store gas during the summer months, was therefore not present," it added.
The "spread" is based on the principle of buying gas cheaply in summer and selling it at higher prices in winter. This year, gas prices rose following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, undermining that seasonal pattern.
How to refill storage faster
Geyer, who also focuses on the summer-winter spread, said storage facilities aren't fuller this time round because it hasn't been economically viable.
"For the future, we need better incentives for filling storage facilities — and risk management on the part of utilities that looks not only at the purchase price but also at how much actual consumption can deviate from projections," he underlined.
Heinermann also called for effective economic incentives to fill gas storage facilities.
"In the medium term, Germany needs a reliable market framework that, through incentives, obligations or a combination of both, ensures sufficient storage levels on a long-term basis while preserving as much market-based flexibility as possible."
This article was originally written in German.

Giorgetti expresses sadness excessive-deficit procedure won't end early

ANSA English Desk

Istat said Tuesday that Italy's deficit-to-GDP ratio for 2025 was 3.1%, confirming the provisional figure it gave in April. The government had been hoping the final figure would be revised down to bring it within the 3% threshold laid down in the EU budget rules to enable Italy to emerge from its excessive-deficit infringement procedure. Russia Delays Civilian Spending as Soaring War Costs Widen Budget Deficit
The Russian Finance Ministry was forced to delay a portion of scheduled government expenditures to later periods to maintain its "everything for the front" priority and keep the budget balanced.
Finance Minister Anton Siluanov announced these measures during the Moscow Financial Forum, as reported by The Moscow Times on September 21.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The most important thing for us right now is defense tasks, the tasks of the front," the minister stated, adding that resolving budget challenges this year required "digging around somewhere" and adjusting both expenditures and the resource base.
From January through August, the federal budget deficit expanded to 5.8 trillion rubles ($72.5 billion), representing 2.5% of GDP. Siluanov noted that this deficit will continue to grow, explaining: "During the execution of the budget, additional needs for financing and expenditures arose.
Additional sources of funding for these costs will also be provided for this purpose. We expect the deficit to be larger than planned, but it will remain within 3% of GDP." He added that the government intends to cover the shortfall using accumulated account balances and borrowing on the debt market, according to The Moscow Times.
In the 2026 budget law, the Russian government originally allocated 12.9 trillion rubles ($161.25 billion) under the "national defense" item.
However, actual spending related to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, including adjacent budget categories, reached 10.687 trillion rubles ($133.58 billion) in the first half of the year alone, according to calculations by Janis Kluge from the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, The Moscow Times reports.
Compared to the same period last year, military and arms production expenditures grew by another 30%. They rose by 65% compared to January–June 2024, and have increased more than fivefold compared to pre-war 2021. Cumulative spending on the military since the beginning of 2022 has exceeded 57 trillion rubles ($712.5 billion).
This stagnation aligns with a previous report, which warned that severe labor shortages and intense military spending have pushed Russia to its absolute productive limits.
It notes that the Kremlin is rapidly exhausting its current human and financial resources, leaving Putin with a fundamental choice: either scale back his military ambitions in Ukraine or implement deeply unpopular domestic measures, such as forced conscription and a Soviet-style command economy, to sustain the invasion.

Economy Ministry continues consultations with business on shelling compensation fund funded by VAT hike
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:18:15 EEST
17:18:15 KST

The Ministry of Economy and Environment is continuing intensive consultations with business representatives, through business associations and think tanks, on advancing and discussing the details of a proposed insurance fund for compensating first losses of up to $10 million, to be funded by raising the value-added tax rate from 20% to 21%, though business remains cautious about the idea.
According to Interfax-Ukraine, active consultations without media presence continued for nearly all of last week, with at least two meetings scheduled for Tuesday and one for Wednesday.
At the same time, none of the major business associations - the American Chamber of Commerce (AmCham), the European Business Association (EBA), the Union of Ukrainian Entrepreneurs (UUE), or the Federation of Employers of Ukraine (FEU) - have yet publicly commented on the proposal, though they are also holding internal discussions on it.
Oleh Hetman, coordinator of expert groups at the Economic Expert Platform, said at the "Think Small First" forum, held by the National Business Coalition with support from the Center for International Private Enterprise (CIPE) on September 21, that small businesses oppose the idea and are asking that an alternative model not involving a VAT rate hike be considered.
FEU council chairman Dmytro Oliynyk had also previously said the federation favored a different source of funding for the insurance fund - an import levy on non-critical goods.
Deputy Finance Minister Svitlana Vorobei stressed at the "Think Small First" forum that the issue concerns the country's food security, since logistics centers, particularly those of food suppliers from whom small businesses also purchase goods, have been among the hardest hit by destruction.
"Is this tool the right one, or 100% ideal? No, because we're increasing the imbalance between taxpayers and non-payers, since the same goods are on our market both with and without VAT: that is, VAT payers will bear more of the burden, greater risks, but this is a way out... It's an extraordinary measure, but one that will spare us disruptions in food supply... If there's another solution you consider more effective, you have ample access to both the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Economy," she said.
Vorobei said the idea will be discussed at a meeting between the Finance Ministry and the Economy Ministry on Thursday.
BDO Ukraine CEO Vira Savchenko, citing her own research, wrote on her Facebook page overnight into Tuesday about 225 private companies and brands whose assets or goods were damaged or destroyed on Ukrainian-controlled territory and which have publicly disclosed this.
"In the third quarter of 2026 alone, there have already been 75 cases of private business being hit - more than in any previous quarter since the start of the full-scale war," she said, adding that there were 15 such cases in the second quarter of this year and 6 in the first.
She noted that loss amounts are publicly known for only 29 of the 225 cases, totaling $0.8 billion, whereas Economy and Environment Minister Oleksii Kravchenko has estimated annual losses at around $10 billion.
Savchenko added that 2.1 million square meters of warehouse space has been destroyed - about 42% of the Class A/B warehouse real estate stock (including space built since 2022) - of which roughly 1.5 million out of 2.2 million square meters, or 68%, has been lost in the Kyiv region alone.
"That's exactly why the Ministry of Economy, Environment and Agriculture's initiative to create a #firstloss mechanism for compensating businesses' war losses is critical. The model isn't final yet: the Economy Ministry, together with the Finance Ministry, the National Bank, the Export Credit Agency, the insurance market and international partners, is currently validating the financial and operational structure," the expert said.
As previously reported, citing Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky and Minister Kravchenko, the plan preliminarily involves a state contribution of about $1 billion to this special shelling-compensation fund, funded by raising the VAT rate from 20% to 21%, a compensation limit of $10 million, and a 2% premium rate to be paid by program participants on the coverage amount. International partners are expected to contribute an additional $1-2 billion to the fund, which could become operational as early as the start of 2027 through the state Export Credit Agency (ECA), though the fund would not cover goods.
The Economy Ministry explains its choice to raise VAT as one of the fund's financing sources by its desire to cover all industries, minimize the inflationary impact, and encourage businesses to come out of the shadows (only VAT payers could participate in the program), whereas alternative sources, such as an additional import duty, fall short on these criteria. According to preliminary estimates, a 1 percentage point VAT increase could raise inflation by 0.8 percentage points.
Yaroslav Zhelezniak, first deputy chairman of the relevant parliamentary committee, told reporters on the sidelines of the annual Yalta European Strategy meeting (YES 2026) that one possible compromise would be raising the VAT rate for just one year.
Verkhovna Rada Budget Committee Chair Roksolana Pidlasa expressed doubt that parliament would vote for a VAT hike to fund such a scheme, while Halyna Tretiakova, chair of the parliamentary Committee on Social Policy and Veterans' Rights, spoke out at the "Think Small First" forum against the idea of passing these losses on to consumers, which she said is effectively what a VAT hike would do.
Business representatives, during discussions, have voiced concerns that money from the VAT hike might not actually reach compensation payouts, that reversing the hike later would be difficult, and that the increase itself would set a bad precedent for raising taxes. They have also called on the government to look at the "gray" and "black" markets as a better source of funding for the fund.

- Blue Ops, the maritime arm of Red Cat Holdings, marked one year since opening its uncrewed surface vessel plant in Valdosta, Georgia.
- The company built its first prototypes with Hodgdon Shipbuilding in Maine before shifting production to the 155,000-square-foot Valdosta facility.
Blue Ops, the maritime division of drone maker Red Cat Holdings, marked one year since it opened a manufacturing plant in Valdosta, Georgia, the company said. The state of Georgia recognized Sept. 21 as the inaugural Blue Ops Day in the city, according to a company statement.
Blue Ops builds uncrewed surface vessels, small autonomous boats used for military and national security missions. The company leased a 155,000-square-foot former boat factory at 601 Gil Harbin Industrial Boulevard in Valdosta, the site of an earlier Regal Boats plant, and announced the move in April with plans to invest about $30 million and create more than 200 jobs. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp announced the facility in April, and state officials said the company planned to hire up to 100 workers in 2026, with more roles to follow as production increased.
Blue Ops president Barry Hinckley said at the time the investment was meant to build “a modern, scalable, and domestic USV manufacturing base from the ground up.”
The company built its first prototype vessels elsewhere. Blue Ops partnered with Hodgdon Shipbuilding, a Maine boatbuilder founded in 1816, to construct its first five uncrewed surface vessel prototypes at facilities in Boothbay and Damariscotta, Maine, before shifting full-rate production to Valdosta.
In April, Blue Ops also partnered with HADDY, a robotic 3D printing company, to add large-scale 3D printing and robotic production systems to the Valdosta plant. The companies said the partnership would roughly double the facility’s manufacturing capacity by using robotic systems to build vessel hulls before workers complete final assembly.
Red Cat Holdings, based in Salt Lake City and traded on Nasdaq under the ticker RCAT, also makes small drones through its Teal Drones and FlightWave Aerospace subsidiaries. The company has positioned Blue Ops as its expansion into uncrewed maritime systems, alongside its existing air-domain drone business.
Blue Ops has not disclosed how many vessels it has built at the Valdosta facility over the past year or named specific government customers for its USV line. The company said in its anniversary statement that it intends to keep expanding production capacity at the site.

Libya’s NOC says armed group shuts oil pipeline valve, sharply reducing main field output
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:13:28 UTC
17:13:28 KST

Muetaz Wannes and Mohammad Sio
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
An armed group has shut a valve on a crude oil pipeline linking Libya’s Sharara field to the western port of Zawiya, causing a sharp drop in production at the country’s main oil field, the National Oil Corporation (NOC) said late Monday.
The NOC said the armed group closed Valve No. 7, halting the flow of crude from the Sharara field, operated by Akakus Oil Operations, to Zawiya Port in western Libya.
The closure caused pressure to build up in the crude pipeline, resulting in a “significant reduction” in production at Sharara, it added.
Located in the Murzuq Desert, around 800 kilometers (500 miles) south of Tripoli, Sharara is Libya’s largest oil field, with production capacity of around 340,000 barrels per day.
The NOC said it contacted the southwestern branch of the Petroleum Facilities Guard and urged it to carry out its duties, but the appeals “had produced no results.” Technical teams had also been unable to reach the area around Valves 6 and 7.
The corporation warned that the continued shutdown would halt production at the Sharara field as well as oil transport and export operations, directly harming Libya’s economy by causing a decline in state revenues.
It also warned that the oil transport system and its facilities will be exposed to technical and operational risks, anticipating that the shutdown will cause the Zawiya oil refinery to cease operations, thereby further increasing the cost of importing fuel from abroad.
It called for the immediate reopening of the pipeline and demanded the relevant authorities secure oil installations and keep them away from protests and other disruptions.
The corporation said it “may be compelled to declare force majeure” if the closure continues.
Force majeure is a contractual provision that suspends liability when extraordinary circumstances prevent parties from meeting their obligations.
The NOC did not identify the armed group responsible for shutting the valve.
The incident comes a week after members of the Petroleum Facilities Guard closed the main Hamada-Zawiya oil pipeline on Sept. 15, causing production and operations to stop at the Hamada and Al-Tahara fields and Station NC5. The NOC also warned at the time that it could declare force majeure if the closure persisted.
The Hamada field is located in the Hamada al-Hamra area of the Ghadames Basin in western Libya, about 400 kilometers (250 miles) south of Tripoli. It is considered one of the key oil and natural gas fields in western Libya and produces around 700 barrels per day.
Members of the Petroleum Facilities Guard have been demanding higher salaries amid a broader wave of labor protests in Libya.

U.S. Army orders more M270A2 launcher upgrades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:09:31 UTC
17:09:31 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Lockheed Martin $200 million in September to rebuild more M270 rocket launchers to the M270A2 standard.
- The upgrade adds a new engine, an armored cab and a fire-control system shared with HIMARS, letting both launchers fire the same precision munitions.
The U.S. Army has awarded Lockheed Martin $200 million to rebuild more M270 Multiple Launch Rocket System launchers to the M270A2 standard, the company said. The September award is the latest in a series of contracts that began in 2019 to modernize the tracked rocket launcher.
The recapitalization strips down existing M270 launchers and rebuilds them as close to new, with a new engine, an armored cab and the Common Fire Control System, the same fire-control system used on the wheeled HIMARS launcher. That shared system lets the two launchers fire the same family of precision munitions, including GMLRS, Extended-Range GMLRS and the Precision Strike Missile, and lets crews trained on one system move more easily to the other.
The Army has awarded similar M270A2 recapitalization contracts nearly every year since 2019, including a $362 million award in 2019, a $226 million award in 2020, a $451 million award in 2024 and a $214 million award last year. Lockheed Martin has said the goal is to keep the M270 fleet in service through 2050. The Army’s fleet includes 225 M270A1 launchers being upgraded to the A2 standard, along with about 160 older, decommissioned M270A0 launchers slated for the same overhaul.
The M270A2 is a tracked launcher that carries more armor and cargo capacity than the wheeled HIMARS, while HIMARS offers greater mobility on roads. Both can fire the Extended-Range GMLRS, which reaches out to 150 km (93 miles), and the Precision Strike Missile, a longer-range weapon still being fielded across the Army. Lockheed Martin has said only the M270A2 and HIMARS can fire those newer munitions, which older, unmodernized M270 launchers cannot use.
The recapitalization work is split among Lockheed Martin’s Camden, Arkansas, plant and facilities in Grand Prairie and New Boston, Texas, with the Army’s Red River Army Depot handling part of the overhaul. Recent contracts have carried completion dates stretching into 2027 and 2030, reflecting the scale of the work needed to rebuild dozens of launchers at a time.
The Army has fielded more than 220 M270-series launchers, and international partners that operate the M270 or HIMARS, including NATO members, are also eligible for the upgraded fire-control system under foreign military sales.

U.S. Army laser weapon shown defeating drones at border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:05:04 UTC
17:05:04 KST

- Newly released footage shows an Army Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser, built with AeroVironment technology, defeating drones at the southern border.
- The system engaged and defeated three hostile drones over two nights in late August under Joint Task Force Southern Border.
The U.S. Department of War has released new footage showing an Army Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser, built with directed-energy technology from AeroVironment (AV), defeating drones along the U.S. southern border, according to a report by Army Verification Alliance (AV).
The laser is deployed under Joint Task Force Southern Border, a U.S. Northern Command unit that supports U.S. Customs and Border Protection. In late August, task force personnel used the system, known as AMP-HEL, to engage and defeat three drones over two nights, Aug. 25 and 26, near the border. The U.S. Army said the aircraft were judged hostile based on their use in direct support of activity that threatened U.S. military personnel and CBP partners.
“Cartel networks are increasingly employing unmanned aircraft systems to facilitate illicit human-smuggling and actively spy on our personnel and law enforcement partners,” said Army Maj. Gen. Curtis Taylor, commander of Joint Task Force Southern Border. “By integrating layered countermeasures alongside advanced directed-energy capabilities like this laser system, we have made it clear that we will not tolerate hostile surveillance.”
The Army has not disclosed exactly where the drones were engaged or confirmed who was flying them, though officials have linked similar incursions to cartel surveillance. AV told Breaking Defense the system used is the product of the Army’s AMP-HEL program but did not say which specific configuration was deployed or whether it was vehicle-mounted.
AMP-HEL is a 20-kilowatt-class laser weapon built to defeat Group 1 and Group 2 drones, the U.S. military’s category for smaller, slower unmanned aircraft. AV delivered the first two prototypes, mounted on Joint Light Tactical Vehicles, to the Army in December 2025 as part of the AMP-HEL prototyping effort. The company markets the underlying laser weapon system as LOCUST, which it says pairs an electro-optical tracking system, a laser rangefinder and a targeting laser with the high-energy laser itself. AeroVironment says the system uses a common gaming controller for weapon control and is designed to plug into a range of sensor types and radio-frequency bands, as well as existing command-and-control networks.
About 8,000 service members are currently deployed under Joint Task Force Southern Border, the Army said. Officials have said hundreds of drones fly near the border each day, and Northern Command leaders have described the border as a proving ground for technology meant to counter them. Weeks after the August engagements, the Army awarded AV a production contract for the laser under a separate program called Enduring High Energy Laser; DefenseScoop reported the deal is worth $464.8 million and covers dozens of additional LOCUST-based systems over the next several years.

Four Corners episodes breached ABC's editorial standards, ombudsman finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:04:59 UTC
17:04:59 KST

Four Corners episodes breached ABC's editorial standards, ombudsman's investigation finds
In short
The ABC breached four editorial standards in stories by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal, its ombudsman found.
The episodes involved have already been withdrawn by ABC News.
What's next
The ABC has said it accepts the report's seven recommendations and has started to implement them.
The ABC's Four Corners program had insufficient verification and fact-checking and a culture of "limiting knowledge" about anonymous sources, its independent ombudsman has found, identifying breaches of editorial standards in two stories by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal .
The ombudsman's report, released this afternoon, found two episodes failed to meet editorial standards for accuracy, fair and honest dealing, and independence.
"Audiences were given a misleading impression of who key contributors were, the basis on which the ABC was relying on them and the level of confidence that could reasonably be placed in their claims," the report said.
The ombudsman made seven recommendations, which include amending the ABC's editorial standard on anonymity, further legal and editorial training for the Four Corners team and more support for less experienced reporters.
The ABC says it accepts the recommendations in full and has begun implementing them.
ABC News had already removed the two episodes covered by the ombudsman's review — Cocaine Nation and Meth Highway — after its own investigation into the anonymous interviewees.
In total, three episodes of Four Corners and two of Background Briefing by Fazal have already been withdrawn by the ABC, with a short segment edited out of another Four Corners episode.
Last month, the ABC said its own review found verification policies on anonymous interviewees were "not followed to a level that meets our editorial standards".
"The ABC is committed to journalism of the highest standard. Maintaining the trust of Australians depends on upholding those standards and we take any concerns about our journalism seriously," it said.
Fazal, a former member of the Mongols bikie club, had his employment terminated in May after an ABC investigation into his appearance on a podcast with a former underworld figure last year.
He had launched an unfair dismissal claim in the Fair Work Commission, but his hearing was removed from the schedule. The ABC said it was aware Fazal was no longer pursuing his claim.
In a social media video post last month, Fazal said he felt like the ABC was "trying everything in their power to stop me from ever working again".
"Even though all my work was approved across different teams and departments, cross-checked and met the standards before broadcast, they've decided there's now different standards that are retrospectively being applied to all of my stories," he said.
"They want to make me a scapegoat? Don't give a s***. I won't stop."
He has previously said he was hired by the ABC for his access to certain sources, but that proximity had then been used against him.
Previously, Fazal's reporting appeared in VICE, The Guardian, Rolling Stone, The Sydney Morning Herald, The Monthly and The Saturday Paper.
Last month, the ABC announced its head of investigations and current affairs, Jo Puccini, was leaving the public broadcaster after a 25-year career.
She had oversight of Four Corners and Background Briefing.
Other senior managers at the ABC at the time of Fazal's reporting, , including news director Justin Stevens, have already left the broadcaster. The ABC's incoming news director Simon Robinson started in the role on September 14.
Last week, ABC managing director Hugh Marks rejected an Australian Communications and Media Authority finding that the public broadcaster breached impartiality obligations in an unrelated Four Corners program about the redevelopment of the Australian War Memorial.
ACMA said on Thursday it had found the program's March 2025 episode, Sacrifice, had "unduly favoured one perspective".
The ABC says it "stands behind the team" that created the episode.
"If this interpretation of the code is applied, including more widely across the industry, it could have a chilling effect on the body of investigative journalism that delivers the important stories that serve the public interest," Marks said in a statement.

A US congressman urged Monday for Israel to end its airstrikes on Syria, saying the attacks “shouldn’t be done,” in an interview with Anadolu on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
“I’m really grateful the president’s envoy, Tom Barrack, has expressed opposition to the Israeli air strikes, and it just shouldn’t be done,” said Rep. Joe Wilson, a Republican from South Carolina.
Asked whether he was calling on the Israeli government to end the strikes on Syria, Wilson responded: “Absolutely.”
“I appreciate the leadership of President Donald Trump, at the request of Türkiye, at the request of Saudi Arabia, to give Syria a chance. And Syria will succeed, and then it’s beneficial to every country in the Middle East,” he told Anadolu.
Wilson also said the “liberation of Syria” — referring to the collapse of Syria’s Bashar al Assad regime in late 2024 — was important for other countries in the region, including Iran and Lebanon.
Barrack, the US special envoy for Syria and Iraq who also serves as ambassador to Türkiye, said in August that Washington was “deeply concerned” over Israeli air strikes on the Abu al-Duhur Airbase in northern Syria, calling them an “unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability.”
Wilson backs Türkiye’s return to F-35 programme
Wilson, who co-chairs the Congressional Caucus on US-Türkiye Relations and Turkish Americans, also underscored the depth of ties between Washington and Ankara, pointing to their cooperation since the Korean War.
“I’m very grateful that Türkiye led the effort for the liberation of Syria, and Syria now having an opportunity of stability, peace and prosperity, it’s going to benefit all of the Middle East, but particularly Türkiye,” he said.
Asked about efforts by Trump and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to address the dispute over Türkiye’s purchase of Russia’s S-400 air defence system and Ankara’s possible return to the F-35 fighter jet programme, Wilson said he was “hopeful.”
Wilson said he supported US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth working with Türkiye, adding that cooperation between Washington and Ankara would contribute to “peace through strength.”
Asked whether he supports the sale of F-35 fighter jets to Türkiye, Wilson replied: “I do. Yes, I do.” He also said he supported removing sanctions on Türkiye, imposed under the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA).
“But the bottom line, let’s go back: Türkiye is a great ally of America, America is an ally of Türkiye, and we want mutual benefit,” he said.
The US suspended Türkiye from the F-35 fighter jet programme in 2019 after objecting to its purchase of the Russian S-400 air defence system, claiming the system would endanger the fighter jets and is inoperable with NATO systems. Türkiye has said repeatedly that there is no conflict between the two and proposed a commission to study the issue.
Several Turkish defence entities were sanctioned under CAATSA.
During his meeting with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Türkiye in July on the sidelines of the NATO summit, Trump said he would “certainly” consider allowing Ankara to buy F-35 fighter jets and wants to remove the CAATSA sanctions on the country.

I IN contrasts concrete architecture with bright colours in Andersson Bell Tokyo store
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:00:21 UTC
17:00:21 KST

I IN contrasts concrete architecture with bright colours in Andersson Bell Tokyo store
Local studio I IN drew on the existing architecture when creating fashion brand Andersson Bell's flagship store in Japan, which is filled with glossy, reflective surfaces and warm red and yellow hues.
Located in Tokyo's Aoyama neighbourhood, the original building from 1993 has an exposed concrete interior that heavily influenced I IN's design for the store.
"It is quite rare to find such a magnificent space in Tokyo, and we were fortunate to have the freedom to take a bold and radical approach to the design," I IN co-founder Yohei Terui told Dezeen.
"Especially, the building's strong composition of mass and void became a major source of inspiration and guided us throughout the spatial planning."
The studio aimed for the interior to be contrasting but not competing with the architecture.
"The idea was to translate the brand's identity of 'contrast' into space design," Terui continued.
"The existing architecture, built in Tokyo in the 90s, already had a very strong character and presence, so rather than competing with it, we wanted to introduce a strong modern layer that would create a beautiful contrast with the existing architecture."
To do so, I IN, which Terui founded with Hiromu Yuyama, introduced warm, saturated colours across the building's three storeys.
Bright red, orange and yellow hues contrast against the boardmarked concrete walls throughout the space, with the red section also visible through the store's large front window.
"The red comes from the brand's signature colour and became the introduction of the store," Terui said.
"As guests move through the space and step upstairs, they experience a gradual transition from red to orange and then to yellow," he continued.
"Rather than simply applying colour to each floor, we wanted this transition to become part of the spatial experience, giving each level a different atmosphere and creating a sense of progression as guests move through the building."
Terui and Yuyama also added pipes that "extend through the existing architecture as if piercing its structure", the studio said.
As well as contrasting the concrete's grey hue with more colourful details, I IN juxtaposed its raw tactility with plenty of glossy and mirrored details, including a glass floor, steel pipes and tables and display cases with shiny, lacquered surfaces.
The furniture pieces used in the 309-square-metre store were tailor-made by the studio and designed to feel like a part of the existing architecture.
"All of the furniture was custom-made for the store," Terui said.
"We followed the same idea of creating a bold presence, taking inspiration from the powerful character and scale of the existing architecture," he continued.
"Rather than treating the furniture as separate elements placed within the space, we designed each piece as a part of the architecture, as if it had always been there, so that the furniture and the space ultimately merge into one."
I IN has previously also designed a tile-clad store for designer Nigo's Human Made brand and a glossy purple lounge for department store Matsuya Ginza.
The photography is by Tomooki Kengaku.
