Cambodian Government Grants Journalists Access to Giant Former Scamming Compound
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
01:39:00 UTC
10:39:00 KST

Cambodia’s government yesterday granted the media access to a massive former online scam compound in the country’s southeast, as it prepares to host a high-profile international anti-scam conference later this week.
Journalists from 39 domestic and international media organizations visited the former cyberscam compound known as “No. 8 Park,” a fortified and self-contained compound in Prey Veng province capable of housing around 20,000 people.
According to a report in the Phnom Penh Post, the No. 8 Park, also known as the Meun Chey Commercial Center, began construction in 2023. The compound covers about 120 hectares and “contains numerous buildings, including residential blocks, offices, a market and shops, with a casino at its center.” It added, “The sheer scale of the site resembled a small, enclosed town.”
Authorities say that they raided the No. 8 Park complex in February, based on information from China’s Ministry of Public Security, the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation and tips and allegations made by individuals who had escaped from the compound.
Inside the complex, journalists were shown evidence of the sophisticated online scams that were recently carried out by No. 8 Park’s huge staff of trafficked workers. According to a report by The Standard, rooms were set up to resemble foreign law enforcement offices, including one with signage for the “Singapore Police Force Commercial Affairs Department” that was used by scammers posing as police and financial crime investigators. Another room featured a Chinese slogan: “Please don’t pretend to work hard, because the result won’t act with you.”
The media visit was intended as a prelude to the two-day International Conference on Combating Online Scams, which opens in Phnom Penh tomorrow, and is set to be attended by representatives from more than 20 countries.
The conference, which will be co-hosted by Interpol, the U.N. Office on Drugs and Crime, and China’s Lancang Mekong Cooperation mechanism, is intended to showcase the extent of the government’s ongoing anti-scam crackdown. Phnom Penh launched the crackdown last year in response to the growing international scrutiny of Cambodia’s central role in Southeast Asia’s scamming economy, which Thailand attempted to weaponize during the two nations’ border conflict last year.
As part of the campaign, the government set up an ad hoc Commission for Combating Online Scams, passed a law outlawing cyberfraud, and launched raids on dozens of scamming compounds across the country. The government claims that it has now investigated over 830 suspected scam sites and dismantled 86 large compounds since July 2025. It also says it has deported more than 20,000 foreign suspects, and Cambodian newspapers have been filled with reports of the arrests of low- and mid-ranking officials for involvement in scams. Late last month, Senior Minister Chhay Sinarith, who heads the government’s ad hoc Commission for Combating Online Scams, declared that “large-scale scam activities have been brought fully under control, and there are currently no online scam compounds remaining in the country.”
While the current crackdown is serious and has far exceeded authorities’ previous efforts, there are good reasons to believe that the political economy that facilitated the country’s takeover by criminal scamming gangs remains more or less intact.
For decades, Cambodia’s political system has conferred special privileges on those with close connections to the ruling Cambodian People’s Party (CPP) and to the family of long-ruling Prime Minister Hun Sen. As I detailed in my 2014 book on Cambodia under Hun Sen, this system grants powerful individuals considerable autonomy to amass wealth – even from business of an illicit nature – and liberates them from the constraints of the law, as long as they remain politically loyal to the CPP and provide the party with financial backing when required.
While the Cambodian authorities were happy to fling open the gates of No. 8 Park to the press yesterday, they are much less keen to trace the threads of accountability for this and other compounds upwards. Over the past five years, reporters and rights groups have assembled an abundant corpus of evidence that scamming operations have flourished in Cambodia due to the protection or backing of powerful businesspeople linked to the CPP.
The businessmen Ly Yong Phat and Kok An, both close allies of the Hun family going back decades, have been sanctioned by the U.S. for their alleged involvement in running scam centers. There have been many others. Last week, two leading U.S. congressmen called on the Trump administration to investigate 28 individuals and entities, most of them Cambodian, for possible links to scam operations and to impose sanctions if warranted. They claimed that “corrupt” senior government officials in Cambodia, as well as in Myanmar and Laos, had “turned a blind eye to this criminal activity at a shocking scale.”
Among the most prominent Cambodian names on the list were Interior Minister Sar Sokha, Deputy Prime Minister and former national police chief Neth Savoeun, and deputy Cambodian police chief Dy Vichea, a son-in-law of former Prime Minister Hun Sen. Also listed was the name of Hun To, a cousin of Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet, who has acknowledged owning a 30 percent share in Huione Pay PLC, a digital payments platform sanctioned by the U.S. government for alleged money laundering and ties to transnational scam operations.
There are also connections between No. 8 Park and Cambodia’s elite. The Blockchain analysis firm Elliptic reported in February that Huione Group’s payment and logistics businesses operated a physical store within the No. 8 Park compound, with the crypto addresses of 10 merchants receiving about $393,000 in Tether in January alone.
Legend Innovation, the Cambodian company that ran No. 8 Park, has also been linked to Prince Group, a sprawling conglomerate that was jointly sanctioned by the United States and U.K. in October for running a “criminal empire built on forced labor and deception.” The sanctions targeted 146 individuals and entities connected to Prince, including its 38-year-old chairman Chen Zhi, who served as an advisor to both former Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen and his son and successor Hun Manet, and was the recipient of the neak oknha honorific, which is granted to the ruling CPP’s most generous benefactors. (The U.S. State Department yesterday announced visa restrictions against 32 additional unnamed individuals linked to Prince Group.)
While the Cambodian authorities did arrest and extradite Chen to China in January of this year, this came only after intensifying U.S. and Chinese pressure to take action on Prince Group. It also came years after the publication of detailed reporting into Prince Group, including a three-part investigative report published by the U.S.-funded broadcaster Radio Free Asia in early 2024 that detailed the extent of Prince’s alleged involvement in criminal activity, including online scams. Again, it is unclear if there has been any reckoning with how such a prominent alleged criminal could rise to the very summit of Cambodia’s elite.
Given this background, there are good reasons to be cynical about this week’s anti-scam conference, which looks less like a well-intentioned attempt to address the political problems that allowed scamming gangs to gain a foothold in Cambodia than an attempt to launder the government’s reputation as a haven for transnational criminals. As Jacob Sims argues in an op-ed for The Diplomat today, the CPP government “is recasting itself as an anti-scam champion while the politically protected elites who abetted the industry remain largely untouched.”
Without full accountability for those who enabled and profited from these operations, it will be hard to take the Cambodian government’s efforts at face value.

Two Republican Senate candidates call for swift end to Iran war, diverging from Trump
- Two Republican Senate candidates, Mike Rogers and Ashley Hinson, called for a swift end to the war in Iran, shifting from their previous support of Trump’s war stance.
- They proposed measures like suspending gasoline taxes and halting diesel exports to ease high fuel costs affecting voters, especially in key states like Michigan and Iowa.
- Democrats criticised the Republicans for flip-flopping, suggesting the calls were election-year tactics amid low Trump approval and rising inflation concerns ahead of the midterms.
AI generated
Two Republicans in tight US Senate races called on Sept 21 for a swift end to the war in Iran, the latest sign that vulnerable candidates are trying to put some distance between themselves and President Donald Trump over a conflict that has pushed up fuel prices, including a surge in diesel to record highs.
Both Mike Rogers, locked in a competitive race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, and Ashley Hinson, who is facing Democrat Josh Turek in a close contest in Iowa, struck a more dovish tone on Iran on Sept 21, after previously backing Trump’s authority to strike Tehran.
The shift was particularly notable for Hinson, a sitting member of the US House of Representatives, who has voted six times against House measures seeking to curb Trump’s authority to continue the war, including as recently as last week.
“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” Hinson wrote on social media, while calling for a suspension of petrol taxes, a pause in diesel exports and other measures, and for the war “to be brought to a successful and immediate end”.
The remarks underscore growing concern among some vulnerable Republican candidates that the nearly seven-month-old conflict is becoming a political liability ahead of the November midterms, which will determine whether Republicans can hold on to narrow majorities in the House and the Senate.
Americans have soured on both Trump’s handling of the economy and the Iran war as inflation remains stubbornly high.
Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 32 per cent, a career low, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Sept 21.
New Rogers ad
Rogers previously backed Trump’s strikes on Iran and argued in a late-July CBS Detroit interview against curbing the President’s authority to continue the conflict while he was negotiating to end it.
But in a campaign advertisement posted on social media platform X on Sept 21, Rogers struck a different tone as he spoke from a grocery store.
“The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly,” he said. “When it does, energy costs will plummet. But Michigan families can’t afford to wait for that to happen. We need to do something now.”
Rogers also called for suspending state and federal petrol taxes and imposing a temporary halt on US diesel exports.
Diesel prices are especially politically sensitive in Iowa, where agriculture plays an outsized role in the state’s economy and farmers depend heavily on diesel-powered equipment and transportation.
Democrats argued that the calls for a swift end to the war by Hinson and Rogers amounted to election-year repositioning by Republicans who had previously supported Trump’s handling of the conflict.
“Mike Rogers is only flip-flopping now because gas hit $5 a gallon and diesel prices hit record highs,” El-Sayed, Rogers’ Democratic opponent, said in a statement.
Hinson’s opponent Turek wrote on X: “It’s easy to send a tweet, but when you had the chance to vote to end this war, you chose not to.”
Other Republicans have recently started to take steps to distance themselves from Trump over the war and other issues.
Last week, Iowa representatives Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, two Republicans facing tough re-election bids for the House, reversed their prior stances and joined Democrats in voting to limit Trump’s war powers in Iran.
On Sept 17, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida released an ad warning that Trump’s immigration crackdown had gone too far and that some Hispanic supporters felt betrayed. REUTERS

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and the prime ministers of Japan and Pakistan arrived in New York to attend the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
 
Lee left Seoul on Monday for a three-day visit to New York City.
 
Soon after he arrived, he visited Korea Town in New York City and “exchanged warm greetings with fellow compatriots who have long nurtured the Korean community here,” according to a statement on the US social media platform X.
 
He is expected to outline his administration's vision for peaceful coexistence on the Korean Peninsula and discuss South Korea’s role in addressing global challenges.
 
Lee is also scheduled to meet with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and seek meetings with US President Donald Trump and other world leaders during his stay.
 
He will later travel to Mexico for a state visit and talks with President Claudia Sheinbaum focusing on trade, investment and supply-chain cooperation, according to Yonhap News Agency.
 
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also arrived in New York after her departure was delayed by around four hours as Typhoon Dujuan brought heavy rain and strong winds to eastern Japan, state broadcaster NHK reported early Tuesday.
 
She is due to deliver her first address to the UN General Assembly since taking office and also meet with Trump on Tuesday.
 
Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also arrived in New York to attend the General Assembly.
 
He is accompanied by Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar.
 
Several other Asian countries are sending their leaders or top diplomats to the 81st UN General Assembly.
 
Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman left Dhaka for New York early Monday and is scheduled to deliver his maiden General Assembly address on Thursday.
 
India's delegation will be led by External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, who is scheduled to address the General Assembly on Saturday.
 
Indonesia will be represented by Foreign Minister Sugiono, who is leading the delegation on behalf of President Prabowo Subianto, according to the state news agency Antara.
 
Malaysia's Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan is set to represent Kuala Lumpur at the General Debate, where he is expected to reiterate Malaysia's positions on UN Security Council reform and international peace and security.

Texas Gov. Abbott freezes environmental permits for AI data centers in expanding state power audit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
01:34:36 UTC
10:34:36 KST

Texas Governor Greg Abbott on Monday barred the state's environmental agency from issuing new permits for data centers until regulators complete a massive audit of the energy-hungry facilities seeking to connect to the Texas electrical grid.
The Republican governor's directive to the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality effectively freezes all state-issued permits to data center developers, which had flocked to the region for its abundant electricity, land and pro-business reputation.
Since the artificial intelligence boom began roughly three years ago, Texas has become one of the fastest-growing data hubs in the world. But intensifying public backlash over the facilities, and fears about AI more broadly, prompted Abbott last month to freeze the connection of new data centers to the state grid and order an audit of the facilities.
By the time of that directive, there were more than 470 gigawatts' worth of data center projects and other large energy users in line to connect to the grid - more than five times the state's peak demand.
The Electric Reliability Council of Texas, which operates the state grid, is in the early stages of auditing data center power use, tax incentives, and water consumption, among other factors.
'Data centers must... protect our grid and water' in Texas
“Simply put, Texans must come first,” Abbott said in a statement. “Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water, and complete the (audits)."
Abbott is among a swelling number of governors who once raced to attract data center investments - and touted their public benefit - but are now tightening restrictions on the developments to ease their constituents' fears about rising power bills and environmental issues caused by the facilities.
Ed Hirs, an energy fellow at the University of Houston, said Abbott was walking back "his earlier pronouncements about data centers leading to lower electricity prices."

EU's Kallas says Red Sea mission needs more than 10 warships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
01:34:29 UTC
10:34:29 KST

The European Union's naval mission to protect shipping in the Red Sea would need to increase its fleet to more than 10 warships, its foreign policy chief said on Monday, as the Houthis rapidly made gains in the waterway.
The EU's Aspides mission was launched in 2024 to protect shipping from attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis, and diplomats have said there are currently six warships operating.
"When Aspides was put in place, then the indication was that it needs at least 10 ships. The situation, I think, is even more grave right now," Kaja Kallas told reporters on the sidelines of the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.
Italy, one of the key countries in the Aspides mission, announced on Thursday it was preparing a naval mission in the area for its own ships, saying it could not wait for the EU to respond to the new crisis.
Kallas said the Houthi attacks were affecting European interests and impacting the global economy.
"The EU operation Aspides is making a crucial contribution to security in the region and global shipping, but the operation needs more naval assets and more air assets to address the increased level of threats in the region," she said.
Kallas sent a letter to the EU's 27 member states on September 19 asking them to up their contributions. The issue would be discussed at upcoming defense and foreign ministers' meetings, she said in the letter.
"This situation, which is still evolving as we speak, is already affecting European interests with repercussions on our supply chains and could have implications for our ability to support our economies, which were already hit by rising fuel prices," she said in the letter.
"For the moment, although the Houthis communicate that they would only target Saudi-linked interests, there is uncertainty over their course of action with respect to vessels that transit through the Strait. Regardless, they are now in a better position to potentially harm maritime shipping."
Houthis have made rapid advances in recent weeks along the Red Sea coast
The Houthis have made rapid advances in recent weeks along the Red Sea coast, further complicating routes in a region that also includes the Strait of Hormuz, where traffic had already dwindled because of the US-Iran war.
A lightning advance by the Iran-backed group this month has extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theater and further threatened global energy supplies. The US has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to join the fight in Yemen.
The New York Times reported that the Trump administration had prepared to launch airstrikes on Sunday against the Houthis after fresh pleas from the Saudi crown prince. But the newspaper said Trump called off the airstrikes at the last minute, even as troops were loading bombs onto aircraft.

UN AI experts warn against ‘apocalyptic’ rhetoric on risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
01:34:00 UTC
10:34:00 KST

UN AI experts warn against ‘apocalyptic’ rhetoric on risks
- UN AI experts warn against using apocalyptic language about AI risks, emphasising the need for scientific understanding rather than fear-driven narratives.
- The International Scientific Panel on AI, formed in 2025, aims to clarify AI risks and inform UN decisions with nuanced, evidence-based discussions.
- Experts call for global, rational debate on AI risks, highlighting uncertainty and differing opinions over alarmist claims of existential threats.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Several experts on a United Nations artificial intelligence committee warned on Sept 21 against the apocalyptic rhetoric used by some professionals in the sector regarding AI risks.
“As scientists, it’s very important to invest in the science, to really understand what we know (from) what we don’t know, and investing in fear is not that helpful,” said Joelle Barral, an executive at Google DeepMind and a member of the International Scientific Panel on AI, an independent body.
She was responding to a question from AFP about recent public statements on AI’s potential dangers, particularly from Jacob Coxon.
The former Anthropic employee, who previously worked at OpenAI, said in early September that AI developers believed the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.
A research engineer who left Google DeepMind in July made similar comments, saying it might already be “too late to avoid” humanity’s eradication by AI.
“We have to change the way we talk about AI risk because for a very long time, it’s either existential and everything is going to die and the killer robots are coming, or it doesn’t really matter,” Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa, an investigative reporter, said on Sept 21 at the same event, held in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
“The truth, though, is far more nuanced and sophisticated,” she continued.
“You can’t turn that into ideology, which is, I think, where (the debate) has been heading.”
The International Scientific Panel on AI was created in 2025, with its members selected in February 2026.
Its mandate is to advance the scientific understanding of AI and inform UN deliberations.
Yoshua Bengio, a panel co-chair who is considered one of the fathers of AI, said it was important to distinguish between what scientists actually know about AI risks and what can only be “plausibly extrapolated” from that evidence – an area where experts still disagree.
“The problem with shouting very loudly is that someone else can also shout very loudly,” he said.
What is needed instead is “a global rational discussion about what is going on, including about the uncertainty, including about the severity of the risks”. AFP

How Hong Kong can keep the talking going when US-China officials don’t
Unknown

Opinion
How Hong Kong can keep the talking going when US-China officials don’t
Hong Kong can’t set the terms of the contest, but with Track 1.5 diplomacy, it can decide if it is the room in which competition is managed
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Neville Lai is the co-founder and CEO of Trigrams Research Group (TRG), an independent boutique research firm dedicated to helping organisations build future-proof capabilities and resilience through market research and strategic foresight to develop critical sectors in Asia. 
When Tung Chee-hwa died, the obituaries predictably described a Hong Kong shipping mogul who became the city’s first postcolonial chief executive. How his government navigated the Asian financial crisis and severe acute respiratory syndrome (Sars) epidemic and its retreat from Article 23 were highlighted. There was less attention paid to the political hybrid he embodied.
Tung sat as vice-chairman of China’s top political advisory body, the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, until 2023 – state-leader rank, no diplomatic portfolio. His working instrument was the China-United States Exchange Foundation, which he established in Hong Kong in 2008, the year marking the 30th anniversary of Sino-US relations, to keep senior Americans and Chinese talking when their governments would not.
Standing without a mandate, exercised through a private vehicle: that is Track 1.5, and Tung was very good at it.
At the recent China-US Track 1.5 Dialogue in Beijing, Liu Haixing, head of the Communist Party’s International Department, said both countries should expand the “pie” of shared interests and reject zero-sum games to reach “normal stability with controllable disagreements”. This is not the stuff of summit headlines but of realistic ambition: neither a friendship nor a divorce, but a managed rivalry where shared interests can grow and the rest is fenced off.

Hunter mistook woman for deer in fatal US shooting, police say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
01:30:00 UTC
10:30:00 KST

Hunter mistook woman for deer in fatal US shooting, police say
Neil Vigdor
WASHINGTON – A hunter is facing a manslaughter charge in the US state of Delaware in the fatal shooting of a woman whom he mistook for a deer while she crossed an open field with three other people, the authorities said.
The man, Walter W. Moorhead, 74, fired his rifle from a ground blind, a tent, shed or other makeshift structure used by hunters to conceal themselves, when he struck Santos Maria Chilel Soto, 39, on a private property on the night of Sept 18 in Ellendale, Delaware, the Delaware State Police said.
Investigators said the shooting occurred around 7.40 pm local time, just over 30 minutes after sunset, in an area dotted with farms, about 120km south of Wilmington, Delaware, and west of Delaware’s well-known coastal resorts.
Soto, who a GoFundMe page said was a mother of five from Guatemala, was with her boyfriend and her boyfriend’s two children when she was shot, according to an arrest warrant. It was not clear why Soto, who lived in Georgetown, Delaware, was on the property.
The victim’s boyfriend told the police that the four of them had been walking together across the field when he heard an explosion and saw Soto fall to the ground with a gunshot wound to her torso, the warrant said.
An older white man, whom investigators identified as Moorhead, approached with a flashlight to search for the deer he thought he had shot, Detective M. Csapo of the Delaware State Police wrote in the warrant.
During an interview with police, the authorities said, Moorhead acknowledged that he had struck Soto.
Moorhead, of Salisbury, Maryland, was also charged with three counts of reckless endangering and possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony. He was released on a US$43,000 (S$54,900) cash bond.
Efforts to reach Moorhead were not immediately successful on Sept 21. It was not clear if he had a lawyer.
Moorhead had been hunting under what is known in Delaware as a crop damage permit, Corporal Raushan Rich of the Delaware State Police said in an email on Sept 21.
The programme allows commercial farms that experience crop damage to hunt antlerless deer, specifically mature does, more frequently than under normal deer hunting regulations.
The state, which expanded the programme in 2026, allows deer hunting from a half-hour before sunrise until a half-hour after sunset, which was about 7.06pm on Sept 18 in Ellendale.
In Delaware, the Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control oversees hunting regulations. It did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Sept 21 or provide a copy of the hunting permit associated with the farm where the shooting occurred.
Details about who owns the property were also not immediately available.
In a Facebook post on Sept 19, Iglesia de Dios Fuente de Verdad Delaware in Georgetown – a Pentecostal church – announced Soto’s death. Organisers of the GoFundMe page were seeking donations to help return Soto’s body to Guatemala. NYTIMES

New Zealand, India ratify free trade agreement
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
09:18:05 CST
10:18:05 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand and India have formally ratified a free trade agreement, paving the way for the deal to enter into force on Oct. 20.
New Zealand Trade and Investment Minister Todd McClay exchanged formal ratification documents with India's High Commissioner to New Zealand Muanpuii Saiawi at parliament on Monday, confirming that New Zealand had completed its domestic procedures for the agreement.
The New Zealand-India free trade agreement will make 57 percent of New Zealand's exports to India tariff-free from the first day, including sheep meat, wool and coal, McClay said in a statement on Tuesday.
More than 95 percent of forestry and wood exports will also be tariff-free on day one, while exporters will receive a second round of tariff cuts on Jan. 1, 2027, he said.
New Zealand exporters will also gain preferential quota access to India for albumins, apples and kiwifruit under the agreement.
McClay said the agreement would improve market access for New Zealand businesses in India, while providing greater certainty for services exporters, investors and companies seeking to expand in the Indian market.
The agreement is expected to help New Zealand exporters diversify markets and build resilience amid growing uncertainty in global markets, the minister noted. ■

4 European nations back India's bid for permanent UN seat, Jaishankar calls it 'historic'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
01:17:06 UTC
10:17:06 KST

Poland, Hungary, Slovakia and Czech Republic on Monday backed India's bid for a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council, with Slovakia foreign minister Juraj Blanár saying India, as a leading country of the Global South and an emerging power in the Indo-Pacific, should have a place at the UN's top decision-making body.The remarks came after external affairs minister S Jaishankar participated in the first high-level Visegrád Group (V4) plus India meeting on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly in New York."We all agree, as V4 countries, that India, as part of the Global South, an upcoming superpower in the Indo-Pacific region, must be at the table as a permanent member of the UN Security Council," Blanár said.
The V4 comprises Poland, Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia. The four countries held their first ministerial-level meeting with India in the new V4+India format during the UNGA high-level week.Jaishankar described the meeting as a "new historic occasion" and said the discussions covered political, economic, defence, technology, space, connectivity and people-to-people ties."We had our first Visegrad Four and India meeting. It was, in a sense, a new historic occasion, and I would like to thank Minister Juraj (Foreign Minister of Slovakia) for convening us today. It was a very, very productive meeting.
What we agreed was that since India's relationship with the European Union itself is deepening, with the V4, we would take some special initiatives to create an annual business forum. As foreign ministers, we would meet annually. That was the consensus. We would also explore in technology and innovation whether we could be doing more. We have a very strong history with all the V4 countries in defense. We want to refresh and take forward that record and that cooperation. We discussed space issues, connectivity, and people-to-people mobility. We have students in each of the V4 countries. Overall, in terms of our cooperation, as well as a very good and useful exchange on the big global crisis, the Ukraine conflict, and what's happening in the Gulf. I think it was a very worthwhile and productive meeting. I'm very pleased about it."
Jaishankar on V4's role in global affairs
Asked about the political importance of the V4 for India on the global stage, Jaishankar said New Delhi viewed the four countries as partners with strong industrial, technological and innovation capabilities."We have very good relations with the V4 countries, and we know that these are countries with a very strong, very distinctive capability. They are industrial economies, economies with great innovation and technology talent. And I think how the V4 come together is for them to decide. But we certainly welcome the opportunity to work."India has been seeking reform of the UN Security Council and a permanent seat on the body. The Council currently has five permanent members, China, France, Russia, the UK and the US, alongside 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms.Jaishankar had formally launched India's campaign for a non-permanent UNSC term for 2028-29 in July, while New Delhi has continued to press for broader reform of the Council and permanent membership for India.
Jaishankar said the meeting also resulted in an agreement to strengthen cooperation through annual foreign ministerial meetings and an annual business forum.In a post on X, Jaishankar said: "Our first meeting in the V4+India format agreed to: Closer political cooperation including annual meetings of Foreign Ministers. Deeper economic cooperation, including the Annual Business Forum. Reinvigorating our defence cooperation. Further development of our cultural cooperation and people-to-people relations."The meeting included Poland's deputy prime minister and foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, Hungary's deputy prime minister and foreign minister Dr Anita Orbán, Slovakia's foreign minister Juraj Blanár and Czechia's foreign minister Petr Macinka.Jaishankar is leading the Indian delegation at the 81st UN General Assembly high-level week in New York and is scheduled to address the General Debate on September 26.

US jury convicts man of attempted murder in shooting of Palestinian students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
01:14:42 UTC
10:14:42 KST

A jury in the US state of Vermont has convicted 51-year-old Jason Eaton of attempted murder for shooting three Palestinian university students near the University of Vermont campus in Burlington in November 2023, The Guardian reported.
Eaton faces up to life in prison following the conviction.
The gun attack left Hisham Awartani paralysed from the waist down and wounded his close friends Tahseen Aliahmad and Kinnan Abdalhamid.
The jury returned its guilty verdict after several hours of deliberation following a week-long trial that heard direct testimony from all three victims alongside competing psychiatric experts.
Eaton, who did not dispute firing the shots, had pleaded not guilty, claiming he was not criminally responsible due to his mental state.
Defence lawyers highlighted his claims that US and Israeli intelligence agencies transmitted instructions to shoot via FM radio, alongside delusions that God commanded him to protect neighbours.
The jury dismissed the insanity defence.
Sentencing remand
Eaton was remanded in custody without bail pending sentencing, showing no emotion as the verdict was announced.
Awartani and Aliahmad, seated in the courtroom's front row, embraced supporters.
"Justice has been rendered for Hisham, Kinnan and Tahseen. After three years of sorrow, loss and struggle, our families finally feel relief," the families affirmed in a joint statement.
They stressed the outcome "affirms something fundamental: Jason Eaton is responsible for what he did", pointing out that Eaton's repeated use of "hateful" language during the trial confirmed his motives: "This was a hate crime. We have said so from the beginning."
The families also drew parallels to the broader plight of their people: "While our children fought to heal from being shot in Burlington, they watched Palestinian children lose their lives, their homes, their land, their families."
"Hisham, Kinnan and Tahseen have spent three years rebuilding their bodies and their lives after a hateful act almost killed them. We are profoundly relieved."

Woman’s death after wellness spa injection is ruled a homicide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
01:10:00 UTC
10:10:00 KST

US woman’s death after wellness spa injection is ruled a homicide
Chelsia Rose Marcius
- The death of 27-year-old Elizabeth Baron after an NAD+ injection at a Bronx wellness spa was ruled a homicide due to a cardiac air embolism.
- Luis Rojas Cabrera, who administered the injection without a US medical licence, faces serious charges; he claims the death was accidental.
- The case highlights risks in the unregulated longevity wellness industry, where treatments lack oversight and safety protections for patients.
AI generated
NEW YORK – The death of a 27-year-old woman who was injected with a substance at a Bronx wellness centre in July has been ruled a homicide, according to a spokesperson from the city medical examiner’s office.
The woman, Elizabeth Baron, of the Bronx, died from a cardiac air embolism, according to the autopsy results. An embolism can occur when air enters an intravenous catheter, and the gas travels straight to the heart.
The ruling paves the way for prosecutors to seek more serious charges against the man, Luis Rojas Cabrera, who administered Baron an intravenous infusion of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, or NAD+, in July.
Baron, who lived less than 3.2km from the wellness centre, died about an hour after receiving the infusion.
Cabrera pleaded not guilty that month to reckless endangerment and unauthorised practice of a profession. It was unclear on Sept 21 whether he had been charged with additional crimes.
Cabrera’s lawyer, Donald Vogelman, said on Sept 21 that “a homicide is not necessarily a murder but may be caused by an accident”.
“Homicide is defined as the taking of a person’s life, regardless of the intent or the circumstances surrounding the death,” he said.
“In this case, if there was a homicide, it was caused by an accident. I am certain that my client will be fully exonerated in court.”
NAD+ is a molecule found in cells that is critical for energy production and other fundamental biological processes. NAD+ has become a popular longevity supplement, but there is little evidence it works in humans, and its use is largely unregulated.
Longevity has become a booming part of the wellness industry, but there are few guardrails to protect patients.
There is no board certification to practise longevity medicine in the United States, and many of the treatments purported to help with ageing, such as peptides and supplements, have scant research in humans and little to no oversight from the Food and Drug Administration.
In New York, a person must be a licensed medical practitioner to administer an intravenous substance. Cabrera does not have a licence to practise medicine in the United States, according to the criminal complaint.
On July 19 at about noon at the wellness spa, Bereshit Lifestyle Center, Cabrera inserted an intravenous line in Baron’s right hand to administer NAD+, prosecutors said.
“She went unconscious immediately,” Cabrera later told investigators, according to the criminal complaint. “I called 911.”
Emergency medical workers took Baron to a hospital, the complaint said. She was declared dead at 1.09pm.
Cabrera, who said he is a licensed doctor in the Dominican Republic, told investigators that he “made a very big mistake”.
“I need to call my family because I have a feeling I will not be home for a while,” he said, according to the complaint.
The case is expected to go to a grand jury before Cabrera’s next court appearance on Oct 8. NYTIMES

After crucial Paramount agreement come relief, anger and concern
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22

After crucial Paramount agreement come relief, anger and concern
Matt Stevens
LOS ANGELES – David Ellison, Paramount’s chief executive, said he was “grateful” for a “path forward” after reaching an agreement to resolve an antitrust lawsuit and move ahead with its US$111 billion (S$142 billion) acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.
Rob Bonta, California’s attorney-general, praised the terms of the settlement but cautioned that it was “not a blessing” of Paramount’s merger.
Governor Gavin Newsom called the agreement “a win for California workers and our creative economy.”
But some critics of the deal in Hollywood are just ticked off: “Gavin Newsom hands huge win to Trump and his billionaire cronies,” actor Mark Ruffalo wrote on social media, referring to the Ellison family’s ties to the president.
US President Donald Trump had yet to weigh in by the afternoon of Sept 21. But the cross-section of union leaders, politicians and media watchdogs who did underscores the breadth of opinions about the deal and reveals the industry’s underlying anxiety about its health.
Los Angeles has been battered by the loss of film and TV production to countries offering large tax incentives and cheaper labour, leading to a sharp decrease in filming and the elimination of tens of thousands of jobs. Many opponents of a Paramount-Warner Bros. deal worry that consolidation would lead to even more job losses and fewer projects.
“My concern has always been that a merger could lead to the loss of thousands of jobs for hard-working Angelenos,” Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said. “For months, the uncertainty of no decision created instability that led to job losses and left workers wondering what it would mean for their futures.”
As part of the agreement unveiled on Sept 21, which needs to be approved by a court, Paramount agreed to a number of concessions.
The company committed to distributing 30 movies in theatres every year, pledged to spend an additional US$1.5 billion on film production over the next five years and guaranteed to increase the proportion of those movies that are made in the United States.
“I do not want to see two of Hollywood’s largest studios consolidated under one company, but now we must focus on holding the companies accountable to these commitments,” Bass added.
After the outlines of the deal became public, the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees, the union that represents more than 170,000 technicians, artisans and craftsmen in the entertainment industry, welcomed the agreement and the commitments written into it. The Directors Guild of America also struck an upbeat tone, offering congratulations to both sides.
But some union leaders seemed to seek to toe the line. The leaders of SAG-AFTRA, which represents approximately 160,000 actors, acknowledged that the settlement “addresses some of our deep concerns about production levels and investment in US production” while also wagging a finger at Paramount.
“We hope that the process of engaging with the attorneys-general has impressed upon them the fact that in addition to collective bargaining, our members rely on the law to help protect our interests,” the union’s statement said. “These are the lowest standards that our employers must meet.”
Others were more downbeat and direct.
In one striking example, Connecticut’s attorney-general, William Tong, a Democrat leading one of the states that joined the antitrust lawsuit, said in a statement that he had sought in particular to “protect the editorial independence of CNN and CBS News”.
Paramount agreed, as part of the settlement, to establish a board of journalists to ensure the editorial independence of the two news organisations. But Tong said that “Connecticut wanted and demanded full divestiture of CNN and CBS News.”
“I am deeply disappointed that we could not do more,” he added.
Seth Stern, the chief of advocacy for the Freedom of the Press Foundation, went further, saying in a statement that “a Paramount-appointed editorial independence board for CNN and CBS is worthless”.
And the advocacy organisation Free Press, which opposes media consolidation, called out Bonta, who it said “went back on his promise to enforce the law and protect consumers and workers”.
“It’s a sad day for all of us who have been opposing this merger because it will cut jobs and raise prices, all as it consolidates the media even more to enable authoritarians,” Jessica J. Gonzalez, co-CEO of the nonprofit, said in its statement. “Based on all reports, this weak deal contains nothing but unenforceable, empty Paramount promises.” NYTIMES

Lithuania ready to 'fight back' but has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM tells BBC
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
02:04:16 BST
10:04:16 KST

Lithuania ready to 'fight back' but has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM tells BBC
- Published
Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrender" if attacked.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told Newsnight that Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.
He told Newsnight if his country was attacked, "we will fight back... we will engage". But he said there were plans for a "variety of scenarios" and used an example of getting elderly citizens out of cities "smoothly" and avoiding traffic jams.
Lithuania, a Nato member, shares a land border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.
"We're thinking about a variety of scenarios, not all of them are being discussed very much publicly," Sinkevičius told the BBC.
"We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us."
Sinkevičius also said the UK needed a "shift in the mindset" in terms of its approach to defence, but noted that Lithuania was "closer to the border and closer to [the] threat".
Last week Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace.
Lithuania has experienced numerous incidents in the past year, which it describes as "hybrid attacks" and blames on neighbouring Belarus, a close Russian ally.
Late on Monday night, flights were disrupted at Lithuania's main airport in the capital Vilnius, because of what the airports operator called a "hybrid attack carried out by Belarus", involving objects that appeared to resemble the shape of balloons.
The president's chief adviser, Deividas Matulionis, said on Tuesday it was unclear whether the objects were balloons.
Germany - a fellow Nato ally - pledged to permanently station a combat-ready brigade in Lithuania in 2023 as a response to the changing security situation in Europe.
It is expected to be operational by 2027 and to number about 5,000 soldiers and civilian employees, though it has failed to recruit enough personnel voluntarily and is now turning to compulsory assignments to fill some positions.
The majority of troops will be based in Rūdninkai, near the Suwałki Gap - a line that borders Lithuania and Poland and also links Belarus with Russia's Kaliningrad.
Nato said that as of December last year it had more than 5,000 troops stationed in Lithuania.
The origins of last week's drone incident over Lithuania have not been confirmed, however Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Newshour that it had come from the direction of Belarus.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace.
"We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory."
Moscow did not comment on the incident.
Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine.
Residents in Lithuania's capital Vilnius were also forced to take shelter in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel.
Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into fellow Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.
Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.
Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one Nato member shall be considered an attack against all members".

IMO chief tells commercial ships to stay out of Hormuz unless Iran and US guarantee safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
01:00:26 UTC
10:00:26 KST

United Nations, New York — Senior UN and maritime officials have warned that commercial shipping is increasingly being used as geopolitical collateral amidst escalating tensions across vital international waterways, including in the Strait of Hormuz, urging global powers to reach political solutions to safeguard crew lives and restore safe passage.
Speaking on the risks faced by commercial vessels at the UN headquarters in New York on Monday, Arsenio Dominguez, Secretary-General of the International Maritime Organization (IMO), urged commercial vessels to steer clear of volatile lanes until binding security guarantees are provided by the warring parties.
"For as long as the conflict is ongoing and we don't have guarantees from the countries involved that no ship is going to be affected, I will ask all ships to stay away from the region," Dominguez said on Monday at a gathering at the UN headquarters in New York, noting that more than 80 vessels have faced attacks in critical transit routes including the Red Sea, Bab al Mandab, and the Strait of Hormuz.
"We are not going to put the lives of innocent seafarers any more at risk. We have already lost too many."
Dominguez highlighted the human and economic toll of the ongoing crisis.
"The impact of this crisis, it’s not only on the global economy and the food security," he said. "It is important that everybody also recognises the innocent seafarers that, of course, are putting their life at risk at no fault in order to make sure that over 80 percent of global trade continues to sail around the world."
The IMO chief noted that approximately 6,000 seafarers remain trapped in the Gulf since the US-Israeli war on Iran began six months ago, unable to leave the region.
The IMO chief underlined that while operational and technical frameworks can be devised to protect navigational freedom in line with international law, genuine security requires political dialogue beyond the maritime agency's mandate to resolve the root causes of the tensions.
Compounding the challenge are restrictions in the Red Sea and Bab al Mandab Strait, he said cooperation between the two coastal states is rooted in IMO conventions and customary international law, with models such as the Strait of Malacca offering potential lessons in building trust.
"The reality is that none of these mechanisms will actually be able to have an effect until there are guarantees that ships and innocent seafarers are not going to be targeted," he stressed. "That’s the main bottom line of why the root causes are so required."
Dominguez underscored the Strait of Hormuz’s outsized role in global supply chains, saying roughly one-third of the world’s fertilisers, 20 percent of global oil, 19 percent of liquefied natural gas, nine percent of automobiles, and 12 percent of container freight originate from or pass through the region.
"We cannot replace that," he stressed.
US and Iran, he said, are prolonging the disruption that poses a severe risk to Gulf Cooperation Council economies.
The IMO chief called for high-level attention, including at the UN General Assembly (UNGA), to resolve the conflict so that resilient shipping operations and free movement of goods can fully resume.
Houthis seized Yemen's Mokha port and Perim Island in mid-September, tightening their grip on the Bab al Mandeb and targeting Saudi-linked ships, plunging Red Sea traffic.
In the Black Sea, Russia and Ukraine keep attacking each other’s ports and vessels, with over 300 ships damaged so far, choking grain exports.
Iran and US have maintained a double blockade on the Strait of Hormuz with traffic remaining a fraction of normal as tankers and crew keep getting targeted.
US and Iran urged to allow transport of fertilisers
Meanwhile, highlighting a potential technical pathway to de-escalation,Jorge Moreira da Silva, Executive Director of the United Nations Office for Project Services (or UNOPS) and coordinator of the UN Strait of Hormuz Task Force, pointed out that operational inspection and verification mechanisms could be swiftly established if political consent is achieved.
He said Iran and US can continue their fight and simultaneously allow the safe transit of an initial five to seven vessels transporting essential commodities such as fertilisers each day.
"This mechanism could act as a stepping stone because trust takes time to be restored," he noted, stressing that the technical obstacles are surmountable and that the primary requirement remains political will.
Both officials warned that simultaneous disruptions across critical maritime chokepoints — including the Black Sea, the Red Sea, and the Strait of Hormuz — carry severe economic consequences for international trade, reiterating that multilateral engagement remains the only viable path to ensure stability across global supply chains.
Da Silva said the double blockade on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz has led to a steep rise in fertiliser prices, adding that 45 million people could face acute food insecurity if vessels carrying fertilisers are prevented from navigating through the strait.
"Well, if we look into the trends, indeed we have a significant increase of the price on the brand, 40 percent since the beginning of the war, 20 percent more or less on urea, sulfur and ammonia, and almost 200 percent increase on phosphate. Unfortunately, if this is not fixed, we'll have 45 million people forced into acute food insecurity, the UN official added.
He said the "key protagonists" — US and Iran — need to agree to allow five to seven ships transport fertilisers in the Hormuz.
"The point that we have been making to both Iran and the US is that we know that you are discussing the big picture. You are trying to find a deal about everything. But in the meantime, because diplomacy and the planting season don't have the same cycles, let's find a short-term time-bound limited solution to let the fertilisers go."

Many other Shivanis: ‘Tailgated, provoked to race, shown the middle finger’ – a day in the life of women riding bikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
00:59:24 UTC
09:59:24 KST

Shivani Chauhan survived a road-rage incident on Gurgaon’s Golf Course Road in which a man in a car chased her and knocked her off her moving bike.
Her injuries will heal, but riding a bike will not be the same again for Shivani Chauhan, who survived a road rage incident in Gurgaon last week in which a man in a car chased Shivani and knocked her off her moving bike on Golf Course Road. “I don't know when I'll start riding again, but whenever I do, I'll have that fear that this can happen again – that another car can come from behind and hit me,” she says.It’s a fear women bike riders understand, and echo, because of what they describe as “unprovoked aggression” that comes their way on roads. Riders TOI spoke to described being chased, tailgated, obstructed, challenged to race and subjected to lewd gestures simply for being women on motorcycles.
Delhi-based rider Neharika Yadav said men have chased her from different angles to take photographs or start conversations, while Gurgaon rider Geetika Khurana recalled an incident of men blocking her way and revving alongside her to provoke a race. Male drivers revving their engines, driving dangerously close, honking incessantly – Mumbai-based motorcycle trainer and motivational speaker Shilpa Balakrishnan (51) describes this as a “routine” experience for woman on bikes.
“Many have tried to corner me when I overtake. They behave this way simply because they see a woman riding,” she says.The India Women Rider Safety and Mobility Report 2026, based on responses from 542 women riders, found that 57% had experienced harassment on the road.For Shivani (27), who started riding only two years ago, the Sept 13 incident has forever changed the “therapeutic experience” of riding her Aprilia. “The incident keeps playing on my mind on a loop every now and then. It has affected me very badly, I think it will be a long time before I’m able to pick up the bike again,” says Shivani, who had kept her biker identity a secret on social media. As ‘Sia’, she felt freedom.
Neharika, a dentist based in Delhi, and Pune-based fashion designer Maral Yazarloo-Pattrick (45) can relate. “I ride a bike because it gives me joy, not because I want to prove anything to anyone. In Delhi-NCR, we get cast into a stereotype. Even in 2026, there are men who can’t seem to digest a woman coming on two wheels. Since traffic here is dense, there are men like (Kalyan) Bainsla (who attacked Shivani) who will not give space to a woman rider. They will keep instigating you. I think they get some perverse joy out of it,” she says.Yazarloo-Pattrick says danger is a tax women bikers pay on roads and freedom is the reason they keep paying it. “Such behaviour is an everyday reality. I’m shocked that anyone in India is surprised,” she says. Earlier this month, she was returning from Ladakh when she noticed a black SUV without a number plate following her. She switched on her GoPro but did not try to outrun it. Instead, she slowed down and pulled into a petrol pump. “If someone is chasing me and I cannot safely get away, I always head towards a crowded place.”Soundari Sindy, a lawyer in her mid-30s based out of Chennai, says attitude towards women riding bikes is similar across the country. “It almost feels like we are hurting the male ego just by being on the road,” she tells TOI. A professional racer, Soundari commands a 150cc bike with her 5ft 1in frame. “Snide comments are common. There are strangers who have made fun of me, saying my feet would not touch the ground,” she says.
'Danger is a tax women bikers pay on roads': Maral Yazarloo-Pattrick - Pune
Suparna Sarkar (39), chief instructor at a motorcycle training academy in Gurgaon, tells TOI what made Shivani’s case different was that the aggression was caught on camera. “It’s just that she had a camera, so it led to widespread anger. Girls I teach biking to often share incidents where either people tried to race from behind or they were hit,” she says. Sarkar has experienced it herself. In 2023, she was riding near Mahipalpur in Delhi when a vehicle hit her. “There were no cameras in the area. I didn’t have a camera either,” she says.Sandhya Das, a 38-year-old IT professional who rides with Soundari, agrees that the sight of her on a bike is somehow “not palatable to some men”, whether she is in traditional attire or in biker gear with a jacket and gloves. “Men have tried to zip past me and tried to throw me off balance,” she says.
‘Even in 2026, there are men who can’t seem to digest a woman on two wheels’: Neharika Yadav, Delhi
Chetana Naik (37) from Mumbai, who twice encountered a group of make bikers intimidating and overtaking her – in Kashmir recently and in Punjab earlier – adds, “For some men, being overtaken by a woman appears to be an insult that must be avenged. They begin intimidating us till their egos are satisfied,” she says.Professional rider Anita Krishnan says even riding gear can be misread by some motorists as an invitation to race. “They start racing with you. It could be a car or even a bike. They will whizz past you at speed, trying to entice you into a race. This is very common,” she says. For long-distance riders, she points out, jackets, helmets and boots are protection from crashes, flying debris, rain, heat and cold, not racing gear.
‘It feels like we are hurting the male ego just by being on the road’ — Soundari Sindy, Chennai
Krishnan says she sometimes tucks her hair inside her jacket so motorists cannot immediately tell that she is a woman. “The gear also camouflages whether you are a woman. If your hair is out, only then people would know you are a woman. So, I would mostly hide my hair,” she says.For 23-year-old Anainah Batiwala, camouflage goes further. The Mumbaikar does not feel comfortable riding in shorts and, after dark, goes out in baggy clothes. “I dress like a guy in baggy pants,” she says. “I wear my actual going-out clothes underneath.”Atulya (23) remembers being scared for her life a couple of years ago while travelling from Gwalior to Hyderabad. A group of men followed her bike relentlessly for about 45 minutes on the highway. “I kept riding for about 10-15km even after I lost them. I was so scared that something would happen to me if I applied the brakes,” she says.
'While going from Gwalior to Hyderabad, a group of men followed me for 45 minutes': Atulya, Rajasthan
Atulya (23) remembers being scared for her life a couple of years ago while travelling from Gwalior to Hyderabad. A group of men followed her bike relentlessly for about 45 minutes on the highway. “I kept riding for about 10-15km even after I lost them. I was so scared that something would happen to me if I applied the brakes,” she says.Atulya, who is originally from Kerala but grew up in Rajasthan, has been riding her bike all over India from the age of 18. While the incident rattled her, she decided to keep going.Delhi-based biker Meenakshi says long group rides can become particularly vulnerable on the return journey because riders who set out together often disperse while heading home. “Often, we get calls from riders asking for help from passers-by, or they call us to say that two or three people are following them,” she says. Krishnan says women travelling alone or in smaller groups also become more selective about where they stop after dark and often share their live location with family members.Organised riding groups have built formal safety systems around that vulnerability. Some assign a leader at the front, a tail rider to make sure nobody is left behind, and a marshal to keep both ends connected. “Men may have the liberty to stop anywhere, but women have to take extra precaution,” says Saify Ratlamwala, who runs riding groups in Navi Mumbai.
Patriarchal conditioning has taught men that women must be watched, judged and corrected — Devika Mehta, Noida
Devika Mehta, a media professional from Noida, narrates how a BMW came dangerously close to her bike on a curved road, nearly running her off.“Remarks, lewd gestures, honking, and constant stares make our freedom rides really ugly. If they don’t hit you, they will come extremely close or follow to just mess with you,” the 40-year-old says, blaming this behaviour on “generations of patriarchal conditioning that has taught men that women must be watched, judged and corrected”. “Add weak impulse control, peer bravado, lax policing and near-zero consequences and harassment starts to feel normal, even entertaining, to them,” Devika says.Geetika (25), a PR professional based in Gurgaon, said catcalling, teasing and obstructing the way are things most women riders have gone through in NCR. “The day I took my first ride, the experience was not pleasant. A group of boys obstructed my way and challenged me to race with them by coming close and revving their bikes. Since then, I’ve only taken my bike out early morning when I’m assured of encountering the least traffic.”Sarkar says it’s “not all bad that women just can’t ride on Delhi-NCR roads”, but agreed there is a “section of people who create nuisance” and that can happen anytime. “It’s not only a women rider problem, but a women safety and road safety issue. When people are on the road, they should behave. When someone is driving a car, there is a base, there is support, it will not lose balance. But when you are on a two-wheeler, even the minutest touch will make you fall,” adds Sarkar.
Just treat us like a normal rider — Riya Yadav, Gurgaon
Though less exposed than those on two-wheelers, women who drive cars say they have also encountered a “sense of entitlement” from strangers on the road, including cab drivers.Pooja (38), who has been driving for 12 years in Delhi, says comments are common, not because she has done anything to provoke it but because it’s a woman at the wheel. “I keep getting told by strangers that the size of my car (a Scorpio) doesn’t ‘match’ mine.”Rupali, an advertising professional from Noida, says she once deliberately slowed down to let a group of men overtake her in their car, just so she wouldn’t be harassed. This did not deter them. “They stopped and waited for me to pass, rolled down the windows and showed me their middle fingers,” the 35-year-old says. After they sped off, Rupali says, she drove at 30kmph so she wouldn’t encounter them again.
Yet the hostility has not stopped more women from taking up motorcycles. Meenakshi says the number of women she sees learning to ride has increased sharply. “Three years ago, if I trained 10 women in a month, the number would be 60-70 now,” she says. The profile, according to Krishnan, is changing too, with women in their 40s, 50s and even 60s increasingly taking up long-distance riding.
Dnyanadaa Mhaskar is an example of that change. The Navi Mumbai schoolteacher began riding at 41, bought a motorcycle while still on a learner’s licence and, by her own account, barely knew how to work the clutch and gears. She later borrowed her grocer’s 100cc Hero for a ride to Pune and joined an all-women motorcycling group. Now 54, she says simply: “Riding is my solace and my bike is my soulmate.”Riya Yadav, a Gurgaon-based professional biker who has been riding since she was a teenager, adds, “People need to realise that we are just riding a bike. We are not doing some rocket science. Just treat us like a normal rider.”Most of these women say they have learnt to live with the unwanted attention on roads. “I think society at large has to change for us to see any meaningful change in men’s mindset towards a female driver. Till then, women need to take utmost precautions while riding. And be brave,” Shivani says.

A journalist with close to 16 years of experience, she has reported on a wide range of topics from crime, to civic infrastructure and education from all over India. With a keen interest in society and evolving trends, she now writes on all things trending at Times of India where she serves as a features writer.

US Sen. Chris Van Hollen called Monday on European countries and other signatories to the International Criminal Court (ICC) to sanction President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio over the administration’s efforts to undermine its work.
“If European countries & other signatories to the International Criminal Court have any self-respect, they'd sanction Rubio & Trump for obstructing investigations of (Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin) Netanyahu's war crimes,” Van Hollen said in a post on the US social media platform X.

The proposed sanctions would target transactions with the ICC itself rather than only individual officials, according to the report. Transactions involving communications services would be exempt.
The ICC issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024, accusing them of alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

Vermont man convicted in shooting of 3 Palestinian students

Berk Kutay Gökmen
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
A jury in the US state of Vermont has convicted Jason Eaton, 51, of attempted murder for shooting three Palestinian college students near the University of Vermont campus in Burlington in November 2023, The Guardian reported Monday.
Eaton faces up to life in prison. The attack left Hisham Awartani paralyzed from the waist down and wounded his friends Tahseen Aliahmad and Kinnan Abdalhamid.
The jury reached its verdict after several hours of deliberation following a week-long trial that included testimony from the three victims and psychiatric experts for both the defense and prosecution. Eaton, who did not dispute that he was the shooter, had pleaded not guilty and argued that he was not criminally responsible because of his mental state.
His lawyers pointed to Eaton’s claims that US and Israeli intelligence agencies had transmitted the orders to shoot the men via FM radio and that God had commanded him to protect his Jewish neighbors. The jury rejected the insanity defense.
Eaton was ordered held in jail pending sentencing, which has not yet been scheduled. He stared ahead as the verdict was read. Awartani and Aliahmad, seated in the front row, smiled and hugged those around them.
“Justice has been rendered for Hisham, Kinnan and Tahseen. After three years of sorrow, loss and struggle, our families finally feel relief,” the families said in a joint statement.
They said the verdict could not erase the trauma but “affirms something fundamental: Jason Eaton is responsible for what he did.”
The families also said that Eaton repeatedly used “hateful” language about their sons during the trial, arguing that his own words showed why they were targeted.
“This was a hate crime. We have said so from the beginning,” they said.
The families thanked supporters in Burlington and Vermont while also highlighting the broader suffering of Palestinians.
“While our children fought to heal from being shot in Burlington, they watched Palestinian children lose their lives, their homes, their land, their families,” they said.
“Hisham, Kinnan and Tahseen have spent three years rebuilding their bodies and their lives after a hateful act almost killed them. We are profoundly relieved.”

Separately, Erdogan met with Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze at the Turkevi Center for bilateral consultations.
Türkiye recognised Georgia's independence in 1991, signing the Protocol on the Establishment of Diplomatic Relations in 1992, with relations between the two Black Sea neighbours currently standing at the level of a strategic partnership.

Lincoln-Goldfinch, speaking on CNN, said that account of the events "doesn't match" what Perez told her, though she provided no details on if he had been stopped by ICE agents before being shot.

Air Force to Get First Next-Gen Tactical C2 Centers By Year’s End
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
00:39:21 UTC
09:39:21 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—A single-pallet-sized tactical operations center is slated to begin shipping to 70 Air Force units by the end of the year following a recent announcement by the company that made it and the Air Force entity responsible for its development.
The Tactical Operations Center-Light is the Air Force’s next-generation method for conducting ground-based air battle management Several years ago, the service contracted with Lockheed Martin and L3Harris to build the first 16 prototypes of the TOC-L, which started delivering in 2023.
In 2025, though, the Air Force tapped Booz Allen Hamilton for a $315 million rapid prototyping contract to scale and produce the second iteration of the TOC-L, dubbed MR2 for Major Release 2 or Material Release 2.
The initial 16 MR1 prototypes let Airmen to get their hands on a prototype system and test it out. MR2 is the kit that will be in place to run air battle management in the near term.
“Material Release 1 is, ‘hey, how do we get the capability they need now so they can fight tonight?” Brig. Gen. Joshua Williams, program acquisition executive for command, control, communications, and battle management, told reporters Sept. 16 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference. “Material Release 2 is focused on deeper integration, improved edge connectivity, and more mature support.”
The system connects to all major aircraft and capabilities the Air Force deploys and can work backward-compatible through the DAF Battle Network, Patrick Hamilton, vice president for defense technology at Booz, told Air & Space Forces Magazine at the conference.
“This is the next-generation C2 system that the Air Force is going to deploy that hopefully will be in place for the next 30 to 40 years for the new C2 fight,” Hamilton said.
Because the TOC-L system can incorporate software changes more readily than legacy ground systems such as the Control and Reporting Center, it can more quickly add in capabilities, applications, and other items from the DAF Battle Network as it grows and more options are added.
“That is the fundamental difference to the prior prototype,” Hamilton said. “Now you’ll be able to, in the future, iterate as future improvements go online in the Battle Network.”
Operational Air Force units have spent the past year taking and testing TOC-L systems “downrange,” Col. Bai Lan Zhu, senior materiel leader for the Advanced Battle Management System, told reporters during the conference media session.
The total number of TOC-Ls to flow across the entire Air Force is still evolving, Zhu said.
“The exact quantities are something that the operational community is going to refine over time,” she said.
The first wave of TOC-Ls will begin shipping to units by or before December. The company plans to deliver 70 units under the current contract, Hamilton said.
The new system can also draw from at least three “enclaves” of data, letting users fuse information from both classified and unclassified sources more easily.
“So, if you have something coming in, let’s say from an FAA unclassified radar, and you want to put that on the situational awareness [common operating picture] that the user is looking at, which is in a secret enclave, you need the ability to move that data up,” Hamilton said.
The TOC-L provides that ability.
The system can also render those enclaves unclassified when powered off, based on National Security Agency data-at-rest standards.
In the past, system users would spend hours at the end of each mission or shift physically removing a series of drives, labeling them and storing them according to protocols, only to have to rebuild the setup the next day, Mike Lewis, Booz’s chief engineer for TOC-L, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“There are a lot of logistics and risk in that type of scenario, so with data at rest being unclassified, it’s a real key to making this tactically relevant from a speed perspective and from a cyber perspective,” Lewis said.
Fewer Pieces, Fewer People
TOC-L replaces the Cold War-era Control and Reporting Center, previously centered around the trusty but bulky AN/TPS-75 radar system.
The legacy system required as many as six C-17 Globemaster IIIs to transport all of its components, using radar dishes, heavy vehicles, and nearly two dozen power generators.
The CRC would require hundreds of Airmen to set up and operate and could take between 24 and 72 hours to set up and tear down.
TOC-L is a feather by comparison.
It fits on a single pallet, with one additional pallet to hold its generator; can be transported inside a single C-130 Hercules; requires about 10 Airmen to operate; and can be set up or torn down in less than an hour.
The TOC-L can squeeze into such a small frame and use far fewer people, partly because of advances in electronics and partly because it can tap into the DAF Battle Network and other networks to access radar and other feeds instead of carrying its own radars into the fight.
The shift in allowing nonproprietary equipment to hook into the TOC-L system also drastically trims down the amount of hardware needed to operate the system’s crucial functions, Hamilton told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“We’re going to collect iterative feedback from ABMS and the user community as it deploys all over the world,” said Hamilton. “And I think over the next 12 to 24 months, that will start to define what [Material Release 3] will look like and what we hear from the user community, what they prioritize for.”

"We had a lengthy discussion on Ukraine and Russia, the need to help our Ukrainian friends more quickly and more strongly in terms of interceptors, because that is the key issue from a defensive point of view," Macron said.
Without going into details, Macron said the two had also focused on the idea of halting strikes on the energy sector, a subject he would bring up when he meets Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy later on Monday.
The French leader said helping Ukraine's energy system remained a priority as the war continued to affect security across Europe and he hoped progress could be made during the annual gathering of leaders at the United Nations. REUTERS

EU's Kallas says Red Sea mission needs more than 10 warships
NEW YORK, Sept 21 - The European Union's naval mission to protect shipping in the Red Sea would need to boost its numbers to more than 10 warships, its foreign policy chief said on Monday, adding that for now there were not that many in the area.
The EU's Aspides mission was launched in 2024 to protect shipping from attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis, and diplomats have said there are currently six warships operating.
"When Aspides was put in place, then the indication was that it needs at least 10 ships. The situation, I think, is even more grave right now," Kaja Kallas told reporters on the sidelines of the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.
The Houthis have made rapid advances in recent weeks along the Red Sea coast, further complicating routes in a region that also includes the Strait of Hormuz, where traffic had already dwindled because of the US-Iran war.
Italy, one of the key countries in the Aspides mission, announced on Thursday it was preparing a naval mission in the area for its own ships, saying it could not wait for the EU to respond to the new crisis.
Kallas said the Houthi attacks were affecting European interests and impacting the global economy.
"The EU operation Aspides is making a crucial contribution to the security in the region and global shipping, but the operation needs more naval assets and more air assets to address the increased level of threats in the region," she said.
Kallas sent a letter to the EU's 27 member states on September 19 asking them to up their contributions. The issue would be discussed at upcoming defence and foreign ministers meetings, she said in the letter.
"This situation, which is still evolving as we speak, is already affecting European interests with repercussions on our supply chains and could have implications for our ability to support our economies which were already hit by rising fuel prices," she said in the letter.
"For the moment, although the Houthis communicate that they would only target Saudi-linked interests, there is uncertainty over their course of action with respect to vessels that transit through the Strait. Regardless, they are now in a better position to potentially harm maritime shipping." REUTERS
