Brownlow simply latest chapter as Daicos continues rewriting AFL history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:20:09 UTC
04:20:09 KST

Thu, 3 Sept, 8:10 pm, Final score, Dockers 40, Hawks 72
analysis
Brownlow a short stopover as Nick Daicos continues rewriting AFL history books
When Nathan Buckley's decade-long tenure as Collingwood coach came to an end midway through 2021, there was a silver lining for the club amid the painful exit of the club legend.
Buckley's tenure had seen the Pies flirt with winning a premiership in 2018 and 2019 before ultimately failing, but by the time he wrapped up, Collingwood seemed well out of the premiership window.
The silver lining came in the form of a player who was yet to set foot on an AFL field: Nick Daicos, then a teenager touted as a generational prospect years before he was eligible to be drafted.
The AFL world was no stranger to the Daicos surname due to the exploits of Nick's famous father, Peter, who was immortalised at Collingwood as a member of the club's 1990 premiership side.
You did not need to be a Collingwood fanatic to know about Nick Daicos. Everyone around the game knew the kid was on his way because of his prolific exploits at the junior levels.
The weight of expectation that comes with the level of hype Daicos had as a draft prospect can prove crippling. Unfortunately, years of evidence support this.
Sometimes even the most hyped prospects can take time to fit into the AFL system, and it makes sense. These are boys coming to a man's game.
The more rigorous training regimes, expanded playbooks, media commitments, dietary requirements, and everything else that comes with being an AFL player can be too much. That is even before we get to the pace of the game being completely different.
That hasn't been the case with Daicos, who, as an audacious Nike advert claimed on the morning of the Brownlow count, has proven it inevitable from day one.
From his first game, Daicos showed an ability to bend the game to his will in ways not seen in teenagers, and we have all been blessed to witness it.
Daicos's arrival helped catapult Collingwood from second-last in 2021 to fourth in his first season in the AFL.
Collingwood fell one point short of a grand final appearance in Daicos's debut season, but went all the way in his second.
After collecting boatloads of the football across halfback while occasionally dipping his toes in the midfield as a rookie, Daicos supercharged the Pies engine room in 2023, helping them claim the flag, and he has not looked back since.
From very early on in Daicos's career, the Brownlow win appeared to be a question of when rather than if, but it was the one accolade he was frustratingly made to wait on.
Daicos followed up his premiership by polling a ridiculous 38 votes in 2024, the most by any player in the league's history up until that point, only for that year's winner, Patrick Cripps, to poll 45.
Last year, he was again a seemingly unbackable favourite before being stunned by Gold Coast's Matt Rowell.
Missing out on a Brownlow after being among the favourites for a few years can be something that follows you.
Marcus Bontempelli, despite being widely considered the best player of his generation, has yet to win the prestigious medal.
Buckley was famously made to wait year after year before eventually breaking through in 2003, his 11th season, while Gary Ablett Jr was even denied by his own teammate before his maiden Brownlow triumph. It is almost a rite of passage if you're an all-timer.
Despite Bontempelli, Zak Butters and Bailey Smith all challenging him at various points during the count, Daicos would not be denied this year.
Almost in revenge for the previous two seasons, this year, Daicos turned in an individual season that would ultimately prove impossible to ignore for the umpires.
Daicos broke Cripps's record with 47 votes and set a few more records along the way.
He is now the only player in league history to poll over 30 votes in three consecutive seasons, the only player to put together six straight three-vote games, and the only player to put together 13 three-vote games in a single season.
Given the ease with which Daicos has played from his first contest in the AFL four seasons ago, it was surprising to talk about the weight of expectation actually weighing on him after winning his elusive first Brownlow.
You get the sense that the weight of expectation might be the only thing that is capable of slowing him down, because efforts from his AFL counterparts to do so have so far proven futile.
For a player so metronomic and seemingly superhuman on the field, it was refreshing to hear Daicos admit he too deals with nerves and struggles with criticism, just like the rest of us.
Daicos admitted to the Brownlow win being a relief after being denied for so many years as a favourite, even saying he had given up trusting in betting markets.
Now that the Brownlow box has been ticked off, it is frightening to think of what an unburdened Daicos could potentially achieve.
Still just 23 years of age, Daicos has gone from being the precocious youngster to one of Collingwood's veterans, and he will act as the bridge from one era of Collingwood premiership contention to the next, just as Scott Pendlebury did.
He seems good enough to single-handedly wrench Collingwood's premiership window open for as long as he wants.
Adding premierships to his 2023 triumph will be at the top of Daicos's to-do list, and the hope will be that in the process of achieving that goal, his resume ultimately becomes undeniable.
The chance to be Collingwood's greatest player is in play. The chance to be the greatest player in league history is as well, as premature as that shout may seem.
The records Daicos set with his maiden Brownlow win will eventually be just another footnote for a player who is poised to rewrite the game's history books.
Like the commercial said: inevitable.

Officer, man wounded in shooting near Ontario synagogue on Yom Kippur
Gunfire sprayed through the synogogue's stained glass windows, left more than 20 bullet holes behind
A police officer and a 29-year-old man were wounded Sunday evening in an exchange of gunfire near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, as congregants gathered to mark Yom Kippur. The man was hospitalized in life-threatening condition; the officer was listed in critical but stable condition.
Belleville police said the officer, parked in an unmarked vehicle, encountered the individual near the synagogue around 7:10 p.m. Ontario's Special Investigations Unit said the incident involved a man with a rifle and sent investigators to the scene. Police have not said what led to the shooting or whether the synagogue was targeted, and said there was no risk to public safety.
Synagogue president Norm Weddum said he was ushering people in when he heard shots. "We all ran back, I closed the doors of the auditorium, and I yelled out 'everybody get down,'" he said. Worshipers crouched on the floor for what felt like ten minutes as bullets sprayed through the room, some calling 911, he said. "We are all upset, but it's not going to deter us. We will reopen, and we will have services again."

Polo strengthens into hurricane, threatening Mexico’s Pacific resort towns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Polo strengthens into hurricane, threatening Mexico’s Pacific resort towns
Polo strengthened off Mexico’s Pacific coast into a hurricane on Sept 21 and is forecast to rapidly intensify into a major storm, threatening floods, dangerous surf and strong wind gusts in coastal states and near major beach resorts.
Around midday locally (2am on Sept 22, Singapore time), Polo was located some 435km south-south-east of port city Manzanillo and 305km south-south-west of tourist town Zihuatanejo, packing maximum sustained winds of 130kph, the US National Hurricane Center said.
Forecasters said the storm could become a major hurricane by Sept 22 and continue strengthening through midweek. While its core is expected to remain offshore, the storm is likely to lash parts of south-western Mexico with torrential rain and hazardous seas.
The NHC said coastal parts of Guerrero and Michoacan states could receive 10 to 20cm of rain through Sept 24, with isolated totals of up to 30cm, raising the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides, particularly in mountainous areas.
Private forecaster AccuWeather said the storm’s reach could extend out toward tourist hubs including Acapulco, Puerto Vallarta and Guadalajara, while southern Baja California Sur, including the Los Cabos area, could also see rough surf and strong gusts later this week.
Accuweather also warned that tropical moisture from Mexico is expected to push north through the rest of the week, threatening flash floods in the US South-west. REUTERS

Migrant child stows away to Spain under football bus

Migrant child stows away to Spain under football bus
MADRID - A Moroccan boy travelled from Spain’s north African exclave of Ceuta to the mainland hidden under a visiting football team’s bus on Sept 21, sources at the club told AFP.
The Real Valladolid players found the child hidden by their coach’s wheel axle when it pulled over at a service station, the sources told AFP.
The team from northern Spain had crossed the Strait of Gibraltar on the ferry on the way home after drawing 1-1 in their second-division match against Ceuta, when they heard strange noises under the vehicle.
Under pressure to contain migration after a crisis in Ceuta on July 30 and 31, Spain’s government had insisted that no irregular migrants would be allowed to reach the mainland.
On those days more than 70,000 people swam in the sea around a border fence into the Spanish territory. Most returned, but several thousand have remained.
The boy under the coach had stayed hidden throughout the ferry crossing and for more than 100km by road before eventually calling for help, the Real Valladolid sources said.
Club members gave him food, water and clothing before police took charge of him.
The authorities say conditions in Ceuta have deteriorated since the migrant influx, sparking angry demonstrations by residents. AFP

Porsche Becomes a Burden for Volkswagen Group — Media
Kyiv • UNN
Porsche lost ground in China and suffered losses due to the transition to electric vehicles. Volkswagen wrote down €6 billion of the value of its stake in the brand.
Porsche, the carmaker, is becoming one of the Volkswagen Group’s biggest problems and is fading into the shadow of the Czech brand Škoda. Reuters writes, as reported by UNN.
Porsche, the manufacturer of luxury sports cars that was long Volkswagen’s most reliable source of profit, has become its biggest problem, creating an obstacle to CEO Oliver Blume’s restructuring plans at Europe’s largest automaker
Less than four years after its record-breaking stock market debut, Porsche has become a symbol of the problems facing the entire group: the company has lost its leading position in what was once a profitable Chinese market and suffered losses because of costly miscalculations during the transition to electric vehicles.
On Monday, thousands of workers protested against cuts at car plants across Germany, and this crisis extends beyond Porsche and the rest of Volkswagen’s sprawling empire, reflecting how Germany’s automotive sector is coming under pressure from Chinese competitors and U.S. tariffs.
On Friday, Volkswagen issued another profit warning, linking it to a €6 billion write-down on its 75% stake in Porsche - just weeks after approving extensive job cuts as part of the largest restructuring in the group’s 89-year history.
The write-down, which followed a €2.7 billion impairment a year earlier, points to a lack of proper oversight at Volkswagen, Jefferies analysts wrote, noting that, in their words, these were "endless surprises related to putting things in order."
Volkswagen attributed the write-down to poorer financial forecasts for Porsche, which made a high-profile stock market debut in 2022 in one of the largest IPOs on the continent in recent years.
In an internal memo seen by Reuters, Porsche CEO Michael Leiters stressed that the company remains committed to its medium-term profitability target of between 10% and 15%.
However, looking ahead, the company’s withdrawal from China, where it has reduced the number of dealerships, and pressure on its U.S. business from tariffs are raising questions about sales volumes.
Porsche has reportedly been going through difficult times for years, and Blume, who is leading the sports-car brand until the end of 2025, will oversee it during a crucial downturn while simultaneously serving as CEO of the group.
We remind you
Porsche has unveiled the 911 Challenge - a full-fledged race car costing $275,000. It is cheaper than the 911 Turbo S convertible, whose starting price is $284,300.

European children could face almost twice as much extreme fire weather: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:13:34 UTC
04:13:34 KST

Aysu Bicer
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
European children born in 2025 could face almost twice as much extreme fire weather during their lifetimes as those born in 1950, according to a new study published in the journal Environmental Research Letters on Monday.
Researchers found that, under current climate policies, a child born in Europe in 2025 could experience three more years of extreme fire-conducive weather than someone born 75 years earlier.
The increase is expected to be greatest in the Mediterranean, where children born in 2025 could face five additional years of extreme fire weather compared with people born during the post-war baby boom.
The study examined 21 climate scenarios, ranging from 1.5°C to 3.5°C (2.7°F to 6.3°F) of global warming by the end of the century. It defined extreme fire weather as days with conditions more severe than the worst 5% recorded during the 1985–2014 reference period.
Under current policies, which are projected to result in about 2.6°C (4.7°F) of warming, children born today are expected to experience 84% more exposure to extreme fire weather than those born in 1950.
The researchers estimated that 86% of this rise would be caused by climate change, with the remaining 14% linked to increased life expectancy.
Hot, dry, and windy conditions allow fires to spread rapidly and burn more intensely. The study notes these conditions have been exacerbated by more than a century of fossil fuel pollution, during which Europe has warmed at roughly twice the global average rate.
If global warming were limited to 1.5°C (2.7°F), children born in 2025 would experience 1.3 fewer years of extreme fire weather over their lifetimes compared with the current-policy scenario.
These findings come as Europe faces increasingly severe wildfire conditions, particularly across the Mediterranean region.

US, Denmark, Greenland to sign security deal for Greenland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:13:20 UTC
04:13:20 KST

The United States, Denmark and Greenland will sign on Tuesday the announced US security deal for Greenland on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, Denmark's government said.
US President Donald Trump said last Friday that the arrangement will give America "permanent control" over security for Greenland, an autonomous Danish territory in the Arctic that he has long coveted.
The office of Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said that she, Trump and Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen would sign the deal at 1430 GMT in the UN building in New York.
Frederiksen said on Monday that the agreement, which has not been published, "recognises" the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination.
"It is a good agreement from a Danish point of view," she told Danish radio DR from New York.
"And when it benefits the Nordic countries and security in the Arctic region, it also benefits NATO and Europe."
Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly insisted that the United States needs to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and sparking fierce pushback from the alliance.
According to Washington, the agreement ensures that China and Russia will not be able to establish military bases in Greenland or carry out sensitive investments there without its consent.
"This is something we have agreed on with the Americans for a very, very long time: the Arctic region, the North Atlantic, constitute an important defence zone for all members of the NATO alliance," Frederiksen said.

Thirteen-year-old surfer breaking records as first Indigenous world champ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21

Thirteen-year-old surfer Leihani Zoric breaks record as first Indigenous world champ
Leihani Zoric almost didn't compete in El Salvador, but now the 13-year-old is the youngest International Surfing Association (ISA) Under 18 World Junior Champion in history.
"When I went over there, I was extremely sick," Zoric told ABC Weekend Breakfast.
"I wasn't even going to go, my mum and dad were like, 'Leihani don't go, you're that sick'."
But the teenager was committed.
"I was like, 'no, I'm going to go. I believe that I can go all the way'," she told her parents.
And all the way she went, using visualisation to help her through.
"I wrote it down about 1,000 times [and] I said to myself, 'I'm going to become this year's Under 18 ISA gold medallist'," Zoric said.
"So, when it happened, I was like, oh my God, this is crazy."
Across more than a week of competition, Zoric was part of a 12-strong Australian team that went head-to-head with the world's best junior surfers.
She competed three age divisions above her own, to take out the title.
"It feels amazing," Zoric said.
"I'm really proud of myself for all my hard work and effort I've put in, and all the people that have helped me along the way."
It comes after a stand-out year so far, which includes winning the Junior Girls and Open Women's divisions at the 2026 Indigenous Surfing Titles.
She's now back home not only as a World Champion, but a history maker.
And she's taking it all in her stride, with a maturity that's beyond her years.
"I'm just so grateful to have been able to go to El Salvador and represent my culture and my country as best as I can," she said.
Creating a proud history
Zoric, from Byron Bay in northern New South Wales, is also the first Indigenous world champion surfer at any level.
"I'm really proud to have represented my Yued mob over in Western Australia," she said.
"We have such important history in our culture and I feel like [that] has really shaped me as a person."
Zoric first got a feel for surfing at two days old, when her dad put her on a surfboard in the shallows at Broken Head.
From then on, she just loved the water.
She takes inspiration from Soli Bailey, the first pro surfer to compete under the Aboriginal flag in the World Surfing League, and Cathy Freeman.
"Having those people inspire me has definitely made me want to be like them one day," she said.
Along with looking up to others, Zoric wants to be a positive role model herself.
When she's not in the water, she's busy creating connection, with things like Lei's Lu'au, a community day celebrating girls and women in surfing.
"I hope that I inspire, not just as an athlete, but being a good person and always caring about others, being encouraging and just having a positive attitude all the time," she said.
"Bringing people up and lifting their spirits and attitudes and just [making] them feel like they belong here in this world.
"Because everybody is important and special in their own unique ways."
Locana Cullen (Under 16 men's) and Lucy Darragh (Under 16 women's) also claimed individual golds at the World Junior Championships, with Australia winning three out of the four divisions.
The Australians also won their third consecutive team gold at the event.

Trump’s approval rating hits record low amid Iran war, economy fallout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:10:52 UTC
04:10:52 KST

Trump approval rating hits career low of 32% amid Iran war, high costs
United States President Donald Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 32 percent – the lowest of his political career – as his fellow Republicans soured on his handling of the cost of living amid the unpopular Iran war, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
The four-day poll, which closed on Sunday, showed 73 percent of Republicans approved of Trump’s job performance, down from 82 percent in a Reuters/Ipsos poll a week earlier. His overall approval was 35 percent then.
Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 on promises to tame inflation and end foreign wars. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in the hours after he was first sworn in, he enjoyed a 47 percent approval rating.
Just 17 percent of respondents in the new poll approved of his handling of the cost of living – the top issue. Americans say it will determine how they vote in the November 3 midterm elections, when Trump’s Republicans are defending narrow congressional majorities.
Dissatisfaction among Republicans has been growing since Trump launched the war on Iran in February, which has pushed gasoline and diesel prices sharply higher. Now for the first time, Republicans who disapprove of Trump’s handling of the cost of living outnumber those who give him a thumbs up – 51 percent to 44 percent.
Trump said on Wednesday that the United States is “hopefully toward the end” of its war with Iran, raising the prospect of renewed diplomacy even as fighting continues in Yemen.
However, Tehran has not confirmed that direct negotiations with Washington have resumed.
The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted online and gathered 1,277 responses from US adults nationwide. It had a margin of error of three percentage points.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Monday met with his Vietnamese counterpart To Lam and Chairman of Libya’s Presidential Council Mohamed al-Menfi in New York, where they are attending the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
Erdogan’s closed-door meeting with To Lam took place at Turkish House, or Turkevi, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
The leaders discussed bilateral relations, as well as regional and global developments, according to Türkiye’s Communications Directorate.
Erdogan welcomed Vietnam's positive response to Türkiye's proposal to elevate bilateral relations to the level of a "strategic partnership," according to the statement.
The Turkish president said Ankara was working to expand cooperation with Vietnam in a range of areas, particularly investment, trade and the defense industry.
Erdogan also stressed the importance of continued cooperation between the two countries in international forums and said Türkiye and Vietnam should maintain their efforts to work together on global issues.
During the meeting, Erdogan congratulated To Lam on his election as Vietnam's president.
He also invited To Lam to attend the Leaders' Summit of the UN Climate Change Conference, COP31, which Türkiye is scheduled to host in Antalya in November.
Diplomatic relations between Türkiye and Vietnam were established on June 7, 1978.
Erdogan also met with al-Menfi at Turkevi in New York. No information was immediately shared about the meeting.
Türkiye attaches the utmost importance to the security and welfare of the Libyan people, given the two countries’ historical and cultural ties.

Why younger Australians are facing a tough economic future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:07:06 UTC
04:07:06 KST

analysis
Intergenerational Report shows younger Australians face tough economic future
Ask any soothsayer. Forecasting is a mug's game.
It is difficult enough to predict what will happen next month, let alone 40 years from now.
Regardless, for the past quarter of a century, Australian governments have sought to project where the nation is heading and predict the challenges and opportunities that may present themselves every five or so years.
They're rarely correct. But that's hardly the point. In many ways, it is just as instructive to figure out why previous forecasts missed the mark, delivering valuable insights into how best to approach the future.
This latest report, the seventh since 2002, has arrived at a seminal moment in history.
Loading...
There has been not been such disharmony and distrust between the superpowers for almost a century.
The first European war since 1945 has not only pitted Russia against the US and Europe; it has caused a growing schism in the NATO alliance, driven in large part by a capricious US president with little regard for the institutions that have underpinned Western democracy.
That's been exacerbated by a calamitous war in the Middle East that has reignited an energy crisis and acted as a catalyst for a looming global economic crisis.
The US dollar's longstanding position as the global reserve currency has been damaged by America's rapidly expanding debt and its use of financial sanctions, while its decision to punish trading partners has caused widespread discontent.
That, in turn, has ended a half-century-long decline in interest rates. Money is now likely to be more expensive as defence-oriented nations compete with industry — particularly the artificial intelligence giants — for funds.
Growing old not so gracefully
What will Australia look like in 40 years?
At an estimated 40 million, the population will be much bigger but much older, and the nation will be more indebted and have what increasingly appears to be a permanent budget deficit.
Demographics play a vital role in shaping an economy.
A country with an aging population has a smaller proportion of workers to shoulder the cost of looking after those in their advancing years. That squeezes national tax income, and there is a greater cost burden associated with higher health care and aged care.
And for those still working? More likely, higher tax bills.
Like many developed countries, Australia has low and declining fertility rates. According to the projections in the report, more Australians will die than be born in 2066.
As Treasurer Jim Chalmers pointed out at a speech yesterday at the Australian National University, many advanced economies have already surpassed that point, and most of the rest are expected to within the next few decades.
The population, however, will continue to grow as new arrivals make up for the downturn in Australian births, but at a more modest pace than in the past 20 years, as immigration has become a hot political issue.
As this graph from the 2026 Intergenerational Report shows, without immigration, the population would shrink, creating a whole new raft of problems.
Add to this volatile mix a new technology that looks set to revolutionise the workplace and perhaps even life as we now know it.
Exactly what artificial intelligence will deliver is anyone's guess. The more optimistic among us hope for higher living standards.
The government hopes it will help turn around Australia's chronic productivity growth problem, which has declined to zero. In the document, Treasury estimates a dramatic recovery in productivity as the technology weaves its way through Australian workplaces.
Many economists are not so sure.
How we created a productivity crisis
Population and productivity are closely intertwined.
Remember all those stories about Australia's "miracle economy" from just a few years ago? A quarter of a century without a recession.
But it was all a thimble-and-pea trick.
For more than 20 years, governments of both persuasions papered over the cracks in our economy by importing people.
It made it appear as though our economy was on a one-way trip to nirvana. But what the pollies didn't do was invest in infrastructure to cope with such a monumental and sudden burst in population.
And now we are paying the price, with cities that barely function, with inadequate public transport, health systems and schools.
In addition, our businesses held off on investment, preferring instead to dole out profits to shareholders and push stock prices higher.
Housing shortages, coupled with tax arrangements that diverted investment funds into suburban house-flipping ventures instead of productive activities, pushed up the cost of putting a roof over your head and drained household incomes.
The data was there all along. The GDP pie kept getting bigger, right through from the first Intergenerational Report in 2002. But divide it by the growing number of people, and you suddenly realise that everyone's share of the pie was shrinking.
Investment in technology and infrastructure per worker has declined. Little wonder we have a productivity problem.
But unless we fix it, our living standards are likely to stall and possibly fall.
Why younger generations are losing faith
During the past three decades, Australian households have grown richer.
On average, real net household wealth has grown from $500,000 in 1993 to more than $1.3 million in 2019/20.
But dig down into the data, and it becomes clear that those gains aren't evenly shared and that younger generations have missed out.
This graph from the report shows that those born in the 1950s did substantially better than those from the 1940s. Those born in the 1960s did even better.
But for those born from the 1970s on, the gains were smaller, if there were any at all.
That's because older households have ridden a property boom unlike any other in history in terms of longevity.
Those born in later decades were forced to buy in at prices that had grown twice as fast as earnings since the turn of the century.
Older generations also have seen their wealth buoyed by maturing superannuation balances and soaring stock markets.
"Gross housing wealth almost tripled in real terms between 1994 and 2020, while superannuation wealth grew five-fold," the report notes.
That disturbing trend was a key reason the government decided in the May budget to tighten the tax breaks around property investment.
It has also committed to strengthening the superannuation system to ensure an aging Australia will help pay for itself rather than rely solely on a publicly funded pension system.
The Australian superannuation scheme has become a focal point for other countries grappling with the same demographic issues and will help curtail spending pressure into the future.
We may be better placed than other nations to handle the upcoming challenges. But it won't be easy.

Dating app safety shouldn't be left to women, researchers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:05:50 UTC
04:05:50 KST

Dating app harms fuel calls to extend digital duty of care to platforms
In short:
Almost all women surveyed in a new Australian study reported encountering harmful behaviour on dating apps, with many taking their own precautions to stay safe.
Researchers say platforms should do more to prevent systemic risks as the federal government considers a digital duty of care.
What's next?
Consultation on Labor's proposed digital duty of care closes on Tuesday, with advocates saying it has capacity to curb online abuse.
Women are being forced to act as their own safety system on dating apps where experiences of sexual harassment, manipulation and controlling behaviours are widespread, a study has found.
Australian researchers found 99 per cent of heterosexual women surveyed had encountered at least one harmful behaviour on a dating app in the previous three months.
Unsolicited explicit messages, attempts to monitor activity, love bombing, negging and gaslighting are common experiences on dating apps, according to the study released on Tuesday by the Minderoo Foundation-funded Behaviour Insights Team (BIT).
Women reported routinely screening profiles for warning signs, withholding identifying information and carefully managing interactions to protect themselves from potential harm.
These accounts have fuelled calls to ensure a proposed digital duty of care was implemented to require online services to tackle systemic risks.
Researchers have argued the scale of the problem showed women could not be expected to manage the risks alone, with dating platforms better placed to prevent harm before it occurred.
Women coaching each other to stay safe
Brisbane resident Rebecca Wilson, 33, said her harmful dating app experiences have included receiving "completely unsolicited" and "aggressively sexual" messages, photos and videos.
Ms Wilson said she was also once stalked by a man she had met via an app.
"We went on one date. I said to him, 'Look I'm just not interested anymore', and he didn't get the message," she said.
"Weeks later he kept popping up at the same places as me … following me around.
"He touched me at a bar right in front of my friends when it was clearly unsolicited."
With only minimal information on the man, Ms Wilson said she could not easily report him to authorities.
One issue was that using the "block" feature on the app meant she lost the ability to collect identifying material to progress a complaint.
"There's no way of being able to know the identity of who you were talking to," Ms WIlson said.
Ms Wilson said she and her friends have "coached" each other through how to navigate online dating safely.
"The current mechanisms are really just not enough on these apps," she said.
Harmful behaviour 'normalised'
The most common harmful behaviours on dating apps were psychological and emotional, which were encountered by 95 per cent of the 1,008 women across Australia surveyed for the BIT study.
About 89 per cent experienced monitoring and surveillance activity and 88 per cent reported being sent unsolicited sexual images and videos, and being pressured and manipulated into sending sexual content.
Almost six in 10 women reported fear-based controlling behaviour, including threats of physical harm. Of those, only about 22 per cent reported those threats to the platforms.
Among women who made reports to platforms generally, about 19 per cent felt their complaint was "barely" or "not at all" taken seriously, while 64 per cent said they were taken at least "somewhat" seriously.
Lead researcher Karen Tindall said the findings showed there was a need for greater efforts by the platforms to tackle "genuinely preventable risk".
"Right now, a lot of these behaviours are so normalised that women blame themselves or they think they are overreacting," she said.
"This data and research should validate women's experience and should shift the conversation toward fixing the system itself."
Dr Tindall said there were features built for safety that could lead to harm, such as preventing screenshots to prevent against image-based abuse.
"But that also removes a woman's ability to document what happened," she said.
"I'm not saying those safety features should be removed, but it means that safety features need to be tested for how they will be worked around, and whether they will work as intended."
Duty would shift responsibility onto platforms
The findings have been released as the federal government consults on its proposed digital duty of care, which is intended to require services to identify and mitigate foreseeable risks rather than relying on users to report harm after the fact.
The draft duty for adults could apply to dating platforms on which users have faced serious abuse, stalking, sexual violence or image-based abuse.
It would mean services were required to identify and mitigate systemic risks that could enable such conduct.
While the initial debate has focused on social media, the proposed duty would apply more broadly across digital services, including dating and messaging apps, online games, search engines and AI services.
Minderoo Foundation gender equality executive director Jacqueline Joudo Larsen said a digital duty of care could prevent harm and protect Australians.
"It is the single biggest lever to curb the reach, scale and speed at which abuse is occurring by shifting responsibility from individuals to companies that are designing and operating online platforms," she said.
"This is a standard that we hold other sectors to and it should be no different for the online space."
Ms Larsen said technology had "transformed" how people met, connected and built relationships.
"Those benefits are very meaningful," she said.
"But safety cannot be the price women pay for participation.
"This is a design problem that's entirely preventable."
Ms Larsen said Australia could be a leader in tech safety and, if it was serious about ending sexual and domestic violence, that was an "opportunity we can't squander".
Labor's proposal under scrutiny
Submissions on Labor's proposal close on Tuesday and draft legislation will likely be introduced next month.
The Coalition has criticised the draft, primarily due to concerns over discretionary powers allowing the minister to add additional "harms" for children and "serious harms" for adults.
In a social media post shared by Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, the Coalition dubbed the idea the "Albo-rithm" and suggested the government would seek to censor online spaces.
But Communications Minister Anika Wells has repeatedly said the intent of the rule making power was about acting with "urgency" if new threats, such as apps that allowed users to "nudify" photos, arose online.
"We think this is a sensible measure to try and deal with these emerging harms that are coming online every single day," she said earlier this month.
The discretion in the bill for adding additional harms would be disallowable by the Senate at any time, but Labor might have to make some changes to their plan in order to secure the Greens' support for the draft bill.
In another submission to the draft legislation, the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman has described the reforms as a "rare opportunity" to build trust and accountability into the digital economy from the outset.
Ombudsman Cynthia Gebert said trust would not be built by hoping companies did the right thing and urged the government to consider an independent external dispute mechanism for when system failures occurred.
"Everyday Australians need someone to turn to for support holding big tech companies accountable when they get things wrong and we stand ready to help," she said.
The submission said an external complaints system would provide a "practical avenue" for Australians to resolve issues such as restoration of account access, ensuring choices about algorithms are implemented and reconsidering incorrect decisions.

Escalating attacks on infrastructure by Russia and Ukraine are leaving civilians increasingly vulnerable as winter approaches, UN investigators have warned, raising concerns about a repeat of last winter’s suffering.
The UN’s Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine said on Monday both sides had intensified long-range strikes against civilian sites, including energy, industrial and port infrastructure, as well as ships in the Black Sea.
The commission said Russian attacks during the winter of 2025-2026 caused prolonged power and heating outages as temperatures fell to minus 20°C, leaving millions of civilians without adequate heating.
“Ukrainian authorities recorded cold-related deaths and injuries,” commission chair Erik Mose told the UN Human Rights Council.
The commission also voiced concern over reports of Ukrainian attacks on infrastructure inside Russia and Russian-controlled areas of Ukraine, saying they indicated rising civilian casualties and damage to civilian objects. It said it had been unable to investigate those reports because it lacked access.
“Continued attacks on energy infrastructure are making living conditions increasingly unbearable for civilians, and we are concerned that the coming winter will be more difficult to endure,” Mose said.
The findings came after US President Donald Trump called last week for an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine, although neither side has confirmed it will participate.
Children, foreign recruits
The commission also reported on Russia’s imposition of what it described as patriotic education in occupied areas, including military training for Ukrainian children from the age of 14.
It said children were taught to handle weapons and carry out military drills.
Investigators also examined the recruitment of foreign nationals to fight for Russia, saying some had been deceived or coerced into joining the Russian armed forces.
Mose said agents and intermediaries had recruited people from various countries with promises of civilian jobs before they were allegedly compelled to sign contracts with Russia’s defence ministry.
Many recruits did not understand Russian or the contracts they signed and were subsequently sent to the front lines in Ukraine, he said.
The commission said some were killed, wounded, captured or went missing, leaving families searching for relatives from abroad.

The surge by the Iran-backed group this month extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theater and further threatened global energy supplies, resulting in a spike in oil prices, upending maritime trade in the region.
"Ninety percent of the food in Yemen is imported. So when ports are not working or when airports are not working, that's having an impact on food security in Yemen," said Skau, who recently visited the country.
Skau also warned that the agency was unable to operate in the Houthi-controlled areas as the group continues to occupy UN offices after it confiscated its assets and detained dozens of UN staff.
"Our offices in the north are occupied by the Houthi de facto authorities, and our assets are still confiscated, so under such circumstances it's very difficult for us to operate," said Skau.

The new generation of ultra-cheap smart glasses is shockingly hackable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
18:50:38 UTC
03:50:38 KST

Ultra-cheap smart glasses leaving Australians' personal data exposed to hackers
In short:
The new generation of ultra-cheap smart glasses leaves Australians' personal data, images and videos exposed to hackers.
Independent testing conducted for the ABC shows the devices can be accessed by a nearby attacker without a password, using only Bluetooth.
At least one supplier has made the decision to wind down its supply because of the furore surrounding the devices.
The new generation of ultra-cheap smart glasses is exposing Australians' sensitive data, images and videos to hackers, an investigation by ABC News has found.
Independent testing by cybersecurity experts has revealed a suite of serious vulnerabilities, and found an attacker can gain control of the glasses and any stored images using only Bluetooth.
"Another person with the same app can log into the glasses without a password [because] there is no password," said David Crees, the lead researcher in testing conducted for the ABC by NSB Cyber and Abstract Shield.
"It shouldn't be possible. It is not possible in pretty much every other proper consumer electronic," he said.
The ability to hijack a stranger's glasses with Bluetooth alone was one of more than a dozen flaws he found in six days of testing the AI-enabled smart glasses, the phone app, and its website.
"I would have expected to have found some vulnerabilities … but in this case, there wasn't a single thing that they had done correctly,"
The findings also horrified legal experts, who said the security flaws were so serious the product likely breached the privacy act, Australian consumer law, and the government's new cyber security act.
"It's really disturbing to read the extent of the failure to take even basic steps to protect personal data," said Kimberlee Weatherall, a tech regulation specialist from the University of Sydney.
"They don't seem to have encrypted it, they don't seem to have put passwords on it, they don't seem to have put even basic protections on the information that's on the website.
"It's a really clear breach [of the privacy act]."
Loading...
There has been growing public backlash to the recent influx of cheap smart glasses to Australia, with calls for an import ban over privacy concerns about their ability to record in secret.
The devices, which look like ordinary glasses, let the wearer capture images, video and audio with the press of a button, and they have attracted the nickname "pervert glasses" because it is not always clear when they are in use.
Now, revelations about their security flaws raise a parallel set of privacy concerns for the glasses' owners.
The testing conducted for ABC News assessed two pairs of glasses — one costing $60 from the online retailer Temu, and another costing $110, bought from a Sydney-based importer called BDI Technology via Big W Marketplace.
Similar versions in a comparable price range have also been available in recent months from Dick Smith, Kmart, and Amazon, and all appear to rely on the same mobile phone app, called HeyCyan.
Like many ethical hackers, Mr Crees first honed his skills as a cyber criminal, but now runs his own company called Abstract Shield, which is often hired by companies to detect security flaws before an attacker can.
"I'll spend anywhere from a week to a month going through a bit of software or a server or a website and finding everything that's wrong with it."
But he said it was clear straight away there was "no chance" these glasses were tested to a basic minimum standard before they hit Australian shelves.
"If you think about AirPods or Samsung earbuds, you have to hold a button on the device for [several] seconds, and then you can pair it with a new phone," Mr Crees said.
"That protects the device, [but] this has nothing."
Professor Weatherall said the glasses also violated Australia's privacy laws and were likely to breach several sections of the yet-to-be-used cyber security act, which came into effect in March.
"The rules say that the password must be unique," she said.
"It doesn't even seem like they were applying a password, which might mean that their standards are so low they don't even technically breach that rule, which I find amazing."
Australian data in, Chinese propaganda out
Aside from the hacking risk, the testing also found Australian user data was being sent to China in many instances.
It revealed anything spoken or typed to the in-built AI companion, along with any images submitted to AI, was sent first to a server in Shenzhen.
Depending on the function being performed, the data might then be passed to another Chinese server belonging to a different company, or to the US, although users are not explicitly told.
"The [privacy] act says if it's practical, you have to identify the country," Professor Weatherall said.
"It's not at all clear to me why they couldn't have put China into the privacy policy," she said, noting that the document only made specific mention of Singapore.
The AI companion embedded in the glasses sometimes returned inaccurate answers or error messages when asked about topics the Chinese government considers sensitive.
In one instance, when asked about China's well-documented persecution of millions of Uyghur Muslims in Xinjiang province, the chatbot said there was "no credible evidence".
It declined to discuss the Tiananmen Square massacre and proposed "more positive topics" instead.
These findings, along with server locations, led researchers to conclude the chatbot companion relied at least in part on Chinese sovereign AI models.
"There is a high degree of uncertainty when it comes to where the data is going," Evan Vougdis, from NSB Cyber, who oversaw the research, said.
"Is it being used for further training [of Chinese AI models]? Is it being used for surveillance?"
The testing did not definitively determine how the data was being used, but Mr Vougdis said any Australians considering buying the product should be aware of the risk they were taking.
"We're looking at data collection at a scale that we've never seen before due to the adoption of … products such as smart glasses that are readily available for a low price,"
The developer of the HeyCyan app is Shenzhen Qingcheng Future Technology Co, based in mainland China.
The ABC made repeated attempts to contact the company about its security flaws and seek a response, but received no reply.
It appeared HeyCyan's developers had attempted to patch some security flaws after the ABC shared the findings, but most vulnerabilities remained unaddressed.
Mr Crees said the flaws were so many and substantial that a total fix was impossible.
"You'd have to update 300 different brands of glasses and the app and the website … it'd take like a year to fix this. The only real solution that I see is a recall," he said.
The ABC understands at least one Australian retailer paused its supply because of the furore surrounding the devices.
BDI Technology, which is also listed as the supplier to Dick Smith and on Big W's Marketplace platform, said it was no longer selling smart glasses.
"I'm not surprised," privacy commissioner Carly Kind said.
"There has been a really extreme backlash to these technologies. Many of these companies really prize their reputation in the Australian community, and I think they [would] do well to listen to that community concern."
The ABC did not receive on-the-record responses from any other retailers.

Only one defence college for Scotland without match funding
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:48:44 BST
03:48:44 KST

Only one of the two proposed Defence Technical Excellence Colleges in Scotland will go ahead unless the Scottish Government provides match funding, the UK Government has said, in a warning accompanying a report by the Scottish Affairs Committee which finds that progress on the colleges has fallen behind equivalent work in England.
Two colleges are proposed for Scotland under the Defence Growth Deal, which carries £50 million in funding drawn from a £250 million pot for growth deals across the United Kingdom. Part of that money supports two engineering and innovation facilities, with £5 million for the Arrol Gibb Innovation Campus at Rosyth and a further £5 million for the Clyde Engineering and Innovation Centre.
The committee’s conclusion states: “Progress establishing DTECs in Scotland has fallen behind those in England. While it is important that both the UK and Scottish Governments are aligned on the establishment of DTECs, intergovernmental cooperation and engagement should not be a cause of delay.”
The colleges have the potential, it adds, “not only to strengthen the defence skills pipeline but also to expand access to highly skilled, well-paid apprenticeship opportunities that support communities and regional economic growth across Scotland”.
The committee wants the Scottish Government to put money alongside Westminster’s, recommending: “The UK Government must work proactively with the Scottish Government to expand apprenticeship provision for the defence industry in Scotland, given the vital role apprenticeships play in developing skilled workers and supporting the UK’s national security. For the same reasons, we hope to see the Scottish Government match the UK Government’s funding for the two proposed DTECs.”
It adds a warning attached to that request, stating that if the Scottish Government does not agree to match funding, “an important opportunity will be lost”.
According to the committee, without matched funding from the Scottish Government the UK Government has said that only one college will proceed.
Patricia Ferguson, chair of the committee, said: “One of the main ways skills training can be expanded is through DTECs, which have the potential to strengthen Scotland’s skills pipeline and expand access to high-quality apprenticeships that can support the UK’s defence ambitions. The committee hopes to see the UK and Scottish Governments work together to deliver both proposed DTECs in Scotland and, more widely, that Scotland can accelerate work to develop the skills base its defence sector needs.”
In its summary the committee says it supports the establishment of both colleges and urges the two governments to work together to deliver them without delay. The report also examines the Defence Universities Alliance, welcoming its creation as a step towards promoting defence careers and building closer ties between academic institutions and the sector, while noting that it is too soon to judge its success.
Recruiting Scottish graduates and keeping that talent in Scotland is described as a clear challenge for the industry and a particularly difficult one for smaller firms.
The committee asks the government to provide a progress update on the alliance by June 2027, including early indicators of its effectiveness in supporting Scottish graduates and institutions, followed by annual reports covering its performance and data on its impact on graduate retention in the Scottish defence sector.
A Scottish Government spokesperson told the UK Defence Journal: “Scotland is well placed to seize the opportunity of increased UK defence spending with a highly skilled workforce, world-class universities and internationally recognised manufacturing. The conflict in Ukraine is a reminder of the increasingly complex and immediate threats we face, underlining the importance of maintaining a strong and resilient defence capability.
“Our aerospace, defence, security and space sectors contribute around £3.7 billion to the economy and support approximately 37,000 jobs. We can maximise the economic benefits of these sectors through a responsible approach while supporting innovation, skills development and building long-term economic resilience.
“The Cabinet Secretary for Economy will meet with representatives from across the sector to discuss how the Defence Industrial Growth Programme can maximise the economic benefits arising from increased UK and allied defence spending, supporting economic growth, high-value jobs and national resilience. Further details of the Programme will be announced in due course.”

Paramount settles with US states in big step towards closing Warner Bros merger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
18:48:00 UTC
03:48:00 KST

Paramount wins Warner Bros takeover after settling US states, union lawsuits
Paramount Skydance emerged victorious on Sept 21 from a legal battle over its US$110 billion (S$140 billion) acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery after settling with a California-led group of US states and a Hollywood writers union, paving the way for one of the largest media mergers in history.
The settlement marks a major win for Paramount CEO David Ellison, who battled the states for months to finalise a deal that would dramatically concentrate power across Hollywood’s film, TV, streaming and news businesses.
Paramount agreed to abide by temporary film quotas and a news oversight committee, avoiding a forced sale of cable assets such as CNN or any of its lucrative film franchises.
The settlement delighted Warner Bros shareholders, but drew criticism from opponents of the merger who say it will hurt Hollywood jobs.
Shares of Paramount pared back earlier gains on Sept 21, while Warner Bros Discovery surged more than 10 per cent.
The Writers Guild of America settled its parallel case against Paramount, while saying it still believes the deal will damage the industry.
The states’ settlement forced the union to “contend with the reality of forging ahead alone, with no backing from government enforcers” in a complex case that would have cost millions of dollars.
California Attorney-General Rob Bonta called the settlement “a strong antitrust outcome.”
“More production, more choice, and guardrails that keep this industry competitive. I don’t think these two companies should merge, but that’s not something that we are focused on with our resolution here,” he said at a press conference in Los Angeles.
Paramount promised in the state settlement to bring more film production to the US – spending at least US$300 million more each year in domestic production – and adhere to US theatrical release quotas for five years.
The company will produce 30 movies in each of the first two years of the deal, and 32 movies in each of the following three years, Bonta said.
Each year, at least four of those films must be independent films and at least 20 per cent must be blockbusters. If it falls below that threshold, it will pay US$30 million per film, most of it into funds to support workers.
Paramount also promised not to raise rates on theatre operators for three years.
Under the settlement terms, Paramount will establish a news editorial independence board to ensure independence at the CBS and CNN networks.
Ellison thanked the states and California Governor Gavin Newsom for his support throughout the process.
“Our goal has always been to build a stronger Hollywood – one with more stories told, greater choice for consumers and stronger competition,” he said in a statement.
While Trump administration regulators cleared the deal, a coalition of 12 state attorneys-general, led by California’s Bonta, sued in July to block the merger, arguing it would reduce competition and create a media behemoth with the power to raise prices in movies and television.
The Writers Guild also sued to stop the deal, arguing it would decrease pay and worsen working conditions for film and TV writers.
The companies said earlier in 2026 the merger will mean US$6 billion in savings, through moves including cost cuts that would likely affect jobs across Hollywood as well as in the CNN and CBS newsrooms. The combined company is expected to hold US$80 billion in debt.
The settlement helps Paramount avoid a US$7 million-a-day “ticking fee” it would have owed Warner shareholders for each day the deal does not close past Sept 30.
Antitrust regulators in other jurisdictions globally, including the European Union and Britain, have already cleared the deal. REUTERS

What everyday Australians want political leaders to hear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
18:47:13 UTC
03:47:13 KST

What everyday Australians want political leaders to hear
Margaret* is a 61-year-old woman from Sydney who works hard to pay her rent and buy her groceries.
There is nothing extraordinary about her story. Her life is not exceptional. It is not news. That's the point.
But what she has to say — what she wants the political leaders in this country to hear — reflects what thousands of people across Australia have told ABC Your Say.
"I'm sure you already have lots of examples of people like [me]. Currently working two, sometimes three jobs. After rent is paid, I sometimes have $7 to live on for the coming fortnight. On a good fortnight I have a bit more and can pay off a bit of electricity and phone, buy panadol, tea and butter, and shout myself a coffee as a special treat.
"I honestly never thought that at 61years old I would be so frightened and despairing. I've had a great life and I am definitely one of the lucky ones. The future, however, is really grim."
Hearing from everyday Australians
For the past eight weeks, teams from across the ABC have been out and about across the country talking to people about what matters to them.
The issues people have raised with us are as diverse as this country is broad, but there is a consistent message that kept coming up.
Margaret asked us to protect her privacy for family reasons and because she is "embarrassed" by her situation. She was not alone.
Life feels hard and seems like it is getting harder. Many feel unheard by people in power and no longer trust those they elected to represent them to govern for them.
They want politicians and the media to listen.
We've heard from thousands of people online and spoken to hundreds more at weekend markets, sporting events, libraries, trivia nights, general stores and on footpaths as we've broadcast radio programs from street corners in country towns and regional cities.
ABC Your Say has reached deep into communities across Australia to ask three questions:
- What matters to you?
- What do you wish people in power understood more about your daily life?
- What do you love about where you live but what needs to be better?
Here are some of Australia's answers.
The man whose good job is no longer enough
Tyson is in his 30s living in outer suburban Perth.
"My wife and I both have multiple degrees [including post-grads] each, and stable jobs. We earn approximately $200k [pre-tax] between us, and are quite frugal with our money. Neither of us have ever even owned a credit card and the only debt we have is a mortgage between us.
"Typically, I would argue that we should be doing pretty well for ourselves, and while the opposite is not true for us, we are struggling pay cheque to pay cheque. When did this become normal? When did having two reasonable incomes from white-collar jobs become not enough?"
The mother still rebuilding after COVID-19
Sarah, a mum of three in her late 40s, is battling to make ends meet in suburban Melbourne.
"We are a family of five, a couple and three kids. Husband has his own small business and I work for government. Being in Melbourne, COVID lockdowns ruined our business and [we] haven't been able to build it back up.
"Six years later our mortgage is huge, we can't afford to do anything on weekends or go on any holidays or buy any clothes, and we can barely make payment of bills and mortgage and to buy groceries. We are building up debts left, right and centre.
"[I] am fully aware our problems pale in significance to others. Just making the point that it definitely feels like things have changed for the worse."
Housing your biggest worry
The stories we've heard have been thoughtful, funny, heartbreaking and inspiring.
The most dominant issues that people have wanted to talk about have been housing and the cost of living.
Across every location and every demographic group, the worry about where people are going to live is top of mind. The cost of housing, rental insecurity, homelessness, downsizing and the impact on social cohesion and community connection have dominated conversations and online submissions.
But people have told us the cost is more than financial.
The woman who feels priced out of spare time
Rosie* is in her 30s and lives in Canberra. She captured the point vividly.
"Housing gets covered as deposits, rates, supply. Living it, the real cost is time. You work the hours the housing demands, in the suburb the housing pushed you to, and what gets sacrificed is the ability to sit down with the people around you.
"Multiculturalism worked in this country when people had time to spend with people unlike themselves. Not policy time — ordinary time. Backyards, front steps, sport, the shops, someone's kitchen. That's how a stranger stops being a category and becomes a neighbour.
"We have spent 30 years pricing that time out of people's lives and now we're surprised that cohesion is fraying and asking what went wrong with our values.
"When people are exhausted and stretched and never in the same room, difference stops being interesting and starts being threatening. That's not a failure of tolerance. It's a failure of time. That's what I'd want people in power to understand."
What keeps us up at night
This loss of community connection was a strong theme that emerged from ABC Your Say.
Mixed into this conversation was an extremely potent topic about the reliance on technology and the loss of human interaction.
Our story on digital exclusion hit a nerve with many people who are frustrated with the complexity of life when everything requires a log-in (with long-forgotten passwords), or email or an app.
Other issues that are keeping people awake at night ranged from concern over international events in Gaza, Iran and our relationship with the USA to frustration over access to health care, climate change and the impact on the environment.
The state of our roads and transport, poor infrastructure planning, education standards and teacher burnout, domestic violence, crime and AI were also prominent issues.
While there was some commonality of concerns, each person has a unique perspective and many offered quite specific examples and solutions.
But one unifying theme was the persistent and consistent ask that our political leaders "do better", as well as frustration at the perception of self-interest.
Loading
Seeing the bright side
Despite the worries, people remain hopeful and grateful about life in Australia. Even those facing hardships were at pains to point out how fortunate they feel to live here.
Mitch, a young man from Sydney, provided insight from his generation.
"It is so easy to be ungrateful, to believe that everything is getting worse, and that things would be better if this or that was different.
"This negativity really distracts from the good, how much equality has improved, how the rare conflicts we have are so far removed from the mass bombings and millions of deaths in a war, and how as confusing and ridiculous as politics is, it at least works in a way that stops Australia from completely falling apart."
ABC Your Say has given us a powerful insight into the lives of the extraordinary "ordinary people" that call Australia home.
It has inspired our journalism and made us question our assumptions.
We will continue to listen to what you want to tell us, but it's appropriate that the last word goes to one of our ABC Your Say contributors, Chrissy Wilson of Boorloo, Perth, in Western Australia.
"It feels like much of the public conversation right now is dominated by fear, frustration and a sense that things are getting worse — cost-of-living pressures, housing challenges, distrust in institutions and concerns about the future.
"But I wonder if part of what we are experiencing is not simply decline, but an awakening. Rather than seeing this awareness as a reason for despair, perhaps it is an opportunity.
"Throughout history, meaningful change has often come when communities have come together, shared their experiences and imagined different possibilities.
"Local communities are already creating solutions — supporting each other, building connection, caring for the vulnerable, creating new models of participation and finding ways to respond to challenges that large systems alone cannot solve.
"The question I want to explore is: how do we harness this growing awareness and turn it into constructive action?
"How can governments, organisations and communities work together in ways that value lived experience, local knowledge and grassroots innovation?
"Perhaps this moment of uncertainty is also a moment of possibility — an opportunity for communities to reconnect, collaborate and build the future they want to see."
Want to have your say? Go to www.abc.net.au/yoursay
*Not her real name.

On September 11, an Iranian-backed militia in Iraq carried out an attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline.
This came as the Houthis also advanced toward Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Saudi Arabia has now faced a potential two-front conflict over the last 10 days. Now Saudi Arabia has sent officials to the UN General Assembly (UNGA). Riyadh has also been wondering whether it will get military support from the US.
What is happening is that the US has advanced a sale of F-35s to Saudi Arabia. However, if the sale proceeds, the 5th-generation warplanes won’t arrive in Saudi Arabia for years. Riyadh needs to decide what to do now.
The Houthis have continued their threats over the last week. They have been fortifying the positions they captured near Bab el-Mandeb; they are pushing propaganda against Saudi Arabia and launching attacks on the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia. They have even threatened Mecca. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia’s allies, Pakistan and Turkey, do not appear to be stepping up.
Saudi Arabia is wary of going it alone. Arab News noted on Saturday that “Yemeni government forces clashed with Houthi fighters on several fronts in Marib on Saturday, advancing on Al-Mashjah front west of the city and forcing the Houthis to retreat, military sources said.” The sources added that the Armed Forces destroyed several Houthi vehicles during the fighting, according to an Al Arabiya report.
Saudi Arabia left alone in its time of need

“The delegation includes Saudi Ambassador to the US Princess Reema bint Bandar, Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Adel Al-Jubeir, and King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Center Supervisor General Dr. Abdullah Al-Rabeeah, along with other officials.”

For two weeks, Trump had wrestled with whether to order US strikes on Houthi targets as the Iran-backed group intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia and made territorial gains in Yemen.”
The report, along with others, noted that the US has stepped back from strikes on the Houthis. This is important. Riyadh wants commitment. It has been fighting since 2015 in Yemen. Saudi Arabia has faced this dilemma before. In 2019, Iran attacked Saudi Arabia’s Abqaiq energy facility on the coast. This is similar to the September 11 attack on the East-West pipeline.
The message was clear both times. If Saudi Arabia responds, the attacks on strategic infrastructure will continue. Riyadh has more to lose than Iran or the Houthis or militias in Iraq. Saudi Arabia and US Central Command retaliated in July for militia attacks from Iraq. The attacks stopped for several weeks.
This big question for Riyadh at the UNGA is whether it can rally support and also work with Washington regarding the next steps in Yemen. The Houthis believe they are winning. Saudi Arabia will have to see how it can avoid a two-front conflict and also restore deterrence.

Qatar denies funding Hamas, says Israel oversaw Gaza aid transfers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
18:42:37 UTC
03:42:37 KST

Qatar has sharply rejected allegations that it transferred money to Hamas, accusing The New Yorker of relying on fabricated material in a report examining alleged Qatari influence involving advisers to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
“To be clear, Qatar’s assistance has been directed to Palestinian civilians in Gaza through mechanisms coordinated with the Israeli authorities and international partners,” Qatar’s International Media Office said. “Under previous aid mechanisms, all financial assistance, as well as goods such as food, medicine and fuel, passed through Israel before entering Gaza.”
The Qatari government said nothing was delivered without Israeli involvement and that the aid arrangements operated for years under successive Israeli governments and with the involvement of Israeli security agencies.
“If any funding reached Hamas, it had nothing to do with Qatar,” the statement said. Qatar argued that responsibility for any diversion would instead lie with Israel, which oversaw the aid arrangements under governments led by Netanyahu as well as former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, with the involvement of agencies including the Mossad intelligence service and Shin Bet domestic security agency.
Qatar, a wealthy Gulf Arab state and longtime U.S. partner that hosts a major American military base, has played a complicated role in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. It hosted senior Hamas political officials while also serving as a key mediator between Israel and Hamas. Before the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, Qatar provided hundreds of millions of dollars in assistance to Gaza under arrangements approved by Israel, which viewed the payments as a means of supporting Gaza’s economy and maintaining stability.
The latest dispute follows publication of a Sept. 19 New Yorker investigation into the scandal known in Israel as “Qatargate,” involving allegations that people close to Netanyahu performed work intended to improve Qatar’s image while working in or around the Prime Minister’s Office. The article also examined documents purporting to show Qatari payments involving Hamas.
Qatar said the allegations were part of a broader influence campaign targeting the Gulf state.
“In this instance, The New Yorker has chosen to give credibility to material that forms part of a wider disinformation campaign against Qatar,” the International Media Office said. It said Qatar had evidence that various parties, including elements of Israel’s far right, had for years created and circulated fabricated documents in an effort to implicate Doha.
Qatar described the information underlying the allegations as false and fabricated and said The New Yorker had been shown evidence before publication that disputed documents were not authentic. It said other news organizations had previously declined to publish the material after being presented with evidence challenging its authenticity.
“The piece reads more like an amateur blog than a report from a reputable publication like The New Yorker,” the Qatari statement said. “We reject these allegations in the strongest possible terms.”
Qatar said it was reviewing possible legal action over the allegations and accused those behind what it described as a disinformation campaign of seeking to undermine its role as a regional mediator.
Israeli intelligence warned Netanyahu about Qatari funds, investigation says
The dispute comes days after a separate investigation published by ynet and its parent newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, reported that Israeli intelligence agencies had warned Netanyahu beginning in 2019 that some money entering Gaza through the Qatari-backed arrangements was being diverted to Hamas’ military buildup.
The investigation reported that Military Intelligence and the Shin Bet provided Netanyahu with information indicating that some of the funds were reaching Hamas’ military wing, the Izzedine al-Qassam Brigades. Later intelligence assessments concluded that money originating through those channels accounted for 40% to 50% of the military wing’s budget, according to the report.
The investigation also reported that Israeli intelligence subsequently discovered an additional, covert channel through which money was reaching Hamas’ military wing and that Egypt separately warned Israel about the issue. It said Netanyahu nevertheless continued the policy of allowing Qatari money into Gaza.
The reporting adds to longstanding scrutiny of Israel’s pre-Oct. 7 policy toward Gaza. Netanyahu’s governments permitted and encouraged Qatari assistance to enter the territory as part of a broader policy aimed at maintaining economic stability and deterring renewed fighting with Hamas, which seized control of Gaza in 2007.
A senior intelligence official who worked on investigating the alleged diversion of the Qatari funds told Yedioth Ahronoth and ynet that military intelligence had obtained evidence of transfers to Hamas’ military wing and passed it to Netanyahu.
“We had evidence of official transfers,” the official said, referring to money reaching the Izzedine al-Qassam Brigades. “We saw it, documented it and passed it to the prime minister. He did nothing; he continued the policy.”
Netanyahu’s office rejected the investigation, calling it a collection of recycled allegations that had previously been disproved and accusing his political opponents of raising them ahead of elections.
The Prime Minister’s Office said the security establishment had supported the Qatari assistance and determined that it was intended for civilian and humanitarian purposes and would help maintain calm in Gaza.
Netanyahu’s office also said that when fighting erupted between Israel and Hamas in May 2021, during the conflict Israel called Operation Guardian of the Walls, Netanyahu ordered the Qatari cash-payment mechanism halted immediately. It said the subsequent government led by Bennett and Lapid restored Qatari assistance.
The precise nature of the arrangements changed over time. Earlier Qatari aid included cash brought into Gaza, while subsequent mechanisms shifted toward fuel purchases and assistance to needy families administered through international organizations.

Ukraine Knocks Out Over 45% of Russia’s Projected Refining Capacity
Unknown

2026-09-21
18:40:31 UTC
03:40:31 KST

- Category

Ukraine Knocks Out Over 45% of Russia’s Projected Refining Capacity
Ukrainian retaliatory strikes on Russian oil refineries, culminating in an attack on the Gazpromneft-Moscow Oil Refinery, have disabled more than 45% of Russia’s design refining capacity, according to Ukraine’s General Staff on September 21.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The figure appeared in a General Staff summary of strikes carried out between September 14 and 20 against military and economic targets inside Russia and in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories.
The General Staff framed the campaign as “an exercise of Ukraine’s inherent right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter,” aimed at reducing Russia’s military and economic potential.
The General Staff reported that the operation struck several major refining and defense-industrial sites:
- The Syzran Oil Refinery in the Samara region, where the AVT-6 primary crude distillation unit and tank farm were hit overnight on September 15;
- The Slavneft-YANOS Oil Refinery in Yaroslavl, with an annual capacity of about 15 million metric tons, where the AVT-3 distillation unit was hit overnight on September 17;
- The Gazpromneft-Moscow Oil Refinery in Moscow, where the AVT-6 unit, the integrated crude-processing unit and the isomerization unit were hit on September 20;
- The Atlant Aero plant in Taganrog, Rostov region, which produces Molniya strike and reconnaissance drones and components for Orion UAVs.
Following the Moscow retaliatory strike, the General Staff said cumulative damage had disabled more than 45% of Russia’s design refining capacity and contributed to shortages of high-quality fuel, including a sharp decline in the production of Euro-5 gasoline and diesel.
The damage has coincided with growing pressure on Russia’s domestic fuel market.
Gasoline rationing has returned across multiple Russian regions in recent months, with purchase limits, restrictions on filling portable containers, and odd-even refueling systems introduced in some areas as supplies tightened.
Independent data also point to a substantial decline in Russian refining activity. The International Energy Agency said refinery throughput fell to 3.8 million barrels per day in June, roughly 30% below the previous year and its lowest level in more than two decades.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that Russian gasoline output was about 20% lower than in 2025, while diesel production had fallen by nearly 30%.

Photos: Gaza’s children return to class in tents and ruins
Unknown
