Trump administration prepares sanctions against International Criminal Court, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
17:11:42 UTC
02:11:42 KST

US President Donald Trump's administration has prepared sanctions against the entire International Criminal Court and plans to announce them soon, two sources familiar with the matter said on Sunday, a move that would step up its attack on the global tribunal that prosecutes war crimes and genocide worldwide.
The ICC was established in 2002 by the international community to prosecute war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. It asserts jurisdiction only if a member state is unable or unwilling to prosecute atrocities itself.
The United States has never been a member.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in July announced a campaign to isolate the court, calling on other countries to withdraw from the tribunal. Washington has imposed sanctions on a number of ICC judges and prosecutors but has so far held off from imposing sanctions on the court itself, although the move has long been considered as one of the options.
The State Department did not respond to a request for comment.
Sanctions may be announced during UNGA summit
Sanctions against the court have been prepared, the sources said, even though the exact timing of an announcement remained unclear. The Wall Street Journal cited officials who said the decision could be finalized as soon as this week during the United Nations General Assembly meeting.
Targeting the entire organization directly, as well as entities that cooperate with it, could severely undermine the court's work.
Any entity-wide sanctions imposed by the US Treasury would prohibit US citizens and companies from providing funds, goods, or services to the court without a license from the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). Banks often over-comply with such US sanctions because they depend on access to the American financial system.
Among the court's operations that could be affected by sanctions against the entire organization are the purchasing of IT services and insurance, the hiring of investigators, and conducting everyday financial transactions, such as paying dozens of American employees, the ICC's registrar and president have warned.

Shooting attack at Ontario synagogue on evening of Yom Kippur, Canadian PM condemns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
17:10:59 UTC
02:10:59 KST

One police officer is in critical condition after exchanging gunfire with a suspect in a shooting near Belleville’s Sons of Jacob synagogue in Canada during Yom Kippur services on Sunday evening, according to Ontario’s Special Investigations Unit (SIU).
The suspected shooter was identified as 29-year-old Sean Ward from the nearby city of Quinte West by Belleville Police Deputy Chief Sherry Meeks.
Ward, who was armed with a shotgun, was shot by a police officer at the scene and is in life-threatening condition. No one inside the synagogue at the time of the attack was wounded.
Meeks highlighted that while the shooter’s motive has not yet been determined by law enforcement, the attack has had a significant impact on Belleville’s Jewish community.
“We recognize the concern and uncertainty many may be feeling, particularly given that this occurred near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue during one of the holiest days in the Jewish faith,” she said. “Let me be very clear. Antisemitism, hate, and violence have no place in our community.”
At a press conference on Monday, SIU spokesperson Kristy Denette stated that an estimated 20-30 total shots were fired and that bullets struck the synagogue in addition to homes, a police vehicle, and civilian vehicles in the area.
Denette said that a team consisting of multiple investigators has been dispatched to investigate the shooting, canvass for witnesses, and look for footage of the incident.
According to Denette, a parallel investigation into the suspected shooter and his motive will be conducted by the Belleville Police Service.
Meeks added that a heightened police presence and increased patrols have been ordered across Belleville, including around places of worship in the aftermath of the attack.
The Toronto Police Service announced that, in light of the shooting, police patrols have also increased around Toronto synagogues.
Synagogue president recounts shooting to CNN
Synagogue President Norm Weddum told CNN that the officer, who had been hired to protect the synagogue during Yom Kippur services, had saved the lives of everyone who had attended the evening services and that the building had been hit with multiple bullets.
The officer was parked near the synagogue in an unmarked vehicle, noticed the shooter approaching the building, and then made contact with the shooter, Weddum told CNN.
Weddum said he heard a series of bangs as he welcomed congregants to the evening services and went to investigate.
“That’s when we heard it again - ‘bang, bang, bang ’-and they were very loud this time so we realized it was definitely shots being fired,” he recounted to CNN. “We all ran back, I closed the doors of the auditorium, and I yelled out ‘everybody get down.’”
Weddum added that once the gunshots stopped, he exited the synagogue, where a heavy police presence had gathered. He said that police cordoned off the area and began investigating the shooting.
Canadian PM Carney, Israel's Foreign Ministry condemns shooting
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney condemned the shooting in a post on X/Twitter on Monday, and vowed that his government will do everything it can to hold the shooter accountable to the fullest extent of the law.
“Jewish people must be able to worship safely. To live free, open, proud Jewish lives,” Carney asserted. “ My thoughts are with the injured officer and his family, and the entire Jewish community.”
Israel’s Foreign Ministry decried the attack as an escalation of the ongoing antisemitism crisis in Canada and called for changes to be made to protect the Jewish community from further violence.
“Our thoughts are with the police officer who acted with remarkable courage and was wounded in the line of duty. We pray for his full and speedy recovery,” the Foreign Ministry said in a social media statement.
The Foreign Ministry continued to cite unaddressed public incitement and anti-Israel policies as factors that fuel the spread of antisemitism.
“Israel stands in solidarity with Canada’s Jewish community, which faces an increasingly threatening reality,” the Foreign Ministry added.
Israel’s ambassador to Canada, Iddo Moed, labeled the shooting as a terror attack and called for immediate action to protect the Jewish community.
“Thanks to the bravery of the police, lives have been saved,” Moed said on X/Twitter. “However, so much more must be done immediately to protect the lives of the Jewish community!”
He added that Israel has repeatedly offered Canada support in efforts to combat antisemitism, and will continue to provide any assistance required.

Türkiye's preparations to host and chair the 31st UN Climate Change Conference, or COP31, are taking center stage in New York this week as world leaders gather for the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
Posters promoting Türkiye's COP31 presidency and featuring President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have been displayed on the Turkish House, or Turkevi, Türkiye's diplomatic complex in Manhattan, under the theme "The Future of the World is in Türkiye."
Promotional vehicles carrying COP31-themed digital displays have also been circulating through New York, including Times Square and routes connecting the area with the UN headquarters.
Türkiye is using the UN General Assembly week to showcase its preparations for the conference and promote its climate agenda ahead of the Antalya gathering in November.
Erdogan is scheduled to take part in a high-level climate meeting organized by UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Wednesday, where he will provide information about Türkiye's preparations to host COP31.
First lady Emine Erdogan, who chairs the UN Zero Waste Advisory Board, is also scheduled to participate in programs related to Türkiye's climate and sustainability initiatives during the UN General Assembly week.
COP31 exhibition at Turkevi

The exhibition, titled "Seeing the Unseen, Hearing the Unheard: SCOPE as a Vision of the Future," will combine artificial intelligence, sound, mapping technologies, immersive displays, and art installations.
Visitors will encounter an interactive installation featuring Caretta, Türkiye's COP31 mascot, as well as a photography experience drawing on the traditional Turkish art of ebru.
Another section will feature a three-dimensional model of the COP31 venue in Antalya. A mapping presentation will be used to illustrate the layout and visitor experience planned for the conference site.
The exhibition will also present Türkiye's COP31 Action Agenda through digital displays.
Other installations will focus on the effects of climate change on oceans, agriculture, soil, and the global climate system. A final section, titled "LET'S COP – Türkiye's Climate Journey," will showcase Türkiye's climate-related work through a large LED wall.
A separate COP31 exhibition will be held at Glasshouse in New York, featuring four presentations focused on climate and nature.
The exhibition will present Türkiye's climate vision and Action Agenda before highlighting works by artists Ilhami Atalay and Ekrem Sahin.
Atalay's "Return of the Birds – Tawaf" will explore the collective movement of birds and the concept of gathering around a common center. Sahin's "Sound of Water" photography exhibition will examine climate change through water.
The program will conclude with a live paper marbling (ebru) performance by artist Garip Ay.
Turkish Minister of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change and COP31 President Murat Kurum is also holding a series of meetings in New York as Türkiye steps up preparations for the Antalya conference.

What will happen to gasoline and diesel prices in the fall, and will the surge in fuel demand lead to higher prices?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:02:54 EEST
02:02:54 KST

What will happen to gasoline and diesel prices in the fall, and will the surge in fuel demand lead to higher prices?
Kyiv • UNN
A-95 gasoline costs UAH 93.33, while diesel costs UAH 98.55 per liter. An expert predicts high, volatile prices and a risk of diesel becoming more expensive.
The Ukrainian fuel market entered autumn with a sharp rise in prices. As of September 18, the average price of A-95 gasoline reached UAH 93.33 per liter, while diesel fuel cost UAH 98.55 per liter. In some networks, diesel has already crossed the psychological threshold of UAH 100. An additional risk factor could be panic-driven demand if drivers and businesses simultaneously begin building up stocks amid fears of new Russian strikes on fuel infrastructure.
What is happening in the domestic fuel market, and what prices should drivers prepare for in the coming month? UNN asked fuel market expert Leonid Kosianchuk.
The energy expert acknowledges that there are currently no grounds for optimistic forecasts regarding the situation on the Ukrainian fuel market, and that the difficulties are indeed real. They are related to the fact that our country currently receives almost 90% of its petroleum products from Europe.
"The situation there (on the European market — editor's note) is very complicated. Especially considering that Saudi Aramco — a state-owned oil company — announced that, as far as supplies to the European market for October are concerned, they will either suspend them or limit them," the expert clarified.
According to Kosianchuk, ORLEN Lietuva could serve as an alternative to Saudi Aramco. It operates the only oil refinery in the Baltic countries, the Mažeikiai Refinery, as well as oil pipelines and the terminal in Būtingė. The company is one of the main suppliers of gasoline and diesel fuel in Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia. Its capacity could help cover certain shortages and prevent the crisis from deepening.
Diesel is becoming more expensive faster than gasoline: what is behind this
The most tense situation has emerged precisely with diesel fuel. In mid-September, its European quotations rose to a record $1,644 per ton. In just five days, the increase amounted to about $172 per ton, or approximately UAH 7.7 per liter when converted. The price later fell back to $1,553 per ton, but this level remains high nonetheless.
Fuel market expert Leonid Kosianchuk, in an exclusive comment to UNN, drew attention specifically to this unusual gap between gasoline and diesel.
"For the first time in all my many years of work in this market, we are seeing diesel fuel cost almost UAH 10 more than gasoline," he said.
Actual prices at Ukrainian gas stations confirm this: on September 21, the difference between the average price of A-95 gasoline and diesel fuel was more than UAH 5 per liter. Moreover, last week some major networks kept diesel at UAH 99.8–99.9, while one network had already set the price at UAH 100 per liter.
Leonid Kosianchuk explains that the reason for this trend is not a shortage of fuel directly at Ukrainian gas stations.
"Ukraine is heavily dependent on imports of finished petroleum products, so the domestic price responds to European quotations, resource availability, logistics costs, and risks to supply routes," the expert explained.
Why prices may rise even after quotations decline
To answer this question, which confounds many Ukrainians trying to understand the issue, it is worth noting that retail prices respond to the external market with a delay. The fuel being sold to drivers at gas stations today may have been purchased when European quotations were at their peak. Therefore, even after they decline, operators continue for some time to receive more expensive batches and pass these costs on to the price displayed on the signs. The Ukrainian market observed such a situation in the second half of September: external quotations had already moved away from their highs, but Ukrainian storage tanks continued to be filled with more expensive supplies.
That is why a quick return to summer prices should not be expected, although as of September 21 there were already signs of some "cooling" in the wholesale market. Demand is currently weak, and some traders are selling supplies below the calculated replacement cost. However, new batches of diesel fuel remain expensive at current European prices.
Commenting on the situation, Leonid Kosyanchuk emphasizes that the issue of resource availability and the issue of its cost now need to be considered separately.
"There is no reason today to say that there will be no diesel fuel or gasoline. However, there is a problem with pricing. The main issue is not whether fuel will be available. The main issue is the price at which it will be offered," the expert explained.
He particularly emphasized that logistics costs, as well as insurance and security risks, are currently added to the external price of fuel. Due to problems along certain routes, traders are forced to change their supply routes. For example, using an alternative route through Moldova can add approximately $25–30 per tonne to the cost of the resource. Additional costs also arise because of delays at the borders or the need to reload the fuel.
Could panic buying push prices even higher?
Several days earlier, society reacted sharply to a call by Serhii Kuiun, director of the A-95 Consulting Group, to build up fuel reserves. One of the reasons was a possible shortage amid the situation on the global oil market and the intensification of russian armed forces’ attacks on gas stations. However, the expert later clarified that he was primarily referring to possible local disruptions caused by Russian strikes on fuel infrastructure. In his assessment, a total shortage like the one in spring 2022 is not expected at present. However, if a large number of consumers simultaneously go to gas stations and begin filling their tanks and additional containers to capacity, this could temporarily alter the balance. Stocks at individual stations would run out faster, forcing operators to urgently transfer resources between regions or purchase additional batches. If external quotations and logistics develop unfavorably, this could accelerate increases in retail prices.
Moreover, Kuiun describes preventing such a scenario as one of the purposes of building up reserves: the reserve should help weather a possible short-term disruption in supply without a simultaneous influx of consumers at gas stations. He stresses that there is currently enough fuel on the market, but does not rule out local disruptions.
However, expert Leonid Kosyanchuk категорically disagrees with him on this point. He explains that even before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the supply of fuel on the domestic market significantly exceeded demand for drivers. Unlike Finland, where gas stations are located at fairly considerable distances from one another and the number of fuel operators is limited, in our country dozens of networks offered and continue to offer their services through an extensive system of gas stations both in cities and outside them.
Therefore, the main near-term risk for truck and passenger-car drivers lies not in a physical shortage of gasoline or diesel fuel caused by the enemy destroying several dozen more gas stations. Difficulties may arise in other areas.
The first is an increase in the price of fuel for retail consumers because the cost of storing fuel in depots located outside Ukraine will be factored into it. Against the backdrop of intensified Russian attacks on infrastructure, operators are increasingly inclined to store significant reserves of gasoline and diesel in depots located in countries bordering Ukraine. Several months of renting such a hub cannot fail to affect the final cost of fuel at gas stations.
Secondly, according to Leonid Kosyanchuk, difficulties may arise with the timely delivery of gasoline and diesel fuel to Ukraine. Mobilization into the army has created a labor shortage in the field of drivers as well. It is currently quite difficult to find a man with a driver's license of the appropriate category and practical experience who could be entrusted with driving a fuel tanker. Involving men aged 60+ in this work could be dangerous for them themselves. After all, many people at this age already have chronic illnesses and may not be physically able to endure days of waiting in a fuel tanker's cab at the border, followed by a long journey carrying a high-risk cargo. Therefore, if the leading players in the fuel market fail to resolve the "staffing issue" in the near future, Ukrainians may soon face a fuel shortage due to delays in supplies.
What to expect from fuel prices in the fall
As Leonid Kosyanchuk explained in an exclusive comment to UNN, the baseline scenario for the coming weeks is the continuation of high and highly volatile prices. Diesel fuel remains at the greatest risk of further increases. If European quotations rise again, the UAH 100-per-liter mark may appear not just at individual gas stations, but at a significantly larger number of them. Market participants recorded potential for a further increase in retail diesel prices even after European prices retreated from their peak levels. If, however, the "retreat" in the external market continues and supply routes operate steadily, the increase in Ukraine may slow down or stop once networks sell through their more expensive stocks. However, an immediate price reduction should not be expected: retail prices respond to changes in cost with a time lag.
The situation with gasoline is somewhat calmer, although there is still little room for a sharp decline here either. Diesel remains more vulnerable because of the more expensive European supply and its greater sensitivity to disruptions in deliveries.
At the same time, according to the expert, fuel businesses and ordinary drivers should not place too much hope in assistance from the state, which will most likely not intervene in pricing policy in any way. This differs from European countries, which are reducing the tax burden on fuel in the face of the threat of an energy crisis.
Recall
On September 17, Ukrnafta and SOCAR raised fuel prices twice.

The Government is aiming to bring forward proposals for new defence readiness legislation later in this Parliament, but has not set a specific date for introducing the measures.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard provided the update in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Stuart Anderson, who asked when the Defence Readiness Bill would be presented to Parliament. Pollard said the Government is examining what additional legal powers may be required to prepare the country for a major crisis or conflict, following a recommendation in the Strategic Defence Review.
He said: “Defence Readiness legislation is being considered to ensure the Government has the powers it needs to keep the UK safe in crisis or war, as recommended in the Strategic Defence Review.”
The legislation has yet to reach the stage where ministers can provide a firm timetable. Instead, the MOD says detailed policy work is continuing to determine precisely what powers are required and what their wider implications would be.
Pollard said: “We are aiming to deliver legislative proposals later this Parliament. It will take time to develop the detailed policy requirements, understand their implications and establish what new legislation is required.”
That wording leaves both the detailed contents and timing of the proposed legislation under development. It also indicates that the Government has not yet concluded exactly which elements of its defence readiness plans will require new primary legislation.
Any eventual legislation will also have to compete for Parliamentary time.
Pollard added: “As is standard with the legislative process, any future legislation will be brought forward when Parliamentary time allows.”
The proposed measures stem from the Strategic Defence Review’s focus on improving the ability of the state, Armed Forces, industry and wider society to respond to a serious security crisis or war. The precise powers to be included have not yet been published. The MOD says officials are working across government on potential measures, with further engagement expected once that work is sufficiently developed.

Tato Architects completes charred timber-clad home in Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:30:46 UTC

Tato Architects completes charred timber-clad home in Japan
Charred-timber cladding is contrasted with warm plywood-lined interiors at House in Mibu, a home in Tochigi Prefecture, Japan, completed by local studio Tato Architects.
The 108-square-metre home was designed for a couple and their three children in the backyard of the client's parental home, tucked off a residential street in the town of Mibu.
As the site needed to accommodate access to an existing garage and workshop, Kobe-based Tato Architects aimed to balance "enclosure and openness" in its design.
According to the studio, this is reflected in the final layout where the first floor overhangs on one side, and the ground floor is sunk 500 millimetres below ground and partially topped with a sloped green roof.
"The core concept is what Dutch architect Aldo van Eyck called the 'in-between' – a realm where enclosure and openness are experienced at once," studio founder Yo Shimada told Dezeen.
"The challenge was to add a whole house without making the yard feel crowded or cutting off the life already flowing through it. Rather than treating these as constraints, we let them shape the building," Shimada continued.
"We sank the living room into the ground and planted its roof with grass: sinking into the earth encloses, touching the earth opens, and the two appear as faces of a single operation."
House in Mibu is entered beneath the overhang of the first floor, where a welcome area with a cloakroom and bathroom steps down into a sunken living, dining and kitchen area.
Full-height windows wrap this lower space to the west, aiming to emphasise its close relationship to the ground while offering views into the neighbouring workshop.
A pair of timber and green-painted steel staircases lead up through a rectilinear void to the home's first floor, where the bedrooms are organised on either side of a raised, loft-like space that can serve as a study or guest room.
The lines of sight created by these stepped levels define the home's interiors, along with walls and ceilings lined entirely in lauan plywood, which Shimada chose for its ability to "record use and age gracefully".
"Sitting in the living room, the ground of the garden spreads out almost at eye level, so family members working in the yard and those inside exchange glances across a slight shift in height," Shimada explained.
"The first floor is the counterpart: a nest-like composition of small rooms – three children's rooms and a bedroom – linked by two staircases, with a loft raised 690 millimetres above the floor that connects the rooms and doubles as a desk or a place to sleep."
Outside, the home is clad in planks of charred cedar and finished with a corrugated metal roof, chosen to nod to the character of the workshop building.
Other homes in Japan recently completed by Tato Architects include a dwelling with similarly open interiors and silver-painted ceilings that help maximise daylight on a compact plot, and a skinny home that is combined with a ceramics studio.
The photography is courtesy of Tato Architects.

26 septembre 2026 - Seul le prononcé fait foi
Déclaration du Président de la République à son arrivée à Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon.
Emmanuel MACRON
Bonjour, heureux de vous retrouver.

Il a évoqué notamment l’essor de secteurs stratégiques comme le spatial, la pêche, le numérique ou l’économie bleue.
À Miquelon, le Président de la République a abordé les effets du changement climatique sur le territoire, alors que le recul du trait de côte transforme déjà l’île.
Revoir le discours du Président sur le devenir de l'archipel :
Ce déplacement a permis également de mettre en valeur la place singulière de Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon dans son environnement nord-américain. Seul territoire français d’Amérique du Nord, l’archipel constitue un point d’ancrage territorial, humain, économique et culturel de la France dans la région.
À l’occasion de ce déplacement, le Président de la République a reçu le Premier ministre du Canada, Mark Carney. Il s’agit de la première visite officielle d’un Premier ministre canadien dans l’archipel, symbole de la force de la relation qui unit nos deux pays.
Les deux dirigeants ont échangé sur les moyens d'approfondir les liens entre l’archipel et le Canada, à faciliter les échanges et à soutenir son développement, notamment dans les domaines économique et humain.
La France et le Canada partagent les mêmes valeurs de liberté, de démocratie, d’État de droit et de respect de la souveraineté des nations, ainsi qu’une même ambition : travailler ensemble pour renforcer leur capacité à décider et à agir par eux-mêmes.
Revoir la déclaration conjointe :
20 septembre 2026 - Seul le prononcé fait foi
Déclaration du Président de la République aux côtés du Premier ministre du Canada à Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon.
Emmanuel MACRON
Monsieur le Premier ministre, cher Mark,
Madame la ministre,
Mesdames les ambassadrices,
Monsieur le préfet,
Mesdames et Messieurs les parlementaires,
Monsieur le président,
Messieurs les maires,
Mesdames et Messieurs, en vos grades et qualités,
Mesdames et Messieurs de la presse,

Bienvenue, Monsieur le Premier ministre. Bienvenue à Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon. C’est une immense fierté pour nous tous de vous accueillir dans cette terre française d’Amérique du Nord : notre République, votre continent. C’est le premier déplacement officiel d’un Premier ministre canadien à Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon. Votre visite aujourd’hui, votre présence et les échanges que nous avons pu avoir marquent d’ores et déjà l’histoire. J’y vois, au fond, le symbole d’une conviction partagée : celle que notre relation ne se construit pas seulement depuis Paris ou Ottawa, mais aussi dans nos territoires et, en l’occurrence, dans ce territoire qui fait de nous des voisins.
Ici, 25 kilomètres de mer seulement nous séparent des côtes de Terre-Neuve. C’est notamment par cette proximité que le Canada et la France ont noué des liens profonds. Par une histoire partagée, d’abord : celle de pêcheurs, de marins, de familles qui, de génération en génération, circulent entre l’archipel et Terre-Neuve. Votre présence témoigne de la solidité de cette relation ancienne qui unit nos deux pays, de cette communauté de valeurs, d’intérêts et de destin que nous avons forgée au fil du temps. Car oui, le Canada et la France portent le même regard sur la période que nous traversons. C’est ce qui donne aussi à votre présence aujourd’hui un caractère tout singulier. Oui, nous croyons ensemble que nos pays sont deux grandes nations indépendantes et qui veulent le rester. Nous croyons, l’un et l’autre, dans la démocratie, l’État de droit, le respect du droit international, le commerce libre et équitable, la science sur laquelle reposent nos décisions et l’autonomie stratégique que nous défendons. C’est ce qui unit très profondément le Canada et la France, le Canada et l’Union européenne.
C’est pourquoi nous soutenons hautement cet agenda de rapprochement, dans cette « alliance du futur » que vous avez nommée, en tant qu’État associé, comme l’a dit la présidente de la Commission, comme membre à part entière d’une Communauté politique européenne à laquelle vous nous avez fait l’amitié de venir, il y a quelques mois, à Erevan : cette coalition des indépendants à laquelle nous croyons l’un et l’autre. La place que le Canada occupe au sein de la coalition des volontaires que nous avons bâtie pour l’Ukraine, les nombreux partenariats qui sont déjà les nôtres et tout ce que nous allons renforcer le montrent ô combien. Votre présence aujourd’hui vient, en quelque sorte, marquer une étape supplémentaire de ce rapprochement, dans la période qui est la nôtre, et de cette volonté d’agir ensemble. Alors oui, nous serons ensemble, l’un et l’autre, dans quelques jours à New York, pour défendre le même agenda lorsqu’il s’agit de la Palestine, de la protection de nos enfants face aux réseaux sociaux ou à l’intelligence artificielle, de la régulation de l’intelligence artificielle. Sur tous ces dossiers, comme sur l’Ukraine, nous sommes côte à côte. Mais, en étant ici, à Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, au fond, nous construisons un caractère encore plus concret à ce rapprochement. Ici, nous sommes déjà forts de trente ans de coopération régionale. Depuis 1996, la commission mixte réunit les provinces atlantiques canadiennes et Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon. Nous voulons que cette commission aille plus loin.
Mais, ensemble, avec Monsieur le Premier ministre, nous voulons donner un nouvel élan. Nous souhaitons évidemment travailler avec nos amis canadiens afin de pouvoir prochainement proposer à l’archipel de nouvelles possibilités en matière de formation professionnelle, en particulier appliquée au domaine de la pêche, ou d’enseignement supérieur. J’ai déjà demandé que le ministre de l’Enseignement supérieur accompagne les étudiants de Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon qui souhaitent suivre leurs études dans les universités canadiennes, en prenant en charge le différentiel des droits d’inscription. Nous avons aussi acté plusieurs rapprochements.
Mais ce que nous avons surtout décidé, c’est qu’ensemble, en lien très étroit avec la collectivité et ses élus, nous allons demander à nos deux gouvernements de travailler à un rapprochement profond entre nos deux pays : en matière de pêche, de sécurité et de missions communes, d’énergie, dans tous les domaines où nous pouvons trouver un agenda qui soit positif pour le Canada et pour la France, qui soit pertinent pour Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon et pour votre pays.
Une page difficile a été écrite, chacun ici le sait, en 1992, et elle a traumatisé Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon. Vous n’étiez pas aux responsabilités. Je n’étais pas aux responsabilités.
Le cours du monde contemporain et votre présence aujourd’hui nous imposent d’en ouvrir une nouvelle. C’est celle que nous allons écrire. C’est celle aussi que nous voulons écrire à travers les grands projets d’avenir. Par les connexions et les câbles sous-marins, pour lesquels le partenariat entre la France et le Canada a du sens, ici en particulier. En matière de spatiale, où le partenariat est essentiel et où nous voulons aussi, évidemment, le déployer ici. Et en matière de climat, qui sera un axe fort de notre partenariat. En effet, dans l’Atlantique Nord, les bouleversements sont déjà là. Les océans se réchauffent, les écosystèmes évoluent, les activités de pêche et les populations sont contraintes de s’adapter. Ces changements sont visibles. C’est pourquoi aussi nous renforcerons la coopération entre nos services météorologiques, pour mieux anticiper les événements extrêmes et prévenir les risques. Nous approfondirons également notre action en matière de systèmes d’alerte précoce, dans le cadre de l’initiative CREWS. Et enfin, nous annonçons aujourd’hui la création du Forum de recherche polaire Canada-France, qui sera organisé alternativement dans nos deux pays et dont la première édition se tiendra ici, à Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon. Le Premier ministre et moi-même avons également parlé de nos économies, de nos liens bilatéraux, de tout ce en quoi nous croyons et de tout ce que nous voulons faire avancer : en matière de défense, de ressources critiques, de minerais critiques, de terres rares, d’énergie, de quantique, d’intelligence artificielle et de technologies maritimes. Et à nous de transformer tout cela en projets, en investissements et en emplois. Je me félicite, à cet égard, du contrat signé vendredi entre Aldoria et le ministère canadien des Travaux publics et des Services gouvernementaux, pour la fourniture de données de surveillance de l’espace au bénéfice de la division spatiale des Forces armées canadiennes. Je salue également le protocole d’entente adopté à l’occasion de cette visite entre CCI France et la Chambre de commerce du Canada.
Et puis, je l’évoquais, nous devons aussi œuvrer ensemble pour sécuriser nos approvisionnements énergétiques et maîtriser les prix du carburant, sujet ô combien sensible aujourd’hui pour la France. C’est la situation au Proche et au Moyen-Orient, évidemment, qui crée cette tension. Les projets canadiens de gaz naturel liquéfié peuvent contribuer — et sont importants pour notre Europe — et contribueront à ouvrir de nouvelles perspectives entre nos deux pays. Nous avons, là aussi, entamé une discussion bilatérale avec Monsieur le Premier ministre sur des projets très concrets. Je veux le remercier d’avoir si vite répondu à notre demande concernant les produits les plus sensibles, afin de pouvoir bâtir des solutions ensemble, le Canada étant un grand pays producteur. Nous continuerons cette discussion dans le cadre bilatéral, ainsi que dans le cadre d’un G7 consacré au sujet énergétique, qui sera très prochainement organisé.
Cher Mark, à Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, la mer est une réalité quotidienne pour celles et ceux qui font vivre ce territoire. Elle est aussi ce qui nous relie. Elle est aussi ce qui fait du Canada non seulement cette puissance qui veut aujourd’hui se rapprocher de l’Europe, mais ce pays si voisin de nous, Français. C’est pourquoi vous avez réparé, au fond, une aberration de l’histoire : qu’il n’y ait jamais eu auparavant de Premier ministre canadien foulant ce sol. C’est une immense fierté pour nous d’être là. C’est une immense fierté que les projets concrets que nous avons décidé d’accompagner et, surtout, d’avoir décidé ensemble d’ouvrir ce nouveau chapitre, ce nouvel élan pour la relation bilatérale et pour Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon. Votre présence ici nous engage et nous poursuivrons.
Vive Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon !
Vive le Canada !
Et vive la France !
À l’issue de cette visite de trois jours, le chef de l'État a répondu aux questions de Saint-Pierre-et Miquelon la 1re. Il est revenu sur les attentes des habitants et a détaillé ses engagements pour l’archipel.

Sarah Bseiso: A Gaza survivor’s story of burns, loss and healing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21

Breadcrumb
Sarah Bseiso: A Gaza survivor’s account of the burns, loss and healing endured during Israel’s genocide
Sarah Bseiso was 17 when she was severely burned during Israel's genocide in Gaza in 2023.
She arrived in the United States (US) for treatment about a year and a half ago and, with support from Heal Palestine, now lives in New Jersey with her mother and sister, having since undergone a large number of operations.
Before the genocide, she was in her final year of secondary school and remembers the moment Israeli violence reached her family home as unlike anything she had experienced before.
"It was not like any other war we had known before," she recalled.
Sarah was inside her grandfather's house when she heard drones and Israeli aircraft around them. Her brothers Ahmad and Hamoud were outside, and when Ahmad called to say that Hamoud was scared, she went outside to calm him down and hugged him. On their way back to the house, she felt something hit her.
"I felt something very hot hit me and push me several steps forward. Then the kitchen caught fire completely, and the flames began burning everything," she explained.
She continued, "While I was trying to understand what was happening, I noticed that my leather shoe had burnt, as had my feet and my medical glasses. I don't know why I forgot that Hamoud was with me and that we were inside the flames."
In sharing this, Sarah noted that she initially thought Ahmad had pulled Hamoud away, before realising that the fire had come from Ahmad’s side and the missile had left his whole body “riddled with holes.”
As she screamed, her father pulled her from the fire, but both of her brothers, Ahmad, 16, and Hamoud, eight, died in the attack, with Ahmad dying immediately and Hamoud succumbing days later to his injuries, fourth-degree burns and smoke inhalation.
Sarah recalls hearing Hamoud's voice and moans from a nearby room while she was suffering from her own burns. No one was able to help him because of the extent of his injuries, the siege and the bombardment.
Her father risked his life under bombardment to take her to a nearby hospital, where doctors gave her fluids to replace some of what she had lost, but they were unable to provide the treatment she needed.
As Sarah explained, “Treatment and medication were unavailable, and the hospital was under siege.”
Sarah eventually travelled to the US as part of a medical evacuation via Egypt, where she stayed briefly. She spent her first three and a half months in intensive care and underwent numerous operations.
"I don't know how many operations there were. Work is still being done to restore my skin, and the movement of my fingers is limited. Some of the operations are to improve the skin," she told The New Arab.
The pain of healing
After a year and a half of treatment, Sarah's recovery remains ongoing. Alongside the physical effects of her injuries, she has had to deal with the deaths of her brothers, the loss of her home and the separation of her family.
She recalls how the Israeli army took over their home for a period, in addition to targeting it. Family members were also dispersed outside Gaza, while the uncertainty of not knowing whether she could reach relatives in the territory remained difficult.
"It is a difficult matter, especially when the internet goes down in Gaza, and we are unable to communicate with them. Every report about a bombing in an area causes a lot of terror, because the media does not specify the details exactly, leaving a lot of speculation and fear about the fate of loved ones," she explained.
Despite those difficulties, Sarah says her physical condition has improved since she arrived in the US. When she first arrived, she was unable to move parts of her face and body and spent her first weeks in intensive care.
"When I arrived, the condition of my face was critical, and I could not move my mouth, neck or joints, but now I am better able to move them," she explained. "In the first weeks, I was in intensive care, and the situation was very difficult. I felt lonely even though I do not have a problem communicating in English."
The adjustment was difficult because she felt separated from the people and surroundings she knew. The nurses who cared for her, however, helped her through those first days.
"I felt that the people around me were not like me, that I did not belong to them and that I did not know them. I felt suffocated in the first days, but I received the affection of the nurses," she recalled.
Physical therapy brought its own challenges, with Sarah describing some sessions as extremely painful. Her therapists and medical staff sometimes used music and dance during treatment, which she remembers fondly.
"I sometimes feel severe pain during physical therapy, as if my whole body is going to tear apart. Sometimes the therapist would stop, and treatment would begin through dance and music, and the staff would join us. I loved them very much," she explained.
The repeated operations also left Sarah afraid that she might die during treatment.
"At first, I was overcome by a strong feeling of fear, in addition to the operations, and I was afraid of dying under the weight of these operations," she recalled.
On one occasion, the pain became so overwhelming that Sarah told a therapist she would not have escaped the fire if she had known what the treatment would be like.
"I once swore in front of one of the therapists, essentially saying that if I had known the pain during the treatment period would be like this, I would not have left the fire," she explained.
The comment frightened the therapist, who requested a psychologist, believing that Sarah might harm herself. Heal Palestine did the same.
Gaza beyond the genocide
For Sarah, however, the difficulties of adjusting to life in the US have also been tied to how she feels Gaza and Palestinians are viewed. She says Gaza was not defined by the genocide, but by the community she experienced there.
"We are not beggars or a charity project. We are not hungry either. Our circumstances were imposed on us," she said.
When Sarah remembers Gaza, she focuses on the sense of safety she felt there and the people who would help her when she got lost.
"Gaza was a beautiful city. I did not feel afraid in Gaza. For example, I have a problem with directions, and I would always get lost and find my way because someone was always there to help," she explained.
That sense of connection extended beyond the people she knew personally.
"I felt that everyone in the street belonged to me, and that no matter how lost I became, there was no reason to be afraid in Gaza," she continued.
That being said, living in the US has not given her the same sense of belonging, despite having lived there for around a year and a half.
"Here, I have been walking down the same street for a year, but I don't feel there is anything there that I belong to," she reflected.
"Gaza was a city that spread its goodness and blessings to everyone, although the circumstances we went through were difficult, and anyone could go through them," she added.
A glimpse of life before
Sarah is now also thinking about what she might do after her treatment. She does not know what she had planned to study, but, coming from a family with many doctors, she would probably have pursued medicine, although she expects her treatment to continue for another year or a year and a half before she can prepare for the required exams and decide on her specialisation based on her grades.
Outside the hospital, moments such as a Heal Palestine camp last summer have helped her reconnect with parts of her life before the injury. She remembers the camp as wonderful because she was surrounded by Palestinians who understood what she had been through.
"We were surrounded by nature and under the shade of trees, alongside Palestinians from Gaza and from different areas who understood what I had been through. During that period, I was able to sleep without any problems," she recalled.
One of the activities at the camp was particularly meaningful because it reminded Sarah of her childhood in Gaza: horse riding. Her father had trained her and her brothers to ride Arab horses from a young age and would challenge them to discover their skills.
"The summer camp was the first opportunity to ride a horse since the incident, and my feelings were indescribable," she said.
She was initially afraid because she had to hold the reins with both hands, knowing that she could not fully move her left hand. She worried that she would lose control of the horse, but she succeeded.
Gaza's patients left waiting
Sarah's story comes as thousands of other Palestinians in Gaza continue to need medical treatment outside the territory.
The latest data from the World Health Organisation indicates that more than 18,000 Palestinian patients and wounded people in Gaza still need medical evacuation, while Israel refuses to grant entry visas to many foreign doctors or doctors of Palestinian origin who want to enter to assist.
One of them is US doctor of Palestinian origin Thaer Ahmad, who has entered Gaza several times before and after the genocide, while on other occasions he was prevented from entering. Ahmad has also spoken about the decision by US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in August to halt medical evacuation visas from Gaza to the US.
In an exclusive interview with The New Arab, Ahmad described the decision as one that would have serious consequences for children who need specialist treatment.
"The decision to halt humanitarian visas for children from Gaza will follow the secretary of state throughout his professional career," he said.
Ahmad has met children who were previously evacuated to the US, including some who were taken to Dallas and Chicago. He pointed to the number of children received by the US compared with other countries in the region.
"Some had previously been evacuated to Dallas and Chicago, and I met many of them. What is striking is that the US received fewer than 80 children, while we hear about other countries in the region receiving more than 2,000 cases, even though the US has specialist doctors capable of helping these children with their injuries, while most of these specialisations are not available around the world," he explained.
Ahmad added that the decision had closed a route for Palestinian families seeking treatment in the US, many of whom, he argued, did not intend to remain in the country.
"The US government decided to close these doors. It is a catastrophic decision in every sense of the word, especially since Palestinian families who come to the US for treatment do not intend to stay," he said.
He also referred to one case he had worked on in which a patient had already returned.
“One of the cases I worked on has already returned, while the family members are living in Egypt, waiting for the borders to open so they can reunite with their families,” Ahmad noted, adding that medical evacuations did not place an unreasonable burden on the US healthcare system.
"Taxpayers' money is not being spent on the children. We did not receive thousands of children, so we could say this puts pressure on our healthcare system, especially since our hospital systems are capable of accommodating them," he explained.
For Ahmad, the issue remains what happens to Palestinians who have travelled abroad for treatment and want to return to their families.
"These people want to return. It is strange. The decision was taken for political reasons, but it is also a very inhumane and tragic decision," he concluded.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

Trump Pressures Ukraine over Rising Diesel Prices Ahead of UN General Assembly Meeting
US President Donald Trump pressed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during a September 20 phone call to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, the Financial Times reported on September 21.
Trump expressed concern that Ukrainian strikes are worsening a global diesel shortage and driving domestic energy prices higher.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
While Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries hit an already fragile market, restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is the primary driver of the current diesel crisis, according to the International Energy Agency’s September oil market report.
Following the Middle Eastern chokepoint’s closure, Persian Gulf diesel and gasoil exports dropped by roughly 1 million barrels per day—accounting for the majority of the combined Middle East and Russian supply decline.
According to a senior Ukrainian official who was on the call, Trump’s messaging focused heavily on “diesel, diesel… diesel,” urging Zelenskyy to order the Ukrainian military to halt its deep-strike drone and missile campaign against Russian fuel processing infrastructure.
Another official familiar with the exchange noted that Trump emphasized his growing concern over rising diesel costs and stressed the need for Russian fuel supplies to reach global markets to ease inflationary pressures, according to the Financial Times.
The conversation came shortly after Ukrainian forces launched a major drone strike on the Russian capital, setting a key oil refinery ablaze in the Moscow region.
In a post on Truth Social following the call, Trump asserted that Russia had “lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry” and reiterated calls to end the war. US diesel prices reached a record $6.51 per gallon on September 21, representing a more than 70 percent increase since the outbreak of broader Middle East hostilities earlier this year, the Financial Times wrote.
Following the conversation, Zelenskyy stated that the discussion was “important” and noted that an upcoming in-person meeting with Trump on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York “could change a lot,” the Financial Times reported.
“There is diplomatic momentum,” Zelenskyy stated, while reiterating in separate comments that Russia continues to escalate its aggression and target Ukrainian civilian infrastructure.
Zelenskyy emphasized that Ukraine’s long-range drone campaign forms “part of the pressure that is actually working and the world can feel it,” maintaining that diplomatic efforts must proceed in parallel.
Ukrainian officials told the Financial Times that while Trump previously suggested both sides had agreed to refrain from striking energy facilities, no reciprocal ceasefire has been implemented as Russia continues its aerial bombardment of Ukrainian power grids and civilian infrastructure.
Despite a relentless campaign of Ukrainian strikes that has knocked out roughly a fifth of Russia’s oil refining capacity, Russian refineries earned unprecedented profits of 938 billion rubles ($11.13 billion) in the first half of the year.
Driven by soaring exchange prices and massive state “damper” subsidies, these windfalls have offset reduced refining volumes, even as direct and indirect damages to Russia’s oil sector mounted and Ukraine expanded its campaign to target shadow-fleet tankers at sea.

Inside the design of New York City's upcoming borough-based jails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:57:00 UTC
01:57:00 KST

Inside the design of New York City's upcoming borough-based jails
New York City plans to relocate inmates from Rikers Island into four jails built from the ground up in Queens, Brooklyn, Manhattan and the Bronx. Here, Dezeen looks at the architecture of each project.
Begun in 2017, the NYC Borough-Based Jail Program (BBJ) is largely overseen by the New York City Department of Design and Construction (DDC), which is working with a variety of architecture studios on each jail, including HOK, Cetra Ruddy and Michael Graves.
With the recent groundbreaking of the Manhattan jail, construction of all four borough-based jails has begun, while the city simultaneously makes steps towards closing the Rikers Island jail complex.
The Brooklyn jail, which is the furthest along, is set to open in 2029. The other three jails are expected to be completed in the early 2030s.
Justice design is a contested field within architecture. Some believe that architects should not be working in this sector at all. In 2020, the AIA New York issued a statement urging studios to "move away" from the design of prisons, jails and other detention centres.
However, others believe that good architecture can better serve the incarcerated population.
HOK, which has designed two of the four BBJ jails and has a dedicated justice design arm, said it does not "shy away" from the projects.
"We think it's our responsibility as architects to help solve some serious social problems, and we don't shy away from them," HOK New York design principal Ken Drucker told Dezeen.
The DDC has a list of design goals for the program, including mental health programming for those in custody, safe environments for staff, visitors and inmates, and "good civic architecture" that relates to its surrounding neighbourhood.
In design documents, cells have horizontally barred windows, a single bed, a desk underneath the window, a stool and a toilet. For the Manhattan project, HOK is integrating circadian-rhythm lighting synced to the outdoors to replace harsh overhead lighting found in older facilities.
In some cells, inmates have access to a reading light they can control.
"This design strategy is really meant to be something that the people can thrive in, and it's not just a place where they always feel like they're on the defence all the time," said HOK director of civic + justice Jeff Goodale.
The DDC and studios are also working to create "welcoming" interior visiting centres, as the projects purport a strong focus on providing dignified spaces not only for those incarcerated, but for visitors and staff.
Interior renders show open waiting rooms clad in "warm" materials, with an emphasis on clear, direct circulation through the space. Spaces for contact and no-contact visitations and children's play areas with bright carpeting and bookshelves are also present in the designs.
Local communities have opposed the projects. Some have held rallies and protests during the past several years as construction moves forward. Some of the projects, such as the Queens facility, are still making design adjustments.
More recently, New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani called Rikers Island one of the "deepest failures of our city government" and said the city is "replacing a system built around neglect with one centred on rehabilitation".
Read on for a closer look at these facilities.
Manhattan Detention Facility, Chinatown, by HOK
Located at 125 White Street in Chinatown, the Manhattan Detention Facility will be the tallest jail in the world when completed.
The design is broken into "four vertical quadrants", with a large, 55-foot-tall (16 metres tall) pedestrian passageway underneath the building. The passageway was meant to integrate the building with its surrounding site at the nexus of Chinatown, Little Italy, Tribeca and the civic district to the south, according to HOK.
The jail, which will replace a former detention centre on the same site, has brought pushback and engagement from the local community, with the DDC and HOK noting the neighbourhood has been "very vocal" in the design process.
Site preparation is underway, but not without concerns about feasibility from local leaders, who recently penned a letter to mayor Mamdani asking for a reassessment of the site.
Find out more about the Manhattan Detention Facility ›
Brooklyn Borough-Based Jail, Boerum Hill, by HOK
Located at 275 Atlantic Avenue on the site of a former jail, the Brooklyn Borough-Based Jail is the nearest to completion. It towers above the low-rise neighbourhoods to the south.
According to HOK, its design focused primarily on bringing daylight to occupants and as deep into the building as possible, with each cell connected directly to an outdoor space completely surrounded by expanded metal security mesh.
"One of the things that we've seen in facilities where people have to be escorted to a central place for outdoor space is that often they don't get there, and with putting the outdoor space directly attached to the living unit, people will be out there daily," said Goodale.
The studio clad the building in fixed fins to control daylighting angles, and terracotta to reflect materials found in the neighbourhood.
Bronx Borough-Based Jail Facility, Mott Haven, by CetraRuddy, Lumen Architects and Urbahn Architects
The 11-storey Bronx Borough-Based Jail Facility is located on the site of a former hospital and New York City Police impound lot.
The facility will contain 40,000 square feet (3,716 square meters) of community and commercial space on the ground floor, dedicated space for on-site services and programming, indoor and outdoor recreation, food services, staff offices and facilities, according to the DDC. It will also contain spaces such as areas for children and nursing mothers.
In the final community design meeting in March 2026, Urbahn Architects associate principal Larry Gutterman explained the building's three-storey podium lines up with the height of nearby residential rowhouses. According to the studio, the mesh-clad tower relates to the scale of surrounding industrial buildings.
A major concern from the community, according to the team, was the scale of the building, which the studio attempted to mitigate by creating several stepped volumes.
Find out more about Bronx Borough-Based Jail Facility ›
Queens Borough-Based Jail Facility, Kew Gardens, by STV and Michael Graves
The Queens Borough-Based Jail Facility is located at 126-02 82nd Avenue, on the same site as the current Queens Detention Center and a large parking lot. It is the only BBJ that includes beds for women and "gender expansive" inmates, according to the DDC. Spaces such as a nursery and a women's "law library" are shown in the design.
The site contains three individual "housing towers" clad in metal mesh around its recreation areas, precast concrete around its base, and metal panels and glass curtain walls on the upper floors.
A smaller parking garage building with a community space was completed in June 2023 as part of the project, which sits off to the side.
In the most recent design meeting, the team said it's working on updates such as replacing natural wood cladding with more durable materials and making the project overall more ADA accessible.

Ukraine’s STING S Interceptor Destroys Dozen Russian Jet Drones

Ukraine’s STING S Interceptor Destroys Dozen Russian Jet Drones
Ukraine’s new STING S interceptor drone has already destroyed around a dozen Russian Geran-4 jet-powered attack drones and several smaller Geran-5 cruise missiles as the system undergoes active combat testing, Ukrainian drone manufacturer Wild Hornets told Militarnyi on September 21.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Developed from the original STING platform designed to counter Russian drones, the Sting S is a high-speed quadcopter interceptor specifically engineered to engage jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles.
Wild Hornets has not disclosed the interceptor’s technical specifications ahead of the start of mass production. The company noted that the STING S’s final characteristics could still be adjusted in the coming weeks based on the results of its combat deployment.
According to Militarnyi, most of the targets intercepted by the Sting S have been destroyed using Hornet Vision Ctrl, a remote-control technology developed for drone operations.
“We expect this will allow us to quickly scale up the use of the new interceptor once mass production begins and deliveries to combat units start,” Wild Hornets said.
The Sting platform has already demonstrated its capabilities against Russian aerial targets at high altitudes. On August 18, Militarnyi reported that Ukrainian drone operators had set a new altitude record after destroying a Russian UAV with a STING interceptor at more than 7 kilometers above ground.
Wild Hornets told the outlet that the “Klever” crew of the “Hrim” unmanned systems unit within Ukraine’s 27th National Guard Brigade intercepted the Russian drone at an altitude of 7,472 meters.
The interception surpassed previously reported altitude records for Ukrainian interceptor drones. Earlier in August, an operator from the Security Service of Ukraine’s Special Operations Center “A” destroyed a Russian aerial target at an altitude of 6,955 meters, according to Militarnyi.
The development of the Sting S comes as other Ukrainian manufacturers advance interceptor systems designed to counter increasingly fast aerial threats. Also on September 21, Ukrainian defense manufacturer Vluchnyk announced the completion of internal trials of its Zorelit v5 interceptor drone, developed to engage high-speed targets, including jet-powered attack UAVs.

Cash-strapped Syria needs $831 million a month to purchase oil
Unknown

2026-09-21

Breadcrumb
Cash-strapped Syria needs $831 million a month to purchase oil: energy minister
Syria needs $831 million a month to purchase crude oil and petroleum products and is facing a significant gas supply shortfall, Syrian Energy Minister Mohammed al-Bashir said on Sunday.
Al-Bashir made the remarks during a briefing to Syria’s People’s Assembly in a session dedicated to reviewing the state of the energy sector, particularly petroleum products and rising fuel prices.
Oil prices climbed back above $100 a barrel last week after new US strikes on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf, while renewed fighting in Yemen has raised fresh concerns over shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
The Syrian government recently temporarily raised the price of a litre of diesel to 175 Syrian pounds ($1.43), an increase of around 40%, while petrol prices rose by more than 25%, triggering the largest protests across the country since the toppling of longtime dictator Bashar al-Assad in 2024.
Syria is emerging from a 14-year civil war that killed more than half a million people and left the country in economic ruin.
"Syria needs $831 million a month to purchase crude oil and petroleum products," al-Bashir said.
Domestic oil production currently stands at 112,000 barrels per day, leaving a shortfall of around 200,000 barrels per day that is covered through imports, he said.
Syria has 78 oil fields, while the ministry is working to rehabilitate production infrastructure and restart oil wells.
The ministry has also formed a committee to assess the country’s oil and gas reserves and prepare a new map as part of a strategic plan to increase production.
"We will achieve self-sufficiency in oil by 2028," al-Bashir said.
In the gas sector, domestic production currently stands at around 8 million cubic metres per day, up from roughly 6 million previously, while the country’s daily demand stands at 24 million cubic metres.
The ministry is drilling additional wells to boost production, although reaching "satisfactory" production levels could take around seven years, al-Bashir said.
To help meet part of its needs, Syria currently purchases 6.3 million cubic metres of gas per day from Azerbaijan and from a vessel at Jordan’s Aqaba port, at a cost of around $140 million a month, according to the minister.
Syria’s domestic refining capacity stands at 150,000 barrels per day, while the country imports a similar volume of refined petroleum products.
Al-Bashir attributed the rise in demand for fuel to an increase in the number of vehicles in the country, from around 2.5 million to 3.6 million. Daily demand stands at 12 million litres of diesel and 8 million litres of petrol, he said.
Average fuel-oil consumption is around 8,500 tonnes per day for power-generation plants and the industrial sector, in addition to approximately 1,300 tonnes of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) for household use.
The minister said the main challenges facing the energy sector include securing the foreign currency needed to purchase crude oil, petroleum products and spare parts, as well as gaps in data and difficulties in securing crude oil supplies.
As part of efforts to strengthen gas supplies, he said the ministry had invited bids to complete the Arab Gas Pipeline linking Syria and Jordan. The project is estimated to cost around $250 million, which would be borne by the Syrian Petroleum Company.
Al-Bashir also said Damascus is considering contracts with "friendly oil-producing countries" to secure its energy needs until Syria achieves self-sufficiency.

Russia Bans Night Movement Along 5-Kilometer Estonia Border Strip
Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) has imposed temporary restrictions on movement, hunting, firearms, and river access across border sections of the Leningrad region facing Estonia, its border directorate announced.
The measures run from September 16 to 26 and include a ban on nighttime movement within the five-kilometer strip along the state frontier.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Border Directorate of the FSB for St. Petersburg and the Leningrad region outlined the controls, citing the need to safeguard the state frontier and protect residents' safety. The directorate stated that the measures form part of an effort to curb offenses in the border and migration spheres and to protect aquatic resources.
According to the directorate, the following are prohibited across the designated zones for the duration of the period:
- presence on the shoreline and the use of small craft on the Narva River between the Bolshaya Cheremukha and Kriusha rivers;
- hunting and movement with firearms within the border zone in Slantsevsky district and the five-kilometer border strip in Kingisepp district;
- movement of people and vehicles after dark outside populated areas in the five-kilometer strip along the frontier in both districts.
The directorate emphasized that the bans apply only within the defined border zones and the five-kilometer strip, not across the entire district.
The border zone falls under Russia's 1993 State Border law, which restricts entry and requires passes for anyone traveling into the controlled area. The directorate noted that the zone's limits in the Leningrad region were set by an FSB order issued in June 2026.
It indicated that passes are issued free of charge through designated offices, including one in Ivangorod. That town sits directly across the Narva River from the Estonian city of Narva.
The controls remain in effect until September 26, according to the directorate. It warned that violations of the border regime carry administrative penalties, which were sharply increased under amendments that took effect in March 2026. The directorate added that foreign nationals who breach the rules may face expulsion from Russia, while equipment used in an offense, such as a boat, can be confiscated.
The clampdown reflects a wider tightening of movement controls inside Russia. Amid rumors of a fresh wave of mobilization, more than 113,000 Russians crossed into Georgia through the Verkhny Lars checkpoint in a single week in August, with over 20,000 passing through on August 20 alone.
Moscow has meanwhile begun using its electronic military registry to bar departures, recording its first known case in early September of a reservist stopped at the border under an enlistment office's travel restriction.

Trump administration gave firm with ties to ballroom donor the green light to do business with a sanctioned Russian bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:56:02 UTC
01:56:02 KST

Trump administration gave firm with ties to ballroom donor the green light to do business with a sanctioned Russian bank
Private equity investor Konstantin Sokolov was also appointed to run a government enterprise fund.
A company linked to a major Trump donor received authorization from the Treasury Department to complete an acquisition involving a sanctioned Russian bank, according to public records.
The Texas-based Dynamic Frontier Holdings purchased Teghut, one of Armenia’s largest copper mines, this summer. Dynamic Frontier’s manager is Konstantin Sokolov, a Russian-American businessman who was one of three dozen private donors to President Donald Trump’s $350 million White House ballroom project.
Russia’s state-owned VTB Bank was Teghut’s primary shareholder and creditor prior to the purchase. The U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned VTB Bank following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, describing it as a “critical artery” of the country’s financial system.
The sanctions prohibit U.S. companies and individuals from transacting with VTB Bank. But on Sept. 3, Dynamic Frontier said in a press statement that it had “received authorization from the U.S. Department of the Treasury” on June 1 to acquire all of Teghut’s shares and outstanding debt.
The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, known as OFAC, can grant a license to individuals or companies to complete transactions that would otherwise be prohibited by sanctions. OFAC states on its website that it may grant a license to do business with sanctioned Russian entities when it is in the interest of the applicant and the U.S. government.
A spokesperson for Sokolov confirmed to ICIJ that OFAC granted a license to Dynamic Frontier to complete the acquisition of Teghut’s shares and debt. The spokesperson also said there was “no evidential basis” to draw any link between Sokolov’s donations and the approval of the license, and that any suggestion otherwise “would be incorrect and wholly misplaced.”
The Treasury Department did not answer questions about the license.
Armenia’s competition commission formally approved Dynamic Frontier’s acquisition of the mine on July 7. However, VTB’s deputy chairman said in an interview with Russian news agency Interfax that the bank sold its interests in Teghut to a “group of international investors” in June. The proceeds from the sale, the deputy chairman said, was 4 billion rubles, or roughly $46.5 million.
As far back as April, VTB’s chairman said that his bank was in “the final stages” of selling Teghut and Armenia’s Radio Azatutyun identified Sokolov as the mine’s likely buyer. In July, the buyer was reported to be a company founded by Sergei Virabyan, a former Armenian government official and banking executive. Virabyan refused to answer when asked whether Sokolov was the true owner of the mine, describing the information as a “commercial secret.”
In a statement, the spokesperson for Sokolov said Dynamic Frontier’s acquisition of Teghut “represents a long-term commitment to one of Armenia’s most strategically important mineral assets,” and that the company’s goal is to revitalize the mine and significantly increase its production. The transaction, the spokesperson said, “will help secure Armenia’s position and sovereignty in the critical minerals space.”
Sokolov was born in the Russian city of St. Petersburg in 1975 and immigrated to the United States at 21 years old, according to his personal website. In the late 2000s, he helped launch an investment fund that backed Russian real estate and hospitality projects.
Sokolov gave $2,300 to support Barack Obama’s presidential campaign in 2008, according to public records. But in more recent years, he has made large donations to Republican political causes. He donated $11 million in 2025 to MAGA Inc., a major pro-Trump super PAC, as well as making over a dozen other donations to other Republican campaigns and political groups. He also donated an undisclosed sum toward the new White House ballroom.
Sokolov was also appointed chairman this summer of a new $200 million State Department enterprise fund to oversee investments in the south Caucasus and central Asia. Armenia is expected to be a primary beneficiary of the fund.
In addition to Teghut, Sokolov has extensive business interests in Armenia’s banking and telecommunications sectors. In Armenia, some politicians have criticized the lack of transparency in his companies’ ownership structures and how he will manage his overlapping public and private roles.
Mesrop Manukyan, a member of Armenia’s National Assembly, told ICIJ that Sokolov’s position “create[s] legitimate questions about…the separation between private commercial interest and decisions involving public or government-backed funds.”

Qatar denies funding Hamas, rejects New Yorker allegations

Breadcrumb
Qatar denies funding Hamas, rejects New Yorker allegations
Qatar has rejected allegations that it provided money to Hamas, saying its aid to Gaza was delivered with the knowledge and involvement of its international partners and Israel.
The Qatari International Media Office said on Monday that claims published by The New Yorker on 19 September were based on what it described as “falsified and fabricated information”.
The office said the magazine had been provided before publication with evidence that documents cited in the report, including material known as the “Blast documents”, were false.
It said the decision to publish the claims despite that evidence raised “serious questions” about the magazine's editorial standards and contributed to what Qatar described as a wider disinformation campaign targeting the country.
The documents were not new and had previously been circulated to other media organisations, the statement said, adding that some outlets had decided not to publish them after being shown evidence that they were fabricated.
Qatar also alleged that various actors, including elements of the Israeli far right, had for several years been involved in creating and circulating false documents intended to implicate Doha in unfounded claims.
The office specifically rejected allegations that Qatar had provided money to Hamas.
It said Qatari assistance had instead been directed to Palestinian civilians in Gaza through mechanisms co-ordinated with Israeli authorities and international partners.
Under previous aid arrangements, the statement said, financial assistance as well as food, medicine, fuel and other essential supplies passed through Israel before entering Gaza.
“Nothing was delivered without Israeli involvement at every stage of the process,” the office said.
Qatar has previously said that its aid to Gaza was transferred through arrangements approved by Israel, including during successive Israeli governments.
The statement said Israeli security agencies were also involved in the mechanisms through which the assistance reached the territory.
It argued that any money that may subsequently have reached Hamas was not the responsibility of Qatar, but of Israel, which had overseen the transfer arrangements under governments led by Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid and Benjamin Netanyahu.
Qatar has repeatedly faced accusations from Israeli officials over its relationship with Hamas. Netanyahu has previously claimed that Doha funded and supported the Palestinian group, allegations Qatar denies.
Doha said the latest claims were part of an effort to undermine its role as a mediator in regional conflicts.
Qatar has played a central role alongside Egypt and the United States in mediating between Israel and Hamas over ceasefires, captive releases and humanitarian access to Gaza.
The office said those behind what it described as the disinformation campaign did not want peace and viewed Qatar’s mediation role as a threat to their political interests.
The statement comes amid continued scrutiny of Qatar’s ties with Hamas and its role in Gaza diplomacy, particularly following the Israeli strike on Hamas leaders in Doha in September 2025.
The International Media Office urged news organisations to exercise caution when dealing with what it called misleading information intended to obstruct efforts to reach peace in the region.
It said journalists and media organisations had a responsibility to apply rigorous standards of verification and analysis, particularly when covering complex geopolitical issues.
Qatar said it was now considering legal options in response to the publication of the allegations, in order to protect its rights and prevent what it described as the misleading of the public.

'Highly recommended': Zohran Mamdani confirms shattafs have made it to Gracie Mansion
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has finally answered one of the more unusual questions surrounding his move into Gracie Mansion - did he actually install bidets in the mayoral residence?
The answer is yes.
Mamdani confirmed last week that the bathrooms at Gracie Mansion have been fitted with the fixtures, months after revealing that installing bidets, commonly known as shattaf across the Arab world, was among the changes he hoped to make after moving in.
The revelation came, fittingly, during a press conference about public toilets.
Mamdani was announcing the installation of 17 new modular bathrooms across New York City on 16 September when a reporter asked whether he had followed through on his own bathroom plans.
"By the way, did you ever put the bidets into Gracie Mansion?" the reporter asked.
"Yes, they're all there," Mamdani replied.
He also gave the new additions his seal of approval, describing them as "highly recommended" and pointing out that the attachments cost around $20.
The exchange revived a small but much-discussed detail from Mamdani's move into Gracie Mansion in January.
Shortly after moving into the official mayoral residence with his wife, Rama Duwaji, Mamdani revealed that he wanted to install bidets in its bathrooms.
The announcement attracted attention in the US, where bidets remain less commonplace than in many parts of the world.
But for many Arabs and Muslims, the idea was far less unusual.
The shattaf, sometimes called a handheld bidet or bidet spray, is a standard bathroom fixture across much of the Middle East and North Africa, where washing with water after using the toilet is commonplace. Similar fixtures are also widely used across South and Southeast Asia.
For Muslims, the practice also has a religious dimension, with cleansing with water after using the toilet traditionally associated with Islamic rules of personal hygiene.
Mamdani, who is Muslim and of Indian-Ugandan heritage, had therefore brought a bathroom custom familiar to millions of Muslims and people across the Global South into one of New York's most famous residences.
Rather than carrying out an elaborate renovation, however, Mamdani indicated that Gracie Mansion's toilets were fitted with inexpensive attachments.
Months after the mayor first floated the idea, New Yorkers now have their answer - the shattafs did indeed make it to Gracie Mansion.
