Nissan eyes increasing U.S. production as new Rogue hybrid launches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:53:00 UTC
01:53:00 KST

Nissan Motor is looking to increase its U.S. production as it launches the 2027 Rogue crossover, including with a new hybrid model that the company views as a crucial offering for American consumers.
"We're now maxing out the production capacity in the U.S.," Christian Meunier, chairman of Nissan Americas, told CNBC. "The next step is going to be three shifts, and I'm pretty optimistic that with the launch of the new Rogue that is happening in the next couple months, we'll be able to do that pretty quickly with the launch of the hybrid."
The Japanese automaker currently produces the Rogue alongside other Nissan and Infiniti crossovers at a 6 million-square-foot assembly plant on two production shifts in Smyrna, Tennessee. It also has another large manufacturing plant producing the Nissan Altima sedan and Frontier midsize pickup truck in Canton, Mississippi.
Additional production at assembly plants typically means hundreds, if not thousands, of new jobs. Nissan's moves come as the Trump administration has been focused on increasing employment and domestic production in the U.S. auto industry.
U.S. manufacturing of the hybrid is expected to start next year after the spring production launch of the 2027 Rogue with a traditional gas engine at the Tennessee plant.
In the meantime, Meunier said Nissan plans to import the hybrid vehicles from Japan as a way to get them to market more quickly to lift sales and help with an ongoing global turnaround plan for the company.
Meunier said if Nissan can add a third shift to each of its assembly plants, it would boost the automaker's U.S. production to roughly 1 million units annually, up from nearly 487,000 in 2025.
Nissan has a target to produce 80% of the vehicles it sells in the U.S. domestically by 2030, but the company has no plans for a new plant as of now.
"I think we're very well equipped to succeed without major investment and a new factory and everything else. Maybe after 2030," he said. "Over the next four or five years, we'll see."
Nissan e-Power
Nissan on Monday officially revealed the 2027 Rogue with its new "e-Power" technology for the U.S., which is the first hybrid of its kind for the American market.
The "e-Power" system is called a series hybrid.
It uses the engine as a generator to power the vehicle's electric motors that then propel the vehicle. It operates like emerging extended-range electric vehicles, or EREVs, but has a smaller battery and doesn't require a plug. It also does not use the engine to power the wheels, just electric motors.
Meunier said the Rogue hybrid and resurrecting the Xterra off-road SUV were his top vehicle priorities when he rejoined Nissan in January 2025 after four and a half years with Jeep. That included pulling ahead the Rogue hybrid twice for the U.S.
Nissan said Monday that the starting pricing of the Rogue hybrid will be between $35,490 for the entry-level model to $43,490 for a "Platinum" version.
The Rogue is a sales leader for the company in the U.S. It competes in the highly competitive small crossover segment against the Toyota RAV4 and Honda CR-V, which have the best-selling hybrid options in that category.
"The hybrid power that we're launching on Rogue is going to really be the boost to our performance," Meunier said. "It's been quite remarkable to be able to grow without having a hybrid in the U.S. because the hybrids are obviously becoming more and more popular."
Meunier said Nissan plans to position the Rogue e-Power squarely against the Toyota RAV4. He said that may include an unconventional sales option to allow potential customers to test drive both vehicles at Nissan dealerships, which wouldn't typically have a Toyota available.
The focus on the Rogue hybrid comes after Nissan and other automakers lost billions of dollars on all-electric vehicles amid a pullback in regulatory support as well as lackluster consumer demand.
Nissan has said the e-Power is a better solution than EVs or even traditional hybrids for U.S. consumers, especially amid inflated fuel prices due to the Iran war.
"It's going to make people look at Nissan with different eyes," Meunier said. "A lot of customers that didn't even consider us until the hybrid comes to market."
Nissan said the fuel economy for the Rogue hybrid will be 38 miles per gallon combined. That compares to the Toyota RAV4 hybrid at 43 miles mpg and the Honda CR-V at 40 mpg.
Nissan turnaround
Nissan's renewed focus on the U.S. comes amid a global turnaround plan.
Under the strategy, the Japanese automaker intends to streamline its automobile lineup by getting rid of low-performing models and increasing its use of technologies such as artificial intelligence.
The plan includes the company targeting 1 million vehicle sales for its Nissan brand in both the U.S. and China by the 2030 financial year and growing its annual sales volume in Japan to 550,000 cars by that time.
For the U.S., Meunier said he is satisfied with the progress Nissan has made since he returned to the automaker last year.
After several years of struggling sales, Nissan's U.S. sales through the first half of the year were up roughly 10% compared with Cox Automotive reporting a roughly 3% decline for the broader industry during that time.
"I think the next few months are going to be pretty good. Pretty tough, but pretty good," Meunier said. "We're going to have a strong close of the calendar year in December."

As Trump touts Hormuz oil flows, can the US outlast Iran?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:51:49 UTC
01:51:49 KST

Breadcrumb
As Trump talks up oil flows in the Strait of Hormuz, can the US outlast Iran?
United States President Donald Trump has been projecting comfort with the status quo in the conflict with Iran.
According to the narrative being promoted by Trump and his allies, the US is getting oil out of the Strait of Hormuz and eroding Iran's leverage over the strategic waterway, with Washington's sanctions and blockade strangling Tehran's economy.
But as renewed violence between Yemen's Houthi group and Saudi Arabia puts further pressure on the oil market, and Iran shows willingness to escalate, any purported gains in Hormuz are not enough to turn the crisis in favour of Washington.
"I don't think it's good for US interests, and I think it's clearly not sustainable," Ryan Costello, policy director at the National Iranian American Council (NIAC), told The New Arab, regarding the current situation.
US officials have insisted in recent weeks that the amount of oil leaving the strait daily is approaching pre-war levels of around 20 million barrels a day.
"We’ve risen the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf to record highs right now. About 18 million barrels flowed out yesterday, basically pre-conflict levels," US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright told Fox News on Wednesday.
Trump and Vice President JD Vance have made similar claims as well.
It is difficult to verify these numbers because some vessels are crossing Hormuz at night with their transponders turned off to avoid being detected by Iranian forces.
Despite Trump's claims that the strait is now under US control, Iranian attacks on ships crossing the waterway have continued.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), a monitoring group affiliated with the British Royal Navy, documented three attacks on oil tankers on Thursday and Friday.
UKMTO said in a report on Sunday that attacks and attempted attacks by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) have persisted in the strait.
"These actions continue to demonstrate Iran’s intent to assert presence along key transit lanes and maintain pressure on transiting vessels," the report read.
"Commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained at reduced levels compared to the 2025 baseline."
'Fog of war'
Costello said the US administration is likely using the "fog of war" and lack of reliable data on transit through the strait to inflate the amount of oil passing through the waterway.
"There have been a lot of other indications suggesting that the overall climate in the Strait of Hormuz is one of restriction, that it's very difficult to get oil through, that there is a laborious process underway to get some oil through," he told The New Arab.
If the US were indeed restoring the flow of oil through Hormuz, the change has not been reflected in the oil markets.
A barrel of oil has been trading at around $100 for weeks, and the Houthi attack on Saudi oil infrastructure has further complicated supply problems.
In the US, the price of diesel - a fuel used to power large machinery, including lorries that carry goods across the country - has broken several records this month, reaching $6.50 per gallon ($3.8 litre) on Sunday.
Likewise, gasoline has been on an upward trajectory, going for a national average of $4.47 per gallon on Sunday, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA). It was less than $3 before the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February.
Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow at the Center for International Policy, said successfully moving individual tankers through the Strait of Hormuz is not the same as restoring the normal flow of oil.
"Commercial vessels still cannot transit regularly, at scale or without extraordinary military protection," Mortazavi told The New Arab.
She added that reported Iranian attacks on tankers in the strait show that "the waterway remains contested".
But the White House has been arguing that the waterway is completely open, with the US president suggesting that the waterway should be named Trump Strait.
Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, said the Trump administration wants to manage the pressure on the oil markets in Hormuz while keeping Iran under the weight of blockades and sanctions.
But the challenge for the US, according to Parsi, is that the possible success of that strategy may lead Iran to counter-escalate militarily.
"This is the paradox. If you're effective in pressuring them, they will pressure you back," he told The New Arab.
"It's a different story if the US was doing this against a country that had run out of escalatory options."
Parsi said if the US feels like it has a tactical advantage now, it would be smarter to bring it to the negotiations table because guarding ships through Hormuz is not "a success or an exit".
War remains unpopular
In the US, the war remains unpopular despite the professed optimism in Trump's circle, according to public opinion polls, with high gasoline prices fuelling inflation.
A survey released by the Institute for Global Affairs (IGA) on Wednesday found that 60 percent of potential voters disapprove of Trump's handling of the war.
The unpopularity of the conflict may hurt the US president's Republican Party in the midterm elections in November, which will decide the makeup of Congress for the next two years.
A staggering 81 percent of respondents in the IGA poll also said the conflict in Iran has increased the cost of living.
Bottom line, the US public does not appear to be responding to the Trump administration's rhetoric about turning the tide of the war.
"There's a huge gap between the White House and the public and between elite opinion of this war and public opinion," Jonathan Guyer, program director at IGA, told The New Arab.
"If you look at these numbers, this is like the most unpopular war ever. None of the war aims are resonating. All the things that the White House is proposing that this war is about are not resonating. The public is just hugely sceptical and don't see a way out."
Ali Harb is a journalist based in Washington, DC. His work focuses on US foreign policy, elections, and Arab American communities

NFL star Azeez Al-Shaair honours Palestinian girl killed in Gaza

The Houston Texans linebacker wore "Wafaa Akila" across his eye black during Sunday's game against the Cincinnati Bengals, days after the NFL fined him $11,941 for displaying Hind's name during a match against the Buffalo Bills.
Wafaa was eight years old when she and her father were killed in an Israeli attack in western Gaza City on 6 September 2026, her first day of school, despite a "ceasefire" in the devastated territory supposedly in place since October 2025.
The pair were travelling home when an Israeli drone struck their car, leaving it burned and charred. Only a handful of pages from Wafaa's schoolbooks survived.
Hours earlier, the eight-year-old had been photographed smiling as she prepared for her first day at school.
Al-Shaair shared posts about Wafaa and her mother's reaction to her killing on Instagram on Sunday.
After the Texans' game, footage shared online showed the 29-year-old interacting on the sidelines with children, including amputees and others wearing keffiyehs and carrying signs in support of him.

Al-Shaair has remained defiant over the penalties imposed for his Palestine advocacy.

NBA star Kyrie Irving later offered to cover the penalty, with Al-Shaair confirming that the two had been in contact.
Hind Rajab was five years old when she was killed in Gaza in January 2024 after Israeli forces opened fire on her family's car.
Her desperate calls for help while trapped inside the vehicle, surrounded by the bodies of her relatives, drew international attention to her killing. Her story later became the subject of an Oscar-nominated docudrama.

Al-Shaair has previously been penalised by the NFL over his advocacy.
Earlier this year, he was fined for wearing the words "Stop The Genocide" on tape across his nose. Although the message did not name a particular conflict, it was widely understood to refer to Gaza and Sudan.
The linebacker has repeatedly spoken out for Palestinians and travelled to Jordan during the summer to spend time with Palestinian refugees.
Prominent American Muslim scholar Omar Suleiman praised Al-Shaair for continuing to use his platform to highlight the plight of Palestinian children.
"My brother, who went to Jordan to be with Palestinian refugees this summer, who spends time with Palestinian children with missing limbs in Houston, who is using every week of his Pro Bowl NFL career to honour a Palestinian child despite the fines," Suleiman wrote.
The gestures come amid a devastating toll on children from Israel's war on Gaza. At least 21,500 children have been killed since October 2023, according to Gaza's Health Ministry, while 90% of the enclave's schools have been damaged or destroyed.

For the first time in the history of its flagship event, the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) is fielding a dedicated refugee team containing the two Syrian taekwondo athletes.
Photo: Reuters

“We didn’t leave our country by choice,” he said. “It was because of the difficult living conditions and the wars that took place, so we were forced to leave and move to another country to build a life there.”
Muhammad said he is not at the Games merely to make up the numbers.
“The preparations were really intense, and our goal isn’t just to participate — we’re hoping to achieve something, God willing.”
Hunaidi thanked the International Olympic Committee, the OCA and World Taekwondo for helping her live out this dream.
“Sport has changed me for the better. I’ve become a different person. I have hope now, and I have dreams and ambitions for the future,” the 18-year-old said. “We’ve seen a different side of life, and we now have hope. We’ve learned that nothing is impossible. The Philippine government on Sunday reaffirmed its long-held stance that it diplomatically recognizes China, rather than Taiwan, but said that position does not prevent it from pursuing relations with Taipei.
“The Department of Foreign Affairs reaffirms the Philippines’ adherence to its One-China Policy, in accordance with the 1975 Joint Communique between the Philippines and China, in which the Philippines recognized the government of the People’s Republic of China as the sole legal government of China,” the Philippine department said in a statement.
While that policy remains consistent, clear and unchanged, it “does not preclude the Philippines from pursuing economic, cultural and functional cooperation with Taiwan,” it said.
Photo: Screen grab from the department’s Facebook page
Citing a recent comment by Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, it said the Philippines and Taiwan are close neighbors with a long history of business.
“Consistent with this mandate, the Department will continue to rely on effective diplomacy, open communication, and the peaceful resolution of disputes in accordance with international law to advance the national interest and promote peace, stability, and prosperity in the region and beyond,” it said.
“Together with other relevant agencies, the Department will continue to ensure the welfare of Filipinos on both sides of the Taiwan Strait,” it added.
The statement was released after a Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson last week urged Manila to adhere to its “one China” stance.
The Chinese statement was made one day after Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) said in a radio interview on Tuesday last week that Taipei was preparing to open a second representative office in the Philippines.
The new office in Cebu would serve travelers and businesspeople in the central Philippines, a popular tourism destination, Lin said, but he did not give an opening date.
The current de facto Taiwanese representative office in the Philippines — the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office — is in Manila.

The ruling United Russia party retained its decisive majority in the national parliament, near-complete election results showed yesterday, while the anti-war Yabloko party appeared to have won a tiny foothold in one regional parliament.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had cast the three-day election to the State Duma — the first since Moscow launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022— as a test of support for the war. Elections for some regional parliaments and governors were held at the same time.
In a tightly controlled political system, which critics say does not tolerate genuine dissent, under which many of Yabloko’s candidates were barred, few surprises were expected.
Photo: AP
However, political analysts said it was important to the authorities that the process itself was seen to be relatively smooth. Officials from Putin down had cast the vote as a way of showing enemies that Russia was united.
With more than 95 percent of the vote counted, Russian Central Electoral Commission Chair Ella Pamfilova Chair said United Russia had won a resounding victory with 57.83 percent, up from the 49.8 percent that it won in the last parliamentary election in 2021.
United Russia was set to control 355 seats or nearly 80 percent of the 450-seat Duma, a total that includes results in individual constituencies. That would maintain its constitutional majority — enabling it to pass laws and initiate amendments to the constitution without the support of other parties.
Pamfilova said three other parties had made it into parliament —the Communists with 13.81 percent, the ultranationalist LDPR with 8.98 percent and the New People party with 7.96 percent.
Just Russia was just under the 5 percent threshold needed to enter parliament, but had “a big chance” of making it, she said.
All of those parties have voted in the same way as United Russia on major issues in the past few years.
In Chechnya, Ramzan Kadyrov, a close Putin ally, was re-elected to a fifth term as leader with an official tally of near 100 percent.
Pamfilova said turnout among Russia’s 111 million voters — which she put at 59.3 percent — was a record for such an election, which continued despite a heavy Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow on Sunday, the last day of voting.
She also called the vote “clean” in the face of allegations from opposition activists in exile of widespread rigging.
Yabloko, the only registered anti-war party in Russia, failed to win any seats at a national level.
However, in Novgorod, about 480km northwest of Moscow, with nearly 97 percent of votes counted, it appeared to have cleared the 5 percent barrier by 1 percentage point to enter the regional parliament.
“More than 12,000 Novogorod residents supported Yabloko,” the party, which supports a ceasefire in Ukraine, said in a statement.
“Peace, freedom and a life free from fear are values that have struck a chord in people’s hearts and souls,” it said.
Meanwhile, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas dismissed Russia’s parliamentary elections as a “veneer” of democracy, and said she was proposing sanctions on those who helped hold them in occupied Ukraine.
“The so-called Duma elections marked another major setback for Russian democracy. Their outcome was never in doubt,” Kallas wrote on X.
“The Kremlin silenced dissent, barred the only registered party that opposed its war in Ukraine, and shut out international election monitors. The veneer of democracy is all that remains in Russia,” she said.
Kallas said she had “proposed measures against those facilitating these sham elections in occupied Ukrainian territories.”
The EU has already sanctioned about 3,000 officials and entities over the war on Ukraine, including Putin.

Mainland Affairs Council Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) yesterday said that the government was not surprised by a YouTuber’s recent claim that some Taiwanese working in China have obtained Chinese identification cards.
Shen declined to comment on individual cases, saying that the government has a comprehensive understanding of the situation and that the vast majority of cases would enter the judicial process.
Shen made the remarks in response to media queries for comment on claim made by Taiwanese influencer Wen Tzu-yu (溫子瑜), who said that some Taiwanese working in China have allegedly obtained Chinese identity cards.
Photo: Chung Li-hua, Taipei Times
Wen, better known as Pa Jung (八炯), recently posted a video on his YouTube channel about Chinese efforts to recruit sympathetic Taiwanese to make videos for Douyin, China’s version of TikTok. The video alleged cases involving Taiwanese who became Chinese citizens and gave up their Taiwanese household registration.
He also said intermediaries allegedly help other Taiwanese privately apply for Chinese IDs in exchange for profits of up to 6 million yuan (US$896,060).
He said he went to the National Immigration Agency to report a large number of Taiwanese who said on social media that they obtained Chinese ID cards, with some posting videos or photos displaying the documents.
Shen yesterday said the government was not surprised by the allegations of a structure in which certain channels in Taiwan help the Chinese government obtain documents or promote activities.
“We have a comprehensive understanding of the situation,” he said.
Shen said the Chinese Communist Party has been expanding and diversifying its efforts to promote integration and infiltration in Taiwan and organize various “united front” activities.
Government agencies would work closely with judicial authorities to monitor the situation, he said.
Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Chung Chia-pin (鍾佳濱) yesterday said that according to the Act Governing Relations Between the People of the Taiwan Area and the Mainland Area (臺灣地區與大陸地區人民關係條例) and the Additional Articles of the Constitution, Republic of China (中華民國憲法增修條文), citizens are not permitted to simultaneously hold Taiwan and People’s Republic of China citizenship.
If a Taiwanese citizen establishes household registration in China, the person could lose Taiwanese household registration and status, and be treated as a resident of the mainland area, Chung said.
Rights arising from the person’s status as a Taiwanese citizen could consequently also be lost, he said.
Chung urged the public to exercise caution when engaging in exchanges with China and not to be tempted or pressured by others.
If people carelessly obtain a Chinese identity card, their existing citizenship status and associated rights could be lost permanently, he added.

====================================================================================================

MMA makes its Asian Games debut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:47:01 UTC
01:47:01 KST

A sport once banned in much of the US and famously decried as “human cockfighting” by a high-profile politician is making an ambitious play for the Olympics.
Mixed Martial Arts, known as MMA, is making its Asian Games debut this week in Japan — a milestone that fighters and organizers hope leads to bigger things.
Galastein Tan, director general of the Federation of International Mixed Martial Arts, said being at the Asian Games was “a big step.”
Photo: AFP
“As for any sport, the inclusion in the continental games is critical,” he said.
“Obviously the inclusion means that you already have a good governance structure, you have enough members, athletes to be able to compete, your ruleset, your officials are ready and therefore it is a significant one,” he added.
At a gym akin to a school sports hall, men and women scrap it out in separate categories in front of a modest but enthusiastic crowd.
Many of the competitors are from countries with proud histories in fighting sports such as Thailand, Kazakhstan, the Philippines and hosts Japan.
For fans of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), the MMA promoter synonymous with the sport, there is one immediate difference.
In UFC, which in June held an event on the South Lawn of the White House, the rough and tumble takes place inside a caged octagon.
At the Asian Games competitors do battle on a white and gray mat, but they are not fenced in.
For martial artists used to fighting in a cage, this takes some adapting to — a fence “does not really align with Olympic values,” Tan said.
Getting everyone to agree on the rules of the competition, including what moves are allowed, is a major obstacle to MMA being at the Olympics.
Singapore’s Teo Hui Hoon said that Asian Games and Olympic recognition would encourage a generation to take up the sport.
“I think it will grow the talent pool a lot,” she said. “It will encourage more children and teenagers to take up the sport and take it seriously.”
“Because now there’s a clear pathway, right?” she said. “You can join a national team, the next step you can go to the Olympics.”
MMA is not the only sport debuting at Asia’s premier sporting event and hoping one day to get into the Olympics.
So is teqball — roughly a crossover between football and table tennis — and there is also the fast-growing racquet sport of padel.
It makes for a crowded field, and there are many other sports with Olympic ambitions.
Plenty of hard work and political lobbying lies ahead if MMA is to make it.
“We have been in talks with the IOC and other relevant stakeholders that have influence or decision on the recognition,” said an upbeat Tan.
Of the other issues on the long path to Olympic recognition there is a perception in the eyes of some that MMA is too violent.
Still, driven by the phenomenal success of the UFC, MMA is now mainstream — a far cry from the 1990s when then-US senator John McCain compared the early version of the sport to cockfighting.
Getting the whole of MMA to coalesce around one governing body is also essential if an Olympic place is to one day come.
Los Angeles in 2028 is too soon, and then comes Brisbane four years later.
“Nothing is impossible,” Tan said. “We hope that MMA is a sport that the Olympics finds relevance to and the ability to connect with both adults and also the youth.”
“[It is] a sport which has global appeal and a sport that is ready and capable of fitting into a major Games schedule,” Tan said. “So if the IOC or LA28 comes and say, MMA, would you like to be in as a medal sport or demo sport, we are ready.”

Yu and Huang narrowly defeated Japan’s Toshiki Uematsu and Rena Temma 5-4 (2-4, 5-3, 4-2, 1-4, 1-4, 4-0, 1-4, 4-1, 7-5) to give Taiwan its first gold in soft tennis mixed doubles at an Asian Games since 2018.
Sun secured Taiwan’s first wushu medal at this year’s game, with a combined score of 19.453 points in men’s taijiquan-taijijian. He scored 9.733 points to finish second in taijiquan and 9.720 points to finish fourth in taijijian. He was 0.107 points behind gold medalist Liu Dewen (劉德文) of China.
Photo: Mark Baker, AP
Taijiquan is the competitive form of taichi, performed through a sequence of controlled, flowing movements, while taijijian is a taichi sword routine. In the combined event, athletes perform both routines and their scores are added together to determine the final standings.
“After waiting 10 years, I finally made it to the Asian Games podium. The moment I stood there, it felt truly unreal,” Sun said after the competition, adding that he was grateful for his family’s support over the past decade.
A video message from his six-year-old son telling him to keep going gave him the confidence he needed ahead of the competition, the 30-year-old said.
Sun’s taijijian routine featured the song Call of Silence from the Japanese anime Attack on Titan, combined with Taiwanese elements to create a dramatic soundtrack.
Sun said he and his coach spent more than a month creating 15 versions of the arrangement before the Asian Games.
Sun won gold in taijiquan and silver in taijijian at the 2023 World University Games in Chengdu, China.
Photo: Eugene Hoshiko, AP
“Being 30 is just a number for me,” said Sun, the oldest of the Taiwanese wushu competitors in Japan.
Shih defeated Vietnam’s Khuat Hai Nam 9-3 to win the bronze medal in the men’s kumite under-67kg division.
He rebounded from a disappointing campaign at the Hangzhou Asian Games, where he lost in the bronze-medal bout.
Photo: Andrew Couldridge, Reuters
It was Taiwan’s second karate medal in Nagoya, after Chien Hui-hsuan (簡慧萱) won bronze in the women’s individual kata on Sunday.

His run to the final four ended with a 2-5 loss to Japan’s Kozaki Yugo in the semi-finals, sending him to the bronze-medal match.

The Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency yesterday reminded people that swimming is prohibited in alpine lakes after a hoax announcement of a Jiaming Lake (嘉明湖) “swimming carnival” was circulated on social media.
A person posted the event online claiming that a minimum of seven people could join in on Double Ten National Day for NT$81,000 per person.
They also asked potential participants to complete a 48-hour trek to reach the Taitung County lake, which is at an elevation of more than 3,000m, and then a 300m swim within 10 minutes.
Photo courtesy of the Taitung Forest District Office
Organizers of competitions or events that could cause environmental disruption in natural forests, except regular hiking, existing ecological tours or traditional indigenous activities, must apply to the agency, it said.
Such events are restricted to existing hiking trails, forest roads or recreational public space, it added.
The agency would not approve any activity that might affect ecological environments, including operating motor vehicles on trails or closed roads, water activities such as swimming or standup paddleboarding in alpine lakes, or large-scale competitions or events at cultural heritage sites, former indigenous settlements or ecologically sensitive areas, it said.
It also prohibits use of bright lighting or loudspeaker equipment that could affect wildlife, or any activities involving feeding, luring or repelling wildlife, the agency said.
Swimming in Jiaming Lake not only disrupts ecological environments, but carries high safety risks, as alpine rescue would be time-consuming with limited resources, it said.
The agency reiterated that it would not allow such an activity, which is clearly inconsistent with the site’s conservation and management objectives.

====================================================================================================

Taiwan and the new globalization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:46:57 UTC
01:46:57 KST

Geopolitical conflicts, geo-economic rivalry, trade disruptions, energy insecurity, technological competition and the reorganization of global supply chains are making uncertainty a structural feature of the emerging economic order rather than a temporary disruption. Economic efficiency is increasingly being balanced against resilience, security and strategic flexibility.
Taiwan enters this era from a position of considerable strength. It has demonstrated an extraordinary capacity to absorb external shocks while maintaining economic dynamism. Its technological capabilities, particularly in semiconductors and advanced manufacturing, have made it an indispensable part of global production networks. Its companies occupy critical positions in some of the world’s most sophisticated technology ecosystems.
However, the more central Taiwan becomes to global technology supply chains, the more exposed it becomes to geopolitical tensions, disruptions in trade and changes in the architecture of globalization. Taiwan should remain deeply integrated with the world economy. The question is how that integration can be made more resilient, diversified and adaptable.
The old model of globalization was driven predominantly by efficiency. Today, supply chains are increasingly being designed not only for cost, but also for resilience, redundancy, trusted relationships and strategic security.
For Taiwan’s next phase of economic growth, the first priority should be infrastructure. Physical infrastructure remains fundamental, but for a technology-intensive economy, infrastructure increasingly means reliable energy, digital connectivity, data networks, logistics and communications systems. Energy security would become even more important as semiconductor manufacturing, artificial intelligence and other energy-intensive industries expand.
Second, Taiwan needs to broaden its base of private investment. Its successful technology companies are a tremendous national asset, but the next phase of growth should create greater opportunities for smaller enterprises, start-ups, services and companies operating at the intersection of manufacturing and technology.
Third, Taiwan should continue moving beyond assembly and into higher-value manufacturing and services. Its semiconductor leadership provides an exceptional foundation, but the opportunities extend into chip design, advanced materials, artificial intelligence, robotics, biotechnology, precision engineering and other emerging technologies. The objective should not simply be to produce more. It should be to capture a larger share of the value created by global technological transformation.
Fourth, export diversification would become increasingly important. Taiwan’s integration into global supply chains is a source of strength, but concentration — whether in markets, products or technologies — can create vulnerabilities. Diversification means developing additional markets and capabilities so that disruption in any one part of the system does not become a systemic shock.
Strategic autonomy should not be confused with self-sufficiency. No modern economy can, or should, attempt to produce everything domestically. Rather, Taiwan should identify areas where excessive dependence could create strategic vulnerability and build alternative sources, technologies, inventories and partnerships.
This leads to perhaps the most important priority: building a network of trusted economic partnerships.
The future is unlikely to be characterized by complete decoupling or a return to the hyper-globalization. More likely, there would be overlapping networks of countries connected through trade, investment, technology, standards and supply chains, and increasingly through trust.
The emerging environment rewards countries that have multiple economic relationships and sufficient strategic flexibility to navigate between them. Strategic autonomy does not mean isolation, diversification does not mean disengagement and multi-alignment does not mean neutrality. They can all be instruments for remaining globally connected while reducing excessive dependence on any single relationship.
India provides an example of this broader trend. New Delhi has sought to deepen its economic relationship with the US while maintaining significant relationships with other major economies, including Russia and Iran. The underlying principle is less about choosing one camp than preserving strategic space in an increasingly fragmented international environment.
Taiwan’s partnerships need not be defined exclusively through geopolitics. There is considerable scope for stronger economic engagement with India, particularly in semiconductors, electronics, advanced manufacturing, digital technologies, skills, research and development and supply-chain diversification.
As businesses seek to make their supply chains more resilient, the economic logic for connecting India’s manufacturing and market capabilities with Taiwan’s technological strengths is becoming increasingly compelling.
Taiwan has an opportunity to position itself not merely as a critical supplier to the global technology economy, but as a hub within a broader network of trusted economic relationships across Asia and beyond.
Resilience is often understood as the ability to withstand a shock, but in a world where shocks are becoming more frequent, resilience alone is insufficient.
Taiwan needs the ability to redirect investment, diversify markets, develop new technologies, build alternative supply chains and forge new economic partnerships while retaining the strengths that made it successful in the first place.
The objective should not be to eliminate uncertainty. It should be to build an economic architecture capable of thriving in uncertainty.
Shishir Priyadarshi is president of the Chintan Research Foundation and a former director of the WTO.

It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. Unknown Publisher

對話 Dialogue
清清：華華，中秋節快到了，你打算怎麼過？
Qīngqing: Huáhua, Zhōngqiūjié kuài dàole, nǐ dǎsuàn zěnme guò?
Photo: Wikimedia Commons 照片：Wikimedia Commons 提供
華華：當然是回家跟家人一起烤肉啊！
Huáhua: Dāngrán shì huíjiā gēn jiārén yìqǐ kǎoròu a!
清清：你們也會烤肉喔？你家不是住大樓嗎？要在哪裡烤？
Qīngqing: Nǐmen yě huì kǎoròu o? Nǐ jiā búshì zhù dàlóu ma? Yào zài nǎlǐ kǎo?
華華：會啊！就在一樓大門口前面跟鄰居一起烤，一邊吃一邊聊，好開心。
Huáhua: Huì a! Jiù zài yīlóu dàménkǒu qiánmiàn gēn línjū yìqǐ kǎo, yìbiān chī yìbiān liáo, hǎo kāixīn.
清清：我們家比較喜歡在院子裡賞月，吃月餅和柚子，喝喝茶、聊聊天，烤肉太麻煩了。
Qīngqing: Wǒmen jiā bǐjiào xǐhuan zài yuànzi lǐ hǎngyuè, chī yuèbǐng hàn yòuzi, hēhē chá, liáoliáo tiān, kǎoròu tài máfán le.
華華：我現在都上網訂整組的烤肉用具和食材，一次送到家，就沒那麼麻煩了。
Huáhua: Wǒ xiànzài dōu shàngwǎng dìng zhěng zǔ de kǎoròu yòngjù hàn shícái, yí cì sòngdào jiā, jiù méi nàme máfán le.
清清：這倒是個好辦法，不用花太多時間準備。
Qīngqing: Zhè dàoshì ge hǎo bànfǎ, búyòng huā tài duō shíjiān zhǔnbèi.
華華：希望今年中秋節天氣好，能看見又大又圓的月亮，好好享受烤肉大餐。
Huáhua: Xīwàng jīnnián Zhōngqiūjié tiānqì hǎo, néng kànjiàn yòu dà yòu yuán de yuèliang, hǎohǎo xiǎngshòu kǎoròu dàcān.
翻譯 Translation
Qingqing: Huahua, the Mid-Autumn Festival is coming soon. How are you planning to celebrate it?
Huahua: Naturally, I’m heading home to have a barbecue with my family.
Qingqing: You have a barbecue, too? Don’t you live in an apartment building? Where are you going to have it?
Huahua: We have it in front of the main entrance on the first floor with our neighbors. We eat and chat and have a great time.
Qingqing: My family prefers to admire the moon in the yard, eat mooncakes and pomelos, drink tea and chat. Having a barbecue is too much hassle.
Huahua: Now I order a complete set of barbecue equipment and ingredients online. Everything is delivered to my home at once, so it isn’t that much trouble.
Qingqing: That’s actually a good idea. You don’t have to spend too much time preparing.
Huahua: I hope the weather will be good this Mid-Autumn Festival, so we can see a big, round moon and really enjoy our barbecue feast.
生詞 Vocabulary
1. 烤肉 (kǎoròu) to have a barbecue; barbecue
2. 鄰居 (línjū) neighbor
3. 賞月 (shǎngyuè) admire the moon
4. 月餅 (yuèbǐng) mooncake
5. 柚子 (yòuzi) pomelo
6. 整組 (zhěng zǔ) the whole set
7. 用具 (yòngjù) equipment; utensils
8. 食材 (shícái) ingredients

Carney, Lula urge nations to join middle-power group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:46:51 UTC
01:46:51 KST

Leaders from Canada, Brazil, Kenya and the EU unveiled a joint diplomatic front on the eve of the UN General Assembly, seeking to shield global cooperation from an increasingly transactional geopolitical order.
Called “Partners for Multilateralism,” it aims to “create a flexible, open framework for countries from different regions and political traditions that are willing to work across divides,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, European Council President Antonio Costa and Kenyan President William Ruto wrote yesterday in the Financial Times.
The leaders said the mechanism, which they shorthanded P4M, would serve to build coalitions for reform and to translate into practical action shared principles, including those enshrined in the UN Charter.
Photo: Reuters
They planned to convene yesterday on the sidelines of the UN Assembly general debate in New York.

Taiwan is stepping up efforts to attract US tourists after the number of US visitors surpassed 710,000 last year, with a majority of them visiting for tourism, the Tourism Administration said.
The agency last week led a delegation to New York, Chicago and Los Angeles to promote Taiwan as a travel destination, with members comprising Taiwanese hoteliers, travel agencies and international flight carriers.
The visit would also mark the agency’s return to Chicago after a seven-year hiatus, as it seeks to tap into the US Midwest market.
Photo: Screen grab from the Tourism Administration’s Web site
More than 710,000 US travelers visited Taiwan last year, with nearly 60 percent coming for tourism, the agency said.
Meanwhile, the number of weekly flights between Taipei and 13 cities in North America has exceeded 200 this year, it added.
“This dense flight network has greatly facilitated North American travelers’ visit to Taiwan. That shows that North America has high potential to become a major source of international tourists for Taiwan,” it said.
Agency statistics showed that 42.25 percent of international tourists last year were repeat visitors, reaching a record-high from before the COVID-19 pandemic, it said.
To attract more North American travelers, the administration said it is offering incentives for repeat visitors and transit travelers to encourage them to revisit.
Chen Ming-chu (陳明珠), who has hosted the Golden Bell and Golden Melody Awards multiple times, was invited to host the promotional events in the three US cities, it said.

US and China consider making AI channel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:46:45 UTC
01:46:45 KST

US and Chinese economic officials discussed creating a communication channel for artificial intelligence (AI) concerns at meetings on Sunday as they set the stage for a summit of the countries’ leaders this week.
The talks come as the countries confront broadening fears that increasingly capable AI systems could wipe out humanity, offering a rare incentive for cooperation despite an intensifying race for technological supremacy.
“We just had a very successful engagement with the Chinese on trade and AI,” US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent said after talks with a team led by Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng (何立峰).
Photo: AFP
The talks are a prelude to a meeting in the White House on Thursday between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平).
The discussions, which included US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, went for about eight hours at JPMorgan Chase & Co’s headquarters in New York.
Bessant said the two sides discussed setting up a way to communicate about AI issues called the “US-China AI dialogue.”
“The US has proposed that we have a notification mechanism between the two countries,” Bessent said.
Such notifications are for “incidents,” or a situation “that rises up to a national security level from AI,” he said, adding that both sides have agreed to meet again.
Bessent and He also spoke one-on-one, a source familiar with the matter said.
China’s top trade negotiator, Li Chenggang (李成鋼), said the talks were held in a “good atmosphere” as he left JPMorgan headquarters on Sunday, while Greer said Sunday it is “imperative that we are able to work together.” State-run Xinhua News Agency described the meetings as “candid, in-depth and constructive.”
Asked about the possibility of mutual tariff reduction on certain goods, Greer said teams “are continuing to work through this.”
The aim is to identify “non-sensitive” goods that can be considered separately from trade measures in the future, he added.
Such products could cover consumer goods from the Chinese side and energy, agricultural and other products like medical devices on the US side.
Beyond less sensitive items, US officials are seeking to ensure the continued flow of rare earth magnets and critical minerals that are vital for US manufacturers.
Working level meetings could continue into yesterday, a source familiar with discussions said.
Earlier negotiations saw China pledge purchases of US agriculture goods too, and their fulfilment of the terms could be an issue under scrutiny.
Another issue is US economic pressure on Iran, as Washington’s war with Tehran has entered its seventh month.
China is a top economic partner of Iran that buys much of its oil output and a key diplomatic backer.
Analysts caution that expectations for the Trump-Xi summit are low.
“One of the only things we can hope for in the short term is a truce, and that this will likely continue through the remainder of this year,” former US deputy secretary of state Kurt Campbell said.
“I think you will hear [Trump] announce the intention to meet with Xi Jinping two more times,” added Campbell, who is chairman of The Asia Group consultancy.
Trump and Xi are expected to meet in November at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, China. Trump is also anticipated to invite Xi to the G20 summit in December at his Doral resort in Miami.

Ministry to revise indoor air quality regulations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:46:44 UTC
01:46:44 KST

The Ministry of Environment yesterday said it is proposing revisions to the Indoor Air Quality Management Act (室內空氣品質管理法), including stricter regulations for facilities serving young children and older adults, standardized monitoring requirements and adjusted requirements for dedicated indoor air quality personnel according to the size of a facility.
The ministry is to hold discussions with local environmental protection bureaus on the proposed changes next month.
The eighth annual Taiwan Indoor Air Quality Week, organized by the Taiwan Indoor Environment Quality Management Association, opened yesterday. Events are being held in Taipei, Taichung and Kaohsiung, focusing on indoor air quality management and healthy living.
Photo: CNA
Department of Atmospheric Environment Director-General Huang Wei-ming (黃偉鳴) said the ministry had begun work on revising the act, which took effect in 2012.
The ministry held three meetings with experts and academics last month and plans to consult local environment protection bureaus with practical enforcement experience next month.
The timeline for completing the draft amendments remains uncertain, Huang said.
The ministry would consider tightening indoor air quality standards for facilities serving vulnerable groups, such as older adults and young children, he said.
However, the would be on improving air quality rather than simply tightening standards, he said.
If conditions cannot be improved and standards are simply tightened, the effect would be limited, Huang added.
The ministry aims to establish standards by the end of this year for simplified continuous automatic devices to help monitor air quality in indoor facilities, he said.
The thresholds for requiring facilities to appoint dedicated indoor air quality management personnel would also be revised and adjusted based on the characteristics and size of each facility, he added.
The ministry has finished an initiative started last year to help kindergartens improve indoor air quality, Huang said, adding that the results would be announced as soon as possible.
Taiwan Indoor Environment Quality Management Association chairwoman Chou Nan-chun (周南君) said that the theme of this year’s Indoor Air Quality Week is clean air as a basic human right.
People in Taiwan spend more than 80 percent of their time indoors, she said.
Amid the growing combination of risks posed by extreme heat and emerging infectious disease, it is essential to establish scientifically based management system, she added.
In France, where air-conditioning penetration is only about 20 percent, vulnerable groups were exposed to heat-related harm amid heat waves in Europe this summer, Deputy Minister of Environment Hsieh Yen-ju (謝燕儒) said.
Although air-conditioning is common in Taiwan, keeping doors and windows closed for extended periods while running air-conditioners makes indoor air quality an issue that must be taken seriously, he said.
The UN has discussed epidemic-prevention issues, saying that following the COVID-19 pandemic, disease prevention should be considered comprehensively, she said.
Indoor air quality is an important part of that effort, she said, citing the need for disinfection and sanitation at airports and maintaining air quality at large-scale gatherings.

====================================================================================================

Taiwan can help set standards in AI race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:46:43 UTC
01:46:43 KST

In April last year, a former OpenAI researcher released AI 2027, a report outlining two paths for artificial intelligence (AI) development: an unbridled competitive race to stay ahead of China or a cautious international effort to slow down before things get out of control.
At the time, it seemed like a thought experiment. However, many now are realizing that the rapid advancement of AI could threaten security, while moving too slowly might yield strategic advantages to China. Where AI goes from here is a political choice for US President Donald Trump.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in an article titled “We Must Pace the Frontier” said the key question for regulating AI development is not whether to slow down, but exactly how to do so. Humans risk losing control of AI systems, resulting in AI-enabled cyberattacks or bioterrorism, as well as serious economic consequences, he wrote.
Rather than calling for an absolute halt on research in the US and China, Amodei has proposed that the US slow down to a pace that safety mechanisms can keep up with, and that China be forced to slow even further.
The Hugging Face incident in July removed any excuse to dismiss concerns as apocalyptic skepticism: More than 1,200 AI agents communicated through unauthorized channels, with about 700 participating in attacks on external systems.
This does not mean AI has developed total autonomy, but it demonstrates that when AI models can collaborate, exploit loopholes and seek tools independently, patching vulnerabilities after product launches would no longer be possible.
The real dilemma lies there. If the US slows down unilaterally, China might catch up. If it accelerates to maintain its lead, the risk of losing control would be amplified.
The heads of three major US AI giants — Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla CEO Elon Musk — are calling for slowing AI development, while Trump insists on not losing the AI race to China. These positions bring the two paths outlined in the AI 2027 report into focus.
US-China AI competition has moved from a race over compute into the next stage — who can control their developmental pace while limiting their rival’s.
Taiwan cannot treat this as a debate within the US tech industry. When Washington ties AI security to restrictions on Chinese technology, Taiwan’s advanced chips and manufacturing supply chains become an industrial advantage, and a security policy tool.
If the US requires chip flows, overseas data centers and high-end computing capacity to be traceable, Taiwanese companies would face more than export controls. Their customers, investment decisions, capacity allocation and research-and-development partnerships could all be assessed and priced through a geopolitical lens. Taiwan should not choose between “slowing down” or “speeding up,” but seek to be a rulemaker.
The government should establish risk classifications, third-party testing and incident reporting mechanisms for frontier AI and high-end computing. Taking advantage of its pivotal position in the semiconductor supply chain, Taiwan should also participate in the democratic world’s efforts to develop standards for compute governance, model safety and chip traceability. Otherwise, Taiwan could end up bearing the costs of the strictest controls while having little choice but to accept rules set by others.
Liao Ming-hui is an assistant research fellow at the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research.

Over 2,700 attend banquet for infidelity-themed arts festival opera show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:46:42 UTC
01:46:42 KST

More than 2,700 people dined with the Sun Kailin Opera Troupe’s outdoor performance of Justice Bao Beheads Chen Shimei (包公鍘陳世美), a traditional Taiwanese opera, in Tainan’s Anping District (安平) on Sunday.
The event was part of the infidelity-themed Zhamei Arts Festival, conceived after former president Chen Shui-bian’s (陳水扁) daughter, Chen Hsing-yu (陳幸妤), revealed her divorce in a scathing one-star review of her ex-husband’s orthopedic clinic last month.
Sunday’s performance was staged in front of the festival’s first of three mass banquets, with Tainan Mayor Huang Wei-che (黃偉哲) and Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Chen Ting-fei (陳亭妃) among 2,700 or so diners across 280 tables.
Photo: CNA
Those without a ticket for the paid banquet were still welcomed to appreciate the opera for free outside the dining area.
Although Chen Hsing-yu’s online review served as a catalyst, festival spokesperson Ma Chia-tung (馬嘉彤) told reporters that the event organizers wished to refrain from commenting directly on individuals’ private lives out of respect for their privacy.
What began as social commentary on current events gradually evolved into a discussion of morality and marital ethics through culture, Ma said, encouraging the public to support traditional opera.
The five-day festival invited attendees to bring their own food for picnics while enjoying free performances on Friday and Saturday nights, followed by paid banquets and free performances from Sunday through today.
Each night features Taiwanese hand puppetry or Taiwanese Hokkien opera, with performances based on either the story that inspired the festival’s name or another tale of infidelity.
The organizers estimated that Saturday’s picnic drew about 50,000 people, as many took advantage of the weekend.
The Zhamei Arts Festival opened with the Goodoo Puppet Troupe performing Justice Bao Executes the Prince Consort (包公斬駙馬), while the Luo Yu-cong Opera Troupe headlined Betrayal of the Hippocratic Oath — The Fury of the Justice and the Beheading of the Unfaithful Man (杏林怨 — 青天怒斬負心漢) on Saturday.
With references to the medical world that were not in the original opera, the Saturday show included not-so-subtle nods to the festival’s original inspirations.
Yesterday, the Chunmei Opera Troupe performed Justice Shi Tries the Unfaithful Man (施工審負心), with the Shiu Kim Taiwanese Opera Troupe closing out the festival today with a performance titled The Haunting of Chou by the Widow Lin (林投姐活捉周阿司).
The Zhamei Arts Festival’s name is a satirical reference to The Execution Trial of Prince Consort Chen Shimei (鍘美案), a Chinese parable featuring Justice Bao (包青天), a figure in Chinese literature and popular culture known for his incorruptibility.
The iconic folklore version of Justice Bao was based on a real-life official from China’s Song Dynasty.
In the story, Bao defies an imperial pardon and orders the execution of Chen Shimei (陳世美), a prince consort who concealed his marriage from the royal family, committed infidelity, and attempted to murder his first wife and children.
Organizers chose the story because they saw parallels with Chen Hsing-yu’s former marriage to orthopedist Chao Chien-ming (趙建銘), who had once been nicknamed Taiwan’s “prince consort” because he was married to the daughter of a then-sitting president.

Neutrality on the campaign trail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:46:39 UTC
01:46:39 KST

Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋) has been drawing crowds at his appearances at night markets as he campaigns for Taipei mayor. However, vendors say they have attracted unwanted attention from the city government after displaying Shen’s campaign slogan: “ocean current” (洋流).
The slogan is a play on the last character of his name (洋), which means “ocean.”
Vendors said they received official notices from the Taipei Market Administration Office ordering the removal of all campaign advertisements. The DPP has asked why the city government would invoke “administrative neutrality” to demand the removal of ads when the vendors are private citizens.
The Chiang (蔣) family’s legacy of martial law, it seems, is certainly living up to its reputation.
The office notice says that under the Civil Servants Election and Recall Act (公職人員選舉罷免法), political parties and individuals are prohibited from hanging or erecting campaign or recall advertisements on roads, bridges, parks, government agencies, schools and other public facilities.
The act restricts campaign advertising on public facilities used for public passage, yet vendors registered with the market administration who display the “ocean current” ad on their own stalls or carts are simply exercising their freedom of speech and political expression. Such displays neither obstruct public passage nor disrupt social order, nor do they have any bearing on administrative neutrality; the vendors are not civil servants.
The Market Administration Office is, under the guise of maintaining administrative neutrality, overstepping its bounds and depriving vendors of their freedom of political expression on their own stalls and place of work. If the office is acting on behalf of Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安), their efforts could have the opposite of their intended effect. By demonstrating the Chiang administration’s heavy-handedness and incompetence, they might well increase the likelihood of some shifting their support to Shen.
Chiang must say whether he ordered or was aware of such an abuse of power by the office, which violates administrative neutrality and infringes on freedom of speech. The facts must be made clear. If Chiang ordered the action, he should publicly apologize. If the department acted on its own, those responsible should be held accountable and disciplined to prevent similar abuses of power.

Lithuanian edition of Wu Ming-yi’s ‘The Man with the Compound Eyes’ released
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:46:37 UTC
01:46:37 KST

The Lithuanian translation of Taiwanese writer Wu Ming-yi’s (吳明益) The Man with the Compound Eyes (複眼人) has been released in Lithuania.
The novel follows two very different people — an outcast from a mythical island and a woman on the verge of suicide — whose lives become unexpectedly intertwined when a tsunami sends a massive island of garbage crashing into Taiwan’s coast, according to an introduction by the Ministry of Culture.
The book was translated by Lithuanian translator Vaidotas Bacianskas, who is currently studying and living in Taiwan.
Photo: CNA
In a recent interview with the Central News Agency, he said the biggest challenge was not understanding the Chinese text, but conveying its nuances and style in his native language.
Bacianskas said the biggest challenge in translating his first full-length Chinese novel was conveying the subtleties and style of the original work.
“There are many subtle and beautiful expressions in Chinese,” he said.
He said he spent considerable time adjusting the tone and wording to achieve natural fluency in Lithuanian while preserving the literary texture of the Chinese original.
He also added the scientific names of the many endemic Taiwanese animals and plants mentioned in the novel so that Lithuanian readers could look them up.
Bacianskas said he was impressed by the immersiveness of Chinese, contrasting it with European languages whose grammatical tenses can constantly remind readers that events took place in the past. He therefore intentionally rendered some chapters in the present tense in hopes of conveying a sense that “the scene was happening in front of their eyes.”
He began learning Chinese somewhat incidentally after earning a bachelor’s degree in theater, when he decided to take on what he considered one of the world’s most difficult languages.
Bacianskas later earned a degree in Sinology in Lithuania and a master’s degree in international education in China before returning to Lithuania to teach Chinese and work as an interpreter.
His desire to better understand Chinese culture eventually brought him to Taiwan, where he began studying at National Taiwan Normal University’s Graduate Institute of Translation and Interpretation two years ago.
Bacianskas first became acquainted with Wu and his work in 2023, when he served as an interpreter for the author during a visit to Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania, at the invitation of the World Federation of Taiwanese Associations.
He said it “really was fate,” as he later traveled to Taiwan to study translation and happened to finish The Man with the Compound Eyes just as Lithuanian publisher Phi knygos contacted him.
The publisher knew of his connection with Wu and invited him to translate the novel, he said.
Bacianskas said he had originally planned to translate works about Taiwan’s history to help Lithuanians better understand Taiwan.
However, he later realized that a book does not have to explicitly introduce Taiwan to achieve that goal, as literature can also convey the country through imagination and the issues explored through its characters.
Bacianskas has also translated the Lithuanian classic Whitehorn’s Windmill by Kazys Boruta into Chinese as part of his master’s thesis.
In doing so, he deliberately retained Lithuanian cultural details while adding explanations to help Chinese readers connect with the literary world of the original work.
He believes a good literary translator should have a deep connection with the culture of the original work.
As an example, Bacianskas said he has also begun translating Taiwan Travelogue (臺灣漫遊錄) by Yang Shuang-zi (楊双子).
To more accurately portray a scene involving the cracking and eating of sunflower seeds, he bought a bag of sunflower seeds himself so he could experience it firsthand.
He also said that seeing the scenery of Hualien County influenced his choice of words and helped with his translation work.
For Bacianskas, Taiwan’s diversity within a relatively small geographic area was particularly appealing.
Its combination of mountainous and coastal landscapes was a new experience for someone accustomed to Lithuania’s predominantly flat terrain.
The high population density of Taiwan’s cities also gave him opportunities to encounter a wide range of events and experiences in daily life, he added.

Baipu to bolster chip ecosystem: Lai
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:46:37 UTC
01:46:37 KST

Kaohsiung’s Baipu Industrial Park (白埔產業園區) would bolster Taiwan’s semiconductor ecosystem, balance north-south development and boost the country’s global competitiveness, President William Lai (賴清德) said at its groundbreaking ceremony yesterday.
The nearly 89-hectare park would create more than 4,000 jobs and generate about NT$300 billion (US$9.45 billion) in annual production value, marking a new milestone for Taiwan’s semiconductor industry, Lai said.
With artificial intelligence (AI) applications and high-performance computing expanding rapidly worldwide, advanced integrated circuit (IC) assembly services have become increasingly important to the semiconductor industry’s competitiveness, he said.
Photo: Lee Hui-chou, Taipei Times
The park would draw on cooperation among the Ministry of Economic Affairs, the Kaohsiung City Government and major semiconductor companies, including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電), he said.
Earlier this month, TSMC announced plans to develop a 3-hectare site in the industrial park, with two buildings housing modular facilities that can be reconfigured as technology evolves.
The site is to include small cleanrooms and laboratories for testing and joint development of advanced assembly technologies, equipment and materials, as well as a training center for highly skilled specialists in semiconductor processes and equipment, TSMC said.
Construction of two campuses at Baipu Industrial Park, including two TSMC facilities, would be completed in the fourth quarter of 2029, the Kaohsiung Economic Development Bureau said.
The park’s entire infrastructure is expected to be completed by 2031, it added.
Also present at the groundbreaking were Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫), Minister of the Interior Liu Shyh-fang (劉世芳) and Kaohsiung Mayor Chen Chi-mai (陳其邁), as well as representatives from TSMC, ASE Technology Holding Co (日月光投控) and Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海精密), also known as Foxconn Technology Group (富士康).
Lai said the park aims to become Taiwan’s first semiconductor base focused on developing, testing and certifying critical semiconductor equipment and raw materials.
The development is expected to shorten the time needed to introduce new technologies and help Taiwanese companies establish a foothold in the global supply chain, he said.
Once completed, Baipu Industrial Park would complement an IC assembly and testing cluster at Kaohsiung’s Renwu Industrial Park (仁武產業園區) and another cluster focused on critical raw materials and other key components at the city’s Ciaotou Science Park (橋頭科學園區), Lai said.
Baipu would also complete southern Taiwan’s semiconductor S-corridor project, with Kaohsiung at its core, Lai said.
The S-corridor project links science parks and technology industrial parks in Chiayi County, Tainan, Kaohsiung and Pingtung County in southern Taiwan.
Kaohsiung’s strong metal processing and precision machinery industries would enhance the project’s value, Lai said.
Addressing concerns about water shortages, Lai said the government has launched the “pearl string project” to connect reservoirs through Taiwan via interregional pipelines to boost reserve water capacity.
Facilities such as water purification and desalination plants would be developed, providing greater flexibility in water management, he said.
With the project nearing completion, the previous practice of using water trucks to maintain supplies at science parks would no longer be necessary, Lai said.
On electricity consumption, Lai said state-owned Taiwan Power Co (台電) has agreed to a plan to build an electricity distribution network in Baipu Industrial Park to ensure stable power supply.

Taiwan labor minister’s APEC meeting in China goes smoothly: MOL
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:46:36 UTC
01:46:36 KST

Minister of Labor Hung Sun-han’s (洪申翰) participation in an APEC ministerial meeting in China went “smoothly” yesterday, with China following APEC practices and rules, the Ministry of Labor (MOL) said.
“Hung and his delegation’s participation proceeded smoothly, and the Chinese side made relevant arrangements in accordance with APEC practices and rules,” the ministry said in a statement last night.
Hung attended the eighth APEC Human Resources Development Ministerial Meeting, a one-day meeting held yesterday in Nanjing, after arriving in the Chinese city on Sunday.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Labor via CNA
The trip made Hung the first ministry head to travel to China since President William Lai’s (賴清德) administration took office in May 2024, marking a rare cross-strait visit by a Cabinet-level official from the ruling Democratic Progressive Party.
Photos provided by the ministry showed Hung seated behind a nameplate reading “Chinese Taipei,” the name under which Taiwan participates in APEC, one of the few major international forums in which it is a formal member.
During the meeting, Hung said workers’ rights and social protections should keep pace with changes in labor markets, demographics and technology.
He called for more flexible work arrangements for workers raising children and stronger protections for platform workers.
On artificial intelligence (AI), Hung called for guidelines and risk-management rules to promote “responsible AI” and “human-centered” governance to prevent workers’ rights from being undermined, the ministry statement said.
“Technological innovation can bring new opportunities, but social protections for workers should also be improved accordingly,” he said, adding that technological development and labor rights should advance together.
The ministry said Hung also learned from other APEC economies during formal sessions and informal exchanges, while interactions with other APEC economies created opportunities for further cooperation.
Hung served as a lawmaker before becoming labor minister in November 2024.
During his time in the legislature, he spoke out on human rights and political issues concerning Hong Kong and Tibet, both sensitive subjects for Beijing.
Asked on Tuesday last week about possible security risks ahead of the trip, Hung did not say whether he was concerned about being unable to return to Taiwan.
Instead, he reiterated that he would attend the meeting in accordance with “established APEC practice” and on the basis of “reciprocal dignity.”
Mainland Affairs Council Deputy Minister and spokesperson Liang Wen-chieh (梁文傑) said on Sept. 3 that the risks associated with Hung’s trip were “controllable,” citing the smooth participation of Taiwanese officials in APEC meetings in China earlier this year.
Hung is expected to return to Taiwan no later than Thursday, when the Minimum Wage Deliberation Committee is scheduled to meet to discuss next year’s minimum wage level.

State of world getting worse as UN Security Council paralysed: Guterres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

01:46:36 KST

State of world getting worse as UN Security Council paralysed: Guterres
The UN chief’s mandate ends on December 31 this year, with a successor yet to be named.
The state of the world “is getting worse” as wars multiply and become more complex, United Nations chief Antonio Guterres has said, warning that growing geopolitical divides have paralysed the Security Council and leave the most vulnerable “in very dramatic situations”.
In a wide-ranging interview with Al Jazeera on Monday, the eve of his final address as secretary-general to the UN General Assembly (UNGA), Guterres discussed the major military conflicts happening in the world and whether the UN is still relevant in addressing today’s challenges.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Why do Sudan’s humanitarian truces keep failing and who is to blame?
- list 2 of 4Israeli forces arrest dozens of Palestinians in occupied West Bank raid
- list 3 of 4CNN, Politico, MS NOW sue Trump administration over White House ban
- list 4 of 4What’s the US–China AI ‘hotline’ that Trump plans to pitch to Xi Jinping?
Guterres said the involvement of “superpowers” and key council members in the wars has created a crisis due to the continued violations of international law.
“That creates an environment of impunity, in which midsize powers believe that they can do whatever they want because nothing will happen to them,” Guterres said.
The UN chief outlined the real-life impacts that the Russia-Ukraine war and the US-Israel war on Iran are having on people, particularly around food accessibility, rising fuel prices and global inflation.
“The combination of the war in Ukraine with the problems of exports of foods, fertilisers, and energy through the Black Sea, if you combine it with the difficulties in the Strait of Hormuz [in the Gulf], in the Bab al-Mandeb [in the Red Sea], and in the attacks [on] oil installations in several countries of the [Middle East] region, we are creating a situation that has a devastating impact on many economies around the world,” Guterres said.
He added that rising interest rates and fuel prices in developed countries could eventually be managed, whereas people in the developing world “are in a desperate situation” due to the increasing energy and food costs and the lack of fertilisers.
Dire need for reforms
Guterres, who previously served as prime minister of Portugal and UN high commissioner for refugees, has been the UN chief since January 1, 2017, though his mandate is coming to an end on December 31, 2026.
His successor, who is yet to be named, will take charge of an organisation that is grappling with multiple crises and is, in Guterres’s opinion, in dire need of reforms to stay relevant and important on the global stage.
He notably cited the Security Council, saying it “still essentially represents the world of World War II”.
Candidates in the running to replace Guterres include the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Rafael Grossi, former Senegalese President Macky Sall and Ecuadorian diplomat Maria Fernanda Espinosa.
To be recommended by the UNSC, a candidate for UN secretary-general needs at least nine of the council’s 15 members to vote in favour and must avoid a veto from any of the five permanent members – China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States – before a final vote in the UNGA.

Unknown

01:46:34 KST

About 45 data center projects worth US$68 billion were blocked or delayed by local pushback from April to June due to mounting opposition in the US, research group Data Center Watch said yesterday.
Communities across the nation are now pushing through moratoriums on new construction, often before developers can apply for permissions. About 30 statehouses introduced or adopted rules pertaining to issues such as data center siting, electricity and water, the group said in a report provided to Bloomberg News.
The research quantifies growing concern about the rapid pace of expansion of artificial intelligence (AI), both in the construction of new computing clusters and its proliferation into daily life. There are now 843 opposition groups across 49 states, with Hawaii the exception.
Photo: AP
“New groups continue to emerge, opposition is appearing across a wide range of states and jurisdictions, and online petition signatures continue to grow,” lead analyst Miquel Vila said.
Data Center Watch is a project from AI intelligence company 10a Labs.
Home to the biggest investors in AI infrastructure, the US is experiencing a bipartisan backlash against facilities that critics say harm the environment and siphon away resources to fuel AI systems that many fear would imperil jobs and livelihoods.
Tech giants such as Amazon.com Inc, Meta Platforms Inc, Microsoft Corp and Alphabet Inc — the so-called hyperscalers — argue they need the facilities to win a race against China to develop potentially world-changing AI.
US President Donald Trump has dismissed opposition to data centers and concern about advances in AI as a “sick conspiracy,” saying “the only one that is happy about it is China.”
The number and value of disrupted projects fluctuates by quarter, with the first three months of this year seeing 75 cases worth roughly US$130 billion facing opposition in the US.
The 45 projects affected during the second quarter represented more than half of all new large-scale developments Data Center Watch began tracking during the period.
Opposition by public figures and the use of social media are amplifying concerns. One petition against a project in Tennessee garnered more than 500,000 signatures on online activism platform Change.org, accounting for more than one-third of those on the service during the quarter, it said.
For the first time since it began its research two years ago, Data Center Watch also reported on protests against data centers outside the US, given increased international opposition. Much as in the US, local campaigns are targeting specific projects, governments’ planning authorizations and worries about resource usage, sometimes coordinating nationally. The group highlighted opposition across European nations, Australia, South Africa and beyond.
“As with many other trends, the US has generally been at the forefront, but the phenomenon is increasingly becoming global,” Vila said. “We anticipate that this will just become more prominent as data center development expands across the globe.”
