Asian Games | Day 2: Yu, 13, sets swimming Asian record, Thai shuttler suspended for doping
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:49:36 CST
22:49:36 KST

by sportswriter Li Jia
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Chinese teenager Yu Zidi's sensational Asian record propelled China's gold-medal charge on day two of the 2026 Asian Games on Monday, while Thai badminton player Pitchamon Opatniputh became the first known doping case of the Games.
Pitchamon, 19, tested positive for the banned substance furosemide and was provisionally suspended.
The International Testing Agency said an out-of-competition sample collected from Opatniputh in Nagoya on September 17 returned an Adverse Analytical Finding for furosemide. The substance is listed by the World Anti-Doping Agency as a specified substance prohibited at all times under the category of diuretics and masking agents.
China claimed two shooting golds, including a world record, and five swimming titles, while Zhang Boheng won the men's gymnastics all-around gold to round off another prolific day for the delegation.
In the pool, 13-year-old Yu maintained her stunning form. She came from behind to win the women's 200-meter individual medley in an Asian record of 2 minutes, 6.10 seconds, with teammate and defending champion Yu Yiting second in 2:07.99. Japan's Mio Narita took bronze in 2:10.40.
Yu's winning time was just 0.40 seconds off the world record set by Canada's Summer McIntosh.
"I feel even happier winning this second gold medal than I did with the first one," Yu said.
Her performance produced the first Asian swimming record of the Games. Yu made her Asian Games debut by winning the 200 butterfly on Sunday.
The excitement peaked in the men's 4x200 freestyle relay. Japan led for the first 750 meters as China stayed close behind. Pan Zhanle narrowed the gap on the third leg before Zhang Zhanshuo took the lead in the closing stages to give China gold in an Asian record of 7:00.17.
Japan took silver in 7:01.05, while South Korea claimed bronze in 7:06.76.
Adding to China's swimming success, backstroke specialist Xu Jiayu successfully defended his men's 50 backstroke title in a Games-record 24.04, while Wan Letian and Wang Xue'er finished 1-2 in the women's 50 backstroke.
China's Dong Zhihao and Japan's Shin Ohashi shared gold in the men's 100 breaststroke in 58.64, while defending champion Qin Haiyang took bronze.
South Korea claimed its first swimming gold of the Games as Kim Yeong-beom won the men's 50 freestyle, while defending champion Siobhan Haughey of Hong Kong, China took the women's 200 freestyle title.
In shooting, China swept the men's 10-meter air rifle individual and team gold medals, setting a world record in the team event.
The trio of Zhang Changhong, Sheng Lihao and Ma Sihan combined for 1,899.0 points to take team gold, breaking the previous world record of 1,898.4. India won silver with 1,890.1, while South Korea claimed bronze with 1,884.2.
In gymnastics, China's Zhang Boheng retained the men's all-around title. Fresh from winning the same event at the Asian championships, the 26-year-old scored 85.065 points to take gold, while Japan's reigning Olympic champion Shinnosuke Oka and 2021 Olympic champion Daiki Hashimoto finished second and third, respectively.
Zhang had finished runner-up to Oka at the Paris Olympics and to Hashimoto at last year's World Championships.
"Gymnastics keeps progressing, and both Japanese all-around gymnasts have very high levels of difficulty and execution," Zhang said.
China's success extended to other disciplines, with Lin Xinyu, Li Mingxu, Huang Anqi and Zhang Xirui winning the triathlon mixed relay in 1:25:54.
Gong Li and Li Qiaoqiao added karate gold medals in the women's kumite 61-kilogram and 68-kilogram categories, respectively.
In team sports, China's women's football team thrashed the Philippines 5-1 in Group G, while the women's volleyball team edged Thailand 3-2 to avenge its defeat in last month's Asian Championship final and advanced to the gold-medal match. China's women's basketball team beat Indonesia 110-41 in Group A.
After two days of competition, China led the medal table with 23 gold, 10 silver and five bronze medals. Japan was second with eight gold, 12 silver and 12 bronze, followed by South Korea with five gold, 13 silver and 15 bronze. ■

'Scorched earth': How Israel is remaking south Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:49:22 UTC
22:49:22 KST

Breadcrumb
'Scorched earth': How Israel is remaking south Lebanon
Beirut, Lebanon - Israel’s military is continuing a “scorched earth” strategy in southern Lebanon, despite a framework peace deal and ongoing direct negotiations between Beirut and Tel Aviv, analysts told The New Arab.
Airstrikes and controlled demolitions have rocked southern towns and villages almost daily, while US-mediated talks aimed at securing an Israeli withdrawal and Hezbollah’s disarmament have stalled ahead of the Israeli legislative elections in October.
Earlier this month, Israeli ground troops took control of the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge - allegedly containing a Hezbollah command centre, tunnels and weapons stores - after months of fighting in southern Lebanon.
“Ali al-Taher is considered a linchpin for the Israeli security system of today,” Elias Hanna, a retired Lebanese army general, told The New Arab.
Hanna added that from this vantage point, Israeli forces can consolidate their position in the previously captured Beaufort Castle and dominate the area south of the Litani River.
But it is not clear whether the Israeli military’s seizure of the Ali al-Taher ridge signals an intent to expand its occupation deeper into Lebanese territory.
The subsequent destruction of the alleged Hezbollah command centre – Israeli troops detonated the hilltop, causing a 4.1-magnitude seismic tremor – has been touted as a strategic and symbolic victory by Israel.
However, Hanna said the Ali al-Taher ridge was not as valuable a stronghold for Hezbollah as it was before this war began, as the armed group has switched to guerrilla-style warfare that precludes the use of large bases.
According to Hanna, Israel’s military, for its part, is also pursuing a new strategy in the south.
“This time it’s totally different from the 1982 invasion – now they are destroying everything,” Hanna said.
Israel historically occupied a swathe of southern Lebanon from 1982 to 2000, when Israeli forces withdrew completely. This time, however, Hanna argued that Israel cannot afford to put a large number of boots on the ground and is opting instead for a “scorched earth” approach.
“If you want to destroy your enemy, you destroy the ecosystem of your enemy, so he won’t be able to ever recover and come back,” Hanna explained.
The remaking of south Lebanon
Israel has flattened entire villages inside the “yellow line”, a 10km-deep ribbon of land occupied by Israel along the Lebanese-Israeli border.
At least 46 of 54 towns and villages in this area have been heavily damaged or completely levelled by airstrikes and controlled demolitions, according to satellite analysis by Bellingcat. More than 340,000 people remain internally displaced.
In August, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz visited southern Lebanon and said the military was destroying underground infrastructure and “all the houses” in the area. Lebanon’s Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has called the destruction a serious violation of international humanitarian law.
“Israel is consolidating its control over this dead security zone that it has demarcated in the south, in which it is attempting to erase any evidence of civilian life and then any possible social or infrastructural base for Hezbollah,” Sam Heller, a Beirut-based analyst with the Center for International Policy, told The New Arab.
The direct negotiations between Lebanon and Israel were announced in April, shortly before the latest ceasefire, despite heavy opposition from Hezbollah.
In June, a framework deal was agreed between Beirut and Tel Aviv that included a plan to launch “pilot zones” in southern Lebanon where the Lebanese army would disarm Hezbollah.
The last round of talks, held in Rome in August, reached a deadlock after Beirut failed to achieve either of its two key objectives: to secure a genuine ceasefire and to make progress on Israel’s withdrawal from the areas it occupies in southern Lebanon.
Israel, by contrast, prioritised Hezbollah’s disarmament and rejected a proposal to launch additional pilot zones.
Asked whether the Lebanese army was capable of disarming Hezbollah, which is widely considered to be the more powerful force, Hanna said: “It’s not about the Lebanese army’s capabilities, it’s about the political will of Hezbollah.”
One of the main obstacles to the negotiations has been the failure to appoint a third party to verify the agreement’s implementation on the ground. Italy and France emerged as potential candidates, but Israel objected to both options.
“The Israelis likely have basically nil confidence in Lebanese authorities’ ability or willingness to really confront Hezbollah or disarm it,” Heller said. “Instead, Israel will seek to legitimate internationally its continued direct role in Lebanon and to make that maximally sustainable politically,” he added.
“Israel has gotten most of what it wanted, which is a step towards the normalisation of relations, the opening of direct negotiations, and the legitimation by Lebanese authorities – as part of this agreement – of Israel’s indefinite presence inside South Lebanon.”
The diplomacy of an indefinite occupation
The next round of talks, which has been postponed to October, is due to take place as Israel gears up for what could be pivotal elections.
“The negotiations themselves have stalled, given the upcoming Israeli elections. The Lebanese President is hopeful that a change in government would yield positive results; the PM and his team are less so,” Mohanad Hage Ali, with the Carnegie Middle East Center, told The New Arab.
While progress on the negotiations before the end of October remains unlikely, Heller doubts that the Israeli elections will deliver a government more amenable to making the concessions Beirut is trying to secure.
The Lebanese government, which says it has no option but to negotiate, is seeking to garner international support for the Lebanese Armed Forces, especially as the UN peacekeeping mission in the south is set to withdraw at the end of the year.
Last week, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun met French President Emmanuel Macron in Paris, as well as Arab, European and US military officials.
While France affirmed its support, observers say this remains largely symbolic, as any meaningful change to the status quo in southern Lebanon will rely heavily on action and mediation from Washington.
“Regardless of how the Lebanese government feel about the prospects of negotiations, the process itself is now all about conflict management and de-escalation, buying time, and the fact is they have no other tools,” Hage Ali said.
Alex Martin Astley is a freelance journalist based in Beirut, covering conflict, foreign policy, and social justice issues

Xinhua Headlines: Fast, focused and forward-looking, China's manufacturing opens new frontier
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:49:19 CST
22:49:19 KST

* Chinese manufacturers are taking a more targeted approach to global markets, moving beyond standardized products to create solutions tailored to specific needs in different global markets.
* Stronger R&D capabilities and faster responses to market needs are allowing Chinese manufacturers to play a bigger role in product design and development.
* From robotics and embodied intelligence to quantum computing, new applications are opening up a wide range of possibilities for manufacturing and creating new links with markets around the world.
HEFEI, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- As Europe was gripped by extreme heat this summer, a production base in Wuhu City, east China's Anhui Province, was racing to meet urgent orders from its European clients: 20,000 mobile air conditioners had to be produced and loaded in just seven days.
The tight deadline set an equally demanding task for the supply chain. More than 1,000 types of components had to be coordinated at the same time, with some rushed to the production line by air and high-speed rail to keep everything on schedule. Once completed, the air conditioners were transported overland across Eurasia to France.
The seven-day turnaround was made possible by a manufacturing system built for rapid shifts in demand -- from adjusting production lines to coordinating suppliers and logistics in real time.
Wuhu is just one part of Anhui's manufacturing landscape. Across the province, manufacturing runs at a scale that can be measured by the minute.
"Every minute, about 190 home appliances, 50 laptops and four new energy vehicles roll off production lines across the province," said Liang Yanshun, Party chief of Anhui, at the ongoing World Manufacturing Convention in Hefei, the provincial capital.
Increasingly, Chinese manufacturers are taking a more targeted approach to global markets, moving beyond standardized products to create solutions tailored to specific needs in different global markets.
TARGETED SOLUTION
In late March, Wuhu-based Tri Waters New Energy Technology Co., Ltd. signed a strategic cooperation agreement with the Maldives' transport authorities to export 32 electric sightseeing boats, each capable of carrying 100 passengers.
Taking into account the Maldives' island geography and demand for greener transport, further plans are in the pipeline to build a photovoltaic energy storage system, charging and battery-swapping networks, and a vessel maintenance base.
"This is a green mobility solution tailored to the Maldives," said Liu Yang, deputy general manager of the company, who noted that the Maldivian side had discussed and planned with the company before reaching a final deal.
"The shift from simply 'taking orders' to 'solving problems' reflects a profound restructuring of the logic of global industrial division of labor," said Han Junhui, an associate researcher at the Chinese Academy of Science and Technology for Development.
For decades, Chinese manufacturers have been engaged in global production networks primarily because of their strong industrial base and cost efficiency, often making products designed by overseas brands, Han said.
"Now, stronger R&D capabilities and faster responses to market needs are allowing Chinese manufacturers to play a bigger role in product design and development," he added.
FORWARD-LOOKING TECH
The same shift is also visible in emerging sectors, where new technologies are still taking shape. From robotics and embodied intelligence to quantum computing, new applications are opening up a wide range of possibilities for manufacturing and creating new links with markets around the world.
At the robotics and embodied intelligence exhibition area of the 2026 World Manufacturing Convention, nearly 200 robots are on display, showcasing applications in logistics, elderly care, services and other fields.
Data from the General Administration of Customs of China show that China exported more than 12 million robots of various types in the first half of this year, with exports valued at 24.85 billion yuan (about 3.68 billion U.S. dollars), reaching more than 160 countries and regions.
"China has a rich range of application scenarios and a strong manufacturing base. The rapid development of artificial intelligence has further strengthened the competitiveness of Chinese-made robots in international markets," said You Wei, chairman and general manager of EFORT Intelligent Robot Co., Ltd., a robotics manufacturer exhibiting at the conference.
Guo Guangcan, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said quantum technology worldwide has accelerated its transition from laboratory research to engineering validation, real-world applications and commercial deployment at scale.
Hefei has now developed a complete technological system covering quantum chips, cryogenic cooling, measurement and control systems, operating software and cloud services, Guo noted.
Through a quantum computing cloud platform open to users worldwide, its computing services have reached 192 countries and regions, with more than 55 million visits and over 1.16 million scientific research and industrial computing tasks completed.
"These applications have demonstrated the feasibility of commercializing quantum computing at scale and provided a practical path for the global open sharing and cross-sector application of quantum technologies," Guo said. ■

Asian Games | Day 2: Yu, 13, sets swimming Asian record, Thai shuttler suspended for doping
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:48:54 CST
22:48:54 KST

Yu Zidi reacts after the women's 200m individual medley final at the 2026 Asian Games in Tokyo, Japan, Sept. 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Zhizun)
by sportswriter Li Jia
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Chinese teenager Yu Zidi's sensational Asian record propelled China's gold-medal charge on day two of the 2026 Asian Games on Monday, while Thai badminton player Pitchamon Opatniputh became the first known doping case of the Games.
Pitchamon, 19, tested positive for the banned substance furosemide and was provisionally suspended.
The International Testing Agency said an out-of-competition sample collected from Opatniputh in Nagoya on September 17 returned an Adverse Analytical Finding for furosemide. The substance is listed by the World Anti-Doping Agency as a specified substance prohibited at all times under the category of diuretics and masking agents.
China claimed two shooting golds, including a world record, and five swimming titles, while Zhang Boheng won the men's gymnastics all-around gold to round off another prolific day for the delegation.
In the pool, 13-year-old Yu maintained her stunning form. She came from behind to win the women's 200-meter individual medley in an Asian record of 2 minutes, 6.10 seconds, with teammate and defending champion Yu Yiting second in 2:07.99. Japan's Mio Narita took bronze in 2:10.40.
Yu's winning time was just 0.40 seconds off the world record set by Canada's Summer McIntosh.
"I feel even happier winning this second gold medal than I did with the first one," Yu said.
Her performance produced the first Asian swimming record of the Games. Yu made her Asian Games debut by winning the 200 butterfly on Sunday.
Xu Haibo, Fei Liwei, Pan Zhanle and Zhang Zhanshuo (L to R) of China celebrate on the podium after the men's 4x200m freestyle relay final at the 2026 Asian Games. (Xinhua/Chen Zeguo)
The excitement peaked in the men's 4x200 freestyle relay. Japan led for the first 750 meters as China stayed close behind. Pan Zhanle narrowed the gap on the third leg before Zhang Zhanshuo took the lead in the closing stages to give China gold in an Asian record of 7:00.17.
Japan took silver in 7:01.05, while South Korea claimed bronze in 7:06.76.
Adding to China's swimming success, backstroke specialist Xu Jiayu successfully defended his men's 50 backstroke title in a Games-record 24.04, while Wan Letian and Wang Xue'er finished 1-2 in the women's 50 backstroke.
China's Dong Zhihao and Japan's Shin Ohashi shared gold in the men's 100 breaststroke in 58.64, while defending champion Qin Haiyang took bronze.
South Korea claimed its first swimming gold of the Games as Kim Yeong-beom won the men's 50 freestyle, while defending champion Siobhan Haughey of Hong Kong, China took the women's 200 freestyle title.
In shooting, China swept the men's 10-meter air rifle individual and team gold medals, setting a world record in the team event.
The trio of Zhang Changhong, Sheng Lihao and Ma Sihan combined for 1,899.0 points to take team gold, breaking the previous world record of 1,898.4. India won silver with 1,890.1, while South Korea claimed bronze with 1,884.2.
Zhang Boheng in action on the parallel bars during the men's artistic gymnastics all-around final at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Jia Yuchen)
In gymnastics, China's Zhang Boheng retained the men's all-around title. Fresh from winning the same event at the Asian championships, the 26-year-old scored 85.065 points to take gold, while Japan's reigning Olympic champion Shinnosuke Oka and 2021 Olympic champion Daiki Hashimoto finished second and third, respectively.
Zhang had finished runner-up to Oka at the Paris Olympics and to Hashimoto at last year's World Championships.
"Gymnastics keeps progressing, and both Japanese all-around gymnasts have very high levels of difficulty and execution," Zhang said.
China's success extended to other disciplines, with Lin Xinyu, Li Mingxu, Huang Anqi and Zhang Xirui winning the triathlon mixed relay in 1:25:54.
Gong Li and Li Qiaoqiao added karate gold medals in the women's kumite 61-kilogram and 68-kilogram categories, respectively.
In team sports, China's women's football team thrashed the Philippines 5-1 in Group G, while the women's volleyball team edged Thailand 3-2 to avenge its defeat in last month's Asian Championship final and advanced to the gold-medal match. China's women's basketball team beat Indonesia 110-41 in Group A.
After two days of competition, China led the medal table with 23 gold, 10 silver and five bronze medals. Japan was second with eight gold, 12 silver and 12 bronze, followed by South Korea with five gold, 13 silver and 15 bronze. ■

Timeline: ‘Mysterious explosions’ and blasts since al Sharaa took charge in Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:42:34 UTC
22:42:34 KST

Since Ahmed al Sharaa assumed leadership of Syria in late 2024, a string of “mysterious explosions” at ammunition depots and military storage sites has unsettled communities and prompted official investigations.
Many involve civil-war munitions and temporary facilities, with causes often listed as under review or later tied to improper storage.
Following the fall of Bashar al Assad’s rule on December 8, 2024, Israel expanded its occupation of Syrian territory and took control of the buffer zone and positions on the Syrian side of Mount Hermon.
Since then, Israel has conducted hundreds of strikes on Syrian military assets, claiming they are aimed at preventing military weapons from “falling into hostile hands”.
Israel has occupied Syria’s Golan Heights since 1967 and unilaterally annexed the territory in 1981, a move not recognised internationally.
Here’s a rough timeline focused on verified incidents of “mysterious explosions” since al Sharaa took charge of Syria.
December 2024 — Tartus countryside
Days after Bashar al Assad was overthrown on December 8, a massive explosion tore through a former Syrian military ammunition site in the Tartus area. The blast was so large that seismic monitoring stations registered what appeared to be a roughly magnitude-3 event. Videos showed a huge fireball and successive secondary explosions.
This occurred amid an intensive Israeli campaign against Assad-era military infrastructure. The Institute for Science and International Security subsequently examined satellite imagery and concluded that an ammunition depot northeast of Tartus was the most likely source of the enormous explosion. The organisation noted that satellite imagery showed fires at the site and that the facility contained bunkered ammunition storage.
December 29 2024 — Adra weapons depot explosion
A major explosion tore through a weapons storage site near Adra, northeast of Damascus, killing 11 people, most of them civilians.
The explosion was likely caused by an Israeli strike, and the incident was widely reported at the time as a suspected Israeli attack. But an Israeli military source told AFP at the time: “We are not aware of IDF [Israeli army] strikes in the area. The IDF did not strike in the area.” A local official described it simply as an explosion of unknown origin.
January 2-3 2025 — al-Safira, south of Aleppo major explosions from confirmed Israeli strikes
Large explosions were reported near al-Safira following what Syrian state television and Reuters described as an Israeli strike targeting military facilities.
Residents reported a series of exceptionally powerful explosions, while Israeli aircraft struck defence factories and research facilities.
January 5 2025 — Kisweh ammunition depots south of Damascus
Explosions hit former-regime ammunition depots around Kisweh, south of Damascus. The blasts may have resulted from an Israeli airstrike. AFP reporters on the ground observed fires and destruction at the site.
Again, however, Israel denied responsibility, telling AFP that its military had not attacked the site.
February 2, 2025 — Deir Ezzor’s former-regime underground weapons depot
A powerful explosion occurred at an underground weapons depot belonging to the former Syrian regime on Mount Harabesh in Deir Ezzor. The site was then under the control of the new administration. No casualties were initially reported.
February 8 2025 — Israeli strike in Deir Ali
The Israeli military said it had struck a Hamas weapons depot near Deir Ali, south of Damascus, saying the weapons were intended for attacks on Israeli forces.
In a brief statement, the army said the weapons depot was hit in the Deir Ali area in southern Syria, claiming that the weapons were stored to carry out attacks against Israeli targets.
Hamas did not publicly respond to the claim at the time.
February 26 2025 — Israeli strikes in Kiswah/Izraa
Israel carried out air strikes against locations around Kiswah south of Damascus and Izraa in Daraa. One strike hit a weapons depot and caused a fire.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz publicly confirmed the strikes and said Israel was targeting weapons in southern Syria.
March 18 2025 — Israeli strikes on former Syrian military sites
Israeli aircraft struck former Syrian army positions around Shinshar and Shamsin south of Homs, according to Syrian security sources cited by Reuters.
Israel had previously acknowledged similar strikes against military headquarters and sites containing weapons and equipment.
April 2–3 2025 — Israeli bombardment in Hama, T4 and Damascus
This was one of the clearest Israeli episodes after Assad's fall.
Israel admitted to striking the remaining military capabilities at Hama airbase and T4 airbase, as well as military infrastructure around Damascus. Reuters reported that the strikes destroyed or badly damaged runways, aircraft, hangars and weapons depots.
The Syrian foreign ministry explicitly blamed Israel, saying Israeli forces had attacked five locations within 30 minutes and had nearly destroyed Hama Military Airport. Damascus called the strikes a violation of Syrian sovereignty and appealed to the international community to stop them.
Israeli Defence Minister Katz subsequently described the strikes as a warning to al Sharaa and said Israel would not allow Syria to become a security threat.
May 2 2025 — Israel strikes near Syria's presidential palace
SANA reported Israeli strikes around Damascus, Hama and Daraa. Israel's military said it had struck a military site, anti-aircraft guns and surface-to-air missile infrastructure.
The same day Israel also struck an area adjacent to al Sharaa's presidential palace in Damascus. Reuters described this as a particularly explicit warning to the new authorities.
The Israeli military confirmed the strike, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz described it as a clear message that Israel would not allow Syrian forces to deploy south of Damascus or threaten the Druze community
June 3–4 2025 — projectiles from Syria followed by Israeli strikes
Two projectiles were fired from Syria towards Israel. Israel responded with strikes on Syrian territory and said it held President al Sharaa responsible.
The Syrian foreign ministry disputed the attribution. It said reports that projectiles had been fired toward Israel had not been verified, and said various parties could be seeking to destabilise the region for their own interests.
A Syrian official specifically mentioned remnants of Assad-era militias linked to Iran as possible actors seeking to provoke an Israeli response.
July 2025: the clearest cluster of unexplained ammunition-depot blasts
July 2 — Kafraya/al-Fu'ah area, Idlib
Explosions were reported at a military site near Kafraya and al-Fu'ah. Syrian state television, citing the defence ministry, attributed successive explosions to high temperatures and said there were no civilian or ambulance casualties.
July 8 — north of al-Fu'ah, Idlib
An ammunition depot containing mines and rockets left from the war exploded about one kilometre from residential areas. The interior ministry confirmed the existence of the depot and said there were minor injuries and fainting cases, but initially did not give a direct cause for the explosion.
July 24 — Maarrat Misrin, Idlib
A much more serious explosion occurred at an ammunition depot, killing at least seven initially and eventually 11 people, with more than 140 injured according to Syrian reporting.
AP reported that the cause was initially unclear; state television referred to the material as remnants of the war.
September 1 2026 — Binnish, Idlib: ammunition-laden vehicle explosion
An ammunition-laden vehicle exploded in Binnish, Idlib countryside, killing at least five people and injuring others. 
SANA reported the explosion but did not establish its cause or identify the vehicle's owner. Other reporting said the munitions were being transferred/unloaded at a warehouse belonging to a local arms dealer, who was reportedly among those killed. 
September 9 2026 — Sarmada, northern Idlib explosion
An explosion occurred at a temporary defence ministry storage facility near Sarmada used to collect and store weapons and remnants of war before their transfer. The death toll rose to 14 defence ministry personnel, with more than 10 others injured, including civilians.
Secondary explosions complicated the emergency response. The defence ministry said it assumed full responsibility and launched an investigation into the cause and circumstances.
At the time of reporting, no external actor was blamed and the cause remained undetermined.
September 18–19 2026 — Ayyash, western Deir Ezzor
An explosion occurred at a Syrian army position in Ayyash, west of Deir Ezzor. SANA initially reported that the cause was under investigation. By September 19, the defence ministry had held a funeral for 11 personnel killed in the blast.
September 21 2026 — Al-Eis, southern Aleppo countryside
A series of powerful explosions struck a Syrian army weapons depot near Al-Eis in the early hours of September 21. Secondary detonations continued for an extended period, sending rockets and other projectiles into the surrounding area.
At least four people were injured, including one by shrapnel. Authorities closed roads, including the Aleppo–Damascus highway, evacuated nearby residents and placed emergency teams on alert. The cause remained under investigation, and no external actor was officially blamed in the initial reporting.
Reuters described it as the fourth similar incident in Syria during September.
While many of the earliest post-Assad explosions were widely linked to or occurred amid intensive Israeli air strikes, the more recent cluster of depot blasts has largely been treated by Syrian officials as accidents or storage failures still under investigation, with not many confirmed to external attributions in official statements.

Makeshift tent schools welcome Gaza pupils for 1st time in 3 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:42:00 UTC
22:42:00 KST

Hundreds of thousands of Gaza children returned to in-person classes over the weekend for the first time in nearly three years, attending lessons in tents or damaged buildings as many families struggled to afford uniforms and supplies.
The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) says 98% of schools in Gaza were either destroyed or damaged during the war and Gaza education officials say about 660,000 students have been deprived of in-person learning and regular participation in education.
The reopening is a fragile milestone for Gaza after a conflict that has killed around 22,000 students and more than 770 education workers, including 532 teachers, according to Ibrahim Ramadan, director of education for East Khan Younis.
"The last time I have been to school was three years ago. Now, we are starting the school year, it is year of joy, happiness and success," said Moayed Abu Mustafa in Khan Younis.
Mustafa said he was determined to learn even though he will sit on the floor in a tent lacking ventilation, he has no decent shoes, nor a notebook and pen, and lost friends during the war.
"Despite all of this we will learn, we will learn even in a tent."
Fifteen-year-old displaced student Samar Abu Salmi, who lives with her family in a tent, is also returning to class.
"We studied on phones and we haven’t seen our teachers ... now, we are back pursuing our dream ... from one tent to another," she said, speaking in the yard of her new makeshift school.
She also lacks much of the essential equipment, which has become unaffordable for her family.
"Before the war, everything was available for us – notebooks, pens, goods, clothes, outings, things that we could get cheaply," Salmi said.
Despite the devastation in the enclave, the Education Ministry, backed by international and local organizations, has moved ahead with the 2026-27 academic year, establishing dozens of temporary schools made of tents, tarpaulins, sheet metal and wood to accommodate pupils.
Some are built on sandy ground, others have classrooms with only some mattresses and a blackboard, into which students cram. Others are still housing dozens of displaced families.
Attending another school was 14-year-old Yamen Abu Samra.
"We used to wake up happy to go to school ... Now, when we come to school, we’re afraid of stray bullets, rockets, strikes, everything," he said.
"Now, I’m sitting in a tent that has absolutely nothing, just the sun and the heat," he added.
At least 540,000 students are expected to attend in-person classes this year in makeshift private schools, temporary learning centers and educational points, with UNICEF support, according to education officials. Online learning will continue for those who can't attend classes or who left Gaza during the war.
Israeli forces remain in control of more than 70% of Gaza despite last year's cease-fire, which halted major fighting but failed to end the conflict.
Israel's 2-year genocidal war killed over 73,000 people, mostly women and children, Palestinian authorities say. The war was triggered by the October 2023 Hamas incursion that caused around 1,200 deaths.
Stationery trader Khaled Aliyan, 30, said Israeli import restrictions have reduced supplies and hiked prices.
"This notebook, which used to cost 3 shekels ($1), now costs 15 (shekels). All stationery items are expensive," he said.

Google fined 403 million euros over location data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:39:51 UTC
22:39:51 KST

Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC) has fined Google 403 million euros for breaching EU privacy rules in its handling of users’ location data, the regulator announced on Sept. 21.
The company has six months to bring its processing into compliance with the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation.
The inquiry into Google Ireland Limited followed complaints from European consumer organizations and covered the period from May 25, 2018, to Feb. 4, 2020.
The DPC found that Google unlawfully and unfairly processed location data through its Web & App Activity and Location History features. It also retained location data for longer than necessary.
For Location Accuracy, Google failed to demonstrate that its processing complied with requirements for lawfulness, fairness and transparency. The regulator also found transparency breaches across all three features.
Google said the case concerned “historical policies that have since been updated,” adding that it had changed its practices and introduced tools to help users manage location data from 2019 onward.
Ireland is Google’s lead privacy regulator in the EU because the company’s European headquarters are in Dublin.

Aviation analytics firm Cirium said 72 of more than 6,000 flights to or from the UK had been cancelled on Monday.
“If this were the end of the day, this level of cancellations is close to normal — around one percent,” Cirium said, adding that it expected operational performance to deteriorate as the day progressed.

In 2023, Britain experienced its worst air traffic systems failure in years, affecting more than 700,000 passengers after hundreds of flights were delayed or cancelled.
NATS has operated under a public-private partnership model since 2001. The British government holds a 49 percent stake and a “golden share” that allows it to intervene in strategic decisions, while the remainder is held mainly by a consortium of airlines.

Stopping Ozempic may raise heart attack and stroke risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:35:30 UTC
22:35:30 KST

Stopping Ozempic may raise heart attack and stroke risk
Stopping GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound may have consequences that go well beyond regaining weight.
- Date:
- September 21, 2026
- Source:
- Washington University in St. Louis
- Summary:
- A large study suggests the cardiovascular benefits of GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound can disappear surprisingly quickly when treatment stops. After two years off the medications, patients had a 22% higher risk of heart attack, stroke, and death compared with those who stayed on them.
- Share:
GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide (Ozempic and Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro and Zepbound) have surged in popularity for treating diabetes and helping people lose weight. About one in eight U.S. adults now use these medications, which are also known to provide cardiovascular benefits. But new research suggests that those heart benefits may fade quickly when treatment is stopped.
Researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis tracked more than 333,000 U.S. veterans with type 2 diabetes for three years. They found that interrupting or stopping GLP-1 treatment for as little as six months was associated with a meaningful increase in the risk of major cardiovascular events compared with remaining on the medication.
The longer patients stayed off treatment, the greater the increase in risk. After two years without GLP-1 therapy, the risk of heart attack, stroke and death was up to 22% higher than among people who continued treatment, largely wiping out the cardiovascular protection gained while taking the drugs.
The findings, published in BMJ Medicine, suggest that stopping GLP-1 medications may have consequences that extend well beyond weight regain. They also point to the importance of uninterrupted treatment for maintaining heart protection.
"There is enormous exuberance about starting GLP-1 drugs, but not nearly enough attention to what happens when people stop," said senior author Ziyad Al-Aly, MD, a WashU Medicine clinical epidemiologist and chief of the Research and Development Service at the VA Saint Louis Health Care System. "Many quit after a few months because of cost, side effects or shortages. When they stop, it's not just weight that comes back; they experience a resurgence in inflammation, blood pressure, and cholesterol. Weight regain is visible; the metabolic reversal is not."
"Our data suggest this metabolic whiplash is detrimental to heart health," Al-Aly added. "Restarting the medication helped restore some protection, but only partially, showing that discontinuation leaves a lasting scar."
Heart protection depends on continued GLP-1 use
GLP-1 medications include the semaglutide drugs Ozempic and Wegovy and the tirzepatide drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound. After observing that about half of users stop taking GLP-1 drugs not long after beginning treatment, Al-Aly set out to examine what happens to cardiovascular health after therapy is discontinued.
The study focused on major adverse cardiovascular events, including heart attack, stroke and death. Researchers analyzed data from 333,687 veterans with type 2 diabetes. Of those, 132,551 had been prescribed GLP-1 drugs, while 201,136 had been prescribed sulfonylureas, another class of diabetes medications.
Sulfonylureas include glipizide (Glucotrol), glimepiride (Amaryl), and glyburide (Diabeta and others). Participants were followed for up to three years.
Researchers reassessed GLP-1 treatment status every six months. During the study, 26% of GLP-1 users stopped taking the medication altogether. Another roughly 23% experienced a treatment gap lasting at least six months before eventually restarting therapy.
Continuous treatment produced the greatest benefit
The clearest cardiovascular benefit appeared among people who remained on GLP-1 medications throughout the full three-year study period.
Compared with participants taking sulfonylureas, those who consistently stayed on GLP-1 therapy had an 18% lower risk of major cardiovascular events. That translated to about four fewer major cardiovascular events for every 100 people over three years.
Participants who stayed on GLP-1 treatment for two years or two-and-a-half years before stopping for the rest of the study also saw meaningful reductions in risk, at 7% and 15%, respectively.
By contrast, people who discontinued GLP-1 therapy before reaching 18 months showed no significant reduction in cardiovascular risk compared with those taking sulfonylureas by the end of the study.
Treatment gaps weakened heart protection
Interrupting treatment and then restarting it also appeared to reduce the cardiovascular benefit.
People who remained on GLP-1 drugs continuously for three years had an 18% reduction in risk, while those who stopped temporarily and later resumed treatment saw an average reduction of 12%.
Even a six-month interruption before restarting therapy was enough to weaken the benefit. Compared with continuous use, those treatment gaps were associated with a 4% to 8% increase in cardiovascular risk.
Longer periods off the drugs were linked to even greater losses of protection. People who stopped GLP-1 treatment for one year without restarting had a 14% higher risk of cardiovascular events compared with continuous users. After two years off treatment, that increase reached 22%.
The pattern suggests that cardiovascular benefits accumulated during GLP-1 treatment can be lost relatively quickly once the medication is discontinued.
Restarting may not fully restore lost benefits
The findings reinforce the importance of continuous treatment if patients and clinicians want to preserve the cardiovascular effects of GLP-1 therapy. They also suggest that reducing treatment interruptions could help maximize the drugs' protective effects on the heart.
"Clinicians should treat adherence to GLP-1 treatment as an important outcome in its own right -- not an afterthought," Al-Aly said. "Health systems need plans in place to help people continue their medication indefinitely, recognizing that GLP-1s treat chronic conditions. That includes proactive management of side effects, candid conversations about the long-term nature of treatment, infrastructure to identify and support patients at risk of stopping and addressing the cost barriers that make GLP-1 therapy unsustainable for many."
Al-Aly noted that this is especially important because cardiovascular protection from GLP-1 treatment appears to accumulate gradually but disappear much more quickly.
For study participants, spending only one year off the medication was enough to lose benefits that had taken years of continuous treatment to build. Restarting the drug restored some of that protection, but not all of it.
The research was funded by the United States Department of Veterans Affairs. The funders had no role in considering the study design or in the collection, analysis, interpretation of data, writing of the report, or decision to submit the article for publication. The contents do not represent the views of the US Department of Veterans Affairs or the US Government.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Washington University in St. Louis. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yan Xie, Taeyoung Choi, Ziyad Al-Aly. Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist discontinuation and risks of major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes: target trial emulation. BMJ Medicine, 2026; 5 (1): e002150 DOI: 10.1136/bmjmed-2025-002150

AI generated
GENEVA – Escalating infrastructure attacks by both Russia and Ukraine are leaving civilians increasingly vulnerable as winter approaches, United Nations investigators warned on Sept 21, expressing fear of a repeat of last winter’s suffering.
For months, Russia and Ukraine have been engaged in intensifying long-range strikes targeting a growing number of civilian sites, including factories, warehouses, and energy and port infrastructure, as well as ships in the Black Sea.
In a fresh update on the situation, the UN’s Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine warned that the attacks raised concerns that already difficult living conditions could worsen dramatically with the arrival of winter, as was the case in 2025.
“During the severe winter of 2025-2026, Russian armed forces continued to launch systematic waves of attacks against Ukraine’s critical energy infrastructure as temperatures plunged to minus 20 deg C,” it said in a statement.
“Millions of civilians endured prolonged power outages, shortages or lengthy absence of heating.”
The commission, which was set up by the UN Human Rights Council shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, cited testimony about temperatures inside apartments “falling to the point where many developed health problems, including psychological conditions”.
“Ukrainian authorities recorded cold-related deaths and injuries,” it pointed out, also highlighting reports about Ukrainian attacks on infrastructure inside Russia and in Russian-controlled areas of Ukraine.
“Those reports indicate an increase in civilian casualties and damage or destruction of civilian objects,” the investigators said.
However, they added that they had been unable to investigate the reported incidents as they lacked access.
“Continued attacks on energy infrastructure are making living conditions increasingly unbearable for civilians, and we are concerned that the coming winter will be more difficult to endure,” commission chair Erik Mose warned in the statement.
The findings of the commission, which does not speak on behalf of the UN, came after US President Donald Trump pushed last week for an energy truce between the two sides.
But the warring sides have yet to confirm that they will take part.
The Kremlin did, however, hail Trump’s “good idea”, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said his country was “ready to support de-escalation” if Russia did the same. AFP

What’s the US–China AI ‘hotline’ that Trump plans to pitch to Xi Jinping?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:32:55 UTC
22:32:55 KST

What’s the US–China AI ‘hotline’ that Trump plans to pitch to Xi Jinping?
Washington and Beijing discuss AI hotline idea amid escalating competition and restrictions on advanced technologies.
The United States wants a new “notification mechanism” with China to warn each other when an artificial intelligence incident becomes serious enough to threaten national security.
The proposal, effectively an “AI hotline”, was discussed on Sunday during talks in New York between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, before a summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Washington, DC, this week.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Doomsday AI: panic, regulation and the China fear
- list 2 of 3Australia seeks big tech support for internet safety, AI regulation
- list 3 of 3Trump says he will create ‘AI Force’ with new ‘AI czar’
The two leaders are expected to consider establishing a broader US-China dialogue on AI, including the proposed notification system, around which details remain limited.
The initiative comes amid an intensifying contest for AI supremacy between the world’s top two economies, along with growing warnings from tech giants that guardrails are necessary around this ever-growing technology.
“I see this as a positive signal, showing that despite intense competition, there is still a willingness to cooperate,” Jiang Tianjiao, associate professor at the Fudan Development Institute in Shanghai, China, told Al Jazeera.
So, what do we know about this so-called hotline, and where is the AI battle between the US and China headed?
What did the US say about this mechanism?
US Treasury Secretary Bessent said Washington had proposed creating a US-China AI dialogue, with particular focus on national security and a notification system covering “common goals and common threats”.
“We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important,” Bessent told reporters after Sunday’s discussions.
Trump’s science and technology adviser Michael Kratsios told Fox News on Sunday that the “key thing” Washington wants to discuss is “avoiding shared risks”.
Exactly what would trigger a notification has not been publicly revealed.
“The US and China absolutely need to be able to share information with each other as threats evolve. This seems like an obvious win for both sides,” Scott Singer, codirector of the China AI Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told Al Jazeera.
“The relationship needs guardrails to keep citizens of both countries safe, and this is a productive first step.”
Chinese academic Sun Chengdao echoed Singer, saying such a mechanism was “increasingly necessary”.
“The value of such a channel is not that it creates trust overnight, but that it can reduce the risk of misinterpretation when something goes wrong,” Chengdao, a professor at Tsinghua University in Beijing, told Al Jazeera.
“Imagine, for example, an autonomous AI agent launching a major cyber-operation, or a frontier model behaving in an unexpected way across borders. The immediate problem would be attribution: was this ordered by a government, carried out by a non-state actor, or caused by an AI system operating beyond its intended boundaries? In a crisis, that uncertainty could be dangerous.”
How did China respond?
Beijing has so far said very little.
China’s official Xinhua news agency acknowledged that He and Bessent discussed issues related to AI, but did not say whether Beijing had accepted Washington’s proposed notification mechanism.
Xinhua said the officials held “frank, in-depth and constructive exchanges” on economic and trade issues.
He and China’s chief trade negotiator Li Chenggang left Sunday’s talks without speaking to reporters.
What other ‘hotlines’ do the US and China have?
The proposed AI mechanism would not be the first time a special crisis channel was established between Washington and Beijing.
In 1997, former US President Bill Clinton and his then-Chinese counterpart Jiang Zemin agreed to create a “direct secure telephone link” between their respective countries.
The two countries have had a military hotline since 2008, designed to allow senior defence officials to communicate during potentially dangerous incidents. It gives both sides 48 hours to respond, though US officials have complained that sometimes no one picks up.
After the US shot down a suspected Chinese surveillance balloon in 2023, then-US Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin sought a call with his Chinese counterpart, but Beijing declined the request.
Why now, and what concerns are there around AI?
Earlier this month, Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei warned in an essay that AI capabilities have been advancing rapidly, and he proposed pacing the development of frontier models to give governments and researchers more time to manage their risks.
“Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails,” he wrote.
His assertions were endorsed by his rivals – OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX founder and Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
Meanwhile, Trump has repeatedly argued that the US must maintain its advantage over China and has resisted calls from technology executives for a slowdown in AI development. He has said, “Whoever wins AI, wins.”
Carnegie Endowment’s Singer does not expect the “fierce competition for AI to slow down”.
“It has the potential to confer tremendous economic and strategic advantage to both countries. But even competitors can find space to cooperate,” he noted.
“Competition and cooperation can coexist. The key for right now is for both sides to act in their own self-interest. Finding some basic areas for cooperation flows very naturally from that.”
Where is the US-China AI war headed?
The US remains ahead in several of the most important features of the AI race, but China has been closing the gap.
US companies continue to dominate private investment and production of leading AI models. According to Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index Report, US companies invested $285.9bn in AI in 2025, compared with $12.4bn in China.
The US also has an advantage in the most advanced semiconductors needed to train cutting-edge models.
However, Chinese companies have demonstrated that they can produce resilient AI models despite US restrictions on their access to the most advanced AI chips.
In January, the release of Chinese AI startup DeepSeek made headlines after it was built using only a fraction of the money its competitors had spent on their own AI programmes. Share prices of US tech companies plummeted.
China has advantages in other areas of the AI supply chain, most notably in the production of critical rare earth minerals used in advanced technology and in generating more than twice as much electricity as the US, giving it access to the vast amounts of relatively cheap power needed to operate AI data centres.
What is the Xi-Trump summit about?
Xi’s state visit to the US will take place from Wednesday to Friday, with Trump expected to welcome him at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.
Trump has said he expects to discuss “almost everything” with the Chinese leader.
Trade remains a central issue, with Beijing and Washington yet to reach a lasting settlement on tariffs, which have dominated Trump’s relationship with China in his second term as president.
Last month, the White House accused dozens of countries of helping China to illegally bypass US tariffs.
Meanwhile, the US Congress last week passed a bill that gives Trump sweeping powers to impose sanctions on Russia’s crude exports as well as steep tariffs on buyers of Russian energy, a measure that will affect Moscow’s biggest customers, China and India.
The US-Israel war on Iran is also expected to feature. Beijing ranks among Iran’s key economic allies, buying a large share of Tehran’s oil exports and attempting to broker an end to the near seven-month-old war.
Other longstanding disputes hang over the summit, including China’s dominance of rare-earth supplies and Taiwan.
The US AI proposal could represent a rare area where the two rivals may find a way to hammer out a deal, experts say.
“I think establishing a permanent channel exclusively focused on AI would genuinely be a major victory. AI has been caught up in the broader ebbs and flows of the US-China relationship, and the 2024 dialogue failed because frontier AI risks got mixed in with other issues,” Singer said.
“This time looks like it might be different, and having an AI risk channel is a necessary precondition to mutually beneficial cooperation.”

Merz's political crisis threatens Germany's obsession with stability
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
14:30:45 BST
22:30:45 KST

Merz's political crisis threatens Germany's obsession with stability
- Published
Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz is a political record-breaker.
The problem for him is these records are overwhelmingly negative and he is at risk of losing his job over them.
The problem for the EU and for Europe more broadly is this has a destabilising effect far further afield.
At a paltry 13%, Merz's popularity rating is the lowest for any German chancellor since polling began.
German voters' ardour for him started lower and fell faster than any of his predecessors. The former corporate lawyer is perceived by many to be arrogant and out of touch with their problems.
He has only been in government for 16 months but under his chairmanship, Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party has suffered three very poor showings in regional elections over the last couple of weeks.
The state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern broke another record on Sunday according to preliminary results: Merz's conservative CDU party did not even reach the 5% threshold to enter the regional parliament.
Conversely, the anti-immigration, nationalist right Alternative for Germany (AfD) - a political party Merz had promised to slash support for when he was running for CDU leadership - has performed spectacularly well.
It became the biggest political faction in two out of those three recent state elections and broke another record: they have a chance at governing in one of those states, Saxony Anhalt, despite the German authorities labelling them in part anti-democratic and far-right extremist.
The AfD also tops opinion polls nationally, a particularly sensitive issue for Germany after its Nazi past.
The party rejects the far-right label. Its German name, Alternative fuer Deutschland, means Alternative for Germany. That is exactly what they say voters now want.
Following this month's regional election surge in success for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, plus its gains in Berlin - where the victors were the hard left Die Linke party - AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said on Monday that her party had effectively replaced the center-right CDU as Germany's true Volkspartei, or catch-all people's party.
The AfD accuses Merz of failing to fulfil his key election promises to improve the spluttering German economy - once seen as the financial engine of Europe - and to find workable solutions to voter fears about immigration and security on their streets.
High time for political change, says the AfD.
Merz's position as German chancellor certainly looks wobbly. There have been rumours for weeks of a brewing palace coup, where he would be replaced by a more popular CDU politician.
Possible candidate names are swirling but no individual will stick out his or her neck in public until they know they have the backing of the party.
I have reported on Germany for decades. This is a stability-obsessed country. This kind of political upheaval is deeply unusual.
Even if Merz stays in post, his political clout and credibility, his room for manoeuvre inside a fractious coalition government, will be restricted.
Looking uncharacteristically forlorn on Sunday evening, Merz jumped to make a televised address even before the regional election results were confirmed.
He would press ahead with tax, welfare and economic reforms to bring about prosperity, he said. "Backbone, steadfastness and patience" were required.
But German patience is running thin.
Voters in Germany, as across much of Europe, have repeatedly elected traditional parties of the centre-left, such as Germany's SPD party, or centre-right, like the CDU, since World War Two - but increasingly they feel let-down and frustrated as they fear for their economic future.
Voter resentment really started to mount after the financial crisis of 2007/8, when these traditional parties were seen bailing out big banks, while families felt their savings and living standards dropped.
Then came the 2015 migration crisis, when more than one million refugees and other migrants arrived by people-smuggler boats across the Mediterranean and made their way across Europe, often by foot, trying to settle in wealthier countries like Germany and Sweden. Germany took in one million people.
Integration into German society has been mixed and Germans have been shocked and scared by a number of headline-making attacks by migrants over the years, some with a history of mental illness, others linked by the German authorities to Islamist extremist groups or ideology.
In December, for example, police said they arrested five individuals suspected of plotting a Christmas market attack in Munich "based on an Islamist motive".
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has had another scarring effect.
Germans pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. The loss of access to cheap Russian energy that German car factories and other industries relied on, plus Donald Trump's trade tariffs and aggressive economic competition from China, have had a heavy toll on this country's export-driven economy.
Germany is Europe's, and therefore the eurozone currency's, largest economy. It is the world's largest single donor to Ukraine right now and it is the biggest net payer into the EU budget.
When Germany's finances are in trouble and the country turns inward because of a political crisis, the knock-on effect beyond its borders can be considerable.
Under financial pressure, Merz has been pushing hard, along with a group of other wealthier EU countries to slash their contributions to the bloc's budget, for example.
This comes at a time when the EU wants to spend more, not less, on common defence projects, migration and AI and tech.
Faced with perceived threats from Russia and China, wars in the Middle East affecting energy supplies and prices, plus the unpredictability - and many in Europe say, unreliability - of the US under Trump, now is a time Europeans must stick tightly together, says Brussels.
The EU is watching Merz's travails, plus the strengthening of the AfD on the right and the hard left Die Linke too, with concern.
These regional German votes come at the start of bumper election season across the EU, where all the big powers - (including France, Italy, Spain and Poland - go to the polls.
Nationalist, Eurosceptic, anti-immigration parties are predicted to do well. And Beijing and Moscow are watching closely.

Why Is Lee Jae-myung’s Approval Rating Dropping?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:29:00 UTC
22:29:00 KST

South Korean President Lee Jae-myung blamed his own shortcomings for a steep loss of public support. His approval rating fell to 37 percent in a Gallup Korea poll released that morning, the lowest level since he took office in June 2025.
At a standing news conference at the presidential Blue House on September 18, Lee described the decline as puzzling at first.
“In the end, I came to think that all of it, taken together, was because of my own shortcomings,” Lee said. And in opening remarks, he noted that he had been flustered by the disappointment that followed the June 3 local elections.
However, the slide began earlier. Support for Lee – who took office in June 2025 – had hovered near 60 percent for months before it started falling in mid-May.
Among respondents who disapprove of him, 20 percent cited housing policy and 16 percent cited personnel appointments in the latest survey.
Aside from specific events, four border trends help explain the slide of the president’s approval ratings.
The first is the fading of the Yoon Suk-yeol effect. Lee won the presidency in a special election following the impeachment of Yoon, who had illegitimately declared martial law in December 2024. For months the contrast with his predecessor helped sustain Lee’s ratings. That contrast has weakened over time. Yoon was sentenced to life in prison in February for leading an insurrection. His wife, Kim Keon-hee, had her sentence increased to four years on appeal in April. Although their sentences will likely need to be confirmed in the Supreme Court, which will take years, the question for voters appears to have shifted from who should be punished to who is fixing daily life. It has already been more than 21 months after the martial law declaration and many South Koreans have moved on.
The second trend is a gap between the image of a hands-on executive Lee cultivated as a mayor and governor and the delegator he now describes. On Friday, he said he has neither the time nor the ability to micromanage everything. Lee has told staff to refrain from involvement in routine ministry business. His principle is to give authority and hold people firmly accountable.
However, the rollout of single-stock leveraged exchange-traded funds (ETFs) shows the risk of this approach. These stock products have hurt retail investors, and South Koreans want an explanation. Former Presidential Policy Chief Kim Yong-beom said in January that he had instructed regulators to review the products. The ETFs went on sale on May 27, days before the local elections. Regulators tightened the rules on July 16 and again on July 29 as losses mounted. The policy chief resigned on September 1, and the Blue House did not give a reason.
In his press conference on September 18, Lee said he did not yet know the details of how the products were approved, although he “received a report at the time,” he recalled. Lee conceded that it seems true that there were shortcomings. In such comments, voters who backed him for getting things done may see a president who owns the results but not the process.
Housing is another area where Lee has failed to convince voters he is solving the problem. It is the most cited reason for disapproval in the Gallup Korea polling. Lee, for his part, pointed out that prices in outlying areas are still climbing even as those in wealthy Gangnam, the emblematic district for wealth in Seoul, soften.
The third problem is communication. Scrutiny of a president tends to sharpen in the second year, and the local elections gave critics an opening. The ruling Democratic Party won 12 of 16 mayoral and gubernatorial races but lost Seoul, where Lee had publicly backed the DP’s candidate, Chong Won-o. During his press conference commemorating his first year in the presidency on June 8, Lee said that losing places the party should have won made the result “at the least, not a success.”
Asked how he would talk to the public about housing, specifically, Lee didn’t seem to have an answer. He said on Friday that he would study a variety of methods and invited suggestions. Lee closed by promising to communicate more, listen more and respect more.
However, voters have other questions for him. The Kospi closed on September 18 about 24 percent below its June 22 peak. The relationship with Washington keeps shifting. North Korea has stopped answering Seoul. On each of those, voters appear to be waiting to hear from the president himself.
U.S. President Donald Trump has pressed Seoul for help in the U.S. war with Iran, especially in reopening the Strait of Hormuz. On March 14, two weeks after beginning strikes against Iran, Trump urged South Korea and four other countries to send warships to the strait.
On August 16, he wrote on Truth Social that he had asked Lee whether South Korea would join “the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran.” South Korea replied, according to Trump, “No thanks!” In the same post, he ordered the Pentagon to substantially reduce joint exercises with South Korea.
During his press conference, Lee ruled out sending troops to take part in the Iran-U.S. war. “There will be no dispatch of troops that involves or intervenes in the war,” he said.
Still, he noted that a naval unit is already stationed near the Strait of Hormuz. And the Blue House said on Saturday that Lee had not rejected the request from Trump for cooperation on Middle East issues. So South Koreans may be left feeling uncertain as to what the Lee administration will actually do in the Middle East.
On North Korea, Lee said Pyongyang “is clearly refusing to communicate with South Korea.” He added that Trump wants dialogue with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and that Seoul is coordinating in advance to make talks possible. He dismissed concerns that South Korea could be sidelined.
The fourth problem for Lee, as mentioned above, is personnel. Five ministerial appointments have been forced to withdraw – starting just a month after Lee took office. His education minister pick, Lee Jin-sook, withdrew in July 2025 amid plagiarism allegations. More recently, Yong Hye-in, a two-time lawmaker in the Basic Income Party who was nominated as gender equality minister, withdrew from consideration on September 13.
In his press conference on Friday, Lee promised a review of how nominees are vetted. “I plan to re-examine the personnel system now,” Lee said, though he could not promise that problems would never recur.
Kim Seung-won, Lee’s justice minister appointee who was attracted critical reporting from the press and belligerence from opposition lawmakers, withdrew the next morning. He was the fifth Lee nominee to fall through since he took office.
When Lee had announced a reshuffle on August 30, his chief of staff, Kang Hoon-sik, said competence was the sole criterion. Nonetheless, South Koreans continued to find flaws with his choices. In a Gallup Korea poll released September 11, 61 percent of respondents called Yong unfit and 43 percent said the same of Kim Seung-won.
In order to take responsibility for the downward slide in Lee’s approval ratings and the recent series of missteps the Blue House has taken, Kang offered to resign on September 21. According to local media reports, Lee said he has not made any decisions on whether to accept his resignation.

Inside Kazakhstan’s push to become a regional AI centre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:26:01 UTC
22:26:01 KST

Inside Kazakhstan’s push to become a regional AI centre
Kazakhstan accelerates AI development but experts warn of impact on the environment and human rights.
A young woman in a sleek bun and a jacket with Kazakh patterns smiles from the screen at a directors’ meeting of Samruk-Kazyna, Kazakhstan’s sovereign wealth fund.
In late 2025, she became the company’s newest board member.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4UK’s Burnham, Canada’s Carney discuss AI risks, defence cooperation
- list 2 of 4What are the world’s biggest AI companies and how much are they worth?
- list 3 of 4Israel weaponises AI for West Bank demolitions
- list 4 of 4Trump says he will create ‘AI Force’ with new ‘AI czar’
But SKAI (or Samruk-Kazyna Artificial Intelligence) is not the first woman to join the all-male board: She is the first artificial intelligence programme with voting rights to support the company’s push for greater transparency and better governance.
In Kazakhstan, AI is the new talk of the town, and part of its new branding and modernisation agenda to improve public services, attract investment and diversify the economy beyond reliance on raw materials.
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev declared 2026 the “Year of Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence” to introduce advanced technologies in all sectors of the economy, develop skills, startups and Kazakh-language technologies.
In 2025, the government created a Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development, and last month, it approved an action plan through 2029 that includes promoting AI literacy in schools and universities, digitalising healthcare, public services, tax collection and the energy sector.
In 2025, Kazakhstan became the second jurisdiction, after the European Union, to pass a law governing AI.
In the futuristic ball-shaped EXPO building in the capital Astana, a new AI museum invites visitors to wander through digital installations and robots, try AI models and immerse themselves in an otherworldly experience.
At the nearby Astana Hub, the largest innovation cluster in Central Asia, which runs the museum, hundreds of schoolchildren are taught programming, generative artificial intelligence, 3D animation, and motion design – for free. For adults, the “Tomorrow School” seeks to develop Kazakhstan’s brightest tech talents.
“We have students from 18 to over 50, coming from various backgrounds who at some point decided to change their profession and become IT workers,” Valeria Tio, Astana Hub’s managing director, told Al Jazeera. “The candidate selection is strict. Of the 25,000 applications that we have received, we took less than 2 percent of the most talented people.”
The candidates first play a logic and memory game to select those with the best potential. Then, during an intensive four-week course called the “Pool”, organisers select a student cohort to participate in training for two years.
While Kazakhstan’s AI push has made it a pioneer, it “is still far away from becoming a Silicon Valley, but it is becoming a regional AI centre”, said Yuri Misnik, chief technology officer at InDrive, a unicorn company actively training a new generation of IT specialists in Kazakhstan.
“Thanks to proximity to China, Kazakhstan can have the best of two worlds: The western innovation and insights from the east … Similar to what happened 15 years ago with digital transformation, the winners change the business, the processes, and the business models.”
‘A real social elevator’
Eighteen months into the Tomorrow School programme, the hub has trained 500 people. Some have secured jobs. This month, pools open in 12 Kazakh regions.
“A girl who worked as a barista in our cafeteria found work as a developer after one year of study. This is a real social elevator,” Tio said.
Astana Hub also has a startup incubator, which helps to create new teams, develop IT products, and sell them to other markets. They partner with hubs in Dubai, Shanghai, Malaysia and the United Kingdom and closely cooperate with the government. Thanks to that, their residents pay zero tax. One percent of their income goes towards the hub’s development.
Over eight years of operation, Astana Hub has helped to incubate Kazakhstan’s first unicorn company – a privately held startup valued at more than $1bn – named Higgsfield, a video-generating programme. By 2030, Tio said, the hub hopes to have five unicorns.
At the nearby Nazarbayev University, another company tries to break new ground. The Institute of Smart Systems and Artificial Intelligence was the first academic entity in Central Asia to operate a supercomputer.
In 2019, scientists realised that neither of the popular AI voice assistants at the time, such as Siri or Alexa, recognised the Kazakh language. The team decided to build its own national product.
When the coronavirus hit in 2020, researchers encouraged local Kazakh speakers and traditional toastmasters who were at home without work to record themselves reading texts using different emotions to train the new Kazakh model. It worked: In December 2024, the company launched its local answer to ChatGPT.
The MagniSoz model works with text and audio in 11 different languages. Oylan, an updated version, which translates from Kazakh into “Think!”, works with images, too, in English, Russian and Kazakh.
“It has deep-thinking, reasoning and web search functions,” said Yerbol Absalyamov, the institute’s executive director.
“To ensure protection of data, we decided to deploy it locally on our servers. It is available open source to all Kazakhstani people, including the government. Our work has two principles: First, AI for good, and second, AI for Kazakhstan.”
While ChatGPT today works in the Kazakh language, too, Absalyamov says a local large language model is still key. First, because the data it collects stays within the country and second, because it represents local culture, history and traditions.
“Our mindset might be different from the European or North American one, so while creating these models, we collect data that represents Kazakhstan, our people, culture, history and identity,” he said.
Concerns over human rights, power supply
But AI development is not without issues.
The decision to create large data centres in Kazakhstan, which require stable water and electricity supply, has raised concerns.
“Kazakhstan still imports power at peak times, and a large share of plants and grids are old. When it comes to the environment, the ministry said cooling will use immersion systems rather than water, but no assessment has yet been made public,” said Tlegen Kuandykov, programme coordinator at CAPS Unlock, a local think tank. “Whatever the engineering answer turns out to be, that transparency gap is a real policy failure.”
Another potential problem is the use – and potential misuse – of data.
“Human rights are a big issue. The new AI law contains protective language, but enforcement is not clear yet and it might not include serious public oversight. Biometric identification and facial recognition are being rolled out rapidly,” Kuandykov said.
