Breadcrumb
Morocco arrests campaigners behind election boycott movement days before vote
Moroccan authorities have detained members of a left-wing political party campaigning for a boycott of the country's upcoming parliamentary elections, days before voters head to the polls on 23 September.
At least six members of the Democratic Labour Way Party, known in Arabic as Annahj Addimocrati Al-Oummali, were detained in the city of Kenitra while distributing leaflets urging people not to vote, according to Moroccan media reports.
The activists were taken to a police station for questioning before being released, while the leaflets in their possession were confiscated, reports said.
Four other party members were detained in Beni Mellal on 12 September in connection with leaflets calling for an election boycott. They were reportedly questioned by the Royal Gendarmerie as part of an investigation overseen by prosecutors before being released.
The party has also reported authorities intervening against its boycott activities in other cities, including Casablanca, Tangier and Al Hoceima.
The Moroccan Association for Human Rights (AMDH) said on Saturday that arrests had taken place in Beni Mellal and Kenitra, while party activists had faced restrictions in Casablanca, Salé, Tangier and Al Hoceima. The rights group described the measures as arbitrary and said peaceful advocacy for an election boycott was protected by freedom of expression.
The party's youth wing separately said that 16 activists had been detained in connection with boycott campaigning by Friday, with another four members in Tangier receiving summonses. Those figures could not be independently verified.
The Democratic Labour Way Party has condemned the campaign of arrests and restrictions against its members and vowed to continue urging Moroccans to boycott the election.
The party formally announced in June that it would boycott the 23 September parliamentary elections, arguing that the vote lacked the minimum conditions for a democratic process.
The arrests occurs amid questions in Morocco over the legal limits of campaigning for voters to stay away from the polls.
Morocco recently strengthened electoral legislation covering attempts to influence voters through false information and other deceptive methods.
Under Article 51, using fake news, false rumours or other deceptive tactics to sway voters or convince them to stay home can carry a prison sentence of two to five years and a fine of 50,000 to 100,000 Moroccan dirhams (around $5,000-$10,000). The rules extend to content spread through social media, online platforms and AI tools.
The government has presented the measures as safeguards against disinformation and manipulation during the election period.
However, the law does not make simply advocating an election boycott a criminal offence.
Moroccan constitutional law researcher Maryam Belil told local outlet Sawt Al Maghrib that abstaining from voting or expressing a political position in favour of an election boycott did not in itself constitute a crime.
She said criminal liability under Article 51 required the use of methods specified by the legislation, such as false information or deceptive practices intended to influence voters.
The detentions come amid wider concern over political disengagement ahead of Wednesday's vote, particularly among young Moroccans.
Only around 3% of Moroccans aged 18 to 24 are registered to vote, according to Reuters, amid widespread frustration over unemployment and distrust of political institutions.

EXPLAINER – Who gets access to advanced AI? US curbs fuel debate over technology and power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:28:38 UTC
21:28:38 KST

The US is tightening controls on who can access its most advanced artificial intelligence systems, extending its technology restrictions beyond chips and hardware as competition with China intensifies.
As increasingly powerful AI systems raise security concerns, government intervention and selective releases by developers are reshaping who can use the technology – and on whose terms.
"The idea of a completely borderless internet was always somewhat idealized," Antonio Calcara, head of the Geopolitics and Technology Programme at the Centre for Security, Diplomacy and Strategy in Brussels, told Anadolu.
Governments and corporations have long shaped digital infrastructure, he said, but national security concerns increasingly influence how technology is developed, shared and controlled.
That tension surfaced in June when the US government ordered Anthropic to block foreign nationals from accessing its Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5 models.
The company took both models offline worldwide, saying it could not reliably distinguish users by nationality. The restrictions were subsequently lifted, but the episode demonstrated Washington’s ability to interrupt access far beyond US borders.
Separately, US President Donald Trump in June ordered federal agencies to develop a voluntary framework under which developers could give the US government access to certain advanced AI models for up to 30 days before releasing them to other trusted partners.
Companies have also limited distribution themselves. Anthropic initially offered Claude Mythos to selected partners, while OpenAI released GPT-5.6 to a small group in June at the US government’s request before widening access the following month.
These arrangements differ from export controls, but together reflect growing scrutiny of who gains access to the most powerful systems.
Milton Mueller, a professor at the Georgia Institute of Technology and co-founder of the Internet Governance Project, said barriers are growing even as the internet’s basic infrastructure remains global.
"We have already created certain forms of fragmentation and barriers," Mueller told Anadolu, explaining that the restrictions largely affect the services people can access rather than the underlying internet itself.
Washington has imposed export controls on advanced semiconductors and other technologies to China. Beijing blocks many major US platforms through its so-called Great Firewall and restricts cross-border data transfers.
Economic incentives favor access to global markets, Mueller said, but national security concerns increasingly drive governments to impose restrictions.
Applying traditional export controls to AI models, however, is particularly difficult.
Weapons, advanced chips and other physical goods can be stopped from crossing borders. AI models delivered through online services can be accessed from almost anywhere, making it much harder to control who uses them.
Mueller compared the challenge to earlier US efforts to restrict encryption exports, which became harder to enforce as the technology moved from specialized hardware into widely available software.
Similar restrictions on AI could require extensive monitoring of who is accessing online services and from where, he said. That would be technically possible, according to Mueller, but difficult and costly to enforce on a global scale.
Control over advanced technology can also give countries leverage over their rivals.
The US, home to many of the world's leading technology companies, can use its legal and regulatory power to restrict who has access to their products and services.
Political scientists Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman call the use of control over critical global networks “weaponized interdependence.”
Their research argues that globalization has concentrated important services and technologies in a small number of countries and companies, giving governments power to restrict rivals’ access.
Closer ties between Silicon Valley and Washington also have advocates within the industry. In their book The Technological Republic, Palantir CEO Alexander Karp and executive Nicholas Zamiska argue that such cooperation is essential to US technological and military strength.
But restrictions can carry diplomatic costs.
Calcara said major powers cannot simply keep technological advantages to themselves while expecting to build strong alliances.
Washington needs partners as well as technological superiority in its long-term competition with China, he said. Restricting access too broadly could undermine the strategic advantages it seeks to protect.
The competition also complicates a debate over how quickly AI should advance.
Some technology leaders want developers and governments to slow work on the most advanced systems, warning that capabilities are outpacing safeguards.
In his essay We Must Pace the Frontier, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for greater coordination among AI companies and governments to slow the pace of cutting-edge development.
He also linked safety to competition with China, arguing that restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports could slow Beijing’s progress and give governments more time to introduce safeguards.
Trump has rejected calls to slow development, saying they risk benefiting China.
“There is a sick conspiracy going on against AI and data centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China,” he posted on his social media platform Truth Social earlier this month. “Whoever wins AI, wins!"
Mueller questioned the premise.
"If this is a race, what is the finish line?” Mueller asked.
AI advances do not automatically increase the power of the country where they originate, he argued. Benefits often flow primarily to the companies and people using the technology, although military applications could provide more direct strategic advantages.
He also questioned whether a slowdown could succeed without agreement among competing powers, seeing little prospect of the US, China and Russia simultaneously limiting development.
Mueller remains deeply skeptical of claims that AI could threaten humanity’s survival and questioned whether proposed safeguards could prevent such an outcome even if the risk were real.
The disagreement leaves policymakers facing the competing demands to preserve a technological lead, prevent misuse and decide how much international cooperation either goal requires.
Although Washington largely justifies technology restrictions on security grounds, Mueller said commercial interests also shape policy.
US companies can benefit when foreign competitors face restrictions, creating incentives to frame business concerns as national security imperatives, he said.
Mueller also questioned whether policymakers sometimes overstate the risks of relying on foreign countries for important technologies and other economic inputs.
Companies seeking market protection also find it easy to convince politicians by framing their interests as national security imperatives, he added.
China has repeatedly criticized US technology restrictions as protectionist, accusing Washington of stretching national security arguments to contain its development.
Yet rivalry has not ruled out cooperation.
Senior US and Chinese officials discussed a proposed notification mechanism for AI incidents affecting national security during talks ahead of a meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping later this week.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters Sunday that greater transparency between the two countries was increasingly important as their AI capabilities advanced.
"We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent told reporters Sunday.
Whether that concern can produce broader cooperation remains uncertain.
Mueller expressed doubt that the leaders’ meeting would significantly alter the technology rivalry, expecting any agreements to focus on narrower trade issues.
Restrictions could also shape technology choices far beyond the US and China.
Developing the most advanced models requires vast computing resources, infrastructure and investment, concentrating capabilities among relatively few companies and wealthy countries.
Calcara said that concentration risks deepening smaller countries’ dependence on foreign providers.
European allies remain closely tied to American technology and transatlantic security structures. Elsewhere, access and affordability could matter more.
Countries in Africa, Southeast Asia and other parts of the Global South could increasingly turn to Chinese technology if it is cheaper, more accessible or subject to fewer political restrictions than US alternatives, Calcara said.
Chinese developers have released increasingly capable open-weight models, allowing users to download and adapt them under the applicable licenses.
That flexibility could increase their appeal where customers want greater control over the technology they use.
Calcara warned that broader restrictions on American systems could therefore strengthen Chinese alternatives in markets where governments and companies can choose between providers.
The divide could also affect scientific research.
Tighter controls could gradually produce more separate US- and China-centered technology systems, with different standards and fewer opportunities for researchers and talent to move between them, he said.
Mueller said restrictions are already affecting academic exchanges, pointing to tighter US policies toward foreign researchers and international students.
Such barriers could make the technology rivalry harder to reverse, even if the two countries reach agreements in other areas.
For Washington, the challenge is therefore not only whether it can restrict access to advanced AI, but what influence it might lose by doing so.
Mueller, however, expects restrictions to persist as long as Washington views China as a strategic threat, with Beijing responding through measures of its own.

Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:25:22 UTC
21:25:22 KST

Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once
Scientists have created a flexible, needle-thin brain implant that can record signals, deliver drugs, and stimulate multiple brain regions at once.
- Date:
- September 21, 2026
- Source:
- Technical University of Denmark
- Summary:
- A new needle-thin brain implant can record neural activity, deliver drugs, and stimulate multiple brain regions using a single flexible fiber. Successful tests in mice suggest it could give scientists a more precise, less invasive way to study the brain and may eventually help treat neurological disorders such as epilepsy.
- Share:
A new type of brain implant could give scientists a more precise way to study the brain and may eventually contribute to treatments for neurological conditions such as epilepsy.
Researchers from DTU, the University of Copenhagen, University College London, and other institutions have developed a long, needle-thin brain electrode equipped with microscopic channels. Known as the microfluidic Axialtrode (mAxialtrode), the device is designed to provide multiple functional points along the length of the implant. This allows researchers to record neural activity and deliver medication to specific locations across different parts of the brain.
The findings were published in the journal Advanced Science.
A Multifunction Tool for Brain Research
For now, the technology is primarily intended as a research tool. Scientists could use it to investigate how signals travel through different layers of the brain during processes involving epilepsy, memory, and decision-making.
Over the longer term, the researchers say the mAxialtrode could also have therapeutic applications. One possibility would be using the device to deliver drugs to precise locations while simultaneously applying electrical stimulation or light stimulation to selected areas of the brain.
Postdoc Kunyang Sui, who developed the mAxialtrode concept together with Associate Professor Christos Markos, says one of the main advantages is that several capabilities can be combined within a single implant. That could allow researchers to perform more precise experiments while reducing the need for multiple devices inserted into the brain.
"Most current brain implants are based on hard materials such as silicon, which can irritate the brain and trigger inflammatory reactions in the tissue. The new implant differs in that it is made of soft, plastic-like optical fibers and has a specially angled tip that makes it smaller and reduces the damage caused when it is placed in the brain," says Kunyang Sui.
Sui cautions that the technology is still far from routine clinical use. Extensive testing, additional development, and regulatory approvals would be required before it could be used to treat patients.
Moving Beyond Conventional Optical Fibers
Brain researchers currently use flat-ended optical fibers in many experiments. These thin fibers, made from glass or plastic, can carry light into deep regions of the brain. They are frequently used in optogenetics, a technique in which specific nerve cells are activated using light.
Conventional fibers, however, have an important limitation. They typically interact with brain tissue only at the end of the fiber, meaning researchers can stimulate or monitor just one location at a time.
The outermost end is called the distal tip, or the "nose" of the fiber. Light is emitted and contact with brain tissue occurs only at this point. As a result, scientists may be limited to measuring or stimulating one brain layer at a time, even though many brain functions depend on communication among several layers and deeper structures.
How the New Brain Implant Works
The needle-thin mAxialtrode begins as a much larger polymer rod. Researchers heat the material and draw it into an extremely thin fiber, somewhat like producing a very fine strand of sugar, but with far greater precision.
A light-conducting core runs through the center of the fiber. Surrounding it are eight microscopic channels that can transport liquids. Those channels can also hold extremely thin metal wires used to measure electrical activity in the brain.
The finished fiber measures less than half a millimeter across. It is also highly flexible, allowing it to move along with brain tissue rather than pressing rigidly through it. This difference in stiffness could be important because harder implants can trigger inflammatory responses when they remain in the brain for long periods.
Tested in Living Mice
The researchers tested the system not only in the laboratory but also "in vivo," meaning in living mice. The electrode was implanted in the animals' brains and connected to light sources, recording equipment, and small pumps used to deliver fluids.
The experiments showed that the device could stimulate nerve cells using both blue and red light. At the same time, researchers were able to record electrical activity from shallow and deeper brain regions, including the cerebral cortex and hippocampus.
They were also able to inject different substances at separate depths, with delivery points spaced almost three millimeters apart. All of these measurements and forms of stimulation were carried out using a single lightweight fiber, which the mice were able to carry without any obvious signs of discomfort.
Potential Applications in Epilepsy and Neuroscience
The in vivo experiments and neurophysiological validation were performed in close collaboration with Associate Professor Rune W. Berg of the University of Copenhagen and Associate Professor Rob C. Wykes from University College London. Their contributions included expertise in analyzing neural circuits and models relevant to epilepsy.
The research team is now working to patent the technology behind the brain electrode. The scientists are also exploring what would be required to begin testing the device in patients within a clinical setting.
Journal Reference:
- Kunyang Sui, Neela K. Codadu, Daman Rathore, Guanghui Li, Marcello Meneghetti, Anders L. Bøcker, Rune W. Berg, Rob C. Wykes, Christos Markos. Multimodal Layer‐Crossing Interrogation of Brain Circuits Enabled by Microfluidic Axialtrodes. Advanced Science, 2026; 13 (18) DOI: 10.1002/advs.202519744

ShanghaiRanking GRAS 2026 rank Iranian universities across 33 academic subjects
TEHRAN – Shanghai Global Ranking of Academic Subjects (GRAS) has evaluated Iranian institutions across 33 out of 57 academic subjects in the fields of Natural Sciences, Engineering, Life Sciences, Medical Sciences, and Social Sciences.
ShanghaiRanking first introduced the world university rankings by academic subjects in 2009, which was officially renamed ShanghaiRanking’s Global Ranking of Academic Subjects (GRAS) in 2016.
 
 GRAS is based on nine objective indicators grouped into five categories: World-Class Faculty, World-Class Research Output, High-Quality Research, Research Impact, and International Collaboration. Each year, GRAS presents around 20,000 subject units from approximately 2,000 universities across some 100 countries and regions.
Iranian universities had a better performance in Engineering and Medical Sciences with 70 and 24 subjects, respectively. The rankings in the five mentioned fields are as follows.
Natural Sciences
In Mathematic subject, Iran University of Science and Technology (with a global ranking of 201-300) is placed first. Amirkabir University of Technology, Azarbaijan Shahid Madani University, and Ferdowsi University of Mashhad rank second (301-400).
University of Tehran has a global ranking of 151-200 in Geography; it ranks 301-400 in Atmospheric Science.

Engineering

Source: European Pravda's Brussels correspondent, citing several European diplomats who spoke on condition of anonymity
Details: The Committee of Permanent Representatives of EU member states (Coreper) is currently considering a proposal from the Irish presidency to extend sanctions against Russia over violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty for 36 months.
Meanwhile, Slovakia continues to insist that Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman be removed from the sanctions list. France also supports Usmanov's removal, citing national interests.
European Pravda sources said a compromise could be approved under which Usmanov and Fridman would be removed from the list in exchange for the extension of the sanctions regime for 36 months.
Two other individuals could also be removed from the list following a relevant court ruling, although details are yet unclear.
The Coreper meeting which is expected to finalise the decision on extending the sanctions began at 15:00 Kyiv time. Such meetings are usually held behind closed doors.
The current sanctions regime, the list for which the EU began compiling in 2014, covers individuals and legal entities responsible for actions that undermine or threaten Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence. Since 2022, the list has included Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin, senior members of Russia's political elite, prominent oligarchs and former Ukrainian president Viktor Yanukovych.
Background:
- On 14 September, Coreper extended the sanctions regime over violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty for seven days, as Slovakia and France continue to insist that two Russian oligarchs be removed from the list.
- European Pravda sources in French diplomatic circles explained why Paris wants to lift sanctions on Usmanov. It later emerged that France plans to "exchange" the removal of Usmanov from sanctions lists for the release of several of its citizens who are currently in prisons in Azerbaijan.
- The last extension of personal sanctions took place on 14 March. Then too, Slovakia pushed until the final hours on that occasion for Russian oligarchs Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov to be removed from the list.

Houthis eye highlands amid report Trump halted strikes last minute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:18:03 UTC
21:18:03 KST

Yemen's Houthi rebels pushed to seize strategic heights Monday to sever the Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed forces, following reports that President Donald Trump aborted U.S. strikes against the group at the last minute.
A lightning advance by the Iran-backed group this month has extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theater and further threatened global energy supplies.
Washington has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to join the fight in Yemen. The Houthis said Saturday they had fired on Riyadh, where loud booms were followed by columns of smoke visible near the airport.
Saudi Arabia has not commented on the first apparent strikes on the capital since the escalation began.
The New York Times reported that the Trump administration had prepared on Sunday to launch airstrikes against the Houthis after fresh calls from the Saudi crown prince. But the newspaper said Trump called off the airstrikes at the last minute, even as troops were loading bombs onto aircraft.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report. The U.S. military's Central Command referred questions to the White House. The White House did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.
Trump spoke Sunday to Rashid al-Alimi, president of Yemen's Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government, who asked him for U.S. military help, four sources told Reuters. Two of the sources, one Yemeni and one Western, said Trump made no direct pledge of military support during the call.
The Houthis, who have controlled Yemen's capital since 2014, seized the country's Red Sea coast this month in an advance that routed forces of the Saudi-backed government.
Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on the fighters' positions in the highlands, the Houthis say.
According to the United Nations, nearly 700 people have been killed and thousands injured in the flare-up in fighting. Nearly 130,000 Yemenis have fled homes within Yemen, and more than 3,000 have fled by boat across the Red Sea to Africa.
Five Yemeni military sources told Reuters the Houthis were now seeking to seize strategic heights, known as the Kahboub Mountains, in two provinces, Taiz and Lahij, which separate the Red Sea coast from the government-held south.
Fighting has centered on the outskirts of the remote mountain al-Wazi'iyah district in Taiz province, and Ras al-Ara along the Indian Ocean coast between the mouth of the Red Sea that the fighters captured last week and the government's base in Aden.
The Houthis aim to secure the rear of their forces around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait leading into the Red Sea by taking control of the heights, according to the sources. That would let them open new fronts and help protect their new positions.
The surge in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis creates a dilemma for Trump, under pressure to help defend Washington's Saudi allies but anxious not to further expand the deeply unpopular war he launched in February against Iran.
The United States bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire with the group and has kept out of the conflict since.
The Houthis' newfound control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait risks cutting off the main alternative route that Saudi Arabia has used for oil exports that bypass disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia has responded by increasing shipments through Hormuz, where a small number of tankers are increasingly shuttling back and forth to bring out oil, charging record fees of as much as a quarter of the value of the cargo to brave the wartime risk. They then transfer the oil to other ships in the Indian Ocean, bound for customers in Asia or elsewhere.
Satellite data shows Saudi exports through Hormuz reaching 2.9 million barrels per day in recent days, up from just 700,000 in August, making up for a halt to Saudi loadings on the Red Sea.
That has helped put a cap on the global price of crude oil, which has retreated closer to $100 a barrel after approaching $110 last week. But consumers and industry are still paying record prices for refined fuels.
The U.S. retail price of diesel, politically sensitive for Trump, hit another all-time high Monday above $6.51 a gallon, from around $3.75 before the war began in February.
In the latest reported attack in Hormuz, Britain's UKMTO maritime security agency said a ship sailing into the strait had been hit with a projectile, causing minor injuries to crew.
Diplomacy in the wider conflict has largely been stalled since a June interim agreement between the United States and Iran collapsed within weeks.
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian is due to fly Tuesday to New York to attend the U.N. General Assembly, the first such visit since Trump launched "Operation Epic Fury" against his country alongside Israel in February.

Guidance: Design Approved Organization Scheme (DAOS)
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:17:33 BST
21:17:33 KST

Design Approved Organization Scheme (DAOS)
DAOS is the means by which the MOD can assess the competency of design organisations.
Documents
Details
Design Approved Organization Scheme (DAOS) provides an independent assessment of the competence of defence contractors and service organisations involved in the design of aircraft systems, associated equipment and airborne explosive ordnance and armament equipment.
MOD policy is to only procure from contractors who have been assessed as competent as stated in Regulatory Article (RA) 1005. A design organization must have a MOD sponsor (typically a DE&S DT) who will apply on their behalf to DAOS Branch Head using DAOS form 80.
Details of the approval scheme are published in MAA Regulatory Article 5000 series.
DAOS organisations will be subject to periodic on site review, based on risk, by the DAOS branch or the CAAi (CAA International).
The CAAi has been contracted by the MOD to undertake on site surveillance audits, for which they will levy a charge. Details of CAA (Civil Aviation Authority) charges can be provided by DSA-MAA-OA-DAOSGroup@mod.gov.uk
Organisations where the scope of the approval covers ITAR, complex weapons, mission software, UK Eyes only design/PDS, will be assessed by the MAA.
The MAA is to be notified of proposed changes which could affect continued possession of the approval submitted to the DAOS Branch Head using the DAOS form 82.
Depending on the nature and magnitude of any change, the MAA may need to carry out an on site assessment before issuing a revised DAOS Certificate.
A list of Approved Organisations within the scheme can be found here.
For further information please contact the DAOS team:
MAA IE&R
DAOS
Juniper 1, Wing 4 #5104
MOD Abbey Wood North,
Bristol, BS34 8QW
Email: DSA-MAA-OA-DAOSGroup@mod.gov.uk

US President Donald Trump barred reporters from the three organisations from entering the White House compound last week. Security personnel turned their journalists away on Saturday morning following the directive.
Trump defended the exclusions, saying he was “tired of reading and seeing fake news” produced by the outlets and disliked “dishonest press.”

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) said Taiwan-US relations remain strong despite concerns about US policy toward Taiwan and growing pressure from China, CNA reported Monday.
Speaking in an interview with Sky News, Hsiao said US officials have repeatedly assured Taiwan that Washington’s policy toward it has not changed. She said the US remains Taipei’s most important security partner, with both sides sharing an interest in maintaining cross-strait stability.
Asked whether US President Donald Trump’s less explicit statements on Taiwan had caused concern, Hsiao said Taiwanese were more concerned about China’s efforts to interfere in domestic politics. She said Beijing seeks to win over political figures, divide society, and spread false information to weaken public confidence.
Hsiao said the Chinese Communist Party’s political operations target four areas: confidence in Taiwan’s democracy, the government and DPP, the military’s ability to defend Taiwan, and Taiwan-US relations. She said such efforts are part of increasingly sophisticated information and psychological operations.
Taiwan must continue strengthening its democratic defenses against such interference, Hsiao said. She added that civil society groups and independent fact-checkers play an important role in exposing false information and improving transparency.
Hsiao also addressed US arms sales and Taiwan’s defense spending. She said the current and previous US administrations have approved major arms sales to Taiwan, while the government has secured legislative support to fund some of the purchases.
Asked whether Taiwan has enough resources to defend itself, Hsiao said it does not yet, but the government is working toward that goal. She said lawmakers have made progress on funding US arms purchases and drones despite disagreements over how defense spending should be approved.
Hsiao said Taiwan’s defense investment reflects China’s growing military capabilities and its position on the use of force. She said Taiwan is increasing defense spending and investing in systems suited to the threats it faces.
Taiwan does not seek conflict and remains committed to maintaining peace, Hsiao said. She said fortifying the nation’s defenses and working with international partners are intended to deter aggression and preserve regional stability.

Li Yuan outlines Taiwan culture strategy through 2030

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Culture Minister Li Yuan (李遠) on Sunday outlined six priorities for cultural development as the ministry prepares to expand programs with a smaller budget than last year.
CNA reported that the priorities cover young people, cultural talent, technology, original intellectual property, investment, and international cooperation. Li said the proposals would guide cultural policy through 2030.
For young people, the ministry plans to expand beyond its Culture Points program by supporting more Taiwan-made stories, videos, and other original content. It also wants to encourage young people to participate in community projects and become more involved in cultural and civic life.
Li said support for cultural workers has become increasingly important. The ministry plans to provide more structured assistance and performance opportunities for people working in traditional arts, cultural heritage, and community development.
Technology is another focus as artificial intelligence changes cultural and creative industries. The ministry plans to work with other government agencies to protect creators’ rights and improve access to AI and computing resources for smaller arts and cultural groups.
The ministry will also continue supporting original intellectual property that can be developed into cultural products. Funding through the Taiwan Creative Content Agency will be combined with efforts to attract more private and corporate investment.
Li said the ministry wants companies to move beyond one-time sponsorships and develop longer-term partnerships with cultural organizations. It will also seek international investment and cooperation to help Taiwan’s cultural industries reach overseas markets.
International outreach is the sixth priority. The ministry plans to promote more Taiwanese cultural content abroad while attracting international cultural professionals to Taiwan and strengthening the country’s role in global cultural networks.
The plans come as the ministry faces tighter funding after the legislature cut about NT$1 billion (US$31.4 million) from its proposed NT$29.6 billion 2026 budget and froze another NT$386 million. The cuts and freezes include funding for Public Television Service and the Taiwan Creative Content Agency.

NASA just powered up Roman’s massive 300-megapixel camera
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:10:58 UTC
21:10:58 KST

NASA just powered up Roman’s massive 300-megapixel camera
- Date:
- September 21, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has successfully activated its 300-megapixel infrared camera, which will capture enormous stretches of the cosmos with Hubble-like sharpness. Its planet-hunting coronagraph is also working as expected, putting Roman another major step closer to beginning science operations in 2027.
- Share:
NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has reached another major milestone in space. Mission teams have successfully powered up the Wide Field Instrument, a 300-megapixel infrared camera designed to survey enormous areas of the universe rapidly while still capturing extremely fine detail.
Roman's planet-imaging system, the Coronagraph Instrument, has also completed an early checkout of its digital, electronic, and mechanical systems after waking up earlier this month.
The tests are part of a months-long commissioning process that will continue as Roman travels roughly one million miles toward its destination at the second Lagrange point, L2.
Roman's 300-Megapixel Camera Comes Online
The Wide Field Instrument, or WFI, is designed to combine an unusually broad view of the sky with the kind of sharp detail associated with space telescopes such as NASA's Hubble. A single WFI image will cover an area of sky larger than the apparent size of a full moon.
That combination of wide coverage and high resolution will allow Roman to carry out enormous surveys of the cosmos. Scientists plan to use those observations to learn more about planets beyond our solar system, investigate mysteries such as dark energy, and study how matter is arranged throughout the universe. Roman's expansive and detailed observations are also expected to create a valuable dataset for many additional scientific studies.
"After years of effort to build and test the instrument on the ground, we now have confirmation that it is operational in space. This is a huge milestone for the team at Goddard, our industry teams at BAE Systems, Inc. and Teledyne, and our science centers," said Josh Schlieder, the Wide Field Instrument scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "There is much to do, but we are on our way to groundbreaking science."
Cooling Roman's Infrared Detectors
Before engineers could switch on the WFI, the instrument spent 10 days drying out and undergoing decontamination. During that period, its detectors were kept at a relatively warm (compared to their final operating temperature) minus 85 degrees Fahrenheit, or minus 65 Celsius.
On the morning of Sep. 11, the team shut off the instrument heater and allowed the WFI to cool to minus 225 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 143 degrees Celsius). At that temperature, engineers were able to activate Roman's 18 infrared detectors. Together, those detectors have a light-sensitive area approximately the size of a laptop screen.
Later that evening, the team turned on the instrument's calibration system. The following morning, engineers began sending test data through the WFI and transmitting it back to teams on Earth.
Testing Roman's Filters and Focus
On Saturday evening, engineers turned their attention to the element wheel, which contains filters, prisms, and other optical components. The system controls which wavelengths of light reach the detectors and can separate light from cosmic objects into individual colors. This marked the first time the mechanism had been tested without gravity.
By Sunday morning, the team was testing the WFI's focusing mechanism. That system will be critical for keeping the hundreds of thousands of images Roman is expected to capture properly focused.
Throughout these tests, the detectors continued cooling toward their final operating temperature of about minus 300 Fahrenheit (minus 183 Celsius).
The results showed that the Wide Field Instrument is functioning as expected. Roman remains on schedule to release its first science images by early 2027.
Roman's Coronagraph Passes Early Checks
Roman's Coronagraph Instrument is built to demonstrate some of the most advanced technology ever sent into space for directly imaging planets orbiting other stars.
The instrument combines optics, masks, self-flexing mirrors, and sensors that are designed to suppress the overwhelming glare of a star. By blocking that light, the coronagraph could allow scientists to detect the much fainter light reflected by planets orbiting nearby.
Scientists and engineers working at the Coronagraph Commanding Center at Caltech/IPAC in Pasadena, California, verified that they can communicate with every major part of the instrument. Those systems include its software, thermal controls, mechanisms, cameras, and the avionics that operate them.
In practical terms, the test confirmed that ground teams can remotely control the instrument's various systems, including movable mechanisms that position its masks, color filters, lenses, and prisms.
Preparing the Coronagraph for Science
Engineers also verified that the coronagraph's thermal system is functioning properly and can warm the hardware to its operating temperature, a relatively comfortable 72 degrees Fahrenheit (22 Celsius).
With the exception of its detectors, the coronagraph is intended to operate near room temperature. That design makes the system easier to test while also helping preserve the material properties required by its deformable mirrors.
"Now that this test is complete, we've been decontaminating: sitting idle with our detectors warm so anything that's stuck to the surface, such as water or trace chemicals, will tend to leave it," said Eric Cady, an optical engineer leading commissioning efforts for the Roman Coronagraph at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "This will continue for 30 days, with occasional stops to do other early calibration activities."

NASA just powered up Roman’s massive 300-megapixel camera
- Date:
- September 21, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has successfully activated its 300-megapixel infrared camera, which will capture enormous stretches of the cosmos with Hubble-like sharpness. Its planet-hunting coronagraph is also working as expected, putting Roman another major step closer to beginning science operations in 2027.
- Share:
NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has reached another major milestone in space. Mission teams have successfully powered up the Wide Field Instrument, a 300-megapixel infrared camera designed to survey enormous areas of the universe rapidly while still capturing extremely fine detail.
Roman's planet-imaging system, the Coronagraph Instrument, has also completed an early checkout of its digital, electronic, and mechanical systems after waking up earlier this month.
The tests are part of a months-long commissioning process that will continue as Roman travels roughly one million miles toward its destination at the second Lagrange point, L2.
Roman's 300-Megapixel Camera Comes Online
The Wide Field Instrument, or WFI, is designed to combine an unusually broad view of the sky with the kind of sharp detail associated with space telescopes such as NASA's Hubble. A single WFI image will cover an area of sky larger than the apparent size of a full moon.
That combination of wide coverage and high resolution will allow Roman to carry out enormous surveys of the cosmos. Scientists plan to use those observations to learn more about planets beyond our solar system, investigate mysteries such as dark energy, and study how matter is arranged throughout the universe. Roman's expansive and detailed observations are also expected to create a valuable dataset for many additional scientific studies.
"After years of effort to build and test the instrument on the ground, we now have confirmation that it is operational in space. This is a huge milestone for the team at Goddard, our industry teams at BAE Systems, Inc. and Teledyne, and our science centers," said Josh Schlieder, the Wide Field Instrument scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "There is much to do, but we are on our way to groundbreaking science."
Cooling Roman's Infrared Detectors
Before engineers could switch on the WFI, the instrument spent 10 days drying out and undergoing decontamination. During that period, its detectors were kept at a relatively warm (compared to their final operating temperature) minus 85 degrees Fahrenheit, or minus 65 Celsius.
On the morning of Sep. 11, the team shut off the instrument heater and allowed the WFI to cool to minus 225 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 143 degrees Celsius). At that temperature, engineers were able to activate Roman's 18 infrared detectors. Together, those detectors have a light-sensitive area approximately the size of a laptop screen.
Later that evening, the team turned on the instrument's calibration system. The following morning, engineers began sending test data through the WFI and transmitting it back to teams on Earth.
Testing Roman's Filters and Focus
On Saturday evening, engineers turned their attention to the element wheel, which contains filters, prisms, and other optical components. The system controls which wavelengths of light reach the detectors and can separate light from cosmic objects into individual colors. This marked the first time the mechanism had been tested without gravity.
By Sunday morning, the team was testing the WFI's focusing mechanism. That system will be critical for keeping the hundreds of thousands of images Roman is expected to capture properly focused.
Throughout these tests, the detectors continued cooling toward their final operating temperature of about minus 300 Fahrenheit (minus 183 Celsius).
The results showed that the Wide Field Instrument is functioning as expected. Roman remains on schedule to release its first science images by early 2027.
Roman's Coronagraph Passes Early Checks
Roman's Coronagraph Instrument is built to demonstrate some of the most advanced technology ever sent into space for directly imaging planets orbiting other stars.
The instrument combines optics, masks, self-flexing mirrors, and sensors that are designed to suppress the overwhelming glare of a star. By blocking that light, the coronagraph could allow scientists to detect the much fainter light reflected by planets orbiting nearby.
Scientists and engineers working at the Coronagraph Commanding Center at Caltech/IPAC in Pasadena, California, verified that they can communicate with every major part of the instrument. Those systems include its software, thermal controls, mechanisms, cameras, and the avionics that operate them.
In practical terms, the test confirmed that ground teams can remotely control the instrument's various systems, including movable mechanisms that position its masks, color filters, lenses, and prisms.
Preparing the Coronagraph for Science
Engineers also verified that the coronagraph's thermal system is functioning properly and can warm the hardware to its operating temperature, a relatively comfortable 72 degrees Fahrenheit (22 Celsius).
With the exception of its detectors, the coronagraph is intended to operate near room temperature. That design makes the system easier to test while also helping preserve the material properties required by its deformable mirrors.
"Now that this test is complete, we've been decontaminating: sitting idle with our detectors warm so anything that's stuck to the surface, such as water or trace chemicals, will tend to leave it," said Eric Cady, an optical engineer leading commissioning efforts for the Roman Coronagraph at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "This will continue for 30 days, with occasional stops to do other early calibration activities."

Ukrainian company unveils interceptor for jet-powered Shahed drones: top speed of 416 km/h
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:10:00 EEST
21:10:00 KST

Ukrainian company unveils interceptor for jet-powered Shahed drones: top speed of 416 km/h
Ukrainian company Vluchnyk has completed internal testing of the Zorelit v5 (Starship), an anti-aircraft interceptor drone designed specifically to counter jet-powered attack UAVs.
Source: Vluchnyk, speaking to Militarnyi, a Ukrainian military news outlet; the company's website
Quote from Stepan Radiboh, Vluchnyk's CEO: "Zorelit v5 has completed all testing and is ready for military use. We are open to direct contracts with military units, and once the product is codified, we will also make it available through the e-Points system E-points are earned by Ukrainian units for confirmed strikes on Russian soldiers and equipment ."
Details: The drone has a stated top speed of 416 km/h and a range of up to 47 km on a single charge. At a cruising speed of around 200 km/h, it can remain airborne for approximately 17 minutes. The UAV is designed to carry a warhead weighing between 300 and 600 g.
The manufacturer says Zorelit v5 is designed to intercept Russian reconnaissance UAVs, Gerbera-type and Geran-2 drones and high-speed jet-powered Geran-3 and Geran-4 drones.
The interceptor can also be equipped with an AI-based system that automatically detects and tracks targets and provides terminal guidance during the final stage of flight. Separately, it can be integrated with the SkyMap system to enable automatic guidance to the target area.
Zorelit v5 was developed from the earlier Zorelit v4 interceptor, which the company says has been used in combat, entered service and received a NATO Stock Number (NSN). Some technical solutions proved in combat were carried over to the new version.
Vluchnyk's website lists the price of one Zorelit v5 at UAH 89,500 (US$2,000).
Background: Ukrainska Pravda previously reported that an interceptor drone developed by the Security Service of Ukraine's military counterintelligence division to counter jet-powered Shahed-type drones had successfully completed testing.

Malaysia's mean monthly salaries, wages up 4.1 pct in 2025

21:09:32 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Malaysian citizens' mean monthly salaries and wages rose 4.1 percent year on year to 3,803 ringgit (about 933 U.S. dollars) in 2025, according to an official survey released on Monday.
The median monthly salaries and wages increased 5.3 percent to 2,940 ringgit, the Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM) said in a statement.
The services sector, which accounted for 71.5 percent of wage recipients, was the main contributor to growth in the number of recipients, which rose 1.8 percent to 7.42 million.
Mining and quarrying recorded the highest mean monthly salaries and wages at 6,175 ringgit, followed by services at 3,993 ringgit, manufacturing at 3,357 ringgit, construction at 3,188 ringgit and agriculture at 2,575 ringgit.
DOSM said the growth in mean and median monthly salaries and wages reflected improvements in the labor market and workers' incomes.
Looking ahead, sustained efforts to enhance productivity, strengthen skills and create high-value jobs are crucial to supporting sustainable real wage growth and workers' well-being, it said. ■

Study finds environmental awareness alone fails to change fast fashion buying
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:09:27 CST
21:09:27 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Awareness of the environmental impact of ultra-fast fashion may not be enough to stop consumers from buying, with price and convenience often taking priority, new research finds.
The study found that shoppers often weighed sustainability concerns against affordability and convenience, using budgets and careful planning to make their choices feel more acceptable, according to a statement released Monday by Australia's RMIT University.
RMIT study co-author Associate Professor Carol Tan said despite this trend, it was important to understand that ultra-fast-fashion shopping was not simply thoughtless or impulsive.
Researchers identified two patterns they called "strategic spontaneity" and "cognitive buffering." The former involved preparing purchases by building wish-lists, parking items in carts, monitoring discounts, and waiting for payday, while the latter involved using budgets, spending limits and other rationalizations to reduce concerns about the environmental impact.
"I know it's bad for the planet, but when I'm on a budget and need an outfit for Saturday, I just block that out," one participant said.
Social media also influenced purchases by exposing shoppers to trends and making it easier to move quickly from discovering an item to buying it, according to the findings published in the Journal of Global Fashion Marketing.
What participants clicked, searched for and saved influenced later recommendations and promotions, keeping them engaged, the researchers noted.
The findings suggest sustainability messages could be more effective if they address affordability and value for money, such as comparing the cost per wear of durable and cheaper clothing. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Thai badminton player Pitchamon Opatniputh has been provisionally suspended from the ongoing 2026 Asian Games over an apparent anti-doping rule violation, the International Testing Agency said on Monday.
The ITA said an out-of-competition sample collected from Opatniputh in Nagoya on September 17 returned an Adverse Analytical Finding for furosemide. The substance is listed by the World Anti-Doping Agency as a specified substance prohibited at all times under the category of diuretics and masking agents.
Opatniputh has been notified of the case and provisionally suspended pending its resolution under the World Anti-Doping Code and OCA Anti-Doping Rules.
"This means that the athlete is prevented from competing, training, coaching, or participating in any activity, during the Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026," wrote the ITA.
Opatniputh has the right to challenge the suspension before the Court of Arbitration for Sport's Anti-Doping Division and to request analysis of the B-sample.
The ITA said it would not comment further while the proceedings are ongoing. ■

China Focus: From clean plates to clean cities, Shaoxing's green push inspires global action
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:09:21 CST
21:09:21 KST

The main forum of the Global Observance of World Cleanup Day 2026 is held in Shaoxing, east China's Zhejiang Province, Sept. 20, 2026. (Xinhua)
HANGZHOU, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- In a restaurant in the eastern Chinese city of Shaoxing, a waiter gently reminds diners to order just enough, pointing to a small sign on the wall that reads, "Clean your plate."
This is no isolated gesture. In Shaoxing's Fushan subdistrict, similar scenes play out almost every day in more than 600 restaurants. Small-portion ordering and free takeout services are now standard at local eateries.
For residents of this historic water town in east China's Zhejiang Province, such small acts have long become part of daily life. The message is simple, but its impact reaches far beyond the dining table.
These grassroots efforts drew international attention to Shaoxing, which hosted the Global Observance of World Cleanup Day 2026 from Saturday to Monday. Themed "From Clean Plates to Clean Cities," it marked the first time China has been chosen to host the event.
The gathering brought together around 800 participants from UN agencies, international organizations, industries and businesses. They called for coordinated action across the entire chain, from reducing waste in homes to building circular, resource-efficient cities.
"From the moment I arrived, I was truly impressed by its water-town charm and clean, well-kept urban landscape -- a beautiful city that combines a rich historical heritage with vibrant modern governance," said Cecilia Andersson, Programme Management Officer and Waste Management Lead at UN-Habitat.
"Reducing food waste can conserve resources, strengthen food security and reduce pressure on waste collection and treatment systems," she added, noting that this year's theme highlights how preventing waste at source can contribute to cleaner, healthier and more resource-efficient cities.
In Shaoxing, such efforts are already yielding results. Some areas have introduced wedding banquet guidelines -- optimizing menus and cutting waste -- which have lowered food loss at rural banquets by an average of 25 percent.
These initiatives are part of a citywide campaign. Since 2023, Shaoxing has completed 514 clean city construction projects, raising public satisfaction from 91.08 percent to 95.02 percent.
Beyond the dining table, Shaoxing's green efforts extend to waste management and various industries.
The city has built nearly 4,500 waste sorting collection points and upgraded its waste management platform. By exploring new incineration technology, Shaoxing is turning household waste, once an "urban burden," into recyclable resources.
Its green efforts are also evident in its industrial sectors. Shaoxing's Keqiao, the world's largest textile distribution hub, has long been renowned for materials used in products ranging from curtains to apparel.
Inside a new materials company in Keqiao, discarded polyester textiles are depolymerized and respun into fabric that rivals virgin fiber. During the 2026 FIFA World Cup, jerseys for several national teams were made from these green fibers.
The green circular economy extends beyond cities and factories into the countryside. Shaoxing is developing green, circular modern agriculture, turning ecological advantages into industrial and income-generating benefits.
The Kuaijishan Ancient Chinese Torreya Community, one of the Globally Important Agricultural Heritage Systems, exemplifies this approach. Local authorities have integrated protection with circular utilization, promoting intercropping under torreya trees with plants such as winter melon and peony.
"This year's theme reminds us that the journey to sustainable cities starts at home," said Anacláudia Rossbach, Under-Secretary-General and Executive Director of UN-Habitat. "The choices we make in our kitchens and communities shape the way our cities function."
Experts noted that the event's debut in China reflects international recognition of the country's green urban-rural development, while also promoting global cooperation in human settlements.
"We will work with all countries to stay true to the original aspiration of thrift, promote sound practices, and build clean homes," said Ni Hong, minister of housing and urban-rural development, calling for systematic policies and collaborative exploration of new urban governance models to keep cities vibrant and sustainable.
Liu Jie, governor of Zhejiang, said the province will continuously improve living standards and contribute more to building a Beautiful China and promoting global sustainable development.
The global event comes as China works to improve nationwide efforts in waste management and environmental cleanup. In January, China released an action plan to significantly expand its solid waste treatment capacity over the next five years, as part of broader efforts to advance a comprehensive green transition across the economy and society.
Meanwhile, China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) outlines initiatives for comprehensive solid waste treatment, stronger environmental risk controls, and significant progress in addressing emerging pollutants.
Established by the United Nations General Assembly in 2023, World Cleanup Day is observed annually on Sept. 20 to raise public awareness of the role cleanup efforts play in sustainable development.
Previous editions have addressed a wide range of global environmental issues, from the challenges of waste pollution in polar regions to efforts targeting textile and fashion waste.
"Every clean place leads to a cleaner neighbourhood. Every cleaner neighbourhood builds a resilient city," said Nga Kor Ming, President of the UN-Habitat Assembly and Minister of Housing and Local Government of Malaysia, in a video address.
"Let the flowing waters of Shaoxing remind us that when resources flow circularly, communities thrive," he added. "Let's turn today's awareness into tomorrow's lasting policy." ■

Militia members Sun Cundong (L), Han Tongyong (C), and Liang Denggao are pictured during a patrol on Kaishan Island in east China's Jiangsu Province, Sept. 13, 2026. Kaishan Island, located 12 nautical miles off the coast of Guanyun County in east China's Jiangsu Province, is a small but strategically important island in the Yellow Sea. With harsh natural conditions and frequent typhoons, the island is home to a rotating team of militia members who take turns guarding it. Their daily duties include monitoring the surrounding waters, patrolling the island, maintaining navigation aids and recording observations, with any unusual activity reported promptly.
Living conditions on the island have improved in recent years. A smart microgrid combining wind, solar and energy storage, along with a seawater desalination system, began operating in 2019, ending the island's reliance on weather-dependent power and rainwater. In 2021, an all-electric kitchen and other facilities were put into operation, further improving conditions for those stationed there.

Asian Games | China's Zhang defends men's all-around gymnastics title (updated)
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:09:13 CST
21:09:13 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- China's Zhang Boheng retained the men's all-around gymnastics title at the 2026 Asian Games on Monday.
Fresh from winning the event at the Asian Championships, the 26-year-old collected 85.065 points to take gold, while Japan's Shinnosuke Oka and Daiki Hashimoto finished second and third, respectively.
Hashimoto, the Tokyo Olympic all-around champion, made a strong start with 14.500 points on pommel horse, while Zhang opened with 13.800 on floor exercise.
Oka's consistent performance kept the battle for gold close. The reigning Olympic all-around champion moved ahead of Zhang and Hashimoto after scoring 14.633 on parallel bars in the fourth rotation.
Zhang responded with 14.700 on the same apparatus in the fifth rotation, taking a narrow 0.167-point lead over Oka into the final round.
With Zhang competing on horizontal bar and Oka and Hashimoto on floor exercise, the title remained up for grabs. Zhang scored 14.033 to secure his second consecutive Asian Games all-around title, while Oka finished with 13.833 on floor to take silver and Hashimoto's 13.433 left him with bronze.
Zhang said competing last on horizontal bar allowed him to adjust his routine based on his rivals' scores. After watching Oka and Hashimoto complete their floor routines, he opted to reduce the difficulty of his routine and lower the risk of errors.
"Gymnastics keeps progressing, and both Japanese all-around gymnasts have high levels in difficulty and execution," Zhang said.
Looking ahead to the 2028 Olympics, Zhang said he needed to develop a broader range of difficult skills and improve his competitive mindset as he aims to deliver a stronger overall performance.
The all-around competition also served as qualification for the team and apparatus finals. China topped the team standings with 255.361 points, ahead of Japan on 254.460, setting up another close contest between the two traditional powers. South Korea qualified third with 238.327.
The women's all-around competition will take place Tuesday, followed by the men's and women's team finals Wednesday. ■

Asian Games | China beats Thailand to reach women's volleyball final

Wu Mengjie (L) of China spikes the ball during the women's volleyball semifinal match between China and Thailand at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Komaki, Japan, Sept. 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Cen Yunpeng)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- China edged Thailand 3-2 in the women's volleyball semifinals at the 2026 Asian Games on Monday, avenging its defeat in last month's Asian Championship final and advancing to the gold-medal match.
China started strongly and built a four-point lead in the opening set, but Thailand responded with improved attacking and blocking. The teams remained level from 12-12 through 18-18 before Thailand pulled away to take the set 25-23.
China regained its composure in the second set, using quick attacks to establish a lead of about four points and holding on to win 25-21 to level the match.
China took control in the third, opening a lead of more than 10 points before cruising to a 25-11 victory and a 2-1 advantage.
The fourth set was much tighter, with neither side able to pull clear. The teams were tied at 26-26 before Thailand produced strong serving at crucial moments to take the set 28-26 and forced a decider.
China dominated the fifth set, using aggressive attacks to steadily extend its lead before closing out the match 15-6.
China head coach Zhao Yong said his players maintained their determination throughout the match.
"Both sides played a fantastic match, but our players showed a slightly greater hunger for victory on the court," Zhao said.
China reached the semifinals with a 3-0 victory over Vietnam in Sunday's quarterfinals, while newly crowned Asian champion Thailand advanced after sweeping Indonesia.
Monday's semifinal was a rematch of last month's Asian Championship final in Tianjin, China, where Thailand overtook China 3-2 to secure its first ever Olympic berth in women's volleyball. ■

Another Chinese water museum joins global network, boosting water heritage protection
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:08:57 CST
21:08:57 KST

YINCHUAN, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- The Ningxia water conservancy museum in Wuzhong, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, was recently admitted to the Global Network of Water Museums (WAMU-NET), becoming the 11th water conservancy and water culture institution in China to join this network.
Previously, 10 such institutions in the country, including the National Water Museum of China, the Yellow River Museum and the Changjiang (Yangtze River) Civilization Museum, had already joined the network.
The latest admission will help raise the profile of Yellow River water culture and Ningxia's irrigation heritage, while giving local institutions access to global expertise in protecting water cultural heritage and managing water resources, according to the Ningxia Water Conservancy.
Headquartered in Italy's Venice, WAMU-NET is a flagship initiative of UNESCO's Intergovernmental Hydrological Programme. It aims to advance the protection, research and promotion of water cultural heritage through global collaboration among water museums, and to raise public awareness of the sustainable use of water resources.
The network now covers more than 40 countries, bringing together over 120 water museums, water culture institutions and individual members.
The ancient Yellow River irrigation district in Ningxia is one of China's four major ancient irrigation districts and an important vehicle for promoting Yellow River culture. In October 2017, it was inscribed on the World Heritage Irrigation Structures (WHIS) list. As of September 2025, it was one of 42 WHIS sites across China.
A WHIS exhibition center officially opened in Yinchuan, capital of Ningxia, in May 2025. The first venue in the Yellow River basin to present 2,000 years of irrigation heritage in a systematic way, it filled a gap in the region's cultural offerings by bringing its water and Yellow River culture together under one roof.
In recent years, Ningxia has stepped up its protection and use of water cultural heritage, enacting China's first local legislation specifically focused on the protection of the WHIS and adding a dedicated chapter on water culture to its conservation plan (2018-2035) for the ancient Yellow River irrigation district.
These local initiatives are part of a broader national push. The Ministry of Water Resources has, notably, been building an institutional framework for protecting water heritage.
In July 2026, it issued guidelines on advancing water culture, calling for a three-pronged framework for protecting, passing on and promoting water culture. These guidelines also set out measures including drawing up technical standards for protecting and managing representative water heritage sites, promoting the digital preservation of water heritage, and encouraging local governments across the country to explore dedicated legislation. ■

China, Madagascar launch first joint operation against telecom fraud
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:08:48 CST
21:08:48 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Chinese and Malagasy police have carried out their first joint operation targeting telecom and online fraud, dismantling multiple criminal dens in the Malagasy capital Antananarivo and other areas, China's Ministry of Public Security (MPS) announced Monday.
The operation comes as telecom fraud syndicates, squeezed out of Southeast Asia by intensified crackdowns, have increasingly relocated to regions that include the Middle East, Africa and Central America.
Madagascar has emerged as one such destination, with its own authorities acknowledging a significant influx of fraud operators from Southeast Asia.
At the invitation of Malagasy authorities, Chinese police sent a working group to assist with the anti-fraud crackdown. Malagasy officials helped repatriate the first batch of 50 suspects to China on Sept. 8. Investigations into the cases are underway.
China has in recent years strengthened law enforcement cooperation with over 30 countries, including Spain, the United Arab Emirates and Myanmar, to tackle cross-border telecom and cyber fraud, developing cooperation mechanisms and achieving results in joint efforts against these crimes.
Since 2023, China and Myanmar have carried out joint operations that led to the dismantling of four major criminal gangs in Myanmar's Kokang region. Earlier this year, police authorities from China, the United States and the United Arab Emirates conducted their first joint law enforcement operation, resulting in the arrest of 276 suspects.
Cooperation with Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, Indonesia, Sri Lanka and other countries has also led to the arrest and repatriation of more than 20,000 telecom and online fraud suspects this year.
Earlier this month, China initiated the International Alliance Combating Telecom and Cyber Fraud, with 46 founding member countries. The alliance is an intergovernmental organization designed to promote cooperation among law enforcement agencies in tackling transnational telecom and cyber fraud and related crimes.
Through this new alliance, China will work with law enforcement partners worldwide to root out illegal fraud hideouts, track down suspects and protect the legitimate rights and interests of people, an official with the MPS said. ■

New US troop rotation on its way to Lithuania, says president

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:20:00 UTC
19:20:00 KST

A new rotation of US troops is on its way to Lithuania, President Gitanas Nausėda said on Tuesday.
"Great news for Lithuania – US troops will continue to be stationed in our country. We are grateful to President Donald Trump and the US administration for this decision, which is important not only for Lithuania’s security but for the security of the entire region," Nausėda said in a statement issued by the presidential office on Tuesday.
New US troop rotation on its way to Lithuania, says president
A new rotation of US troops is on its way to Lithuania, President Gitanas Nausėda said on Tuesday.
"Great news for Lithuania – US troops will continue to be stationed in our country. We are grateful to President Donald Trump and the US administration for this decision, which is important not only for Lithuania’s security but for the security of the entire region," Nausėda said in a statement issued by the presidential office on Tuesday.
According to the president, the exact number of US troops has not yet been confirmed, but it will not be lower than previously.
Presidential adviser Deividas Matulionis told LRT RADIO that he did not have the information on Tuesday morning, but official confirmation about the US troops had reached him by lunchtime.
"It has been confirmed that the troop rotation is on its way, already on trains, and is expected to arrive in Lithuania in the near future," the presidential adviser said.
He also confirmed that the number of US troops would definitely not be lower than the previous deployment. "I cannot say exactly because the Americans have not yet given us the number. The only thing I can say is that it will not be lower than before," Matulionis said.
Discussing the deployment of US troops to Lithuania, Matulionis said Washington had not imposed any conditions on Lithuania concerning fertiliser exports from Belarus and that Lithuania had been among the first countries to respond to a US questionnaire on defence commitments.
"No, definitely not, there were no conditions," the adviser said.
The US is currently reviewing the deployment of its forces in Europe. More than 1,000 US troops completed their rotation in Lithuania this summer.
The US has regularly deployed battalion-sized units to Lithuania since 2019. Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Washington changed the status of its forces in Lithuania to continuous rotational deployments.
These reinforced battalions have typically consisted of 1,000 or more troops, along with various types of combat equipment.
Lithuania has previously said it is prepared to host up to 1,500 US troops.
In August, the US sent a questionnaire asking European countries to demonstrate progress toward taking primary responsibility for the defence of the continent, following an agreement to increase defence spending.
