Erosion of Germany's political centre exposes Merz's weakening grip on power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:54:01 UTC
20:54:01 KST

Erosion of Germany's political centre exposes Merz's weakening grip on power
BERLIN, Sept 21 - Germany's far right and far left both made big gains in Sunday's state elections, exposing yet again the erosion of the political centre in Europe's largest economy as well as Chancellor Friedrich Merz's weakening hold on power.
The anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) confirmed its strength in the formerly communist eastern states by taking first place in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state, building on its triumph two weeks ago in Saxony-Anhalt.
The AfD also recorded its best-ever result in Berlin, where the far-left Left Party came first and looks set to replace Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) in the mayor's office.
Merz called the result in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — the worst in CDU history — "a disaster". But he defied speculation he might step down, pledging to remain to pass a package of tax and pension reforms that he hopes will help revive Germany's sluggish economy.
For now, at least, the party has stood behind him, although the result will add to pressure within his coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD), some of whom want to water down parts of the reform agenda.
"We have to analyse, as a government, why there is this sense of uncertainty in the country," SPD co-leader Lars Klingbeil said.
A pervasive sense of economic malaise and disillusion with traditional political parties point to further turbulence ahead, with a raft of state elections in western Germany due next year.
"Germany is entering a period of political instability where viable coalitions are harder and harder to build, and that doesn't bode well for Europe when Germany is the de facto leader," said Sudha David-Wilp, a senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States.
The AfD wants to expel foreigners with no right to stay in Germany, restore energy ties with Russia and quit the euro, while the Left Party wants to cap rents and nationalise large parts of the Berlin housing market.
By contrast, Merz's pursuit of what he says are painful but necessary reforms has yet to yield improvements that voters can feel.
"We can see how difficult it is to win people over while in government and from the centre of society," said Stefan Evers, the CDU's lead candidate in Berlin.
DISASTER
Even before the election, Merz's approval ratings were at a record low and his party has trailed the AfD in national polling for months. "People would tell us that as long as he had a say in things, we wouldn't vote for you," said one CDU election campaigner in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
From the start of his time in office, when a normally routine parliamentary vote to confirm him as chancellor turned into a humiliation requiring a second round of voting, Merz has struggled to establish his authority.
There have been repeated gaffes, from saying people in Germany needed to work longer hours to identifying as "middle class" while working as a highly remunerated supervisory board chairman of asset management firm BlackRock.
Surveys indicate that his communication lapses and his difficulty in establishing an emotional connection with voters anxious about their economic future both contributed to the outcome of all five state elections this year.
But Germany's deep-seated economic challenges — an ageing population, poor growth and the erosion of its industrial base under increasing pressure from China — resist easy solutions.
The reforms themselves caused problems in formerly communist eastern Germany, where despite more than three decades of economic transformation, more voters than in the west earn the minimum wage and rely completely on the state pension in retirement.
Manuela Schwesig, the SPD state premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, whose success in limiting the AfD's gains in her state was one of the few bright spots for the government, said she was "surprised" by Merz's refusal to change course.
Her campaign was heavily critical of Merz, whom she accused of showing indifference towards voters struggling with soaring fuel prices. She also called for changes to the pension reform that would require people to work for longer — a particularly unpopular issue in the east, where many have not built up the same level of savings as those in the west.
FIREWALL UNDER PRESSURE
Days before the vote, as speculation grew that his position might be in danger, senior CDU leaders rallied around the chancellor, aware that replacing him would put the reform programme at risk without solving underlying problems.
So far, the policy — known as the 'firewall' — under which the mainstream parties refuse to cooperate with the AfD has kept it from sharing power.
But there are growing doubts about whether it is possible to exclude a party which enjoys the support of more voters in Germany than any other.
Despite reservations about cooperating with a party with elements that are classified by the domestic security services as extremist right-wing, there are growing calls in the CDU for a rethink.
"This 'firewall' hasn't done anything for the CDU and they need to think about that," said Leif-Erik Holm, the AfD's lead candidate in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Opinion polls have shown deep disillusion among many voters with a political system that has seen a succession of coalitions between the formerly fiercely antagonistic mainstream parties of the centre-right and centre-left.
Under former Chancellor Angela Merkel, the "grand coalition" of CDU and SPD, seen only once before at federal level during the 1960s, became standard. Merz, once seen as a firebrand conservative, repeated the exercise after another coalition, headed by SPD Chancellor Olaf Scholz, collapsed in 2024.
"It's just allowed a vacuum on the right and the left for these parties to emerge," David-Wilp said. REUTERS

US refusal to issue visas to Palestinian delegation violates international agreements: Hamas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:50:46 UTC
20:50:46 KST

Lina Altawell
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
Hamas on Monday condemned the US refusal to grant visas to a Palestinian delegation seeking to attend UN General Assembly meetings.
“The decision constitutes a flagrant violation of the international conventions and agreements governing the work of the UN headquarters and a continuation of the policy of complete US bias toward the Zionist occupation,” Hamas spokesperson Hazem Qassem said in a statement.
The restriction has continued for a second year. In 2025, Washington denied visas to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and other officials to attend the meetings, forcing Abbas to participate by video link.
On Thursday, the UN General Assembly adopted a resolution allowing the State of Palestine to participate in the general debate of its 81st session through a prerecorded address by its president to be shown in the Assembly Hall.
The resolution was backed by 152 countries, opposed by three, with four abstentions.
On Thursday, the Palestinian Foreign Ministry rejected Washington’s decision to extend visa restrictions on Palestinian officials over alleged failures to meet commitments toward the US, calling for the measure to be halted and for direct Palestinian-US dialogue to begin.
Under the 1947 UN Headquarters Agreement between the organization and the US, Washington, as the host country, is required to facilitate access to the UN headquarters in New York for representatives of states and entities participating in UN activities.
Palestine has held the status of a non-member observer state at the UN since 2012.
Of the UN’s 193 member states, 160 recognize the State of Palestine, which is also a member of more than 100 international organizations and treaties, according to the Palestinian Foreign Ministry.
Israel and the US oppose such recognition, while Washington has used its veto power at the UN Security Council to block Palestine from obtaining full UN membership instead of its current status.
Since Oct. 8, 2023, Israel has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000 others in its genocide in Gaza, most of them women and children.
Successive US administrations have provided Israel with military, financial and diplomatic support, including protection from accountability at the UN Security Council through the use of the veto.
In 1948, Israel was established on lands seized by armed Zionist groups that carried out massacres and displaced at least 750,000 Palestinians. Israel later occupied the remaining Palestinian territories and continues to reject withdrawal and the establishment of a Palestinian state as stipulated in UN resolutions.

“Ninety days from the date of the first arrest are going to be over on September 25, so we will have to file the chargesheet, otherwise, they (the accused) will get default bail,” Mehta said.The bench, comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, also perused a detailed status report submitted by the SIT in a sealed cover.Under Section 167(2) of the CrPC, an accused becomes entitled to statutory bail if the investigating agency fails to file a chargesheet in the trial court within the stipulated period of 60 or 90 days.The bench had earlier directed the probe team to complete its investigation expeditiously and take it to its logical conclusion. It had also asked the SIT to file a status report in a sealed cover on the progress of the probe into the alleged theft of donations.

Explainer-How Putin may leverage Russian ruling party's election win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:49:02 UTC
20:49:02 KST

Explainer-How Putin may leverage Russian ruling party's election win
MOSCOW, Sept 21 - The pro-Putin ruling United Russia party retained its decisive majority in the national parliament, near-complete election results showed on Monday, in a tightly controlled political system that excluded most candidates who oppose Moscow's war in Ukraine.
Here are some of the reasons why the vote may be useful to President Vladimir Putin:
A MANDATE FOR MORE WAR?
As president or prime minister for more than a quarter of a century, Putin's grip on Russia has never been tighter. But the war has lasted much longer than many Russians expected and fallout from the conflict is now being felt much more sharply on the home front.
Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia itself have escalated, and Moscow was targeted on Sunday in the biggest attack of the war so far. While civilian casualties are far lower than in Ukraine, they have sharply increased this year. Strikes on oil refineries have caused fuel shortages, while businesses are grappling with drone attacks on their warehouses and polls suggest some Russians are increasingly anxious.
Having framed the election as a test of support for the war, Putin is likely to point to the results to say that most people back his decision to fight on until key war aims are met.
CREATION OF A 'NEW ELITE'
Putin has said that those who fought in Ukraine are "warriors", part of a new "elite" he has promised will have prestigious careers. With many of the 200 or so veterans who stood from a range of parties on track to enter parliament, Putin is expected to point to their success as an example of how Moscow looks after those who risked their lives for the motherland, and of how service on the battlefield can lead to a high-profile political career. It could also encourage more people to sign up to fight in Ukraine.
CONTRAST WITH UKRAINE
Putin has repeatedly suggested that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy is illegitimate, pointing to the fact that his five-year term ran out in May 2024 and that Zelenskiy has not held a new election since. Martial law, introduced in Ukraine in 2022, bans any wartime election and the constitution says the president serves until a newly elected one takes office. But Putin - who has faced criticism from Western politicians about Russia's own political system - may use the vote to say that Russia - unlike Ukraine - has stuck to its electoral timetable regardless of the war and has given people a chance to vote.
SENSE OF NORMALITY
Putin has been keen to show Russians that despite the conflict and everything associated with it they can largely carry on life as before. Increasingly deep and destructive Ukrainian drone strikes have made that harder to achieve in this fifth year of the war. But holding a relatively smooth parliamentary election across 11 time zones in the world's largest country, while also waging war in Ukraine, could help Putin reassure Russians that pre-war practices are being respected and that life - up to a point - goes on despite the conflict.
MOBILISATION/CENSORSHIP
Putin this month dismissed as "nonsense" suggestions by Ukraine and Western media pundits that Russia would carry out a post-election mobilisation to expand the ranks of its army in Ukraine suggesting it was a malicious suggestion designed to sow panic.
However, domestic and foreign critics of the war fear he could use the outcome of the election to justify such a move, given what Western intelligence agencies say are heavy Russian losses on the battlefield and what they say is Moscow's desire to urgently speed up the pace of its territorial gains.
Those same critics fear that the authorities may deploy more repressive measures once the election results are in and a pre-election feel-good mood is no longer required.
They point in particular to plans previously floated by the authorities to have mobile service providers charge customers extra for using more than 15 gigabytes of foreign data in a month, a move seen as targeting people who use VPNs or virtual private networks to access websites and apps banned inside Russia. The authorities have given no public indication they intend to resurrect the plan imminently. REUTERS

US President Donald Trump expressed concern Sunday over rising fuel prices during a telephone discussion with Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy, urging Kyiv to cease strikes against Russian oil refineries, the Financial Times reported on Monday.
"Diesel, diesel... diesel," served as the primary thrust of the American leader's message as he pressed the Ukrainian military to halt missile and drone bombardments of Russian refining installations, a senior Ukrainian official present during the call told the newspaper.
A second senior Ukrainian official familiar with the exchange confirmed that Trump conveyed acute anxiety regarding surging diesel expenses, which have intensified domestic political pressure on his administration as critical congressional midterm elections approach in November. According to the American Automobile Association (AAA), national average gasoline prices in the US stand at $4.48 per gallon, marking an increase of 9% from $4.11 a month ago and a jump of more than 40% from $3.19 a year ago.
"Russia has unfortunately lost control of its diesel oil industry due to its war with Ukraine," Trump wrote later on his social media platform Truth Social, adding that numerous refineries have been destroyed and remain “out of commission.”
He argued that the war "must be ended," lamenting that "the whole world suffers" as an estimated 25,000 people, primarily soldiers, die each month.
The White House did not immediately issue a public response regarding the telephone conversation or the FT report.
Confirming the call in a statement on messaging service Telegram, Zelenskyy said the discussion addressed wide-ranging matters and produced an agreement to hold an in-person meeting during this week's UN General Assembly in New York.
"We just spoke with President Trump. An important conversation, and many things were discussed. We have arranged a meeting in New York, and this meeting can change a lot," Zelenskyy said on Sunday.
Trump earlier publicly insisted that Ukrainian forces spare Russian energy infrastructure, maintaining that attacks on refining facilities hurt the global economy by provoking worldwide diesel deficits. The US president has repeatedly attributed record American and international fuel prices directly to Kyiv's refinery campaign rather than the concurrent Iran war in the Gulf.
On Sept. 14, Trump claimed on his social media platform Truth Social that Washington had brokered a mutual energy truce between Moscow and Kyiv, though Ukrainian officials later clarified that the proposal remained an unfinalized American framework rather than a formal accord.

Morocco's 2026 elections explained: Everything you need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:39:19 UTC
20:39:19 KST

Breadcrumb
Everything you need to know about Morocco's 2026 legislative elections
Moroccans will go to the polls on 23 September to elect the House of Representatives, the lower house of parliament. It will be the sixth legislative election since King Mohammed VI came to the throne and the fourth since the constitutional reforms introduced in the aftermath of the Arab Spring in 2011.
Expectations are high that the new parliament will help address persistent weaknesses in health care, education and employment. The vote also comes as Morocco takes on a series of strategic commitments, from advancing its autonomy plan for Western Sahara to preparing to co-host the 2030 World Cup with Spain and Portugal.
At home, the government faces pressure to consolidate Morocco’s social-state reforms, reduce unemployment and make room for a new generation of political leaders. Yet the election takes place against a backdrop of declining political engagement, particularly among young Moroccans and parts of the country’s political and professional elite.
Rachid Lamsallam, a Moroccan journalist and political analyst, identifies two immediate tests for the next parliament: whether it can produce a legislature capable of confronting the country’s political and economic challenges, and whether the resulting government can deliver the major economic, development, and infrastructure projects on its agenda.
The elections also present a test of Morocco’s political system itself. Lamsallam argues that participation must be revived and that practices that have eroded confidence in political life must be addressed. The prosecution of several parliamentarians in corruption cases, he says, has further contributed to disengagement among younger voters and political elites.
For Rachid Lazraq, head of Morocco’s North Africa Centre for Studies and Research, the more fundamental challenge is restoring trust in elections and representative institutions.
That means ensuring genuine competition, improving the quality of political programmes, curbing the influence of money and patronage, maintaining administrative neutrality and giving political forces more equal access to traditional and digital media.
Lazraq also argues that electoral violations should be met with swift and effective sanctions where they are proven.
For Morocco’s next parliament, therefore, the question is not simply who wins seats, but whether the election can restore confidence in a political system facing growing demands for better representation and delivery.
Falling turnout
Turnout in the upcoming elections poses another challenge for the state and political parties across the ideological spectrum.
A low participation rate would revive memories of Morocco’s 2007 elections, when turnout fell to just 37%, potentially casting a shadow over the political reform process pursued since the Arab Spring.
The Moroccan House of Representatives has 395 seats, whose holders are elected through proportional representation under a two-tier system.
A total of 305 seats are elected from 92 local multi-member constituencies, with each constituency having between two and six seats.
The remaining 90 seats are elected from 12 constituencies distributed across Morocco's regions, with between three and 12 seats, mainly reserved for women.
According to Moroccan Interior Ministry data, about 57% of current parliamentarians (227 members, including 204 men, 20 women, and three parliamentary advisers) are seeking to retain their seats in the 23 September elections.
Voting demographics
The number of registered voters stands at 15,801,162, compared with 17,983,490 in the 2021 elections, a decrease of about 2.18 million registered voters, or just over 12%.
Men account for 54% of those eligible to vote, compared with 46% women.
According to Moroccan Interior Ministry data, older age groups make up the largest share of the electorate, with those aged 60 and above accounting for about 30% of all voters, or approximately 4.74 million voters.
By contrast, youth participation in the electoral rolls remains limited.
Those aged between 18 and 24 account for only about 3%, or approximately 474,000 voters, despite the number of young people who have reached voting age standing at around 3.89 million.
When the 25-34 age group is factored in, accounting for about 15% of registered voters, under-35s make up no more than 18% of the total electorate.
28 parties in the parliamentary race
A total of 28 political parties are taking part in the 23 September elections, with 1,848 candidate lists comprising 1,783 male and female candidates across local and regional constituencies, in addition to two lists of independent candidates.
A comparison with the 8 September 2021 legislative elections reveals a notable discrepancy.
The number of participating parties has fallen from 31 to 28, while the number of lists has risen from 1,704 to 1,850, and the number of candidates has risen from 6,815 to 7,288.
This indicates that the competition has become more crowded despite the lower number of participating political forces.
Moroccan Interior Ministry data show that the parties with the strongest presence in local constituencies are the Authenticity and Modernity Party, the Istiqlal Party, the Party of Progress and Socialism, and the Justice and Development Party.
Each has submitted 92 local lists, the maximum possible under the system used for these constituencies, while each party has 305 candidates.
The National Rally of Independents, the leader of the current government coalition, comes directly behind these parties in terms of coverage.
It has submitted 92 local lists covering all local constituencies, in addition to 11 regional lists.
Differences in the number of lists submitted by the parties taking part in the elections reflect the scale of each party's presence.
They also provide an initial indication of the breadth of competition and the number of forces competing for parliamentary seats across the kingdom.
Election boycott
The Justice and Charity Association, Morocco's largest Islamic movement, is boycotting the legislative elections, citing the absence of "conditions for free and fair political competition".
It said elections in Morocco "have failed to move the country towards democracy, freedom and justice".
The Democratic Labour Way Party, the radical left-wing party, has also formally announced its decision to boycott the legislative elections, renewing its position of boycotting electoral events in the kingdom since its establishment.
The party linked its boycott decision to the fact that "the current political and constitutional conditions do not allow for fair and competitive elections capable of bringing about real change".
Limited presence of women
The nominations for the next House of Representatives have sparked anger over the limited presence of women at the top of lists in local constituencies and the rejection of some nominations on lists headed by women.
The difficulty women face in obtaining party endorsements to run for office has been notable.
They will head 121 local lists out of 1,615, accounting for only 7.5% of all local lists, according to Moroccan Interior Ministry statistics.
Women's main presence in the upcoming elections remains within regional lists reserved exclusively for them under the "quota" system, with 235 such lists.
Few independent parties
For the first time in the history of Moroccan elections, the state has adopted a package of direct incentives to lower the barrier for young people entering legislative institutions.
These include financial support covering 75% of campaign expenses for candidates under the age of 35, capped at 500,000 dirhams (about $55,000), and facilitating independent candidatures for young people to reduce their reliance on traditional parties' "endorsements".
These endorsements have been subject to "suspicions of exploitation" and are often granted to local notables.
Despite these incentives, official statistical data issued by the Interior Ministry revealed notably limited interest among non-affiliated candidates in taking part in the elections.
Only two lists containing five male and female candidates were submitted for the local constituencies in the 23 September elections, compared with candidates running under the names of 28 political parties across 92 constituencies.
Independent candidates were absent from the 12 regional constituencies.
Proxy voting for Moroccans abroad
The Moroccan Interior Ministry announced the launch of an online platform for arranging voting proxies for Moroccans living abroad who are registered on the electoral rolls.
This came as debate over their participation in elections in their countries of residence returned to the fore. Their participation has long been discussed without a final solution being found.
At least six million Moroccans live outside the kingdom, spread across Europe, North America and the Gulf.
They have significant economic and social weight in the country given their large remittances and the economic and tourism activity generated by their visits to their families and relatives every summer.
The platform allows each voter living outside Morocco to appoint a voter of their choice who is registered on the general electoral roll of one of the municipalities or districts in the kingdom to vote on their behalf on election day.
The demand for direct political participation by Moroccans living abroad in elections has remained on the table for years, amid various obstacles preventing this.
These are related to the method of voting, appropriate electoral boundaries and the proportion of representation, as well as the political sensitivity of party affiliation among Moroccans living abroad.
Crackdown on disinformation
The 23 September 2026 legislative elections are being held under new legal provisions that toughen penalties for producing fake news and fabricated digital content or publishing it with the intention of defaming voters and candidates or undermining the integrity of the electoral process.
The organic law governing the House of Representatives provides for imprisonment of between two and five years and a fine ranging from 50,000 to 100,000 dirhams for anyone who broadcasts or distributes a composition consisting of a person's statements or image without their consent.
The same applies to anyone who publishes, broadcasts, transmits or distributes false news, claims and facts, or fabricated or falsified documents, with the intention of violating the privacy of or defaming a voter or candidate.
The same penalty applies to anyone who creates content using digital media, artificial intelligence tools or otherwise containing false or fabricated material with the intention of undermining the integrity and credibility of electoral operations.
$48 million for election campaigns
The Moroccan government has allocated 450 million dirhams ($48.3 million) to finance the election campaigns of political parties taking part in the September 2026 vote.
It has also allocated 50 million dirhams ($5.2 million) from this amount to candidate lists headed by or including candidates aged 35 or younger, with the aim of encouraging youth participation and strengthening their presence in representative institutions, provided that the applicable legal conditions are respected.
As a result, the amount of public funding allocated to election campaigns has increased significantly compared with the 2021 elections, when the state's contribution did not exceed 160 million dirhams.
Meanwhile, the law has set an election spending ceiling of 600,000 dirhams (about $64,000) per candidate, requiring them to submit a detailed statement of the sources of their campaign funding and how it was spent to the relevant authorities.
How do voters cast their ballots?
Voters cast their ballots under a proportional representation system based on the largest remainder rule.
Seats allocated to each constituency are distributed among candidate lists based on an "electoral quotient", determined by dividing the number of registered voters in the relevant constituency by the number of seats allocated to it.
After the electoral quotient is determined for the relevant constituency, each list is awarded several seats equal to the number of times the total number of votes it received contains that quotient.
Each list retains the votes remaining after the seats it has won through this process have been calculated.
The seats that remain vacant after this process are then distributed according to the largest remainder rule, with seats successively going to the lists with the largest number of remaining votes.
Therefore, the number of seats each list receives is determined not only by its ranking according to the total number of votes, but also by the size of the remainder it retains after the first stage.
Who oversees the elections?
The Central Committee for Election Monitoring is responsible for ensuring the integrity and transparency of the electoral process at all stages and verifying compliance with the legal rules governing it.
The central committee consists of the interior minister and the prosecutor-general.
Regional and provincial committees also support its work at the local level.
The former comprises governors and public prosecutors, while the latter consists of provincial governors and prosecutors, with the aim of ensuring the integrity of electoral operations and monitoring them on the ground.
A total of 3,006 male and female observers, including delegations representing 20 international and regional bodies and organisations, will be able to monitor the various stages of the legislative elections scheduled to take place in Morocco on 23 September.
Since 2011, election observation in Morocco has been provided for in the constitution and regulated by law.
Morocco uses an independent election observation system rather than monitoring.
Observers only record violations in reports submitted to the relevant authorities, while monitors have the authority to intervene to stop any violations affecting the electoral process.
Who are the main contenders?
Twenty-eight parties and two independent lists are competing in the 23 September elections, but the main competing forces are divided into two camps.
The first consists of the parties in the current government majority, represented by the National Rally of Independents, which is seeking a second term at the head of the government, and the Authenticity and Modernity Party, the second party in the current government coalition.
The Authenticity and Modernity Party aspires to oust its ally, the National Rally of Independents, and achieve its longstanding goal of leading the Moroccan government after failing to do so in three previous elections (2011, 2016 and 2021).
While the "polarisation war" between the two parties expected to lead the party scene after 23 September was one of the most prominent features of the political scene on the eve of candidate registration and during the election campaign, the Istiqlal Party, Morocco's oldest party, is seeking to benefit from the "battle to break the bones" between its two allies.
It is seeking to seize first place, paving the way for it to head what is known in Morocco as the "World Cup government".
Meanwhile, opposition parties, represented by the Socialist Union of Popular Forces, the Party of Progress and Socialism, the Popular Movement and the Justice and Development Party, are seeking to spring a surprise or at least improve their position in the post-23 September political landscape.
Over recent days, Moroccan parties of different political orientations have raced to present their plans, answers and promises to address the economic and social challenges negatively affecting the lives of Moroccan citizens.
Party programmes have shown broad areas of overlap regarding economic and social priorities.
The main areas of convergence include consolidating the foundations of the social state, continuing to reform the universal health coverage programme, strengthening social protection, supporting targeted housing for low- and middle-income groups, promoting youth employment and economic recovery.
National Rally of Independents
The National Rally of Independents' programme aims to create one million jobs during the next term, while reducing the unemployment rate from 10.8% to 9% by 2031.
It proposes raising the minimum wage to 5,000 dirhams a month, linking social support to inflation, and providing a tax credit of up to 5,000 dirhams annually for each child for families.
It also pledged to create hundreds of thousands of jobs linked to industry, services and the digital economy.
It presents these targets based on an assumed growth rate of 4.5% in 2025 and expected inflation of 0.9%, while maintaining fiscal balances.
The party, which is seeking to lead the government for a second consecutive term, also proposes extending the "pioneer" schools and middle schools programme by 2028 and secondary schools by 2031.
One of its plans includes increasing the number of universities from 12 to 27, upgrading 1,600 primary healthcare facilities, and establishing 200 additional facilities and 100 mobile units.
Authenticity and Modernity Party
The party, which aspires to lead the Moroccan government for the first time in its history, aims to create one million net jobs between 2027 and 2031.
These would include 360,000 linked to the 2030 World Cup and related activities, 270,000 in the knowledge economy and high-value-added services, 250,000 in industry and import substitution, 80,000 in agriculture in rural areas, and 40,000 in the sports economy.
It also promised to reduce unemployment from 10.8% to 7% by 2031, meaning the creation of at least 200,000 net jobs annually.
It also promises to raise the minimum wage to 5,000 dirhams, increase the minimum pension to 3,000 dirhams, exempt gross salaries below 15,000 dirhams from income tax, and provide free electricity bills below 100 dirhams.
Istiqlal Party
The party proposes providing financial support of up to 5,000 dirhams (about $500) to young people preparing to marry, training 100,000 young people and preparing them to integrate into the global digital economy, and creating 2,000 specialist emergency doctors by 2031.
The party says it will equip all schools with internet access by the end of the primary education term, impose a 40% tax on the profits of monopolistic activities, and provide a tax deduction for families that bear the costs of educating their children.
The party also says it will introduce 16 measures to protect families' purchasing power, including gradually raising wages and pensions and digitising 100% of public services.
Socialist Union of Popular Forces
The party pledged to create 250,000 industrial jobs, increase industrial exports by 40%, add 1.5 percentage points annually to growth through industrialisation, reduce unemployment to below 8%, reduce youth unemployment to below 10%, and raise women's participation in the labour market to more than 30%.
It also promised to increase the number of healthcare providers to 4.5 per 1,000 people and reduce waiting times by 50%.
In education, it proposed increasing the research budget to 2% of gross domestic product, reducing overcrowding by 40%, raising graduate integration to 60%, creating 10 new university hubs and digitising university services by 100%.
Party of Progress and Socialism
The party's programme is based on creating one million jobs, including 100,000 in the digital sector, employing 500,000 workers in the industrial sector, and increasing industry's contribution to gross domestic product from 15% to 20%.
It also proposes raising wages by 15% in two stages, increasing the minimum wage and linking it to inflation, raising direct social support for families to 1,000 dirhams (about $100), and mobilising additional investment and resources in health, education, digital transformation and artificial intelligence.
The programme also includes tax reforms aimed at tax fairness and combating rent-seeking, establishing a public investment bank, and supporting small and medium-sized enterprises and domestic production.
Popular Movement
The party's programme includes a promise to establish a social tax account for families, allowing them to deduct private education, healthcare and basic service expenses from their taxable income.
It also proposes launching a national price platform with an intervention mechanism when the price of a basket of basic goods rises by 20% within 30 days, and digitising administrative and tax procedures for businesses.
The party is also focused on expanding access to housing support in rural areas, strengthening services in mountainous and rural regions, and expanding Amazigh-language teaching.
According to Ouzzine, it criticises reducing the Amazigh budget to around 1 billion dirhams without sufficient impact on the ground.
Justice and Development Party
The Justice and Development Party is contesting the elections with an election programme centred on five main areas, including strengthening the democratic choice, education and training, healthcare and employment.
Under its healthcare proposals, the party plans to allocate annual funding from the general budget in exchange for public health centres and hospitals taking responsibility for providing these services.
The party also proposes extending health coverage to parents as part of the rights of insured people. It is calling for a comprehensive review of medicine pricing policy, particularly for expensive medicines, as well as a review of the decree regulating the sector.
On taxation, the party proposes imposing a 40% corporate tax rate on companies and businesses operating in sectors characterised by monopolistic, near-monopolistic or oligopolistic conditions.
Left Alliance
The alliance proposes a birth grant of 5,000 dirhams (about $500) for every mother who gives birth in a public hospital, establishing 3,000 free nurseries, and a monthly grant of 1,500 dirhams for unemployed graduates for a period not exceeding one year.
It also proposes creating 150,000 jobs for unemployed young people, raising the minimum wage to 5,000 net dirhams by 2029, providing a monthly independence allowance of 1,500 dirhams (about $150) for people with disabilities, a monthly dignity income of 1,500 dirhams for elderly people without pensions, and increasing pensions by 2,000 dirhams (about $200) a month.
It further says it will allocate 70.9 billion dirhams to education and universities and 80.2 billion dirhams to health, increasing the research and development budget to 1.2% of gross domestic product, employing 15,000 healthcare professionals and between 8,000 and 10,000 research professors.
It also says it will reduce medicine prices by between 30% and 50% and fully exempt basic goods and medicines from value-added tax.
What happens next?
The Moroccan Interior Ministry is expected to announce the results the day after the vote, on 24 September.
However, the results will not become final until the Constitutional Court rules on the appeals.
After the results are announced and the leading party is known, the process moves from the electoral law to the constitution, with the Moroccan monarch appointing the head of the political party that won in the elections as prime minister.
It has been the political convention for the king to choose the party leader for the position.
Once appointed, the prime minister holds consultations with the country's other political parties to form a government coalition that secures a parliamentary majority.
After an agreement is reached with the government, the appointed prime minister proposes the names of its members to the king, who appoints them in accordance with Article 47 of the constitution.
The government is not considered official until it receives the confidence of an absolute majority of members of the House of Representatives, or at least 198 votes.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) warned Monday they will strike new targets and deploy new weapons if the U.S. launches further attacks, the Fars news agency reported.
"If a new aggression occurs, we will certainly change the weaponry and the geography of the war," IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said, adding that Tehran was prepared for a prolonged conflict.
Almost seven months into their war, Tehran and Washington remain locked in a stalemate, though neither side appears willing to return to full-scale war.
In a statement, Mohebbi warned that "there will certainly be significant changes in our defense and our counteroffensive" in the event of a new U.S. attack.
"We will introduce new weapons with new capabilities into the battlefield and the world will be surprised," he said.
"Our targets will not necessarily be the same as before either. We have new targets that have not yet been attacked," he added.
The Guards also said they were prepared for a "prolonged war".
On Saturday, the central command of Iran's military said the U.S. was planning new action against Tehran, according to state television, but it did not elaborate.
Fighting between the U.S. and Iran has eased in recent days after a flare-up at the end of last month, though Tehran continues sporadic attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
Meanwhile, Two crew were wounded when an "unknown projectile" hit a tanker Monday in the Strait of Hormuz, a maritime agency said.
"Military authorities have informed UKMTO that a tanker conducting an inbound transit was struck by an unknown projectile," said the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
"Two crew have sustained minor injuries and the vessel is reported to be continuing to its next port of call under its own power," it added.
The UKMTO said the vessel is reportedly continuing to its next port of call under its own power. No reports indicated any environmental impact at this time.
British security firm Vanguard Tech said U.K.-flagged tanker La Stephanie was hit by a drone while sailing towards the Gulf, also reporting minor injuries to two crew members.
Tehran is seeking to maintain a stranglehold on the vital waterway in its war with the United States, while Washington has kept up a counterblockade of Iranian ports.
Tehran has asserted control over much of the Strait of Hormuz since the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28 . In peacetime, about 20 million barrels – roughly a fifth of the world's oil supply – passed through Hormuz each day.
Some tankers are again traversing the strait, but traffic is well below what it once was, with both sides maintaining rival blockades in the waterway in an effort to exert pressure.

Chronic stress may be quietly reshaping your heart

Chronic stress may be quietly reshaping your heart
- Date:
- September 21, 2026
- Source:
- Medical Research Council (MRC) Laboratory of Medical Sciences
- Summary:
- Chronic inflammation tied to stress, lifestyle, mental health, and socioeconomic conditions may silently change the heart for years before any symptoms appear. People with the highest inflammation levels faced a 43% greater risk of heart attack and stroke, raising hopes that earlier testing and anti-inflammatory treatments could help prevent serious heart disease.
- Share:
Chronic stress linked to everyday life may leave a lasting physical mark on the heart, potentially damaging cardiovascular health and shortening lifespan.
That conclusion comes from a study of nearly half a million adults in the UK, led by researchers at the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (LMS) and Imperial College London. The researchers believe it is the largest study of its kind.
Their findings suggest that chronic inflammation, which is associated with lifestyle and socioeconomic circumstances, may contribute to harmful changes in the heart's structure. It was also linked to a greater risk of heart attack and stroke.
Importantly, these changes may begin years before a person notices any cardiovascular symptoms, allowing the damage to build silently over time.
Hidden Inflammation May Change the Heart
Professor Declan O'Regan, British Heart Foundation Chair of Cardiovascular AI at Imperial College London and Head of the Computational Cardiac Imaging Group at the LMS, said: "Our study, which is the largest of its kind, suggests that millions of people could be living with hidden inflammation, which is slowly changing their heart and causing long-term damage - increasing the risk of heart attack and stroke. Chronic inflammation is complicated, but we know it's tied to our health and driven by a range of lifestyle and economic factors - meaning people may be at more risk just because of their surroundings, their economic status, their family's health and their lifestyle."
"But while tackling health inequalities remains an issue, there are things that we can do about inflammation, including reducing risk factors like smoking and obesity."
Chronic inflammation occurs when the immune system remains mildly activated for long periods rather than switching off after an immediate threat has passed. This persistent, low-level immune activity has been associated with several diseases, including cancer and diabetes, and researchers increasingly suspect that it may also play an important role in heart disease.
For the new study, the team examined UK Biobank data from nearly 480,000 adults in the UK. They assessed inflammation using a blood marker called glycoprotein acetyls (GlycA) and combined those measurements with heart imaging and genetic information.
A 43% Higher Risk of Heart Attack and Stroke
People with the highest inflammation levels (the top 20%) had a 43% higher risk of heart attack and stroke than participants with the lowest levels (the bottom 20%).
The researchers also found signs that inflammation was associated with physical remodeling of the heart. People with higher inflammation tended to have thicker heart walls, smaller heart chambers and poorer heart filling - all changes which may develop quietly for years before progressing to heart failure.
Inflammation was also strongly associated with socioeconomic disadvantage and psychological distress. More familiar cardiovascular risk factors, including smoking and excess body fat, were linked to higher inflammation as well.
People whose inflammation remained elevated over time had a 43% greater risk of heart attack and stroke, even when they had no previously existing heart disease.
The findings suggest that inflammation may provide one biological route through which pressures from everyday life, including poverty and mental health problems, can affect the body and increase cardiovascular risk.
Social Factors, Mental Health, and Genetics
Professor Declan O'Regan added, "The surprising thing was how much social factors and mental health are linked to inflammation and damage to the heart -- as well as more well-known risk factors like smoking and inactivity. There was also a strong genetic factor, with some people being naturally more resilient or susceptible to the inflammatory damage that comes from different lifestyles."
The researchers emphasize, however, that genetic susceptibility or difficult life circumstances do not make heart disease inevitable. There are still opportunities to reduce persistent inflammation and lower cardiovascular risk.
The analysis also highlighted inflammatory proteins in the interleukin-1 and TNF families as possible contributors to the observed heart damage.
Several of these proteins are already being targeted by drugs being tested in clinical trials. That raises the possibility that anti-inflammatory therapies could eventually help prevent cardiovascular disease before symptoms begin.
Blood Tests Could Help Identify People at Risk
The researchers also suggest that inflammation blood tests could potentially be combined with genetic risk scores to identify people who may benefit most from early intervention.
Professor Bryan Williams, Chief Scientific and Medical Officer at the British Heart Foundation, said: "Inflammation is part of the body's healing process, but there is also a darker side to it. This large-scale study found people with higher levels of inflammation experienced silent changes to the structure of their hearts and had a higher risk of major cardiac events including heart attacks and strokes."
"The research provides valuable insights into how our genes and lifestyle factors, such as smoking, poor mental health and socioeconomic status, can converge to trigger inflammation. It also identifies several inflammatory proteins that appear to play a key role in the heart changes linked to chronic inflammation, and it is to be hoped that anti-inflammatory medicines could become an important tool in preventing cardiovascular disease.
"These findings reinforce the importance of tackling the causes of inflammation and poor cardiovascular health, while also supporting people to make lifestyle changes that can help protect their hearts."
The study was funded by the Medical Research Council and British Heart Foundation.
The work was also supported by the NIHR Imperial Biomedical Research Centre, a translational research partnership between Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust and Imperial College London.

People protest against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Austin, Texas, after a federal ICE officer shot and wounded a person. (AFP Photo)
The United States has deported more than 25,000 people under secretive agreements with 35 countries to take migrants with no ties to those nations, according to an investigation published on Sept. 21.
Since U.S. President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, Washington has been signing deals with developing countries to take migrants who cannot legally be sent home.
The investigation by Forbidden Stories found the administration has earmarked $410 million to be paid directly to the receiving countries, or to U.N. agencies to facilitate the returns.
At least 25,447 people had already been deported to third countries by Aug. 31, according to data compiled by Forbidden Stories with a consortium of international journalists.
The vast majority, around 20,000, were sent to Mexico, but the rest were dispersed to 27 other countries across Latin America, Africa, and the Pacific, and agreements have been finalized with seven more.
The deals vary, including over which nationalities can be deported and whether people with criminal records can be accepted.
An AFP investigation earlier this year found Washington is using visa bans and restrictions on African countries to strongarm them into accepting deportees.
Lawyers told AFP that deportees were being thrown into a “legal black hole,” held without charge in countries where they have no ties and few if any rights.
A little-known State Department division called the Office of Remigration, created in May 2025, has handled most of the negotiations and payments, according to Forbidden Stories.

Tablet fragment found in Türkiye adds piece to world’s oldest known peace treaty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:29:11 UTC
20:29:11 KST

Tablet fragment found in Türkiye adds piece to world’s oldest known peace treaty
Fragment discovered at ancient Hittite capital Hattusa identified as part of a copy of the Kadesh Peace Treaty
Yasemin Kalyoncuoglu
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
ANKARA
A fragment of a cuneiform tablet found in Hattusa, the ancient capital of the Hittite Empire in central Türkiye, has been identified as part of a copy of the Kadesh Peace Treaty, Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said Monday.
The fragment was found during excavations at Buyukkale, an area of the ancient city, and contains lines from provisions dealing with people who fled one country and sought refuge in the other, according to the ministry.
“We have found traces of peace dating back thousands of years in the soil of Anatolia,” Ersoy said in a social media post. “Scientific examinations have determined that a fragment of a cuneiform tablet found during excavations at Buyukkale in Hattusa, Corum, belongs to one of the copies of the Kadesh Peace Treaty.”
“The new fragment contains lines from provisions of the treaty regulating the treatment of people who took refuge in one country after fleeing another,” he said.
Ersoy said the readable sections of the newly identified fragment include references to people fleeing the lands of Egypt and Hatti, the ancient Hittite kingdom, as well as provisions concerning the destruction of homes.
He said the discovery, announced on Sept. 21, World Peace Day, demonstrates Anatolia’s longstanding role in the history of peace and diplomacy.
“The statements concerning the destruction of people’s homes carry a powerful message from thousands of years ago to the present day,” Ersoy said.
In his post, Ersoy also referred to the situation in Palestine, saying the ancient heritage reminded people of their responsibility to protect human life and dignity.
“We wish for a future in which all people, particularly our Palestinian brothers and sisters, can live in safety, peace and tranquility,” he said.
Identified after a year of examination
The tablet fragment was found near Building E at Buyukkale during archaeological excavations, according to the ministry.
One side of the fragment has survived, and it underwent detailed scientific examination for about a year.
Researchers determined that it belongs to one of the copies of the Kadesh Peace Treaty concluded between Hittite King Hattusili III and Egyptian King Ramesses II.
The treaty is widely associated with the end of the conflict between the Hittite and Egyptian kingdoms following the Battle of Kadesh, fought in the 13th century BC. It is considered one of the earliest known written peace agreements.
The newly identified fragment contains lines from provisions covered in Articles 12 to 20 of the treaty concerning the treatment of people who fled from one of the two countries and sought refuge in the other.
The surviving text is fragmentary and incomplete, but its readable sections refer to people fleeing Egypt and Hatti and contain references to the protection of homes from destruction.
New addition to Hattusa treaty fragments
The Egyptian version of the Kadesh Peace Treaty was inscribed in hieroglyphs on temple walls in Egypt, while fragments of clay tablets containing its Akkadian version were discovered in Hattusa during the first excavations at the site between 1906 and 1912.
Hattusa, located near the modern-day town of Bogazkale in Corum province, was the capital of the Hittite Empire, which became a major power in Anatolia and the wider region during the second millennium BC. The archaeological site was added to UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 1986.
Previously discovered fragments of the treaty are held in the collections of the Istanbul Archaeological Museums, the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations in Ankara, the Vorderasiatisches Museum in Berlin and the State Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg.
The newly identified fragment is expected to contribute to efforts to reconstruct the clay tablet copies of the treaty found at Hattusa.
Excavations at Buyukkale are ongoing, with researchers hoping to find additional missing fragments of the treaty.

Taiwan’s BizLink teams up with AMS-Osram on AI data center links
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:24:40 UTC
20:24:40 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — BizLink Holding Inc. is tapping the growing convergence of optical and copper connectivity to advance interconnect technology for AI data centers.
The connectivity solutions provider announced Monday that it is partnering with Austria-based optical and sensor solutions provider AMS-Osram. BizLink will contribute its optical expertise and high-volume production capabilities, while AMS-Osram will provide its laser technology, according to UDN and LTN.
The cooperation comes as AI systems scale up, requiring reliable interconnect solutions that balance power consumption, latency, and density. The companies said their architecture addresses these requirements by spreading data across many parallel, lower-speed channels instead of sending large amounts of data through fewer, more complex high-speed channels.
The companies hope to bring the architecture into mass production. They have already built key components of the system, including a two-dimensional array of individually controlled tiny lasers that operate at 850 nanometers to transmit data, along with BizLink’s fiber-to-fiber connectors and optical packaging.
As AI data centers expand and connectivity speeds increase, both copper and optical technologies are expected to play important roles. Copper connections can continue handling shorter links within a rack, while light-based optical links are increasingly used for longer distances between racks.
The industry therefore expects AI data center connectivity to rely on the complementary use of the two technologies rather than a complete shift from copper to optical, according to LTN.

Why do Sudan’s humanitarian truces keep failing and who is to blame?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:22:40 UTC
20:22:40 KST

Why do Sudan’s humanitarian truces keep failing and who is to blame?
As the US pushes for a 90-day humanitarian truce, Sudan’s warring factions continue to prioritise military victories over mediation efforts.
Efforts to bring about truces in Sudan are continuing to hit a dead end, with fighting continuing and worsening the country’s dire humanitarian situation.
Renewed efforts, including by the United States, to implement temporary truces to allow desperately needed aid into the country have repeatedly failed. Fighting has intensified in recent months, with the United Nations warning that the humanitarian system in Sudan is on the brink of collapse.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Hundreds of thousands lack adequate shelter at Sudan’s Tawila camp
- list 2 of 4UN extends partial Sudan arms embargo for a month
- list 3 of 4Gold mine collapse kills at least 70 people in Sudan’s West Kordofan
- list 4 of 4At least 26 killed in clashes along Sudan-South Sudan border region
Aid groups have urged immediate truces to alleviate the humanitarian crisis, but rival factions continue to maintain their momentum on the battlefield and break local ceasefires.
Political survival prioritised
Sudan’s civil war erupted in April 2023 after months of tensions between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) group. It expanded into 13 out of Sudan’s 18 states and has forcibly displaced 14 million people, creating one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises and killing tens of thousands of people.
Several international mediation efforts have attempted to broker ceasefires to end fighting and bolster humanitarian efforts, amid cases of starvation.
The first major initiative, the Jeddah Declaration in May 2023, was mediated and guaranteed by the US and Saudi Arabia. While it temporarily facilitated limited humanitarian access to affected communities, it soon collapsed after both factions repeatedly violated the terms.
Regional efforts via the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) and the African Union (AU) similarly failed when localised, short-term truces broke down, sometimes just hours after they were implemented.
The US has significantly ramped up its diplomatic engagement over the past year, spearheading the Aligned for Advancing Lifesaving and Peace in Sudan (ALPS) initiative in Geneva. Alongside Switzerland, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, the UAE, the UN, and the AU, Washington has pushed for direct negotiations and localised humanitarian pauses.
Responding to the escalating crisis, US Senior Advisor for Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos last week committed $375m to humanitarian efforts in Sudan and reiterated that “there is no military solution to this conflict.”
The US has reportedly renewed calls for a 90-day humanitarian truce in Sudan and for allowing affected communities to access emergency aid.
Fighting continues on multiple fronts in Sudan. In South Kordofan, the SAF has claimed gains, while Al Jazeera sources reported that the army had repelled an attack by the RSF in Blue Nile state. Conversely, the RSF has claimed a major victory over the army and its allies in Abu Qauod, west of El Obeid. With both sides claiming to be winning, it could make the prospects of a peaceful outcome to the war even harder to achieve.
Battle for control
Analysts suggest the failure of these truces is ultimately tied to the political ambitions of the warring leaders – Lieutenant General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan of the SAF and the RSF’s head Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti.
Fathi Abu Ammar, a Sudanese academic and editor-in-chief of Al-Wasat newspaper, argued that the military leadership is deliberately stalling negotiations to maintain its grip on power.
“All these efforts that serve the interest of the Sudanese people primarily were rejected by the army, rejected by al-Burhan and Yasser al-Atta (chief of staff of the SAF), and they all tried to obstruct them by setting broad lines for the peace they want,” Abu Ammar told Al Jazeera.
He said recent comments from the two military commanders hint that al-Burhan is preparing to formalise his rule over Sudan, perhaps for decades.
Supporters of SAF believe that after a series of victories on the battlefield, it is now operating from a position of strength and does not need to compromise.
Mohammed Ibrahim al-Rashid, director of the Center for International Political Relations Studies (Ma’alim), believes the RSF is facing a comprehensive defeat and that an SAF victory will end the war.
“The defeat now is not military; the defeat is diplomatic, a defeat in the corridors of the Security Council. The militia’s (RSF) load and its support are now in a critical position,” al-Rashid told Al Jazeera.
“Therefore, the government is reassured as days go by with the military advance … we can talk about breakthroughs with … a peace that achieves the interest of the Sudanese people, not one that reproduces the crisis and reproduces the militia.”
Flawed mediation efforts
While the fighting in Sudan continues, experts believe that international diplomatic efforts to end the war are essentially dead.
Cameron Hudson, former adviser to the US envoy to Sudan, believes that applying punitive measures while excluding the warring parties from negotiations is counterproductive.
“I think that there is one approach the United States has not tried since the beginning of this war, which is providing incentives and motives for peace. The United States used only pressures: Pressures through sanctions, and also accusations of using chemical weapons, and even pressure by ignoring both parties and not travelling to Sudan, and not inviting Sudanese officials to participate in international conferences,” Hudson told Al Jazeera.
“The issue of accumulating pressures one after another has not succeeded and has not worked, and therefore the United States must acknowledge that this approach has not succeeded. And until their position is revealed with the end of the war, I do not think that either of the fighting parties will proceed to stop the fighting.”

US President Donald Trump called off planned airstrikes against Houthi targets in Yemen shortly before they were to be carried out, The New York Times reported Sunday.

The decision to hold off on strikes also comes against the backdrop of previous US-Houthi understandings reached through mediation in Muscat, Oman.
Houthi representatives have said a 2025 ceasefire with the US remains in effect and that they do not intend to target American shipping.
Recent cross-border Houthi attacks have injured civilians in southern Saudi Arabia, while renewed fighting has disrupted shipping routes and displaced civilians inside Yemen.

Xinhua News Agency: China just announced President Xi’s state visit to the United States. Could you please share more information about the schedule and China’s expectation for China-U.S. relations?
Guo Jiakun: At the invitation of President Donald J. Trump, President Xi Jinping will soon pay a state visit to the United States. During his visit, President Xi will have an in-depth exchange of views with President Trump on major issues concerning bilateral ties and world peace and development.
Head-of-state diplomacy plays an irreplaceable role in providing strategic guidance to China-U.S. relations. The exchange of visits by the two presidents within the span of half a year will mark a milestone of historic significance. China will work with the United States to enrich the dimensions of the China-U.S. constructive relationship of strategic stability, strengthen dialogue and cooperation, and properly manage differences, so as to deliver greater benefits to our two peoples and further contribute to world peace, stability and prosperity.
China News Agency: On the fifth anniversary of the Global Development Initiative (GDI) put forward by President Xi Jinping, could you update us on the implementation of the initiative over the past five years? Is China considering hosting events on the initiative on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly?
Guo Jiakun: Five years ago today, President Xi Jinping put forward the GDI at the general debate of the 76th session of the UN General Assembly. Focusing on development, a timeless theme for humanity, the initiative pools together international efforts to put development high on the global macro policy agenda, aims to expedite the implementation of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and has injected strong impetus into revitalizing global development. The initiative has received extensive recognition from the international community.
Over the past five years, under the guidance of President Xi Jinping and with the joint effort of various parties, fruitful outcomes have been made in implementing the GDI. The GDI has turned from a Chinese proposal into a global consensus, with people-centered development philosophy enjoying increasing popularity. The GDI has played a greater role in driving global development by real actions. Under the framework of the initiative, more than US$23 billion have been mobilized, and more than 2,000 cooperation projects have been carried out. In particular, practical cooperation under the framework of the Global Development and South-South Cooperation Fund has yielded fruitful outcomes in 70 plus countries, benefiting more than 40 million people. The GDI has developed better cooperation architecture across various sectors, laying the groundwork for advancing international development cooperation as well as realizing UN Sustainable Development Goals.
The general debate of the 81st session of the General Assembly starts tomorrow. On the sidelines of the general debate, China will host the High-Level Dialogue on the Fifth Anniversary of the Global Development Initiative at the UN headquarters in New York on September 25. We look forward to working with the broader UN membership to take stock of the achievements and useful experiences over the past five years, share development opportunities, explore cooperation on development, facilitate the implementation of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and build a community with a shared future for humanity.
The New York Times: A U.S. official said last week at a briefing that China has not fully resumed rare earth deliveries despite agreeing to do so at previous summits of the two leaders. What is China’s position?
Guo Jiakun: I’d refer you to competent authorities for the specific question. China is committed to keeping the global industrial and supply chains of critical minerals safe and stable. China and the United States should jointly implement the important common understandings reached between the two presidents and maintain the steady growth momentum of China-U.S. economic and trade ties.
Shenzhen TV: Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson stated on September 18 that Russia had sent a note of protest to the Japanese side regarding the deployment of Typhon missile systems on Kyushu Island. The Kremlin considers the deployment unacceptable and demanded that the Japanese side fully recognize the results of WWII and abandon its remilitarization policy. China also recently sent a note to the Japanese side to express its concerns. Can you confirm that and share more details on that?
Guo Jiakun: The deployment of Typhon missile system, a strategic offensive weapon, is yet another example of Japan’s accelerated remilitarization. Such move will only push up the risk of military confrontation and arms race, threaten strategic balance and regional stability, and harm the legitimate security interests of neighboring countries. The international community is on high alert, with people from multiple Asian countries voicing their opposition to the deployment. China has also lodged strong protests against Japan through diplomatic channels on multiple occasions, and has recently sent a diplomatic note to Japan to reiterate China’s solemn position.
On the occasion of the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trials, China urges Japan to do serious soul-searching on its history of aggression, face up to the call from regional countries, and stop advancing its remilitarization agenda.
Reuters: The New Zealand Defence Force said today that two of its naval ships have transited the Taiwan Strait. The New Zealand PM called this a routine activity and said he was not expecting any backlash from China. Does China have any comment on this event?
Guo Jiakun: China’s position on foreign military vessels’ transit through the Taiwan Strait is consistent.
Beijing Youth Daily: According to preliminary results, the United Russia Party is leading in Russia’s State Duma elections held from September 18 to 20. What’s China’s comment?
Guo Jiakun: China extends congratulations over the smooth conclusion of the Russian State Duma elections. The elections are a major event on Russia’s political calendar. The results of the elections represent the will of the Russian people. As a friendly neighbor and comprehensive strategic partner of coordination for a new era, China firmly supports the Russian people’s independent choice and stands ready to continue working with the Russian side to act on the important common understandings between the two presidents to make fresh progress and bring bilateral relations to new heights.
The New York Times: Is China amenable to an extension of the November 10 deadline for expanded restrictions on rare earth exports, and if so, for how long?
Guo Jiakun: I’d refer you to competent authorities for anything specific.

Guo Jiakun: China strongly condemns this attack. We mourn for the loss of lives and extend sincere sympathies to the injured and the bereaved families.
Terrorism is a common enemy of humanity. Fighting terrorism is in the shared interests of all countries. China will continue its steadfast support for Pakistan’s counter-terrorism efforts. We call on all countries to join forces in tackling the threat of terrorism and safeguard global security and stability.
The New York Times: China’s restrictions this year on rare earth exports to Japan have affected American supply chains. Will this also be discussed at the summit later this week in Washington?
Guo Jiakun: I’ve just shared relevant information on the summit.
On the rare earth exports restriction you mentioned, in accordance with laws and regulations, China prohibits the export of all dual-use items to Japanese military users and for Japan’s military use, and any export that could help enhance Japan’s military capabilities. The aim is to thwart Japan’s remilitarization and attempt to possess nuclear weapons. China’s position of keeping the global industrial and supply chains of critical minerals safe and stable has not changed. All parties have the responsibility to play a constructive role to this end.
The New York Times: Do you have any further details regarding what progress may have been made in the conversations in New York City between Vice Premier He Lifeng and Treasury Secretary Bessent?
Guo Jiakun: The Chinese side has released a readout, which you may refer to. I have no further information to offer.
The New York Times: CNN reported at the end of last week that the U.S. military had been falsely responding to an AI report that a Chinese vessel was moving military components to the Middle East. Do you have any comment on this?
Guo Jiakun: I am not aware of what you mentioned.

Tens of thousands of German auto workers protest to save jobs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:18:00 UTC
20:18:00 KST

German auto workers stage mass protests in bid to save jobs
FRANKFURT – German automotive workers held nationwide protests on Sept 21, calling for government and management action to protect jobs and factories in an industry facing headwinds.
Growing Chinese competition, compounded by weak domestic demand and US tariffs, have hit the German car industry hard.
Volkswagen plans to cut 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade, the biggest restructuring ever in global automotive history. Mercedes-Benz and BMW are also downsizing.
Almost 180,000 people took part in the protests at over 280 sites across Germany, the IG Metall union said.
Janik Hitzemann, 31, an assembly line worker at a VW plant in Hannover – one of four in Germany that have been slated for potential closure – told AFP news agency he was protesting to pressure management to find another use for the site.
“All we really want is for the board to take our demands for an alternative solution seriously,” he said.
“Losing your job would be devastating for the individual concerned,” he added.
Speaking at VW’s iconic Wolfsburg factory, the largest in the world by floor area, IG Metall leader and VW supervisory board member Christiane Benner said: “Things have really hit the fan.
“Companies like VW, BMW, Audi, Bosch, Mercedes and Porsche were synonymous with fantastic cars and high quality.
“Now, management is driving the industry at full throttle into a brick wall.”
Many blame the industry’s woes on the management for starting too late with the transition to electric vehicles and being too slow to invest in software.
Others point to Chinese government support for its domestic carmakers which many in Europe say has unfairly led to overcapacity in the global car industry.
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said last week he would press for the European Union to further protect the continent’s carmakers from Chinese competitors, saying it was important to not be “naive”.
Speaking on Sept 21, Benner called on the government to make energy cheaper, provide financial help for suppliers who need to retool and promote domestic production with “Made in EU” rules.
“Colleagues in these tumultous times need to be able to count on the protection of comprehensive welfare and industrial policy,” she said.
Painful truths
Also speaking at Wolfsburg, Daniela Cavallo, the head of VW’s works council, told colleagues some “painful” truths.
“Europe’s automotive industry will be remade,” she said. “Long-established carmakers will fall by the wayside. Others will have to merge.
“The battle over how to share the burden has already begun,” she added. “The question is not what we as employees will be asked to take, but rather how we collectively can distribute sacrifices fairly among ourselves.”
Wolfgang Schroeder, a political scientist at the University of Kassel who researches labour relations, told AFP that the protests were a sign of “real fear over the future of the industry”.
“A nationwide action that is not related to pay negotiations or to specific disputes with companies but to a whole sector and its problems, that’s rather new,” he said.
“It’s the expression of real fear over the future of the industry.” AFP
