China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:17:30 CST
20:17:30 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- For Hunaidi Talal Hassan, reaching the Asian Games is a dream years in the making. "For us, this is not just a competition, it is a dream we have worked towards all our lives," the 18-year-old told a press conference on Monday. "We always had hope. And today we are here living that dream."
Hassan and fellow taekwondo athlete Muhammed Mahmoud Jasem make up the first refugee team to participate in the Asian Games. Both are from Syria and now live in Jordan. At Aichi-Nagoya 2026, they bring ambitions for the competition ahead, along with stories of how sport helped them see a future when one had seemed out of reach.
Hassan took up taekwondo at nine. The sport, she says, has changed many things in her life for the better. Being at the Games is a source of happiness and pride, made all the more meaningful by the difficulties she has faced.
"We faced many challenges, but we kept going and never gave up on our dreams," she said.
Jasem began practicing taekwondo at 14. For him, its importance has long extended beyond training and competition.
"This sport means a lot to me. It was my only hope," he said.
Living in a refugee camp, Jasem had struggled to imagine what lay ahead. Taekwondo gave him reason to believe a better life was possible. He kept training, and years of effort brought him to the Asian Games, where representing refugee athletes is both an honor and a responsibility.
"I'm not just participating in a regular competition. I'm carrying a story with me. I hope it will be a success story," he said.
Both athletes want to do well. They also want people to understand the journeys that brought them here. Speaking through an interpreter, they thanked their coaches, families and others whose support and belief had helped them reach the Games.
Introducing the pair, Olympic Council of Asia Deputy Director General Vinod Kumar Tiwari emphasized that they had earned their places through training and sacrifice, just like every other competitor.
Their presence also carries a wider meaning, he said. For people forced to leave their homes, sport can offer purpose, belonging and hope.
Beyond competition, both athletes also spoke about their experience at the opening ceremony. Through an interpreter, they expressed pride in attending as members of the first refugee team at an Asian Games.
Shiva Keshavan, vice chair of the OCA Athletes Committee, had met them at the athletes' accommodation and spoken with them again before the press conference. They had told him about the people they encountered and the athletes they met while entering the opening ceremony.
For Keshavan, those encounters are part of what sport makes possible.
"They are part of a family. We welcome them with open arms," he said. "The human connections, the bonds that they will make here will last a lifetime."
The questions on Monday also looked beyond the Games: how could the opportunities opened up in Nagoya be sustained once the competition was over?
OCA officials said they would discuss the athletes' needs with them and build on the training support already in place in Jordan. Tiwari expressed hope that refugee team would continue to take part in future Asian Games, drawing on the IOC's experience.
Speaking after the press conference, Mohammad Tayyab Ikram, president of the International Hockey Federation and chair of the OCA Coordination Committee for the 2026 Asian Games, said plans included reaching athletes in more locations and providing access to suitable training facilities.
National Olympic committees and international federations would work together to assess athletes' backgrounds, sporting ability and eligibility, he said. Helping them establish stable lives and continue their sporting careers was particularly important.
Ikram also said he expected the number of refugee athletes participating in the Games to increase. ■

Sri Lanka has recorded 1,849 fatal accidents so far in 2026. Compared with the same period last year, fatal accidents have increased by eight and deaths by 16, he said. ■

According to CEC data, after 95.18 percent of the ballots were counted, United Russia led with 57.83 percent of the vote, followed by the Communist Party of the Russian Federation with 13.81 percent and the Liberal Democratic Party of Russia with 8.98 percent. New People and A Just Russia garnered 7.96 percent and 4.96 percent of the vote, respectively.

The State Duma is Russia's permanent legislative body, composed of 450 deputies. Half of the seats are distributed proportionally in accordance with party lists, while the remaining 225 are elected through single-mandate constituencies nationwide under a relative-majority voting system. A total of 10 political parties participated in the election.
The final results are expected to be announced on Friday, said Pamfilova. ■

Feature: Zhu Yuling begins new table tennis chapter after eight-year Asian Games absence
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:17:06 CST
20:17:06 KST

by sportswriters Sun Zhe and Huang Haoran
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- For Zhu Yuling, the table tennis arena at the Asian Games felt both familiar and unfamiliar.
She had been here before, winning the women's team gold medal with China at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta. But eight years later, Zhu returned to the continental championships in a different jersey, representing Macao, China.
And in her first match at the Aichi-Nagoya Games, Zhu found herself across the table from her former teammates as her team faced China, the dominant force in women's table tennis, in the group stage.
"I was still very nervous in my first match," Zhu said. "Standing on the court at a continental multi-sport event, the feeling was very hard to describe."
Her first opponent could hardly have made the moment more emotional: Wang Manyu, the current women's singles world No. 1.
Zhu, 31, also once the world's top-ranked women's singles player herself, took the first two games 11-9, 11-9. Wang fought back to win the third 11-7, but Zhu closed out the match 13-11 in the fourth.
Later, Zhu faced another former teammate, Sun Yingsha, losing 3-0 as China eventually won 3-1. But her performance had already won warm applause from the crowd.
"My condition was even better than I had imagined," Zhu said. "Before the match, I went to my coach and told him I wanted to play first and face the strongest opponent. I wanted to find out where I was at and also fight for the chance to play the second match. In fact, I did it."
For Zhu, simply being there was already a victory.
Eight years ago she was a key member of China's team that won gold in Jakarta. She was then pushing toward the Tokyo Olympics, seemingly on a clear path at the highest level of the sport.
Then her life took an unexpected turn.
In August 2020, Zhu was diagnosed with a fibroadenoma, a non-cancerous breast lump. More than a year later, after undergoing surgery, she was forced to put down her paddle. She missed the Olympics, left China's national team and gradually disappeared from the spotlight.
But Zhu did not remain defined by what she had lost.
In 2022, Zhu began pursuing a doctorate in management at the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, researching career transitions among elite athletes, a subject closely tied to her own experience. She later joined Tianjin University as a physical education teacher.
Another chapter began in February 2024, when Zhu obtained Macao residency through the Macao Special Administrative Region government's talent recruitment program and began representing Macao, China in international competition.
Zhu was starting her second career in table tennis virtually from zero, while juggling classes to teach, a doctoral dissertation to finish, and training sessions and tournaments to prepare for.
Yet less than a year after returning to the international table tennis circuit, she had climbed back into the world's top 10.
Now, at the Asian Games, she has a new goal.
Macao, China opened its second women's team match with a 3-1 victory over Nepal on Monday.
"My goal is to create the best result in Macao's history," Zhu said. "This is very significant for us. We hope that, through our own efforts, we can inspire more young people in Macao."
After watching Zhu fight for every point against China, her Macao teammate Leung On Na broke down in tears.
"Seeing her fight for every single ball, I was really moved," Leung said.
For Zhu, however, this is not a story of hardship, but of gratitude for having another chance to compete.
"I think my life has been quite smooth," she said. "Although I am no longer at the top of the pyramid, being able to stand on the court itself means that, for me, I have already overcome myself." ■

20:17:01 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- An Australian vaccine platform demonstrated in animals could soon become a "plug-and-play" system to rapidly adapt to future mosquito-borne disease threats in humans, researchers said.
Building on more than a decade of work, University of Queensland (UQ) researchers have developed the ISVac platform, which uses a mosquito-specific virus genetically engineered to generate virus particles that are non-infectious to humans or animals, according to a UQ statement released Monday.
The particles have been used as vaccines against Japanese encephalitis virus in pigs and West Nile virus in crocodiles, said UQ Associate Professor Jody Peters.
"This next stage is a huge leap forward, developing a potential new tool to protect humans against emerging mosquito-borne diseases," Peters said.
"With the changing climate there's been an expansion of where mosquitoes are thriving, and it is pushing mosquito-borne diseases into new regions," she said, adding that Japanese encephalitis, which can cause severe neurological illness, lifelong disability and death, was not seen in Australia until 2022.
If successful, the platform could support the development of vaccines against other mosquito-borne diseases, including dengue, Zika, yellow fever and West Nile virus, the researchers said. ■

The findings point to a problem extending beyond the availability of jobs, with graduates increasingly facing a mismatch between their qualifications and the skills demanded by employers. Similar pressures have been reported across Asian economies, although the scale differs considerably between countries.
Technological change could further complicate the situation. The IMF noted that artificial intelligence has the potential to improve productivity and economic growth, but could also increase labor-market pressure on young workers if adoption advances faster than skills development. ■

Asian Games | Feature: Lee Hyun-jung powers South Korea to gold after years chasing NBA dream
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:16:53 CST
20:16:53 KST

by sportswriters Li Bowen, Cao Yibo, Yue Chenxing
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- The final buzzer sounded and the scoreboard read 67-57. South Korea's players poured off the bench and crumpled into one another at midcourt. Lee Hyun-jung stood among his teammates, and the tears came before he could stop them.
"I always seem to cry when I win a championship. The feeling of winning is so wonderful, and I think that is why the tears came. I also know how hard my teammates fought for this gold medal," Lee said after the game.
Lee had played nearly the entire final against host Japan, shooting 8 for 12 from the floor and 5 of 8 from three-point range. He finished with 27 points, 18 rebounds, three assists the whole game.
The teams were tied 28-28 at the break. In the fourth quarter, Lee kept rising to hit, stretched the lead to 13 and snuffed out Japan's last run. South Korea had its first Asian Games men's basketball gold in 12 years.
"I'm unbelievably happy. More than anything, I'm extremely grateful to my teammates," Lee said afterward.
The medal carried weight beyond the podium. South Korea's conscription law requires able-bodied men to serve roughly 18 months in the military. Winning a gold medal at an Asian Games is one of the few ways of achieving an exemption. At 25, Lee had played this final with his career clock on the line. 18 months away from top-level competition would have ruined any chance he has left of reaching the NBA.
That is a dream he has chased for years.
Born on October 23, 2000, in Seongnam, Lee grew up inside a basketball-playing family. His mother, Sung Jung-a, took a silver medal while representing South Korea at the 1984 Olympic Games. His father, Lee Yoon-hwan, played semi-professionally before becoming a high school athletic director and coach. His older sister, Lee Ri-na, played for South Korea's under-16 national team.
Lee did not take the red carpet laid out at home. He moved alone at 17 to the NBA Global Academy in Canberra, Australia, played for the BA Centre of Excellence and learned English at Lake Ginninderra Secondary College. From there he committed to Davidson, the small North Carolina school where Steph Curry played, choosing the Wildcats over an offer from Washington State.
At Davidson, Lee became the fourth South Korean to reach NCAA Division I. He averaged 8.4 points as a reserve freshman in 2019-20 and made the Atlantic 10 all-rookie team. As a sophomore he started every game and became the first player in program history to shoot at least 50 percent overall, 40 percent from three and 90 percent from the free throw line in the same season. As a junior he averaged 15.8 points and 6.0 rebounds, scored a career-high 32 against Charlotte and was named first-team All-Atlantic 10.
Then came the fall. A foot injury kept him from the NBA scouting combine. A prospect once viewed as a late second-round talent went undrafted in 2022.
He kept going. He joined the Santa Cruz Warriors of the G League in February 2023, averaged 5.5 points in 12 games and played for the Philadelphia 76ers in that year's Summer League. When it did not lead to a roster spot, he signed with the Illawarra Hawks of Australia's National Basketball League and helped them win the 2025 NBL championship.
That July, Lee signed with the Nagasaki Velca in Japan's B. League. He helped the team win that year's championship and was named MVP, making him the first South Korean to earn that honor in the B. League.
This summer he returned to the NBA circuit for his third Summer League, this time with the San Antonio Spurs, and the Portland Trail Blazers later gave him an Exhibit 10 training-camp deal.
Lee thought of his national team coach, Nikolajs Mazurs, while he wept on the Nagoya floor. The coach, alone in a foreign country, reminded him of his own younger self, the teenager who had left for Canberra with no support staff, no family nearby, no guarantee.
Mazurs arrived under anything but certainty. The 45-year-old Latvian was hired in December 2025. Before the Asian Games, South Korea had lost more games than it had won under him, including two straight warm-up defeats to Japan, and doubt followed the team into the tournament.
"A lot of people said that it would be difficult for us to win the gold medal," Lee said. "But under our coach's system, we worked hard to become more coordinated as a team. We did not allow ourselves to become discouraged by outside opinions. I think the fact that we stayed focused on one another and developed our chemistry led to this result."
"Despite everything, he did not become discouraged. He adapted well to us, and we managed to win the gold medal together. I am extremely grateful to him, and maybe thinking about the coach was one of the main reasons I cried so much," Lee added.
South Korea did not win this with Lee alone. Lee Jung-hyun added 14 points and seven assists beside him. Much of Lee's work was more than his three-pointers, 18 rebounds, many snatched over Japan's bigger frontcourt for second shots. A wing who built his reputation as a shooter had played like a center on the glass when it mattered most.
"I kept thinking the same thing: if I had an opportunity, I would take the shot, and I had to run one more step and make one more effort for my teammates. That was all I was thinking about," Lee said. ■

Türkiye leaves its mark in Africa with peace diplomacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:16:00 UTC
20:16:00 KST

Türkiye has built a reputation as a reliable power broker and mediator in international affairs under the leadership of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. On the International Day of Peace, observed on Monday, this role is under the spotlight, especially in Africa. Experts say Türkiye’s approach to Africa through mediation, diplomacy, humanitarian aid, development and capacity building contributes to peace and stability processes across the continent.
The country obtained observer status with the African Union (AU) in 2005 and was declared a strategic partner of the continent in 2008. Peace and security are also among the priority areas of cooperation within the Türkiye-Africa partnership.
Speaking to Anadolu Agency (AA), Dr. Alioune Aboutalib Lo, a researcher at the Africa Coordination and Training Center (AKEM), an Istanbul-based think tank, and Dr. Tarık Nur, a Sudanese academic and faculty member at Bilecik Şeyh Edebali University in Türkiye, assessed the country’s efforts toward peace and stability on the continent.
Lo said promoting peace and mediation had become an important component of Türkiye’s Africa policy over the past 20 years, noting that Ankara has been involved in various processes on the continent at both multilateral and bilateral levels.
Türkiye’s engagement with the continent gained unprecedented momentum after Ankara declared 2005 the “Year of Africa.”
Ankara has repeatedly presented itself as a fairer player than the continent’s former colonial powers, touting cooperation based on “equal partnership and a win-win principle.”
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has made more than 50 visits to African nations both as prime minister and president during the past two decades.
Pointing to Türkiye’s contributions to peace efforts in Sierra Leone under initiatives carried out within the framework of the United Nations (U.N.), as well as to the U.N. Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in the Central African Republic (MINUSCA) and the U.N. Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), Lo said that at the bilateral level, Ankara has used diplomacy to bring parties involved in disputes closer together.
Lo said the Ankara Process between Somalia and Ethiopia was one of the most concrete examples of this approach, adding that Türkiye has also facilitated talks between Somalia and Somaliland, played a role in the Libya file and undertaken diplomatic initiatives regarding the dispute over Nile waters between Ethiopia and Egypt.
Emphasizing that the relations Türkiye has developed with African countries over the years have enabled Ankara to engage with different sides, Lo said: “Türkiye’s advantage is that it can talk to all parties involved in a conflict.”
Lo said Türkiye’s strengthened bilateral relations on the continent had put it in a position to initiate dialogue between different actors and made mediation one of its diplomatic tools.
Referring to the dispute between Somalia and Ethiopia, Lo said Türkiye’s political, diplomatic and economic relations with both countries had been instrumental in bringing the two sides together in Ankara.
Talks that began in July 2024 under Türkiye’s facilitation culminated in the Ankara Declaration, adopted on Dec. 11, 2024, under the auspices of Erdoğan. Somalia and Ethiopia reaffirmed their respect for each other’s sovereignty, unity, independence and territorial integrity.
Commenting on the situation in West Africa and the Sahel, Lo said the region was becoming increasingly complex in terms of peace and security and that terrorism was one of the main challenges facing countries in the region.
Noting that Türkiye’s relations with countries in the region had strengthened in recent years, Lo said Ankara had developed ties not only with West African countries but also with countries belonging to the Alliance of Sahel States (AES).
Lo said Türkiye’s role in the region extended beyond diplomatic and economic relations to the security sphere, adding that some Sahel countries were benefiting from Turkish defense industry products to develop their counterterrorism capabilities.
Sudanese academic Nur said Türkiye’s peace efforts in Africa should not be assessed solely through the lens of traditional mediation activities, noting that diplomacy, development cooperation, humanitarian aid, education and institutional capacity building were also components of long-term peace.
Citing Somalia as one of the clearest examples of Türkiye’s multidimensional approach, Nur emphasized that the Ankara Process also demonstrated Türkiye’s capacity to facilitate talks directly.
“It would be more accurate to view Türkiye’s role in Africa as a facilitation model that helps parties develop their own solutions, rather than producing a solution on behalf of one side,” Nur said.
Commenting on the ongoing war in his country, Nur said Türkiye could play a role in creating diplomatic space in Sudan, delivering humanitarian aid and supporting an inclusive political process that Sudanese parties could agree on.
Nur stressed that Türkiye’s coordinated efforts with the AU, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the U.N. and Sudan’s neighboring countries could produce more effective results, saying: “Peace should not be viewed as being limited to a cease-fire.”
Nur emphasized that restoring the functioning of state institutions, universities, and education and health infrastructure in Sudan after the war would be important for sustainable peace.
Nur said Türkiye could increase its coordination with Africa’s own peace mechanisms, adding that post-conflict reconstruction and human resource development were also among the areas in which Türkiye could contribute to peace processes on the continent in the coming period.

====================================================================================================

Spain and Türkiye: Five centuries of evolving ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:13:24 UTC
20:13:24 KST

For centuries, Turks and Spaniards imagined each other, long before they ever truly met.
In 16th- and 17th-century Spain, "the Turk" appeared in paintings, plays, festivals, sermons, and battle accounts. The Ottoman Empire was then one of the great powers of the Mediterranean and also one of the main rivals of the Spanish monarchy.
Across the sea, however, Spain generally occupied a less constant place in Ottoman concerns.
This contradiction (imagining the other a lot and knowing little about them) was a recurring theme at a congress held in Istanbul to commemorate the Spanish-Ottoman Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1782.
For two days, Spanish and Turkish historians reconstructed a relationship more complex and nuanced than the simple story of rivalry, peace, and subsequent reconciliation.
Because Spain and Türkiye have been meeting for five centuries. What has changed is the way they do it.
From its earliest centuries, the Ottoman Empire held a prominent place in the Spanish imagination.
Both powers vied for control of the Mediterranean Sea; corsairs linked to the Ottoman regencies in North Africa, such as Algiers and Tunis, raided the Iberian coasts, and thousands of people directly experienced war or captivity.
The Battle of Lepanto in 1571, a historic naval confrontation in which the prominent writer Miguel de Cervantes , author of Don Quixote, participated, left an indelible mark on the geopolitics of the time and ended up becoming the great symbol of that rivalry.
But in those times, “the Turk” was much more than a military adversary. He appeared in plays, romances, celebrations, and paintings.
A project led by art historian Ivan Rega Castro on the construction of the Turkish imaginary analyses precisely how these representations adapted to the needs of each era.
In Hispanic painting of the 16th and 17th centuries, his presence was relatively discreet but constant, extending even to the monarchy's American territories.
Over time, moreover, the Turk became a recognisable image of the “enemy”: he could appear as a defeated captive, a fearsome warrior, or even as a ridiculed figure, and was even used anachronistically to represent conflicts that occurred centuries before the Ottoman expansion.
The problem is that those images could be much more intense than the actual knowledge of the other person.
Even enemies negotiated
The image of the Turk as a great Mediterranean adversary did not prevent Spaniards and Ottomans from talking to each other when necessary.
By the end of the 16th century, after decades of conflict, both empires began to seek ways to reduce a rivalry that was becoming increasingly costly.
No permanent embassies existed between Madrid and Istanbul, but emissaries, intermediaries, merchants, and agents carried messages between the courts.
Diplomatic contacts, secret negotiations, and even projects aimed at achieving a more lasting peace existed.
During the Istanbul congress, historian and expert on the early modern Ottoman period Evrim Turkcelik succinctly summarised the situation with the phrase: “Negotiating without normalisation”.
This helps us understand a reality often lost when history is reduced to the Battle of Lepanto and the Mediterranean Wars. Spain and the Ottoman Empire could be at war at one time and, at the same time, maintain open channels of communication.
Furthermore, the Mediterranean in the 16th and 17th centuries was not divided into two completely isolated worlds.
Goods and news circulated through its ports, but so did freed captives, converts to Islam, interpreters, merchants, and religious figures.
The border separated, but it also connected.
This coexistence of rivalry and diplomatic interaction also explains why the treaty signed in 1782 did not emerge from nothing.
Rather, it was the decisive step from occasional diplomacy, dependent on intermediaries and specific circumstances, to a much more stable relationship.
The big change came at the end of the 18th century, when the period marked by the Battle of Lepanto and the great naval and military rivalry was behind us, and both powers had new priorities.
Spain was looking more and more towards the Atlantic and America, while the Ottoman Empire had to face, among other challenges, the advance of the Russian Empire towards the Black Sea and southeastern Europe.
In 1782, they signed a Treaty of Peace, Friendship, and Commerce in Istanbul, ratified the following year. Rather than ushering in a sudden friendship, the agreement transformed the former adversary into a stable partner.
As historian Elsa Medina Iglesias summarised during the congress, it was the convergence of “two reasons of state”.
From then on, the relationship no longer relied solely on occasional envoys and paved the way for more regular legations, consulates, and commercial contacts.
From political to cultural rapprochement
The next major change came in the 20th century. After the collapse of the Ottoman Empire, the Republic of Türkiye was proclaimed in 1923 under the leadership of Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, and just a year later, Spain signed a Treaty of Friendship with the new state.
A prime example of that era was Yahya Kemal Beyatli, one of the great Turkish poets of the 20th century and author of Dance in Andalusia, who arrived in Madrid in 1929 as a diplomat and the first plenipotentiary minister of the new Republic in Spain.
He perfectly encapsulates how culture and diplomacy were beginning to intertwine in a relationship very different from that of previous centuries.
For decades, however, the relationship remained relatively discreet. A genuine rapprochement began to become more visible in the 1980s and 90s.
Spain had emerged from a 40-year dictatorship and joined NATO and the then European Economic Community.
Meanwhile, Türkiye, a member of the transatlantic alliance since 1952, was also strengthening its ties with Europe. Official visits became more frequent, and both governments began to maintain a more regular political relationship.
One of the clearest symbols of this new era was the Alliance of Civilisations.
Proposed in 2004 by the then Spanish prime minister, Jose Luis Rodriguez Zapatero (2004-2011), and co-sponsored by Türkiye under the government of Recep Tayyip Erdogan, the initiative stemmed from a simple idea: in an increasingly interdependent world, the security, development, and prosperity of some societies could not be understood in isolation from others.
Based on this premise, it sought to generate a common political will to combat prejudice, misperceptions, and polarisation, especially between Western and Muslim societies.
The United Nations formally incorporated it in 2005.
It is difficult to find an image further removed from Lepanto: Spain and Türkiye presenting themselves together, not as representatives of civilisations destined to clash, but as promoters of dialogue between them.
Today, the relationship between Spain and Türkiye is no longer built solely on governments and embassies.
It is an increasingly broad and diverse relationship, encompassing businesses, universities, tourists, students, and books, and it promises to continue deepening as exchanges between the two societies grow.
In 2025, trade between the two countries exceeded $20.5 billion, a record figure.
That same year, more than 452,000 Spaniards travelled to Türkiye. Istanbul, Cappadocia, and the Aegean coast are now increasingly popular tourist destinations for Spaniards.
Contact between the two countries is thus beginning to extend beyond diplomatic summits.
Cultural ties have also strengthened. The Cervantes Institute has operated in Istanbul since 2001, and the Yunus Emre Institute has had a branch in Madrid since 2018.
Both serve as spaces to promote their respective languages and cultures through courses, cultural activities, and meetings that bring the two societies closer beyond official relations.
Added to this is a growing circulation of books and ideas: Turkish authors such as Orhan Pamuk , Zulfu Livaneli , and Ahmet Hamdi Tanpinar can now be read in Spanish, bringing themes such as Istanbul, memory, modernisation, and the tensions between tradition and change closer to Spanish-speaking audiences.
At the same time, Spanish works continue to find new readers in Turkish.
History has not simply been a leap from enmity to friendship. The process was more complex and gradual: Spaniards and Ottoman Turks first imagined each other, then learned to negotiate, later built permanent relationships, and finally began to get to know each other more directly.
The Mediterranean Sea, which separated the worlds of Philip II in the 16th century and the Ottoman sultans, remains in the same place. The distance between its two shores, however, seems to be shrinking.

WASHINGTON – CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued President Donald Trump and other members of his administration on Sept 21 for banning them from White House grounds, saying the action violated their rights to free speech and a free press under the US Constitution’s First Amendment.
The news outlets are seeking a temporary restraining order to block Trump’s action in federal court in Washington DC, with a hearing scheduled for Sept 23.
“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the lawsuit stated.
“Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference,” the outlets wrote in a joint statement.
“The government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.”
Trump announced the ban on Sept 18 on social media, saying the outlets “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States,” and defended it in another post on Sept 21.
“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” Trump wrote on Sept 21, without providing evidence of a national security threat.
Past presidents have battled with the press, but Trump’s campaign against the media has been unprecedented.
He has upended decades of tradition by denying basic access to many major news organisations, launching personal attacks on journalists for their reporting and elevating media outlets seen as more sympathetic to the administration. He also has filed lawsuits against multiple news outlets.
The White House launched a “Trump TV” stream on the evening of Sept 21, days after Trump banned the media outlets from the White House.
The White House said the stream will run videos and highlights of what it calls the Trump administration’s achievements but a press freedom advocate said it amounted to “a steady diet of government propaganda”.
A 60-second trailer displayed the Republican leader’s 2024 presidential win and the first video streamed after the platform went live was Trump’s remarks on July 3 at Mount Rushmore. The stream had only about 8,000 live views 15 minutes after it was launched on YouTube.
“This just makes it even clearer that the real goal here is to ensure that the American public is fed a steady diet of government propaganda,” Jameel Jaffer, executive director of the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, said.
White House television pool
CNN is one of the five news organisations – along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC – that make up the primary White House television pool. They share the costs of covering the president, take turns organising coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.
CNN had been scheduled to cover Trump’s trip to New York for the United Nations General Assembly on Sept 21, but was not able to provide a pool feed.
In response, the other major TV networks suspended presidential pool coverage. This effectively eliminated the most widespread video source for White House events just as Trump is set to meet with numerous world leaders on the sidelines of the General Assembly and host Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington later in the week.
“This is to advise that, effective today (Monday), the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage of the President,” Bryan Boughton, who runs the Fox News Washington bureau and is the current TV pool chair, said in an email on Sept 21. “There will be no replacement pool put in place.”
Otherwise, it was business as usual in the White House press room on Sept 21 as reporters planned for the day’s events, including an afternoon ribbon-cutting ceremony for the Republican president’s new Marine One helipad on the South Lawn.
The audio on the White House’s own live stream of the ceremony, which it promoted as an alternative to the pool feed, was inaudible.

Trump has been “very unhappy” with coverage of the midterm elections, the source added, and his frustration intensified after last week’s Supreme Court ruling that blocked his attempt to limit mail-in voting.

- The conflict threatens global oil supplies by risking closure of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait; Saudi Arabia reroutes oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, raising fuel prices worldwide.
AI generated
DUBAI – Houthi fighters were pushing to seize strategic heights in Yemen on Sept 21 to cut off the Red Sea coast from remaining areas held by Saudi-backed forces, after a report that US President Donald Trump had called off US strikes on the group at the last minute.
A lightning advance by the Iran-backed group in September has extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theatre and further threatened global energy supplies.
Washington has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to join the fight in Yemen. The Houthis said on Sept 19 that they had fired on Riyadh, where loud booms were followed by columns of smoke visible near the airport.
Saudi Arabia has not commented on the first apparent strikes on the capital since the escalation began.
The New York Times reported that the Trump administration had prepared on Sept 20 to launch air strikes against the Houthis after fresh pleas from the Saudi Crown Prince. But the newspaper said Trump called off the air strikes at the last minute, even as troops were loading bombs onto aircraft.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report and the US military’s Central Command did not respond to an e-mail seeking comment.
Fighting in highlands
The Houthis, who have controlled Yemen’s capital since 2014, seized the country’s Red Sea coast in September in a lightning advance that routed forces of an internationally recognised Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia and based in the south.
Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on the fighters’ positions in the highlands, according to the Houthis. But the air power advantage has so far done little to slow the advance of the fighters as Saudi-backed government forces have melted away.
According to the United Nations, nearly 700 people have been killed and thousands injured in the flare-up in fighting. More than 120,000 Yemenis have fled homes within Yemen, and thousands more have fled by boat across the Red Sea to Africa.
Five Yemeni military sources told Reuters the Houthis were now seeking to seize strategic heights, known as the Kahboub Mountains, in two provinces, Taiz and Lahij, which separate the Red Sea coast from the government-held south.
Fighting has centred on the outskirts of the remote mountain Al-Wazi’iyah district in Taiz province, and Ras al-Ara along the Indian Ocean coast between the mouth of the Red Sea that the fighters captured last week and the government’s base in Aden.
The Houthis aim to secure an area around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait leading into the Red Sea by taking control of the heights, which would allow them to open new fronts, according to the sources. That would help protect exposed positions the Houthis captured during their advance around Dhubab on the Red Sea and on Perim Island in the strait.
Saudi oil exports
The surge in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis creates a new dilemma for Trump, under pressure to help defend Washington’s close Saudi allies but anxious not to further expand the deeply unpopular war he launched in February against Iran.
The United States bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire with the group and has kept out of the conflict since.
The Houthis’ newfound control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait risks cutting off the main alternative route that Saudi Arabia has used for oil exports that bypass disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia has responded by increasing shipments through Hormuz, where a small number of tankers are increasingly shuttling back and forth to bring out oil with their transponders off, charging record fees of as much as a quarter of the value of the cargo to brave the wartime risk. They then transfer the oil to other ships in the Indian Ocean, bound for customers in Asia or elsewhere.
Satellite data shows Saudi exports through Hormuz reaching 2.9 million barrels per day in recent days, up from just 700,000 in August, partially making up for a halt in Saudi loadings at its Red Sea port of Yanbu.
That has helped put a cap on the global price of crude oil, which has retreated closer to US$100 a barrel after approaching US$110 last week. But consumers and industry are still paying record prices for refined fuels.
The US retail price of diesel, politically sensitive for Trump with midterm elections in six weeks, hit another all-time high on Sept 21 above US$6.51 a gallon. It was around US$3.75 before Trump launched the war alongside Israel in February.
In the latest reported attack in Hormuz, Britain’s UKMTO maritime security agency said a ship sailing into the strait had been hit with a projectile, causing minor injuries to crew.
Diplomacy in the wider conflict has largely been stalled since a June interim agreement between the United States and Iran collapsed within weeks. Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian is due to fly on Sept 22 to New York to attend the UN General Assembly, the first such visit since Trump launched Operation Epic Fury against his country alongside Israel in February. Returning from unauthorized absence under the new rules: where to apply and what awaits the servicemember
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
14:02:41 EEST
20:02:41 KST

Returning from unauthorized absence under the new rules: where to apply and what awaits the servicemember
Kyiv • UNN
After September 20, returning from unauthorized absence is handled through the Military Law and Order Service or a reserve battalion. The procedure takes longer, and a unit is not always chosen.
After September 20, service members who have gone absent without leave may voluntarily return to service under the general procedure. This was reported by UNN, citing the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
To do so, they must contact the Military Law and Order Service or report to a reserve battalion. At the same time, the procedure will now take longer, and it will not always be possible to independently choose a military unit in which to continue serving.
Details
As explained by the ministry, through September 20, 2026, inclusive, a simplified return procedure was in effect for service members whose unauthorized absence from their unit had been recorded before June 12. After the end of this program, voluntary return after going absent without leave is carried out under the general procedure through the Military Law and Order Service, reserve battalions, and other mechanisms provided for by law.
The Ministry of Defense noted that this means a longer return process, a longer wait for the restoration of monetary allowances, as well as the inability to independently determine the military unit for further service.
A service member who has decided to return may contact the Central Directorate of the Military Law and Order Service in Kyiv and the Kyiv region, territorial directorates, or regional departments of the Military Law and Order Service. At the Military Law and Order Service unit, the service member will be provided with information about the reserve battalions to which they may report to continue their service and, if necessary, will be issued an appropriate directive. At the same time, a service member may independently report to one of the reserve battalions; a list of them can be obtained from the Military Law and Order Service.
After the service member arrives, the commander of the reserve battalion must, within three days, issue an order adding them to the list of temporarily arrived personnel and assign them tasks. In addition, law enforcement agencies will check whether information about the service member’s unauthorized absence has been entered into the Unified Register of Pretrial Investigations. The reserve battalion also notifies the unit that the service member left without authorization of their arrival.
If the service member has the written consent of the commander of a combat unit designated as a priority unit for staffing, this will be taken into account when determining their subsequent assignment.
The Ministry of Defense clarified that reserve battalion commanders may also take into account letters of recommendation from combat brigades that need personnel reinforcements. At the same time, letters of recommendation from support units are not taken into account.
The ministry separately reminded service members of the possibility of exemption from criminal liability. This may apply to a service member who went absent without leave for the first time during martial law.
To do so, the service member must submit a report and obtain the written consent of the commander of the military unit or reserve battalion to continue military service. It is also necessary to contact an investigator, prosecutor, or court with a motion expressing the intention to return to service. After that, the materials concerning the service member’s exemption from criminal liability are submitted to the court. The final decision is made by the court.
Let us remind you
Earlier, UNN reported that returning after going absent without leave does not mean automatic reinstatement in service.

Couples searching for a third partner report stronger bonds but often ignore the newcomer’s desires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:00:21 UTC
20:00:21 KST

Couples who search for a third person to join their sexual or romantic relationships frequently focus on their own pleasure while minimizing the desires of the person they pursue. A recent qualitative analysis of people in these relationships also reveals that the search process itself often strengthens the existing couples’ bonds and communication. The findings were published in the journal Psychology & Sexuality.
In consensual non-monogamy, partners agree to have romantic or sexual encounters with other people. One increasingly visible practice involves established couples seeking a third person to join them. This third person is colloquially known as a unicorn because they are perceived as rare and highly sought after. The practice is often associated with a man and a woman looking for a bisexual woman to join them.
Polyamorous communities sometimes criticize couples who search for a third person. Critics argue these couples often prioritize their own needs and protect their established relationship hierarchy. This framework can treat the newcomer as an accessory to be used and discarded.
Engaging with a third person can provide a positive experience for everyone involved and can challenge traditional relationship norms. Direct research on couples seeking a third person has remained sparse. To better understand this dynamic, researchers led by Alena Bondarchuk-Mclaughlin at La Trobe University in Melbourne, Australia, set out to explore the perspectives of the people conducting the search.
The researchers recruited 80 participants through social media and an online survey platform. All respondents indicated they were currently or had previously been part of a couple looking for a third person. Participants answered five open-ended survey questions about who they wanted to join them, what their goals were, and how the search had affected their primary relationship.
The research team analyzed the text responses using a qualitative method. They looked for recurring patterns and grouped the answers into four main categories. These categories covered the desired characteristics of the third person, the effects on the couple, the ideal relationship dynamics, and the reality of their actual encounters.
When describing who they wanted to join them, most participants specifically sought a woman. The majority of these requests specified a bisexual woman. The desires were more varied than the typical stereotype suggests, as nearly a quarter of respondents said gender was irrelevant. Others looked for men, other couples, or specific personality traits like friendliness.
Couples overwhelmingly described the search process as having a positive impact on their relationships. Nearly 80 percent of participants reported that looking for a third person brought them closer together. They noted improvements in communication, honesty, and trust. Discussing fantasies and boundaries openly often heightened their sexual experiences as a couple.
A small minority reported that the search had a negative effect on their primary relationship. In these cases, participants noted that initiating the search coincided with disagreements, pressure, or a breach of trust. Some participants also described struggling with feelings of jealousy when confronting traditional relationship expectations.
The researchers found a major gap between the type of relationship couples wanted and what they actually experienced. A majority of participants desired a predominantly sexual relationship with the third person. They wanted to fulfill specific fantasies, experience novelty, or enhance their own shared pleasure. Many explicitly stated they wanted minimal romantic involvement.
In contrast, about 40 percent wanted an emotional connection, ranging from friendship to a loving, cohabitating relationship. Yet some responses revealed an expectation that the third person would serve mainly to fix a void or provide a service. These participants often specified that the newcomer must respect the existing couple’s priority and not disrupt their bond.
Only a small fraction of the participants mentioned the third person’s own desires or sexual pleasure as an important part of the ideal scenario. When describing their actual relationships with a third person, many couples maintained purely sexual boundaries, often sticking to one-night stands. About a quarter managed to form ongoing social or romantic relationships.
Expressions of care for the third person were rare in the actual relationship descriptions. Only 12 percent of responses mentioned prioritizing the newcomer’s feelings or treating them as an equal. The researchers noted that many couples entered the search focused heavily on their own personal gain.
Couples also frequently reported struggling to find a willing third person. Almost half of the participants described difficulties in their search. Many could not find the right match, faced a scarcity of interested people, or encountered mismatched expectations.
The researchers suggested this lack of success might stem from the couples’ failure to consider the third person’s interests. Treating the search like a request for a specialized service rather than the formation of a new interpersonal connection can easily lead to disappointment for all parties. The authors suggest that couples should express genuine care for the person they seek.
The study relies on self-reported data from a sample of 80 individuals, rather than interviewing both members of the couple. The researchers only surveyed the people doing the searching, leaving out the perspectives of the individuals being pursued. Future research will need to examine the experiences of the third person to provide a complete picture of these relationship dynamics.
The survey prompts may have influenced how participants answered the questions. For instance, the question asking who they wanted to join them included “bisexual woman” as an example, which might have prompted respondents to use that exact phrase. The survey also did not ask about the gender of the participants’ partners, which limits the ability to analyze how the gender makeup of the original couple shapes the search process.
The study, “Searching for a third: couples’ experiences of unicorn pursuit, desire, and ethical tensions,” was authored by Alena Bondarchuk-Mclaughlin, Nat Amos, and Joel R. Anderson.

Ukrainian Hackers Raid Russia’s Naval Files, Walk Away With Secrets From 70 Projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:00:10 UTC
20:00:10 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukrainian Hackers Raid Russia’s Naval Files, Walk Away With Secrets From 70 Projects
Ukrainian hackers gained access to a large collection of Russian naval files, obtaining technical documentation linked to 70 projects involving submarines, warships, navigation systems, sonar technology, and autonomous underwater vehicles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The cyber operation, dubbed “Poseidon,” was carried out by Ukrainian Militant, the group said on September 20. According to the hackers, the compromised data covers Russian naval research, engineering, testing, and operational documentation, including files marked “secret” and “top secret.”
The materials reportedly contain information on nuclear-powered and diesel-electric submarines, frigates, corvettes, landing ships, and vessels designed for Arctic operations.
Among them are Project 949AM Antey nuclear-powered submarines and Project 636.3 Varshavyanka diesel-electric submarines, as well as ships belonging to Projects 22350, 20386, 23550, 11711, 23770, and 23900.
For some of these projects, Ukrainian Militant said the files reveal details of navigation equipment and modernization, onboard hardware placement, cable connections, information interfaces, and testing results.
The archive also reportedly includes technical requirements, operating manuals, structural and functional diagrams, algorithms, accuracy and reliability specifications, testing procedures, and acceptance documents.
Beyond individual ships and submarines, the breach reportedly covers a broader range of Russian naval technologies, including ship and underwater navigation, integrated control systems, sonar, radio navigation, inertial navigation systems, digital hydrography and mapping, and marine robotics.
Some of the documented research concerns autonomous navigation for submarines and underwater vehicles using terrain and geophysical fields, technologies intended to allow them to determine their position without relying solely on satellite navigation.
Ukrainian Militant also identified a series of systems and development programs in the obtained files, including Simfoniya, Chardash, KAMA-NS-VK, Sprut-N1, Priliv, 14Ts217, AKNG/PNG-23820, and ISU NK-23550.
The group said the archive contains materials associated with major Russian organizations involved in naval and underwater technology, including the Rubin and Malachite submarine design bureaus, the Elektropribor research institute, Okeanpribor, Elara, the Vega concern, and Russia’s State Research Navigation and Hydrographic Institute.
According to Ukrainian Militant, the documents also provide information on cooperation between contractors, research and development stages, testing, and the status of individual programs.
In total, the hackers said the obtained files concern Russian scientific and technical work supporting 70 ship, vessel, and submarine projects currently under construction or modernization. The full scope and authenticity of the archive have not been independently verified.
The naval breach follows other major leaks involving Russia’s defense industry. In November 2025, Ukrainian-linked hackers obtained classified documents related to Russia’s PAK DA strategic bomber and Su-57 fighter, exposing technical details of key aircraft components and the programs’ reliance on foreign manufacturing equipment.

Russia’s Molniya Attack Drone Shows Up in Africa—and Gets Shot Down in Mali
A Russian-made Molniya attack drone was reportedly brought down near the town of Dioura in central Mali, where Russian Africa Corps personnel and Malian forces have been conducting operations against the al-Qaeda-linked JNIM militant group.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Sahel-focused outlet Alerte Sahel on September 21, footage from the area showed the wreckage of what appears to be a Russian Molniya-type fixed-wing drone following its crash near Dioura in Mali’s Mopti region.
Alerte Sahel reported that Russian Africa Corps personnel had used the drone against positions held by Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) before withdrawing from the area. The outlet claimed the aircraft was subsequently shot down.
The available footage shows a damaged fixed-wing drone with a long fuselage and straight wings consistent with the design of Russia’s Molniya UAV. However, the video only shows the aircraft after it came down and does not establish what caused the crash or independently confirm that it was shot down.
The Molniya is a relatively simple Russian fixed-wing attack drone designed to carry an explosive payload. The aircraft has a reported operating range of roughly 30 to 40 kilometers and can carry a warhead weighing up to seven kilograms. Variants of the platform have also been used for reconnaissance and artillery fire adjustment.
The reported loss comes amid continuing fighting around Dioura following a major JNIM assault on a Malian military camp there on September 10.
The Malian Armed Forces acknowledged the attack and subsequently announced air and ground operations against militants in the area. On September 19, Mali’s military said its forces, supported by partners, continued targeted strikes around the Dioura garrison and the outskirts of the town.
The scale of the September 10 attack was substantial. AFP reported on September 18, citing military, security and local sources, that at least 100 Malian soldiers and five Russian Africa Corps personnel were killed. JNIM separately claimed that it killed 150 soldiers and captured 93, figures that have not been independently verified.
Russia has expanded its military presence in Mali through the Africa Corps, which replaced the Wagner Group as Moscow’s principal security force in the country. The reported deployment of a Molniya drone near Dioura would indicate the use in Mali of another Russian unmanned system originally developed and widely fielded for combat operations in Ukraine.

Justice in action: Five lessons for Ukraine from the conviction of Kosovo’s former president
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
14:00:00 EEST
20:00:00 KST

Justice in action: Five lessons for Ukraine from the conviction of Kosovo’s former president
On 16 September 2026, a verdict was delivered in The Hague against one of the most prominent political figures in post-war Kosovo. Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaçi and three other former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) – Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi – were found guilty of war crimes committed during the 1998–1999 armed conflict.
Thaçi and Krasniqi were sentenced to 25 years' imprisonment, Veseli to 18 years and Selimi to 13 years. The Court found them criminally responsible for the unlawful or arbitrary detention of 385 people, the torture of 303, the cruel treatment of 49 and the murder of 96 people.
More than a quarter of a century passed between the crimes and this first-instance judgment. During that time, Thaçi went from being one of the KLA's leaders to Prime Minister and later President of Kosovo. Political circumstances, the international environment and institutions all changed. At the time of the war, there was no mechanism capable of providing a legal assessment of these crimes. This differs from the situation in Ukraine, where we are building such a mechanism amid the realities of an ongoing war.
This is one of the most interesting features of the case. The Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established only in 2015. Their structure combines national and international components. The Chambers were established under Kosovo's Constitution and legislation, are integrated into the different levels of its judicial system, and apply Kosovo law alongside international law. At the same time, they are based in The Hague, while their judges, prosecutors and staff are international. The Specialist Prosecutor's Office is also based in The Hague and operates independently of other Kosovo institutions.
In practice, this is a hybrid justice mechanism that combines national jurisdiction with international participation and allows particularly complex cases to be heard outside Kosovo.
In my view, such a model could also be appropriate for Ukraine. This does not, of course, mean replicating the Kosovo model. Ukraine has its own Constitution and judicial system, a significantly greater volume of proceedings concerning international crimes, and an already established system of cooperation with international institutions. At the same time, combining national jurisdiction with international expertise and participation could strengthen Ukraine's capacity to adjudicate the most complex cases while keeping such proceedings within the Ukrainian justice system.
The trajectory of the Thaçi case itself illustrates how long it can take for such an opportunity to emerge. The indictment was confirmed in 2020. Thaçi subsequently resigned as President, was taken into custody and transferred to The Hague. The trial began in April 2023. The evidentiary proceedings concluded at the end of 2025, and in February 2026 the parties presented their closing arguments. The Court heard evidence from 273 witnesses, admitted 5,467 items of evidence, and the trial transcript ran to 29,238 pages.
The indictment contained ten counts. Six concerned crimes against humanity and four concerned war crimes. The outcome of the proceedings was significant not only because of the severity of the sentences imposed.
The accused were acquitted on all counts of crimes against humanity. The Court concluded that the prosecution had failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt the existence of a widespread or systematic attack directed against a civilian population.
This is precisely why the Thaçi case is far more relevant to Ukraine than simply as the story of one former president. It shows what happens to information about a war decades later, when the political context has already changed and every allegation must withstand judicial scrutiny.
What of the material collected today will withstand such scrutiny in ten, twenty or thirty years? Is it enough to have thousands of documented incidents? Where is the line between information and evidence? How do we move from a specific crime to the responsibility of a particular commander or political leader?
The Thaçi case offers at least five lessons that Ukraine should take into account today.
Lesson One. It Is Necessary to Prove Not Only the Crime, but Also the Responsibility of a Specific Individual
International criminal justice does not put positions or titles on trial.
It is not enough to establish that a person was a commander, minister, general or political leader at the time the crimes were committed.
In the Thaçi case, the Court separately examined the role of each accused, their powers, specific actions, involvement in decision-making and contribution to the common criminal purpose. The Court examined their actual influence. This is fundamentally important for Ukrainian cases concerning Russia's military and political leadership.
A chain of command positions does not in itself establish a chain of criminal responsibility. It is necessary to determine who made decisions, who issued orders, who received reports, who had information about the consequences, what measures were taken after such information was received, and what the actual contribution of a particular individual was to the commission of the crime. This is why proving international crimes requires more than documenting a crime scene. An evidentiary link must be established between a specific incident and a specific individual.
Lesson Two. The Number of Crimes Does Not in Itself Prove the Existence of Crimes against humanity
This is perhaps one of the most important conclusions from the case for Ukrainian investigations.
The Court established that hundreds of people had been victims of murder, torture, cruel treatment and unlawful deprivation of liberty.
Yet this was insufficient to secure convictions for crimes against humanity.
The reason lies in the legal structure of this international crime. It is not enough to prove numerous individual murders, acts of torture or unlawful detentions. The contextual elements must be established separately, including the existence of a widespread or systematic attack directed against a civilian population and the connection between the specific act and that attack.
In the Thaçi case, the prosecution, in the Court's assessment, failed to meet this standard.
For Ukraine, this has direct practical significance. When documenting Russian crimes, it is not enough to accumulate individual incidents. At the same time, material must be collected that makes it possible to identify and prove the broader system: recurring patterns of conduct, their geographical and temporal dimensions, categories of victims, methods of committing crimes, patterns in target selection, command links, orders, internal documents, policies and practices, as well as the leadership's response to crimes of which it was aware.
It is possible to have thousands of well-documented incidents and still have a weak evidentiary basis for establishing the contextual elements of crimes against humanity.
Numbers matter. But arithmetic is no substitute for proof.
Lesson Three. Information Is Not Yet Evidence
Another important aspect of the case concerns information about individuals whom the KLA regarded as opponents.
The Court examined the activities of the KLA's intelligence structures and the role of Kadri Veseli. The judges found that the four accused had made substantial contributions to a common criminal purpose directed against individuals regarded as opponents of the KLA's political and military objectives. These included Kosovo Albanians affiliated with other political or military forces, individuals suspected of links to the Serbian or Yugoslav authorities, and members of national minorities.
For Ukraine, a broader principle is important here.
Intelligence, operational, military or open-source information may be extremely valuable in criminal proceedings. It may help formulate an investigative hypothesis, indicate a direction for the investigation, and assist in identifying witnesses, documents, locations or other sources of evidence.
But information and a proven fact are not the same thing.
For Ukraine, which is currently accumulating a vast body of information about the war, including operational, digital and intelligence data, not least through the work of the newly established Directorate for Documentation of Violations of the Law of Armed Conflict Committed during Hostilities within the Military Law Enforcement Service of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the question of verification has very practical significance. Such information must be cross-checked against other sources, its provenance and authenticity established, and only then can its evidentiary value be assessed.
Lesson Four. The Legality of War and the Rules Governing Its Conduct Are Assessed Separately
The proceedings in The Hague were not an assessment of the political objectives of the Kosovo Liberation Army or of the idea of Kosovo's independence itself. The Court considered a different question: whether specific individuals bore individual criminal responsibility for specific acts committed during the armed conflict.
This legal distinction is also important for Ukraine. Ukraine is defending itself against Russian aggression, exercising its inherent right of self-defence under the UN Charter. At the same time, international law separately regulates the legality of a state's resort to force and the rules governing the conduct of hostilities.
Accordingly, the legal assessment of a specific incident during the war concerns compliance with international humanitarian law. It neither changes nor calls into question Ukraine's legal status as a state exercising self-defence against armed aggression.
This is why credible information about possible violations by the Ukrainian side must also receive proper legal assessment. This in no way equates the aggressor with the state defending itself. These are different questions of international law and involve different matters to be proved.
Moreover, a state's ability to examine the conduct of its own military personnel and, where sufficient evidence exists, ensure accountability demonstrates the capacity and resilience of its legal system. For Ukraine, this also has very practical significance. Proper domestic investigations allow the state itself to establish the facts, distinguish substantiated violations from unsubstantiated allegations, and examine its own mistakes in order to prevent their recurrence.
This is also important at the international level. Genuine and good-faith criminal proceedings at the national level are relevant to the principle of complementarity on which the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court is based. At the same time, it protects the state from situations in which third countries initiate investigations under the principle of universal jurisdiction.
There is another aspect that is particularly important in the context of information warfare. If the state itself does not establish what happened in a particular incident, the resulting vacuum is filled by unverified reports and manipulation, which the Russian authorities use to construct their own narrative. A professional investigation helps prevent this.
Legal assessment of possible violations by one's own side therefore demonstrates the ability of the legal system to function even under the most difficult conditions of war, to establish facts regardless of whom they concern, to learn from its own mistakes, and to ensure accountability where evidence exists.
Lesson Five. Evidence Must Outlast the War
More than a quarter of a century passed between the events at issue in the Thaçi case and the first-instance judgment.
But these were not 27 years of a single trial. The trial itself began only in 2023. Before that came years of accumulating information, international investigations, establishing a specialised mechanism, setting up the prosecution office, working with witnesses and preparing the case. The Specialist Chambers were established only in 2015, many years after the events they are now adjudicating.
In 1998, no one could have known that Hashim Thaçi would become Prime Minister, then President of Kosovo, and that two decades later he would leave office and appear before a court that did not even exist at the time of the events.
Likewise, today we do not know what the political circumstances will be in ten or twenty years, or when particular individuals suspected of crimes against Ukraine may actually appear before a court.
But there are things Ukraine can influence now. Will the evidence be preserved? Will it be possible, twenty years from now, to establish its provenance? Will it be clear who obtained a particular digital file or physical object, when and where it was obtained, and under what circumstances? Will the chain of custody be preserved? Will it be possible to reconstruct command relationships and decision-making processes?
The Thaçi case therefore does not provide grounds for mechanically transplanting the Kosovo experience to Ukraine. The conflict is different, the scale is different, the jurisdictional framework is different, and the factual circumstances are different.
But it demonstrates something universal. Political circumstances change far more quickly than the question of individual criminal responsibility disappears. In ten, twenty or thirty years, governments, international relations, official positions and individuals' status may all have changed. A judicial mechanism that does not yet exist today may emerge. New legal avenues for holding particular individuals accountable may become available.
For Ukraine, therefore, the central question today is not only when and where future trials will take place. More important is what we will bring to those trials. Will we have evidence of individual crimes and of their broader context?
The political window for justice may open years from now. More than a quarter of a century passed between the crimes for which Hashim Thaçi and the other KLA leaders were convicted and the first-instance judgment. During that time, political circumstances, individuals' status and institutions changed.
The question of individual responsibility did not disappear.
For Ukraine, this may be the central lesson of the case. Justice may come decades later, but the case that it will one day adjudicate begins today.

Gaza students return to in-person schooling for first time in three years
- Hundreds of thousands of Gaza children returned to in-person schooling after nearly three years, mostly in damaged or makeshift buildings with limited supplies.
- About 660,000 students missed regular education due to war damage; UNICEF reports 98% of schools were destroyed or damaged.
- Despite hardships, including unaffordable supplies and unsafe conditions, Gaza's education officials and organisations opened temporary schools to continue learning.
AI generated
CAIRO/GAZA – Hundreds of thousands of children in Gaza returned to in-person teaching on Sept 19 for the first time in nearly three years, albeit in damaged or makeshift school buildings and tents, and with uniforms, notebooks and pens unaffordable for many families.
The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) says 98 per cent of schools in Gaza were either destroyed or damaged during the war, and Gaza education officials say about 660,000 students have been deprived of in-person learning and regular participation in education.
The reopening is a fragile milestone for Gaza after a conflict that has killed around 22,000 students and more than 770 education workers, including 532 teachers, according to Ibrahim Ramadan, director of education for East Khan Younis.
“The last time I have been to school was three years ago. Now, we are starting the school year, it is year of joy, happiness and success,” said Moayed Abu Mustafa in Khan Younis.
Mustafa said he was determined to learn even though he will sit on the floor in a tent lacking ventilation, he has no decent shoes, nor a notebook and pen, and lost friends during the war.
“Despite all of this we will learn, we will learn even in a tent.”
Fifteen-year-old displaced student Samar Abu Salmi, who lives with her family in a tent, is also returning to class.
“We studied on phones and we haven’t seen our teachers... now, we are back pursuing our dream... from one tent to another,” she said, speaking in the yard of her new makeshift school.
She also lacks much of the essential equipment, which has become unaffordable for her family.
“Before the war, everything was available for us – notebooks, pens, goods, clothes, outings, things that we could get cheaply,” Salmi said.
Mattresses and a blackboard
Despite the devastation in the enclave, the Ministry of Education, backed by international and local organisations, has moved ahead with the 2026-27 academic year, establishing dozens of temporary schools made of tents, tarpaulins, sheet metal and wood to accommodate pupils.
Some are built on sandy ground, others have classrooms with only some mattresses and a blackboard, into which students cram. Others are still housing dozens of displaced families.
Attending another school was 14-year-old Yamen Abu Samra.
“We used to wake up happy to go to school... Now, when we come to school, we’re afraid of stray bullets, rockets, strikes, everything,” he said.
“Now, I’m sitting in a tent that has absolutely nothing, just the sun and the heat,” he added.
At least 540,000 students are expected to attend in-person classes in 2026 in makeshift private schools, temporary learning centres and educational points, with UNICEF support, according to education officials. Online learning will continue for those who can’t attend classes or who left Gaza during the war.
Israeli forces remain in control of more than 60 per cent of Gaza despite the 2025 ceasefire, which halted major fighting but failed to end the conflict.
The Palestinian authorities say more than 73,000 people have been killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel in October 2023.
Stationery trader Khaled Aliyan, 30, said Israeli import restrictions have reduced supplies and hiked prices.
“This notebook, which used to cost 3 shekels (S$1.20), now costs 15 (shekels). All stationery items are expensive,” he said.
Israel’s COGAT military agency, which controls access to Gaza, did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on restrictions on supplies and strikes on schools. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of using schools for military purposes, which Hamas denies. REUTERS

The European Union announced new sanctions against russia following the "elections" to the Russian State Duma, including in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. UNN writes about this, citing a statement by the EU High Representative on behalf of the European Union dated September 21.
Details
"The elections to the State Duma held in russia on September 18–20 highlighted the ongoing and deepening erosion of democracy in russia, which is taking place amid an increasingly authoritarian political environment. The absence of any level playing field was further exacerbated by russia’s illegal war against Ukraine and the continued illegal occupation of Ukrainian territories," the EU statement said.
The statement noted that "the Russian authorities continue to intensify systematic and institutionalized domestic and transnational repression in order to exclude any democratic opposition forces from the possibility of challenging the status quo." "In the period preceding the elections, independent analysts and observers had already reported significant abuse of administrative and judicial resources aimed at eliminating everyone who opposes russia’s illegal war of aggression, depriving Russian voters of a genuine choice regarding the future of their country, and severely restricting Russians’ access to independent information," the statement said, mentioning the exclusion of candidates from the Yabloko party from participating in the elections under the federal list.
The bloc also noted that the EU regretted the decision of the Russian Federation not to invite OSCE observers to these elections.
Regarding the russian "elections" in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine
"Furthermore, the European Union unequivocally condemns the illegal organization by the Russian Federation of so-called "elections" in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, namely in the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol, as well as in parts of the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. These so-called "elections" constitute yet another blatant violation by russia of international law, including the UN Charter, as well as of Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity," the statement said.
The European Union calls on russia to respect Ukraine’s internationally recognized borders and sovereignty. The European Union reiterates that it does not recognize and will never recognize either the holding of these so-called "elections" in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine or their results. Those involved in organizing these sham elections or nominating candidates in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, as well as those responsible for undermining the possibility of holding free and fair elections in russia, will be subject to sanctions
The European Union reiterated its unwavering support for Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders. "russia must end its illegal war of aggression against Ukraine, agree to a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire, and immediately, fully and unconditionally withdraw its military forces and equipment from the entire territory of Ukraine," the statement stressed.
