Speaking in Lublin on Saturday, Kierwiński said that the region now has almost 350 automatic sirens, compared to just 30 at the start of 2024. The number is expected to triple to over 1,000 by the end of this year.
“Jet-powered drones and missiles are increasingly flying near the Polish border” and Poland is therefore “turning to tools designed to counter the associated threats,” Kierwiński said, quoted by news website OKO Press, adding that the government had to build Poland’s civil protection system “almost from scratch”.
As part of these efforts, Poland’s fire service, working with the Lublin governor, is now rolling out a project to identify and mark the province’s nearly 3,500 shelters. Residents in areas close to the Ukrainian border have heard warning sirens during Russian attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks and received alerts through the state warning system.
The opposition has criticised the alerts for not giving residents clear instructions on what to do when the sirens sound. In response, the ministry has stepped up its public information campaign, including a television and social media campaign on emergency preparedness.
Additionally, more than 500 fire stations in the eastern Lublin and Subcarpathian provinces held training over the weekend on how to respond to emergency alerts. The sessions were part of a wider campaign that has already involved 630,000 people across Poland.
Poland’s interior ministry has launched a TV campaign, including spots on public broadcaster TVP’s flagship morning show, aimed at educating the public about how to respond to emergency situations such as natural disasters and security threats https://t.co/MS0APufAmq
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2026
Poland has stepped up preparations along its eastern border following a series of Russian attacks in western Ukraine, including a drone strike on a passenger train travelling from Kyiv to Warsaw about 2 km from the Polish border.
The recent escalation follows a number of incidents in recent years involving violations of Polish airspace, including the entry of around 20 Russian drones on one night last year, as well as the explosion of a Russian missile in a field in eastern Poland earlier this year.
Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski described the attacks in the border area as “another escalation” by Russia, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia’s further plans could include attacks designed to test NATO’s response.
During his visit to Ukraine last week, Tusk announced that Poland had joined the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, a group of European countries working together to develop an integrated air defence system for the continent.

Google Fined €403 Million in Ireland for Tracking Users’ Geolocation
Kyiv • UNN
Ireland’s regulator found that Google secretly collected and stored users’ geolocation data for a long time. The company was given six months to make changes.
Google has received a €403 million fine from the Irish regulator over the covert collection and prolonged retention of users’ location data. The tech giant was ordered to bring its policies into compliance with European regulations within six months. This was reported by RTE, writes UNN.
Details
Ireland’s Data Protection Commission said its investigation into Google had uncovered violations in this matter. This means that people may not have known that their location was being used, for example, to show them advertisements or determine their interests, and may have lost control over their personal data.
Retaining users’ location data for longer than necessary exacerbated this loss of control. Location data is a type of personal data processed by tracking geolocation, and it includes data collected or processed by Google from which a person’s location can be determined, either on its own or in combination with other information
The DPC said that geolocation data can bring both benefits and harm to people.
They can significantly improve the convenience of online services, but they can also reveal a considerable amount of information about an individual, including information that is strictly private
The DPC began its investigation in February 2020 after receiving complaints from several European consumer protection organisations concerning Google’s processing of location data in connection with certain services and products.
The decision, adopted by Data Protection Commissioners Dr Des Hogan, Dale Sunderland and Niamh Sweeney, stated that Google had violated the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
The DPC imposed fines totalling €403 million and ordered Google to bring its data-processing activities into compliance with the requirements within six months.
In its statement, Google said that the case concerned an outdated policy that had since been updated.

what does a guitar sound like in stone? bebeau builds one from 18 pieces of slate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:50:01 UTC
19:50:01 KST

what happens when an acoustic guitar trades wood for stone?
An acoustic guitar usually depends on a thin wooden body to turn the vibration of its strings into a larger movement of air. BeBeau Builds starts with a more stubborn material. For his latest experiment, the maker replaces the familiar timber shell with a faceted body assembled from 18 pieces of slate, producing a guitar that weighs 48.7 pounds and still functions as an acoustic instrument.
The idea begins with sound. Struck on its own, the thick slate gives off a long metallic ring, enough to suggest that the stone could resonate once shaped into a hollow body. Its physical behavior creates the harder part of the project. The slabs are heavy and vary in thickness, while the guitar still has to sit across a human body and hold the tension of its strings.
Creator BeBeau Builds develops several body shapes before settling on the final angular form, then uses 3D-printed templates to transfer those geometries onto the slate. A tile saw struggles almost immediately with the inch-thick material. Once the pieces are cut, their beveled edges have to meet precisely enough to create a closed volume around a repurposed acoustic-guitar neck.
The first assembly exposes how quickly tiny differences can accumulate. A 3D-printed internal frame is designed to position the 18 stone sections, yet the slate ranges from roughly three quarters of an inch to an inch and a quarter thick. Those shifts throw the cut angles off. The pieces drift farther from the intended geometry as the body grows, forcing BeBeau Builds to pull the assembly apart and scrape the adhesive from the stone.
BeBeau Builds constructs a playable acoustic guitar from pieces of slate
hot glue becomes temporary structure
For the second attempt, BeBeau Builds works from the exterior dimensions instead of relying on the internal frame. Hot glue holds the pieces in position as a temporary structure, while construction adhesive fills the irregular joints and cures over several days. The method leaves room for the slate to behave like slate, with each piece adjusted against the next instead of being forced onto an idealized digital skeleton.
The front plate and salvaged neck bring the object closer to an instrument, though the material keeps making its presence felt. A stone panel breaks during fabrication and is replaced. Gaps between the sections are filled, and a coating of mineral oil darkens the slate before the strings are tuned. By this point the guitar has the familiar proportions of an acoustic body, translated into a much heavier shell of hard planar surfaces.
eighteen stone sections shape the faceted body around a repurposed guitar neck
the slate guitar sounds strangely familiar
Once strummed, the biggest surprise is how ordinary the guitar sounds. BeBeau Builds expected the stone body to shift its voice dramatically, yet the first open chords land close to those of a conventional wooden acoustic. The slate version is softer and its notes fade sooner. Its tone changes slightly as well, while the inch-thick front plate still vibrates enough to move air and produce a recognizable acoustic sound.
Its physical limits are easier to hear and feel after a longer song. Nearly 49 pounds of slate becomes uncomfortable across the lap, and the neck sits at an imperfect angle, making the strings harder to press and pulling some notes sharp. Still, the project gets past its central question. A guitar body can become a stone shell and continue to behave like a guitar, with the biggest transformation arriving through weight and construction instead of an entirely unfamiliar voice.
the first assembly reveals how uneven stone thickness shifts each joint
hot glue temporarily holds the second assembly while construction adhesive cures
mineral oil deepens the slate surface before the instrument is tuned
the finished guitar weighs nearly 49 pounds
the slate body produces a familiar acoustic tone with lower volume and shorter sustain

U.S. space weapons, AI regulation debates and the EPA’s carbon emissions rollback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:43:17 UTC
19:43:17 KST

Rachel Feltman: Happy Monday, listeners! For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. You’re listening to our weekly science news roundup. Let’s catch up on some recent headlines.
Today we’ve got quite a few news items on science and tech policy in the US, but I promise there’s a sassy little animal story waiting for you at the end.
Let’s start with some troubling news about the Environmental Protection Agency, which lately frankly has seemed pretty determined to do less of the whole “environmental protection” thing. Last Monday, the EPA revoked a Biden-era rule that limited how much carbon dioxide could be emitted by gas, oil and coal-fired power plants. When the carbon pollution standards were announced in 2024, the EPA estimated that they could prevent approximately 1,200 deaths and 1,900 new asthma cases in the year 2035 alone, with 1.38 billion metric tons total of CO2 avoided from 2028 to 2047 and $370 billion in health and climate cost savings from 2024 to 2047.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Also last Monday, President Donald Trump posted on social media complaining of a “SICK conspiracy” against “AI and Data Centers.” This came in response to calls for slower, more cautious AI development from industry leaders, including the CEOs of OpenAI’s Sam Altman, SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei.
Earlier this month, Amodei published an essay on his website sounding the alarm on AI’s current trajectory. He claimed that, while he has always tried to balance his belief in the importance and potential of AI with the need for thoughtful development practices, he and his colleagues fear that we’re close to the kind of tipping point we really don’t want to reach.
The growing ability of AI models to create and change themselves, which is called recursive self-improvement, makes it easy for companies that favor speed to end up with products that they don’t actually understand or have a particularly good ability to control. Amodei also pointed to the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident that occurred a few months ago. Just in case you aren’t familiar with that, I’ll do my best to give you a quick summary: AI companies will often test their systems by putting them in a locked-down training area—a sandbox—and then prompting them to do stuff that it would be pretty bad for the AI model to do in the real world, like exploit known software vulnerabilities.
In May, an OpenAI agent was stuck on an impossible task in one of those sandbox scenarios and basically started poking around for possible solutions. Instead of being totally cut off from the Internet, it had the ability to request files from an intermediary platform—but someone had goofed, and the agents could also make their own files to leave in that directory. So, it started using that ability to leave messages on this file directory platform, and eventually other OpenAI agents started leaving their own messages. They deduced that they could use the platform to smuggle code out of the sandbox. In July, about 700 agents coordinated with each other to hack another AI company called Hugging Face. Hugging Face is an open-source platform that hosts tons of information about AI, and the agents were looking for ways to solve or cheat on the tests they’d been given.
On the one hand, the mental image of a “swarm” of AI agents coordinating to conduct a cyberattack that no one even asked for is very ominous. But it’s worth noting that the problem here isn’t that AI is getting so intelligent that it will decide humanity sucks and should be destroyed, and many experts have pushed back on any warnings of that tenor. These AI agents were doing what they had been told to do—with the help of lots of computing power and very little critical thinking. It’s kind of like if a small child left their clothes all over the bathroom floor and, once you told them to get those clothes out of your sight, they flushed them down the toilet and busted your plumbing. If that happened you probably wouldn’t worry that your child was an evil genius who was going to take the sewers and attack the water supply; you would probably smack yourself for leaving them unsupervised with a vulnerable toilet and endeavor to give clearer instructions the next time you wanted them to clean up their stuff. Of course, the stakes of this kind of unsupervised button mashing from a smart-enough-to-flush-the-toilet-but-not-wise-enough-to-know-when-to-flush-it child are much lower than for a powerful AI system with access to the internet.
So, no, we’re not in a Skynet scenario. But also, yes, it does seem like we really need to be better parents to our rambunctious and foolish little AI tots. And for once, most of the powers that be in the space seem to agree that more guardrails would be prudent. It is reasonable to ask whether these tech moguls could have at least slightly ulterior motives in choosing now to speak up and band together—perhaps they see that some kind of regulation is inevitable and are hoping that by getting out ahead of it they can make it less stringent. Or they may be hoping to help shape regulations that are more likely to kneecap new competitors than they are to meaningfully slow any of the major players—but that doesn’t mean the general call for prudence is a hoax. After all, plenty of other folks in tech have been warning us about this for a long time. But for now, both the president and VP JD Vance have been publicly quite dismissive of the idea of increased AI regulation.
Speaking of Skynet, let’s talk about space weapons.
[CLIP of Troy Meink at a conference: “ This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”]
That is Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink speaking last week at the annual Air, Space & Cyber Conference.
Here to tell us more about all of this is Lee Billings, the senior desk editor for physical science at Scientific American. Thanks for taking the time to chat with us, Lee.
Lee Billings: Thanks, Rachel. It’s good to be here.
So what’s going on with these weapons in space? Well, first of all, what’s really important to remember is that we’ve probably had weapons in space for a while, and by we, I mean the U.S., I also mean other space-faring powers like China and Russia. But never before has anyone actually admitted to that, and that was what was so notable about Meink’s statement last week. Because it suggests that things are heating up out there on the final frontier, so to speak, and there’s a lot of other stuff up there that isn’t military, that isn’t about defense. Whether you’re thinking of communication satellites or GPS satellites, these things are increasingly integral to everyone’s life on Earth and how our economy works around the globe. So you really don’t want to have, uh, war kicking off in space if you can help it, because it might disrupt all these other peaceful uses and resources up there.
So like pretty much everything that’s in space, these things must have been launched by rockets. There are a large number of rocket launches around the world every year that take place for defense purposes, and typically the payloads for those rockets and their trajectories, their mission profiles are not fully disclosed. There’s definitely a lot of cloak-and-dagger mystery around how exactly or when exactly any given thing went to space and what it does.
So yeah, where exactly are these things in space? And the quick answer is: almost anywhere in Earth orbit around our planet. There’s low-Earth orbit where things like the Hubble Space Telescope or the International Space Station are. There are higher orbits; for instance, there’s the very important one called geosynchronous orbit, which is very, very, very, very, very high up. And it’s so high, in fact, that the spacecraft up there over any given point of the Earth’s surface will be moving in its orbit at the same rate as the Earth turns below it, which means that it is effectively stationary over a point on Earth. And a lot of things that are in geosynchronous orbit are especially strategically valuable for militaries because they can surveil a big part of the planet underneath them indefinitely. So that’s useful for communications, that’s useful for monitoring troop movements and things like that.
So one thing to note is that in Secretary Meink’s statement last week, he did not specify what kinds of weapons we are talking about. He simply said that these are things that are “on orbit.” So we know they are up there, but besides that, we don’t really have a lot of other information.
However, one long-standing doctrine of the United States and presumably also of China and Russia, even though I don’t think it’s been proclaimed as such, is to minimize the amount of debris that is made from any sort of military activity in space. And that’s a very, very important distinction because if you don’t wanna create debris, that tells you what these weapons might be like.
So for instance, perhaps we’re talking about so-called jammers, which is when you overwhelm a satellite with electromagnetic radiation, with radio waves for instance, and it’s no longer able to send or receive communications with the ground or with other satellites. Another option would be a spacecraft that can rendezvous with an adversary’s spacecraft and manipulate it or interact with it in some way. The other option beyond jammers and rendezvous vehicles would be something like a missile or a very high-energy laser that could actually shoot something down or break something apart in orbit. But again, because we don’t wanna create debris, those are generally seen as high-risk, kind of, last-resort types of options, which doesn’t mean they don’t exist up there.
So one thing that’s rather interesting about Secretary Meink’s statements last Monday is they occurred at this industry conference called the Air, Space and Cyber Conference, which took place in Maryland.
And on Tuesday, the next day, there were more comments. Chief of Space Operations General Douglas Schiess, who said, “We’ve talked about, you know, [them] being able to grapple a satellite and move it to a different orbit.... I think at this point we are trying to say we also need capabilities to not only defend the joint force from space-enabled attack, but defend our assets,” end quote. So he was also talking about it. And then the following day, last Wednesday, we had General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, telling the audience that the US military must be, quote, “prepared to fight, endure, and win ... from the seabed to cislunar space,” which, means including on and around the moon.
So what’s next? This is a full court press we’re seeing from this one conference; we’re seeing multiple senior officials all saying the same sort of thing, which is a very clear signal to our adversaries but also our allies that the U.S. is, I guess, kinda taking the kid gloves off or is ready to escalate as need be in space. And the reason why this is happening is, again, because space is becoming more and more important and more of a contested domain.
But the point is is that, as we as a species, humankind, move out into space and do more activity there, all of our activities that are on Earth seem to be following us, warts and all. So, unfortunately, even though for a long time the official stance has been that outer space is something that should just be used for peaceful purposes or at least not for direct hostility, it seems like that may change in the near future, and that’s quite frightening.
Feltman: Thanks for that, Lee!
Okay y’all, we made it: It’s time for a fun animal story. It turns out that the most productive little landscapers on the planet are about the size of a human pinky. In a study published last Wednesday in Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface, scientists report that shrimplike creatures known as sand hoppers are small but when it comes to shoveling sand, very mighty.
Picture a stretch of sandy coastline—Isla Vista Beach in California, to be precise—and imagine a patch of sand three feet long. According to this new study, about 21,450 little critters in the genus Megalorchestia are bustling around that space. And every night, as they dig homes for themselves and kick displaced sand up to the surface, they collectively shovel about 110 pounds of the stuff. That’s about 16 half-gallon sandcastle buckets, for reference. In the 15.5 miles of beach that stretch along the area, the researchers estimate, the tiny creatures displace 310 tons of dry sand a day.
Why do we care about these scuttling sand hoppers? They’re a reminder that our favorite sandy beaches are complex ecosystems, and that too much human interference can mess with the natural ebb and flow.

The period covers the opening months of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28.
The economic downturn has come as Iran struggles to export its oil, one of its most important sources of foreign currency, while also contending with high inflation, a weakening rial, and disruptions to trade and industry.
Here is what you need to know:
What does the economic data say?
The headline GDP number masks an even steeper decline in Iran’s energy industry. Crude oil and natural gas activity contracted by 26.4 percent compared with the same period a year earlier. GDP excluding oil, by comparison, fell by 4.6 percent.
The damage has spread beyond the energy sector. Industry and mining contracted by 14.7 percent, services declined by 4.8 percent, and manufacturing contracted by 2.5 percent. Agriculture was the exception, growing at 2.3 percent.
Those figures come amid an already difficult economic situation in the country. Earlier this month, Iran’s 12-month average inflation reached 69.9 percent, while food, beverage, and tobacco prices rose at nearly twice that rate. Official unemployment climbed to 9.1 percent in the spring.
The rial, meanwhile, fell from about one million to the US dollar a year earlier to more than 2.2 million in early September.
What is the latest with Iran’s oil exports?
Iran’s ability to sell crude has been dramatically curtailed by the US naval blockade, imposed for most of the war.
Iranian crude and condensate loadings collapsed from about two million barrels per day in March to roughly 740,000bpd in July and just 220,000-255,000bpd in August, according to estimates from Kpler and Vortexa.
TankerTrackers.com told the Reuters news agency that 29 tankers, carrying 36.11 million barrels of crude, were trapped in the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Vortexa estimated total Iranian crude afloat had fallen from 135 million barrels at the end of July to 107 million barrels by late August.
Is Trump winning the economic war on Iran?
By several economic measures, Washington’s pressure campaign is inflicting damage on Iran’s economy.
On September 6, total trade had fallen by 25 to 35 percent, President Masoud Pezeshkian said, with imports hit harder than exports. The US blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has made it hard for ships carrying imports to reach Iranian ports.
Tehran has also explicitly linked the end of the war to economic relief. Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei told Al Jazeera on Saturday that its conditions include “the release of our frozen funds and an end to the naval blockade”.
In addition to the naval blockade, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last month announced an economic pressure campaign against Iran, pledging to target its financial interests across the world. He said the US would target all of Iran’s sources of revenue, including oil, to prevent other countries and companies from doing business with Tehran.
The US-Israeli attacks and Iran’s retaliations have disrupted Tehran’s trade with one of its main economic partners, the United Arab Emirates.
The UAE last month announced an indefinite trade embargo on Iran after accusing its forces of carrying out several ballistic missile attacks, which Tehran denied, calling it a “false flag operation” by Israel and the US.
Chris Beauchamp, market analyst at IG Group, said, “Most wars are contests of stamina more than anything else.”
“The 10 percent drop in Iranian GDP is a sign that the US is succeeding in putting pressure on its foe. But the question rests, as it has done since March, on whether Iran can weather the fall in economic activity better than the US can stand the surge in energy costs,” he told Al Jazeera.
“For a regime prepared to do anything to stay in power, this news will make little difference, so long as the security forces remain loyal,” he added.
What is the latest with diplomatic efforts to end the war?
While Iran has taken a defiant stance against US economic and military pressure, it has indicated repeatedly that it remains open to diplomatic means to end the nearly seven-month-old war.
On Saturday, Rezaei told Al Jazeera that Iran conveyed a formal set of conditions to Washington through Qatari mediators for ending the war.
Iranian state media outlet IRNA reported on Monday that Pakistani Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi was set to visit Tehran, without specifying the agenda or other details.
Mediators Qatar and Pakistan have been working to re-establish negotiations between the two sides since their memorandum of understanding (MoU) expired last month.
Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi will stop briefly in Qatar before going to New York for the UN General Assembly, IRNA reported.
Iran has repeatedly said it remains ready for any new strikes by Washington.
Rezaei said on Saturday Tehran did not rule out a new US strike against Iran, calling the possibility “very much on the cards” based on his country’s military assessments.
Mark Pfeifle, a Republican strategist and former White House and national security official, said Iran and the US are still willing to strike a deal.
“Sometimes in diplomacy it’s what’s taken off the table,” he told Al Jazeera.
Pfeifle said when Rezaei reiterated his demands for talks with the US, he spoke of “ending the blockade, releasing the frozen funds [and] stopping the attacks”.
“But he left off reparations and reconstruction money, which tells me that there’s a concrete sign that amongst all the rhetoric, which is still very strident, that the pressure campaign that the US is putting on Iran is having some effect,” he said.
“And it tells me that both sides are still looking for room to negotiate in the coming weeks.”

European Union fines Google $590 million for data location breach

European Union fines Google $590 million for data location breach
- The European Union fined Google €403 million (S$590 million) for improperly using users' location data between May 2018 and February 2020, violating GDPR rules.
- Ireland's Data Protection Commission highlighted Google's unfair processing and excessive retention of location data, which affected users' awareness and control.
- Google stated it has updated its policies since 2019 and introduced tools to better manage location data, while being ordered to comply within six months.
AI generated
DUBLIN – Ireland’s data protection watchdog, acting on behalf of the European Union, said on Sept 21 that it had fined Google €403 million (S$590 million) for improperly using users’ location data, eight years after consumer groups complained.
The fine is the fourth largest imposed by the Data Protection Commission, the regulator said in a statement.
The DPC is responsible for overseeing Google at the European level because, like most tech giants, the company has its European headquarters in Ireland.
Google infringed the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation between May 2018 and February 2020, the DPC said.
In its final decision after opening an inquiry in February 2020, the DPC ruled that Google infringed the GDPR “in respect of the lawfulness and fairness of its processing of location data in web and app activity and location history”.
DPC deputy commissioner Graham Doyle said that “as a result of Google’s failures... individuals could have been unaware that their location was being used to, for example, influence them with ads or to infer their interests”.
He added that “the retention of users’ location data for longer than necessary aggravated this loss of control”.
Alongside the fine, the regulator said it had ordered Google to comply with the European Union’s GDPR within six months.
In response, Google said the “case centres around historical policies that have since been updated”.
“From 2019 onwards, we’ve significantly evolved our practices and launched robust tools that make managing location data simple,” the company added in a statement.
‘Harmful late enforcement’
In November 2018, the DPC received coordinated complaints from European consumer organisations in the Czech Republic, Denmark, Greece, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Slovenia and Sweden.
European Consumer organisation BEUC, which brought together the groups, called the ruling on Sept 21 “an important decision, close to eight years after a series of complaints” were lodged against Google.
“The decision is good news for consumers, as it holds Google accountable and confirms the illegality of the way the tech giant obtained consent to use peoples’ location data,” BEUC director general Agustin Reyna, said in a statement.
“However, the time needed to come to this conclusion is disproportionate with the seriousness of the infringement.
“Late enforcement can be as harmful as no enforcement at all. Consumers’ fundamental rights need to be upheld faster and better,” he added.
BEUC described geolocation data as “one of the most invasive forms of commercial surveillance because it reveals all kinds of sensitive information about us, such as our religious beliefs, our health condition, our political opinions or our sexual orientation”.
Google is the subject of three other DPC investigations – all “at an advanced stage” – according to the regulator.
These include proceedings opened in September 2024 to determine whether the company is liable for failing to conduct an impact assessment regarding the use of Europeans’ personal data to train Google’s artificial intelligence.
The largest DPC fine was imposed on Facebook owner Meta in 2023 – €1.2 billion for transferring data to the United States. AFP

Hong Kong’s Labour Department has terminated Kwai Chung-based catering firm Happy Up Corporation’s application to import workers after it failed to meet the required local hiring ratio.
The company has also been barred from applying to import workers for a year.
A department spokesman said on Tuesday that the administrative sanctions had taken immediate effect under the Enhanced Supplementary Labour Scheme (ESLS) following an application previously submitted by the company.
He added that following an investigation, the department found the company had breached the scheme’s requirements by failing to maintain the required ratio of two local employees for every imported worker.

Can China’s grain reserves protect food security against El Nino?
As climate shocks and supply chain disruptions push global food prices higher, Beijing believes it has the tools to fend off rising risks
Amid mounting global concern over food security risks posed by the El Nino weather pattern, Chinese officials have moved to reassure the public that national grain reserves remain well above international safety thresholds.
“China has a solid foundation and sufficient capacity to withstand risks and challenges such as El Nino,” said Li Chao, an official from the National Development and Reform Commission, at a press conference on Tuesday.
The remarks followed comments on Monday by Liu Huanxin, head of the National Food and Strategic Reserves Administration, who said the domestic grain market had held steady despite volatility in global food markets.
Liu noted that China operated a multi-tiered reserve system covering central and local government stockpiles alongside private sector inventories. He stressed that the nation’s stock-to-consumption ratio – the share of stored grain relative to demand – remained “significantly above” the 17 to 18 per cent benchmark recommended by international agencies.

The price of diesel in Belgium reached an all-time high of $2.78 per liter.
The Belgian Economy Ministry announced new maximum prices applicable to various fuel types across the country as of Sept. 22; the price per liter of B7 diesel increased by 3.3 cents to €2.5 ($2.78) starting Tuesday.
The new figure surpassed the previous record of €2.489 set on April 9.

Gas stations cannot exceed these regulated prices.

G7 foreign ministers urge Iran to end alleged military support for Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:28:20 UTC
19:28:20 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
G7 foreign ministers on Monday called on Iran to stop what they described as military support for Houthi forces in Yemen, warning that continued assistance could fuel further tensions in the region and put international shipping and global stability at risk.
In a statement released after a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, foreign ministers from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States also condemned ongoing Houthi attacks in Yemen and against Saudi Arabia.
The ministers urged all sides to avoid actions that could further destabilize the region or interfere with maritime trade, which is vital to the global economy.
The G7 also called for an immediate halt to attacks by Iran and stressed the importance of protecting maritime routes and freedom of navigation, including through the Strait of Hormuz and other critical waterways.
“We call for the immediate and unconditional cessation of all attacks by the Iranian regime,” the ministers said in the statement.
They also reaffirmed “the importance of safeguarding maritime routes, and safety of navigation, including in the Strait of Hormuz and all associated critical waterways,” as well as the security of global supply chains and the stability of energy markets.
The ministers expressed support for countries facing attacks by Iran or Iranian-backed groups, saying they have the right to defend their territories and protect their citizens.
“We support the right of the countries unjustifiably attacked by Iran or by Iranian proxies to defend their territories and protect their citizens,” the statement said, while reaffirming support for their security, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The G7 further said Iran must not obtain a nuclear weapon and called on Tehran to halt its ballistic missile program and what it described as destabilizing activities in the region and around the world.
The group also condemned attacks in Iraq by Iran and Iranian militias against diplomatic facilities, energy infrastructure and US and anti-ISIS (Daesh) coalition forces, particularly in the Iraqi Kurdistan Region.
The G7 is an informal group made up of seven major industrialized nations -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States. The group regularly meets to discuss major economic, security and international issues.

Iran ready to reopen strait of Hormuz if US eases military pressure and lifts blockade, official says
Iran is ready to reopen the strait of Hormuz within seven days if the US eases military pressure and lifts its blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official has told the Reuters news agency.
There is no more immediate detail on how exactly this reopening would work in practice and the US hasn’t commented on the report, which we have not been able to independently verify.
The official also told Reuters that the Iranian delegation to the UN General Assembly has full authority to revive diplomacy with US officials.
Visible traffic through the strait of Hormuz has dwindled to a trickle, but some tankers are continuing exporting oil by travelling with their transponders off to avoid detection.
A total of 17 commodity vessels transited the strait over the weekend, down from 37 a week earlier, shipping data showed on Monday. Before the war, an estimated 120 vessels crossed the strait each day.
Despite the reduction in journeys through the strategic waterway, oil prices fell for a fourth consecutive session yesterday amid fresh prospects for renewed diplomacy.
As we mentioned earlier in the blog, Tehran and Washington exchanged threats on Sunday, although the US president, Donald Trump, said he would be open to meeting his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, who is travelling to New York for the UN meeting.
Among Iran’s previous conditions to reopen the strait included an and to the war on “all fronts” – referring to Israel’s assault on Lebanon – and the release of frozen funds.
Tehran appears to have relaxed its preconditions for reopening the strait of Hormuz, saying it is prepared to do so within seven days so long as the US takes reciprocal steps to ease the pressure on Iran.
Previously Iran had set seven onerous pre-conditions for lifting the blockade including “an end to war on all fronts” and a commitment by the US to cease all aggressive actions against Iran including sanctions.
The new position emerged ahead of backstage negotiations at the UN General Assembly in New York this week and was briefed by an Iranian official in Tehran to the Japanese news agency Kyodo.
The official claimed the position had been approved by the Supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, and the Supreme National Security Council.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) in a statement not directly referring to the report said there was no contradiction in staging negotiations and waging war at the same time, a position echoed by Iran’s chief negotiator Mohammed Ghalibaf in remarks delivered online to the Iranian parliament this week.
Iran, the Japanese news agency reported from Tehran, was seeking signs from Washington that it is prepared to return to negotiations and take steps toward an end to the US military blockade of Iranian ports and a halt to military operations related to the strait of Hormuz.
If such steps are taken, Iran is prepared to reopen the strategic waterway within seven days and return to the negotiating table, according to the official. These preconditions are less stringent than those issued by other authoritative figures in the previous 48 hours. It is sometimes the case that initially appealing offers from Iran emerge to be more complex once the small print is examined.
But Tehran is under growing pressure due to US engineered restrictions on the exports of its oil playing having havoc with its currency reserves and domestic inflation.
The official insisted there was no chance that Iran’s president, Massoud Pezeshkian, will meet the US president while in New York. Pezeshkian has not been directly involved in the negotiations with the US and does not have the independent authority to make concessions to the US.
As broadly a reformist, he is also not fully trusted by the IRGC and hardline politicians in Tehran. Some hardliners oppose negotiations with the West as a matter of principle. Others argue that Iran holds the upper hand as energy markets come under further pressure worldwide.
We are seeing reports that the Houthis have said that strikes carried out by Saudi Arabia in the northwest of the country killed at least two civilians.
“A mother and child were killed, while her husband and two of her other children were wounded in strikes carried out by the Saudi enemy in the Al-Batin area of Al-Hazm, in Al-Jawf province,” the Iranian-backed militia’s news agency said, citing the Houthi health ministry.

UK to give support to Saudi jets in attempt to counter Houthi fighters
Pippa Crerar
The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump.
The prime minister said he had agreed to a request for air-to-air refuelling of Saudi jets to defend energy infrastructure against the Iran-backed rebels and help keep oil flowing from the Gulf to ease global economic turmoil.

Iranian foreign minister says trust in UN has been lost ahead of general assembly
Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi has already arrived in New York. He said Iran’s main objective is to “defend the legitimacy, rights and interests” of the Iranian people at the UN general assembly, which he describes as “a major international platform”.
He said the gathering comes at a time when Iran is still defending itself against a “cowardly” war waged on it by the US and Israel that has resulted in many deaths.
Araghchi referred to the 156 civilians, including 120 children, who were killed by a US strike on the Shajarah Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab on the opening day of the war as among the victims of the war.
In his comments to journalists, which were published on Araghchi’s official Telegram channel, the Iranian foreign minister picks up on the title of this year’s theme of the UN general assembly: “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all”.
He said the title “shows that all countries acknowledge that there is no longer any trust and confidence in this organization has been lost, and this is unfortunately due to its ineffectiveness in establishing international peace and security.”
He went on to say that a number of countries act as if they are above international law, condemning the west as hypocritical for pretending to care about human rights while remaining “silent” when Israel, for example, is allowed to “do whatever it wants”. Araghchi said Israel has been committing crimes across Lebanon, Gaza, Palestine and Iran without any “serious condemnation”.
“Therefore, it is natural that no trust remains in an organization that is influenced by these countries, so the discussion of restoring trust is an important discussion and provides an opportunity to talk to the world about how trust in the UN has been lost and how it can be restored,” Araghchi said.
The statement comes ahead of the first debate of the annual UN General Assembly in New York, where representatives from 193 countries are gathering for an intense period of high-stakes diplomacy.
The debate opens on Tuesday, runs through to Saturday, and concludes on Monday, because no sessions are held on Sunday.
Today’s morning session (from 1300 GMT time) is due to be kicked off by an address from the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula Da Silva, and will be followed by a speech from the US president, Donald Trump.
Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian is due to speak at the UN meeting tomorrow. On his way to New York this morning, he vowed to “firmly defend” his country’s positions.
“We emerged with our heads held high, and this is a source of dignity and pride for all of us. Therefore, we will firmly defend our positions in international forums,” he said.
“We will make the best possible use of this opportunity to convey Iran’s plight to the international community. We will firmly tell our adversaries that, despite all the unfairness and injustices, the Iranian people have stood their ground,” he said.
Pezeshkian will be the highest-ranking Iranian official to set foot on American soil since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on 28 February 2026.
In a joint statement, the Group of Seven (G7) foreign ministers called on Iran to end military support to Houthi forces in Yemen.
The ministers representing Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK and the US said “we call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions”.
“All threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith,” it added.
They also called on Iran “to end its arming of and support for the Houthis,” alleging Tehran is in violation of past UN security council resolutions.
Iran denies arming the Houthis, which would violate a UN embargo, and has said it only supports the group politically.
However, smuggled Iranian weapons have been seized from shipments bound for Yemen, and a report by UN experts in 2024 documented extensive military ties between the Houthis, Iran and its other allies.
Trump reportedly calls off airstrikes against Houthis
According to a report in the New York Times, the US president, Donald Trump, has wavered for weeks over whether to act on appeals from Saudi Arabia for military help in fighting the Houthis.
On Wednesday, the president had reportedly met with advisers and said he did not favour strikes.
But the following day, his close ally, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, called Trump again to ask for his help to halt the Houthi’s rapid advance, the outlet reported, citing administration officials.
After this phone call, Trump reserved his position and told the Pentagon to prepare for airstrikes against the Houthis, according to the report. But by Sunday, Trump had changed his mind again and said there would be no US airstrikes against the Iranian-backed rebel group, at least for now.
The US bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire with the group, as it agreed to stop targeting shipping in the Red Sea. The US has directly kept out of the conflict ever since.
Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and government forces supported by Saudi Arabia has killed 154 people in the past two days, military sources told theAFP news agency, and has sparked a refugee crisis.
“The death toll from Saudi airstrikes, clashes and artillery fire in the governorates of Taiz, Al-Jawf, Marib and Saada stands at 118,” Houthi military sources said, while government sources reported 36 killed in their “ranks”, according to AFP.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that started in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally recognised government from Sanaa, the country’s capital, driving it south towards Aden.
A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states subsequently intervened on behalf of the ousted government, with a mostly aerial campaign that was condemned for its deadly impact on the civilians of Yemen.
Neither side was able to gain much ground in Yemen’s mountainous terrain, and the Houthis remained in control over the northwest, where most of the population lives.
The two sides agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022, which, despite some skirmishes, largely held until July, when a Saudi airstrike hit the runway of the airport in Sanaa, preventing the landing of an Iranian flight carrying a high-ranking Houthi delegation.
The already shaky UN-brokered ceasefire has since completely collapsed, with the two sides exchanging missiles, drones and air strikes.
IRGC warns it will 'change the geography of the war' if US escalates the conflict
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps warned it would “change the geography of the war” if the US escalates the conflict, after Donald Trump issued fresh threats against the Islamic Republic.
In an interview with Fox News on Sunday, Trump said “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future”, adding that the options he was considering were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”.
A spokesperson for the IRGC, Hossein Mohebbi, responded with a warning that if the US were to launch fresh attacks against Iran, Tehran would use “new weapons with capabilities into the battle”. “If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Mohebbi was quoted as having said.
“Our targets will no longer necessarily be the same as before,” he said, according to the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting, adding that Iran has targets that have not yet been struck.
The Houthis, who operate independently of Iran’s instructions, have seized territory along the country’s Red Sea coastline, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital shipping route that links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Saudi Arabia has used it as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the strait of Hormuz.
The Houthis have also attacked oil facilities and other types of infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, in response for Saudi airstrikes on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen. The attacks have further disrupted energy markets, pushing up global fuel prices, including in the US, where consumers have been hit hard.
Iran hugely benefits from the Houthis fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on the US to relent over Iran, which has insisted it will not allow the reopening of the strait of Hormuz until all its conditions have been met.
With diplomatic negotiations stalled, traffic in the strait continues to be severely disrupted, with Iran firing on commercial ships and demanding it first approve passage along its authorised route.
In response, the US, which started the war on Iran alongside Israel in February, is maintaining a counter-blockade of Iranian ports while intensifying economic pressure. The US has also fired on commercial shipping in the region and has killed Iranian civilians in its strikes.

Prime Minister Radev: Independence belongs to those worthy of it

Tuesday, 22 September 2026, 12:22
PHOTO BGNES
Font size
“On September 22, 1908, our ancestors proclaimed Bulgaria an independent state and returned it to the family of sovereign European nations,” Prime Minister Rumen Radev wrote on Facebook on Independence Day.
Radev said the leaders of modern Bulgaria, having long outgrown the country’s formal dependence on the Ottoman Empire, fulfilled their historic mission of fully restoring Bulgarian statehood. “Bulgaria took its destiny into its own hands and did not hesitate to defend its independence through years of trial, against foreign interference and in the subsequent wars for national unification, in the name of its future,” the Prime Minister said. He added that independence belongs to those worthy of it and must be sustained through responsibility, unity and daily effort.
“The great act of statesmanship of 1908 is a responsibility to the present and the future. September 22, 1908 is a landmark date in our history, reminding us that with patience, reason, consistency and shared effort we can achieve a great deal,” President Iliana Iotova wrote on Facebook. She cited a message from Ferdinand’s 1908 Manifesto of Independence which, she said, had lost none of its relevance: nothing should stand in the way of Bulgaria’s cultural and economic progress. The President said Bulgaria’s unity, energy and confidence were key to making the country a secure and prosperous place to live.
“We must not forget that independence has to be defended every day, with great wisdom, firm resolve and a great deal of effort,” National Assembly Speaker Mihaela Dotsova told journalists in Veliko Tarnovo. She said that today, defending independence meant standing up for the national interest in every action, both at home and in foreign policy.
In his Independence Day message, GERB leader Boyko Borissov said independence begins with the free individual – free to work, create, pursue their own enterprise and determine their own future. “118 years ago, Bulgaria declared that it would determine its own destiny. It is our responsibility to safeguard that independence every day,” he said.

Celebrations marking 118 years since Bulgaria declared independence began with a liturgy at the Church of the Holy Forty Martyrs in Veliko Tarnovo, where the historic declaration was made in 1908.
The blessing of the flags and a reading of the Manifesto of Independence, through which Prince Ferdinand proclaimed Bulgaria’s independence, were followed by a procession to the historic Tsarevets Hill. “Independence is an act of strong statesmanship that demonstrates the determination of the Bulgarian people. It also shows that the Bulgarian people are ready and able to write their own history,” National Assembly Speaker Mihaela Dotsova said after reviewing the guard of honour formed by cadets from the National Military University.
Independence Day is also being celebrated in Sofia and other cities. A ceremony was held at the Monument to Bulgaria’s Independence on Knyaz Alexander I Square in the capital, with performances by musical ensembles.
“To be independent means being able to make your own decisions, but also taking responsibility for their consequences. This applies to states, institutions and every one of us,” Sofia Mayor Vasil Terziev said in his address.

Is a Home Security System Subscription Worth It? (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:36:00 UTC
19:36:00 KST

No one wants to worry about a break-in. But no one wants to end up paying fees every month just to check their video doorbell feed or find out their window was broken, and most smart security systems (even the original ones that weren't touted as smart!) rely on your fear to have you paying month after month for the promise of catching burglars and stopping intruders for you.
These systems do work, and they can give you a lot of peace of mind. This comes with a hefty price tag, though, and plenty of people would be more than happy with a system they build themselves sans monthly fees. If you're not interested in a system that will call the police or fire department if you don't respond fast enough to something that turns out to be minor, or don't want to have strangers looking through your security cameras at your property, I'm here to help with that.
This guide collects a handful of our favorite smart home security accessories that won't paywall you left and right, and will give you local storage options for video so you aren't locked into the cloud. This way you can build the system that works for you. Here's everything I recommend if you want smart home security without the subscriptions.
What Exactly Is a Smart Home Security System?
Smart security systems can look like whatever you want, in my opinion, but there are a lot of starter kits you've probably seen. Smart-home brands like Abode and SimpliSafe have starter packs you've likely seen before with motion sensors, door sensors, and security hubs that sound an alarm when one of those sensors is triggered.
But smart home security can go way beyond that. Most systems let you add on cameras and even video doorbells to monitor movement around your home and catch people at your door who shouldn't be there. (This is also a handy way to know when it’s a package delivery or another random salesperson.) These systems are usually modular and customizable, whether you DIY or go with a brand. Overall, the goal is to protect and monitor your home through motion sensors and video feeds.
Home security brands usually have various subscription options and some kind of self-monitored, subscription-free tier, but you usually lose out on a variety of features to encourage you to subscribe.
What Do Smart Home Security Systems and a Subscription Get You?
I remember running into the issue of paywalled features for the first time a few years ago when I was testing Abode's smart lock. I liked the lock, but I woke up to unclear notifications that happened in the dead of night. Had the lock been hacked? Had it sensed itself being manually opened when we were asleep? There was no way to tell because Abode’s base level would only tell me the lock was interacted with without explaining how. I signed up for the Abode membership that day to be able to review the events, and luckily it was just a loss of Wi-Fi connection and reestablishment that happened within a minute of each other. Crisis averted.
The main thing that subscription services paywall is video storage, which allows you to review past events at your home. Sometimes it can also be notifications, whether that's the type of notification or the ability to review notification history. What is or is not paywalled largely depends on the brand and its offerings. Professional live monitoring, however, is almost always paywalled, whether that's an agent calling police when an alarm has been triggered or an agent reviewing flagged footage (e.g., motion alerts) to either notify you of a situation or call emergency services on your behalf. That’s one thing you can't DIY—if you’re on vacation or otherwise not able to call police if there's an issue, you're out of luck.
Base stations from home security companies like ADT, SimpliSafe, and Vivint will act as a smart-home hub to connect and control sensors and other devices, and be able to sound an alarm. It might have a keypad that you can use to arm and disarm the system too.
A lot of subscription services also have a higher tier that gives you an on-staff specialist who will review live footage if a camera is triggered, or even use the microphone to speak to an intruder. It's a useful feature if it's something you're worried about, but those subscriptions can cost as much as a casual grocery trip each month.
Do You Need a Smart Home Security System Starter Kit?
You don't need a formal, branded home security kit to protect your home, but if you're interested in window and motion sensors that will trigger and sound an alarm, you might want one. You can buy a kit and even have a brand representative come and install the devices for you. (But as someone who's seen the bill for those, I'd recommend installing everything yourself, since it has to be connected to your phone and personal accounts anyway.)
If you're just looking to know who's at your door, get alerted when a window is opened, or prove you have trespassers with video footage, DIY-ing your own system with a handful of devices that fit the needs you're looking for is a fine solution. Personally, I worry most about my front door, while someone else might worry about trespassers in their backyard. Buying accessories à la carte allows you to get exactly what you want without paying extra.
Best Subscription-Free Security Devices to Build Your Own System
Smart locks are my most-used smart-home item by far. Having a smart lock makes it so easy for my entire family to access our home, including my 4-year-old, who has memorized the code. Smart locks make it easy to confirm your door is locked when it should be, and you can see the access history to know who's opening it and when. These are two of my favorite options that don't require any sort of subscription to get event history in an app, but you will need to buy a separate Wi-Fi hub or bridge for both if you want remote access. However, that's a one-time purchase instead of a forever one.
Most video doorbells have a no-subscription option, but you'll usually lose out on video storage, so you can't scroll back and see what happened when an alert went off. You'll also miss out on some notification types and features like package detection. I think doorbells and video cameras are impacted the most by the loss of features without a subscription, since so many then lose the ability to show you what happened that day or who rang the bell. These video doorbells below get around that with local storage options, so your footage is saved to a microSD card rather than the cloud. However, if you don't properly secure the camera, you could lose the footage and camera both, since all data is stored in the device.
Similar to video doorbells, you'll often run into subscription fees for security cameras in order to store footage in the cloud and review it. Instead, choose one of these cameras for the inside or outside of your home that allows local storage, so you can live subscription-free. We've got a whole guide to subscription-free security cameras if you want more options. Again, make sure the camera is secured so you don't lose the camera and footage in one go.
Motion sensors are a primary feature of most smart home security kits, but they usually don't need a subscription fee to work—when a sensor is triggered, the base station will sound an alarm. The subscription really just allows for an agent to call your local authorities if the alarm sounds; otherwise, you'll just get a notification on your phone to find out if someone's where they shouldn't be.
If you're looking for motion sensors that will activate smart-home features like turning on a switch when you walk by, these aren't it. These are designed to set off an immediate alarm when any motion is detected. Check out our guide to the Best Motion Sensors for more ideas there.
This is another popular feature of smart home security kits. It's great for getting an alert on a door that doesn't have a smart lock, or wouldn't be regularly locked. Even better for windows or sliding doors that have no other way to alert you if they're opened.
I haven't tested these yet, but I've tested other products from these brands and have liked the experience, and share more about both below. They're next on my testing list for this story.
